papers.abstract: Recent efforts have demonstrated the strong capabilities of Multimodal Large Reasoning Models (MLRMs) in geographic reasoning. By jointly analyzing subtle visual cues, these models can infer the locations of photos, thus enabling doxing even by non-expert adversaries. Existing defense methods struggle to balance the shareability of photos with effective protection, and often fail to sufficiently disrupt the implicit geo-evidence chains embedded in scene semantics. To this end, we propose GeoEdit, an adversarial de-evidencing framework for silent geoprivacy protection via image editing. Specifically, we apply minimal edits to high-risk evidence anchors in the image, thereby disrupting the underlying spatial reasoning chains while preserving overall scene semantics. We identify these anchors by combining structured knowledge with adversarially discovered geographic cues. To further navigate the large editing action space, we adopt a learnable policy to iteratively refine editing decisions, distilling successful trajectories into transferable natural-language insights for consistent and efficient editing. Evaluated on LifePhotoBench, GeoEdit achieves strong protection against 6 mainstream MLRMs, outperforming visual perturbation baselines by over 0.59 in image fidelity.
bullets: Targets implicit visual evidence chains that MLRMs use to infer photo locations.
Identifies geographic evidence anchors using structured knowledge and adversarially discovered cues.
Uses a learnable policy to iteratively refine edits and distill successful strategies into natural-language guidance.
On LifePhotoBench, protects against six mainstream MLRMs and exceeds visual-perturbation baselines by over 0.59 in image fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall architecture of GeoEdit. ❶ De-Evidencing Image Editing: A policy 𝜋 explicitly reasons and acts within a ReAct loop, invoking the core tools 𝑇𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑘 , 𝑇𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑡 , and 𝑇𝑒𝑣𝑎𝑙 to identify evidence, generate semantic edits, and verify protection quality. ❷ Self-Evolution via Insight Distillation: A test-time optimization mechanism that constructs group-relative joint reward signals from rollout trajectories, distilling them into natural-language protection insights (K) to guide future edits.

Figure 4: Overview of Self-Evolution via Geoprivacy Protection Insight Distillation. By contrasting successful and unsuccessful editing trajectories, GeoEdit distills a group relative advantage into a shared Insight Buffer (K).

Figure 1: Comparison of social media sharing scenarios. The landmark check-in (a) exemplifies intentional location sharing. Conversely, the daily life photo (b) inadvertently leaks sensitive location data via implicit geo-evidence, resulting in non-consensual exposure and severe doxing risks.

Figure 2: Comparison of geoprivacy protection mechanisms. (a) The unprotected image. (b) Image Obfuscation hides sensitive areas but ruins the visual experience. (c) Visual Perturbation tricks visual encoders to protect geoprivacy, but its adversarial nature is often lost during unpredictable image processing and causes noticeable artifacts. (d) Geo-Evidence Editing (Ours) blocks the localization reasoning chain to defend against both MLRMs and human analysis while keeping visual appeal.
Figure 5: Visualization of different protected images. GeoEdit achieves silent protection while preserving naturalness.

papers.selection_reason: Directly targets and disrupts spatial/geographic reasoning chains in multimodal models, offering transferable insights into spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GeoEdit: Adversarial De-Evidencing for Silent Geoprivacy Protection via Image Editing
papers.tldr: GeoEdit protects image geoprivacy by minimally editing high-risk geographic cues while preserving the scene’s overall meaning and shareability.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal place recognition (CMPR) matches natural language descriptions against databases of geo-tagged reference images, enabling localization without visual queries. Despite its potential for language-guided navigation, existing vision-language models lag far behind visual place recognition (VPR) baselines, even after task adaptation. Unlike general-purpose text-to-image retrieval, place recognition relies on subtle local cues to distinguish visually similar locations. We therefore hypothesize that a primary bottleneck in CMPR is capturing fine-grained correspondences between image regions and text details, which requires higher visual token granularity, strong text representation capacity, and local cross-modal matching. To address this challenge, we propose CrossPlace, a two-stage CMPR framework. Stage 1 performs global retrieval by pairing a jointly aligned DINOv2-B/14 visual backbone with a progressively fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, while Stage 2 refines top candidates using a lightweight token-level cross-attention reranker. Through systematic analysis, we isolate the drivers of retrieval accuracy and show that visual token density provides the largest performance improvement, while text encoder capacity and task fine-tuning offer complementary gains. To evaluate robustness under realistic conditions, we also extend CMPR evaluation to city-scale and severe weather and illumination settings. Across all existing and new benchmarks, CrossPlace achieves double-digit Recall@1 improvements over prior cross-modal methods, closes the gap to unimodal text retrieval, and narrows it to unimodal VPR. Code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/oferidan1/CrossPlace
authors: Ofer Idan, Dan Badur, Yoli Shavit
bullets: CMPR matches natural-language descriptions to geo-tagged reference images, but trails visual place recognition because subtle local details are difficult to align.
A two-stage pipeline first performs global retrieval with DINOv2-B/14 and a fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, then reranks candidates with lightweight token-level cross-attention.
Analysis identifies visual token density as the largest accuracy driver, with text capacity and task fine-tuning providing complementary gains.
Evaluation includes existing benchmarks plus city-scale and severe weather/illumination conditions.
CrossPlace reports double-digit Recall@1 gains over prior cross-modal methods and narrows the gap to unimodal VPR.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of our two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 retrieves a top-K shortlist via cosine similarity between LoRA-tuned BGE and DINOv2 global embeddings. papers.title: Towards Closing the Performance Gap in Cross-Modal Place Recognition
papers.tldr: CrossPlace improves cross-modal place recognition by combining high-resolution visual tokens, a stronger text encoder, and token-level reranking to better match fine-grained image–text cues.

papers.abstract: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.
authors: Tomas Hodan, Vineet Bhat, Martin Sundermeyer, Jonathan Tremblay, Yash Patel, M\'ed\'eric Fourmy, Stephen Tyree, Junwen Huang, Varun Burde, Martin C\'ifka, Eric Brachmann, Vincent Lepetit, Stan Birchfield, Jiri Matas, Carsten Rother
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering everyday and industrial objects from 9 diverse BOP datasets.
Pairs images with VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions and derives 2D/3D ground-truth boxes from object models and 6DoF poses.
Evaluates 17 proprietary and open-weight VLMs across Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families.
The best reported model achieves 72.6% 2D AP but only 12.4% 3D AP, even with more lenient 3D IoU thresholds.
3D predictions are generally image-centered but often have large depth errors, indicating metric scale and object-size priors as the main limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Comparing 3D boxes. The ground-truth box b is green and the predicted box b̂ red. (a) NCD is the mean distance between corresponding corners, such as ci(b) and ci(b̂) (gray line), divided by the diagonal d of the ground-truth box. (b) IoU3D is the intersection volume (gray) divided by the union volume. S ranges over the symmetry transformations S of the target object and π over the 24 corner labelings of the box b (Sec. 3.1). Of the 225 BOP-Refer objects, 78 have an annotated discrete or continuous rotational symmetry. papers.abstract: Scene rearrangement is an essential task for 3D content creation applications, requiring generation of diverse, aesthetic and functional scene rearrangements. We present SceneDesigner3D, an agentic evolutionary search method for 3D indoor scene rearrangement that systematically explores the design space of 3D scenes and generates multiple solutions according to common interior design principles. Given an input scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D represents the rearrangement as an editable program and evolves a population of candidate layouts. Starting from distinct design ideas, a VLM agent mutates the programs by refining promising candidates, exploring new rearrangement strategies or redesigning from scratch, while verifying the layouts for physical validity. Proposals are scored by a VLM judge for adherence to the input prompt and satisfaction of design principles such as balance, zoning and emphasis, as well as numerically computed principles such as circulation and clutter. An archive of top-performing, structurally varied candidates further increases diversity of rearrangements. Experiments on the SAGE-10k and SceneSmith datasets show that SceneDesigner3D improves prompt adherence and computed design principle scores over baselines by up to 5.1% and 15.2%, respectively. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Represents scene rearrangements as editable programs and evolves populations of candidate layouts.
A VLM agent mutates candidates through refinement, exploration, or redesign from scratch, with physical-validity checks.
A VLM judge scores prompt adherence and qualitative principles, while numerical metrics assess circulation and clutter.
An archive preserves high-performing, structurally diverse solutions.
Experiments on SAGE-10k and SceneSmith report up to 5.1% better prompt adherence and 15.2% better computed design-principle scores than baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. Given an input 3D scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D evolves a population of programs that rearrange its objects. The prompt is decomposed into requirements, design seeds are initialized and objects are described by a VLM. An agentic evolutionary search explores the design space through various strategies (colored paths: object movement relative to parent). Each candidate is judged by a VLM against its parent on the prompt requirements and design principles, and combined with numerically computed principles into its fitness. An archive keeps diverse candidates as inspiration for future iterations, giving diverse layouts that follow the prompt and design principles.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing scene understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret queried targets in relation to nearby objects and surrounding structures, which serve as spatial references or define the scope of an answer. However, standard answers and bounding boxes often leave these contextual relationships implicit. Thus, we construct GeoContext-5K to make them explicit in 5,394 training pairs for visual question answering (VQA), with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions. GeOPD uses these annotations for on-policy distillation, guiding a frozen teacher with region marks on the full image and a visual fact while preserving surrounding spatial references. It prioritizes teacher corrections that agree with the shift in the student's next token distribution when evidence is restored. A complementary objective weights the contrast between the student's scores on the two views by how much masking lowers the teacher's log probability for the same sampled token. Experiments on five remote sensing VQA benchmarks show that GeOPD outperforms the evaluated open-source MLLMs and matched post-training baselines, improving over the 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average. The dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/YeeCharm/GeOPD.
authors: Yichang Luo, Hourun Zhu, Shixiong Liu, Kan Wei, Shi Liang, Yidan Zhang, Lei Wang
bullets: GeoContext-5K contains 5,394 VQA training pairs with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions.
GeOPD performs on-policy distillation with region-marked full images and visual facts while preserving spatial references.
It prioritizes teacher corrections supported by changes in the student’s next-token distribution when evidence is restored.
A contrastive objective uses how masking affects the teacher’s token likelihood to weight student-view comparisons.
Across five remote-sensing VQA benchmarks, GeOPD improves over 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of GeoContext-5K construction. papers.abstract: Generative driving planners may produce trajectories that appear feasible at their reference points but violate environmental constraints over the full vehicle body. We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative planning framework that enhances vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) through body-scene spatial grounding. The proposed method constructs spatial queries from actual vehicle-body corners and dynamically updates visual sampling locations using evolving trajectory estimates across Flow steps. Retrieved local visual features condition subsequent Action Flow-DiT velocity predictions, allowing trajectory generation to guide spatial information retrieval. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation, followed by planning-supervised VLM-Action Alignment. Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis reveals safety differences under identical trajectories but varying vehicle geometry. On NAVSIM, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% relative to the base planner and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8. Under NAVSIM v2 evaluation, EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Ablation and body-clearance analyses further demonstrate the safety benefits of body-scene spatial grounding.
authors: Bo Leng, Baoyun Wang, Wenxin Wen, Ming Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Ran Yu, Chongfeng Wei, Zhuoren Li, Lu Xiong
bullets: Addresses collisions caused by evaluating feasibility only at trajectory reference points rather than across the vehicle body.
Builds spatial queries from vehicle-body corners and updates visual sampling locations as trajectory estimates evolve during Flow steps.
Uses retrieved local visual features to condition Action Flow-DiT predictions, enabling trajectory-guided spatial retrieval.
Adds Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning and planning-supervised VLM–Action Alignment.
On NAVSIM, reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8; NAVSIM v2 EPDMS rises from 86.5 to 88.3.

papers.abstract: Dense global attention is crucial for capturing cross-view geometry in visual geometry foundation models, yet its quadratic complexity limits efficient inference on long image sequences. Existing sparse attention methods primarily select entries of the global attention matrix based on attention probabilities and construct masks independently across layers, overlooking value redundancy and cross-layer information reuse. By analyzing attention distributions and clustering value representations across layers, we reveal two forms of \emph{cross-layer consistency}, characterized by highly similar attention probability distributions and localized changes in value redundancy structures. Building on these observations, we propose \textbf{DuCo}, a training-free sparse attention framework that exploits historical attention information and value redundancy for efficient geometric inference. Specifically, DuCo leverages historical attention information to estimate current-layer dense attention probabilities and introduces value clustering to exploit redundancy, with clusters efficiently refined through local updates across layers. Both factors are integrated through probability-weighted value distortion to jointly optimize four cluster representation states under an attention budget for sparse mask construction. Experiments across three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs.
authors: Liangyu Xiang, Junyu Gao, Xiaofeng Wang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Dense global attention captures cross-view geometry but has quadratic cost on long image sequences.
DuCo estimates current attention from historical layers and reuses clustered value representations with efficient local updates.
Probability-weighted value distortion jointly optimizes cluster states under an attention budget to construct sparse masks.
Experiments on three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks show favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.
authors: Yurun Chen, Biao Yi, Qihang Yu, Keting Yin, Shengyu Zhang
bullets: Introduces three settings: explicit-instruction Computer-Use, prerecorded Offline Ego Use, and continuously observed Online Ego Use.
Builds 693 tasks from over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings.
Separately tracks observations, user requirements, and website state to model task evolution.
Groups evolving tasks into Graft, Refresh, and Clarify based on how information changes.
Advanced models achieve substantially lower success in Online Ego Use than Computer-Use, exposing challenges in maintaining contextual alignment.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. Project Page: https://marslab-navigent.github.io/navigent.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/MarsLab-Navigent/Navigent

Uses a frozen multimodal large language model with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC).
GEC checks action-to-motion consistency and motion-to-landmark consistency using visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates.
Detected discrepancies trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery; historical visual memory tracks progress.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.
authors: Luoxi Zhang, Tianyi Tan, Jiawei Liu, Xingyu Zeng, Min Yang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for separating perception, rule application, and planning failures in visual grid games.
Combines Sokoban solving with recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state-tracking probes, using both image and equivalent text-grid inputs.
Across seven MLLMs, proprietary models mainly struggle with multi-step planning, while open-source models struggle with rule application or visual grid indexing.
Targeted vision-module fine-tuning improves a perception-limited model’s Sokoban success from 5.8% to 20.4% and transfers to an unseen maze game, while solver-solution training provides no gain.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a diagnostic benchmark to analyze failure modes in Multimodal LLMs during spatial planning tasks, providing insights into the gap between visual perception and planning in embodied agents.
papers.title: Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning
papers.tldr: GridProbe shows that similar MLLM planning failures can arise from different bottlenecks—visual grid indexing, rule application, or multi-step planning—and diagnoses which component to train.

papers.abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.
authors: Luoxi Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Yanlin Luo, Peiyang He, Junlin Zhu, Chun To Choi, Yang Xiong, Jiang Wu, Xingyu Zeng, Min Yang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Introduces a three-way benchmark: Answerable, Guessable, and Unanswerable.
Contains 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, with controlled wording and visual-input perturbations.
Evaluation of 10 Video LLMs attributes failures mainly to insufficient evidence-sufficiency judgment, not evidence perception.
Targeted guess-level supervision increases appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals.
Conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions, highlighting the need for graded supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for Video LLMs to handle partial evidence, addressing critical challenges in spatial reasoning and understanding within multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
papers.tldr: ClueProbe shows that Video LLMs often perceive partial visual clues but fail to judge when evidence supports a cautious guess rather than a definite answer or refusal.

papers.abstract: Overall part-discrimination accuracy can conceal failures when image position favors the wrong bilateral part. We examine whether dense descriptors distinguish the correct part under this conflict and whether their discrimination scores help select matching coordinates. We evaluate position agreement and conflict within the same target images and annotated part pairs, using a bounding-box-side score to define the conditions. We compare the original descriptors with their even and odd components under horizontal reflection, examine feature upsampling with the backbone and adapters fixed, and test candidate-selection rules based on odd scores. On SPair-71k, odd discrimination accuracy falls from 86.66% under agreement to 19.63% under conflict for frozen DINOv2, compared with 95.27% to 86.16% for MARCO. With MARCO's input geometry fixed, odd accuracy in box-side conflict was 34.12% on the native grid and 88.84% after learned upsampling and pooling back to that grid. Odd-score rules improve on the original hard-peak matchers overall for DINOv2 and DINOv3 and on conflict queries for MARCO. With MARCO's soft decoder fixed, reranking the cosine peaks changes mean per-pair PCK by +0.47 pp. For supervised GeoAware-SC, using the odd score to select the localization window center yields only 15 net additional correct matches, with 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors. Evaluating discrimination under position conflict reveals failures hidden by aggregate accuracy. Reporting corrections and introduced errors separately also shows whether a discriminative score produces useful matching decisions.
bullets: Aggregate part-discrimination accuracy can hide errors when image position favors the wrong bilateral part.
The study compares descriptor behavior under horizontal-reflection agreement versus conflict, including even/odd components, upsampling, and odd-score-based candidate selection.
On SPair-71k, frozen DINOv2 odd accuracy drops from 86.66% with position agreement to 19.63% under conflict; MARCO drops from 95.27% to 86.16%.
For MARCO, learned upsampling raises conflict accuracy from 34.12% on the native grid to 88.84% after pooling back to that grid.

Odd-score rules improve some hard-peak matching results, but localization gains are limited: MARCO reranking changes PCK by +0.47 percentage points, while GeoAware-SC yields 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors.

papers.abstract: Given a continuous RGB-D stream and a language request, streaming 3D affordance grounding requires an agent to decide when to respond and where to locate the requested functional part using only observations available so far. Existing 3D affordance grounding methods typically assume complete scene observations, while streaming vision-language models lack fine-grained 3D functional grounding. Our goal is to jointly determine response timing and functional-part localization during continuous scene observation. We propose StreamAff, an evidence-guided response strategy that makes both decisions from the grounding model's own visual evidence. The model scores the visual patches of the frames it reads: their combined support, weighed against a wait option, decides when to respond, and the highest-scoring patch selects the frame to ground in. A conditional look-back policy lets the model answer from an earlier observation at the moment of the request or wait for new evidence, and zoom-and-refine grounding segments the part named in the answer on the 3D points of the selected frame. We further introduce StreamFun3D, a benchmark derived from real-world 3D scenes that evaluates response timing and grounding across four evidence settings: Current, History, Future, and Unobserved, together with StreamIoU, a metric that credits a mask only when the response is timely and grounded in a valid source frame. We adapt offline 3D affordance grounding methods and build external-decider baselines that pair vision-language models with our mask decoder. StreamAff achieves 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams, a 40.6% relative improvement over the strongest of these baselines.
authors: Wenting Luan, Weilong Yan, Siqi Lu, Ming Li, Beibei Lin, Yongbin Zheng, Robby T. Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline 3D affordance grounding and streaming vision-language interaction.
Uses visual-patch evidence to weigh responding now against waiting for more observations.
A conditional look-back policy can select an earlier frame or wait for new evidence.
Zoom-and-refine grounding segments the named functional part in the selected frame’s 3D points.
Introduces StreamFun3D and StreamIoU; StreamAff improves 40.6% relatively over the strongest external-decider baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of StreamAff. RGB-D observations are stored as 3D-aware visual tokens. Scores denote probability masses in this look-back read. Where to ground: the outlined top-scoring patch selects an earlier frame (i⋆ = 4). The model answers from the look-back read and uses its part phrase to segment that frame’s 3D points. Zoom re-encodes phraseselected windows at higher resolution and adds their features to the frame’s 3D features; Refine corrects the decoder mask voxel-wise.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Streaming (a,b): all methods see only arrived frames. StreamAff responds on time by retrieving past evidence (a) or waiting for visibility (b); Qwen3-VL deciders respond late or mask the wrong object. Offline (c,d): masks are shown on the 3D points of the same valid source frame. StreamAff better isolates target parts using only frames available at response, while Fun3DU and T-FunS3D use full streams. Yellow: annotated part; green: StreamAff; magenta/blue: baselines.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-modal homography estimation is challenging because appearance differences obscure shared geometric structures. Separating modality transfer from homography estimation helps reduce these differences, but accurate alignment still requires effective geometric representations and consistency constraints on the two subtasks. We propose GeoCo (Geometry-Aware and Consistency-Constrained Homography Estimation), a framework that addresses these two requirements without cross-modal transformation labels. Its homography estimator, RVHomo, adapts hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model (VFM) and fuses them with local CNN features to capture structural context and spatial detail. Two geometric consistency constraints encourage modality transfer to preserve geometry and homography predictions to remain consistent under synthetic geometric transformations. Through two-stage progressive distillation, we further obtain GeoCo-D, which uses the lightweight RVHomo-D estimator. An intermediate model first learns to perform cross-modal matching without modality transfer, then transfers prediction and feature knowledge to the student, eliminating online VFM extraction. Experiments on GoogleMap, OPT-SAR, FSD, and VIS-IR show that GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4-46.7% relative to the best-performing baseline on each dataset. GeoCo-D also outperforms all compared baselines while using 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the complete GeoCo teacher.
authors: Zhuoran Yang, Junchen Yu, Runmin Zhang, Linshan Li, Chenghao Zhang, Hui-liang Shen, Si-Yuan Cao
bullets: Addresses appearance gaps between modalities that obscure shared geometric structure during homography estimation.
RVHomo fuses hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model with local CNN features to capture both context and spatial detail.
Geometric consistency constraints enforce geometry preservation during modality transfer and prediction consistency under synthetic transformations.
Progressive distillation produces GeoCo-D, which avoids online foundation-model feature extraction through a lightweight estimator.

Across four datasets, GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4–46.7% versus the strongest baseline per dataset; GeoCo-D uses 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the teacher while outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Understanding manga requires connecting who appears and who speaks with the events, character states, and relationships that unfold across panels. We study manga visual parsing through local story understanding: analyzing each double-page spread independently to capture and organize its story information in a reusable structured representation. We propose MangaParser, an agentic reading framework that jointly performs character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding within a shared multimodal conversation, without additional training or fine-tuning. The agent uses structured story memory to guide character and speaker identification, inspecting relevant image regions when uncertain and refining its predictions and story records together as evidence accumulates. Quantitative evaluations show that our parser substantially outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones. Parsing examples illustrate how a unified representation links the character and speaker predictions with narrative content and supporting evidence. We further test reusability through story question answering using outputs generated before the questions are provided. The results confirm output reusability, offering a foundation for manga translation, content retrieval, and question answering.
authors: Yingxuan Li, Jiafeng Mao, Arata Furukawa, Mayu Otani
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting who appears and speaks with events, character states, and relationships across manga panels.
Uses an agentic multimodal conversation to jointly perform character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding.
Maintains structured story memory, selectively inspects image regions, and refines predictions as evidence accumulates.
Outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones in quantitative evaluations, according to the abstract.
Its parsed outputs support downstream story question answering and applications such as translation and content retrieval.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Introduces 2,341 multiple-choice questions from 379 videos across 17 quantitative kinematics tasks.
Covers object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object kinematic relations using monocular RGB input.
Uses validated trajectories, hidden geometric/temporal signals, and fixed kinematic rules to produce verifiable answers.
The best evaluated model reaches only 41.2% overall accuracy, while spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage.
Shows that general spatial intelligence does not reliably transfer to quantitative understanding of dynamic scenes.

papers.abstract: Free-text 3D grounding, segmenting in a CT volume the region described by one sentence of the radiology report, could link reports to images at scale, but it is unclear where current models fail. We analyse the publicly released VoxTell model on all 381 findings of the 200-scan ReXGroundingCT validation set, where it grounds 53.5% of findings. Its failures are rarely about which lesion or side is meant. No miss lies on the side opposite to the one named, and findings are almost never confused with one another. Instead, predictions are too large, land on a neighbouring lesion on the correct side, or are missing for small findings, and diffuse findings are rarely grounded. Removing location words halves performance, to the level of label-only prompting, and anatomical rules derived from the sentence never improve the full-sentence output. The same pattern holds on the hidden 300-scan test set. Further progress therefore depends on extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity rather than on anatomical post-processing.
authors: Abdullah Arif Sheikh, Kamalaker Dadi, Raju S. Bapi
bullets: VoxTell grounds 53.5% of 381 findings in the ReXGroundingCT validation set.
Errors rarely involve the wrong lesion or opposite side; predictions are often oversized or shift to a neighboring lesion on the correct side.
Small findings are frequently missed, while diffuse findings are rarely grounded.
Removing location words halves performance, and anatomy-based post-processing does not improve full-sentence predictions.
The same failure pattern appears on the hidden test set, emphasizing extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity as priorities.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies increasingly operate without explicit HD maps at inference, raising the question of what road knowledge they actually internalize. To probe this knowledge through model outputs, we introduce Road-KSU, a framework that automatically converts HD maps and actor annotations into a road-centric scene graph. From this, we derive road-focused question answering and reasoning targets, complemented by map-based trajectory compliance metrics. Pairing Road-KSU with geographically disjoint splits yields a $2 \times 2$ evaluation crossing output modality (language vs. action) with place familiarity (seen vs. unseen roads). On NAVSIM, 95% of test samples lie within 10m of a training sample, and scores of 13 published planners on turns rise steeply with the number of training drives through the test location, pointing to memorized road geometry. Retraining on geographically disjoint splits and probing with Road-KSU confirm that action-space performance degrades most on unfamiliar turns, with failures dominated by geometric compliance. Language accuracy, however, drops on road-centric VQA on straight and curved roads alike, and remains stable on dynamic scene content. Scaling the training data further reveals a double dissociation: more drives through the same places improve driving on unseen roads but leave road question answering unchanged, whereas spreading a fixed data budget over more places increases road question answering with little change in driving performance. These findings show that improved driving scores need not imply broader road understanding on unseen roads, and identify geographic diversity as key to transferable road knowledge.
authors: Lena Wild, Christian Helten, Katie Z Luo, Jakob Thumm, Rafael Valencia, Patric Jensfelt, Marco Pavone
bullets: Introduces Road-KSU, which converts HD maps and actor annotations into road-centric scene graphs, questions, reasoning targets, and trajectory-compliance metrics.
Evaluates language versus action outputs across geographically seen and unseen roads using disjoint splits.

On unfamiliar turns, action failures are mainly geometric; language accuracy falls on road-centric questions but remains stable for dynamic-scene content.
More drives in the same places improve driving on unseen roads without improving road QA, while broader geographic coverage improves QA with little driving change.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new paradigm and method for giving large language models spatial understanding. Standard language models operate exclusively over discrete words (secondary representations of things rather than continuous space itself), forcing them to guess geometry verbally. Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.
bullets: Motivates continuous geometric representations—poses, boundaries, and relations—as distinct from image-based spatial grounding.
Interleaves word tokens with continuous object tokens encoding pose and signed-distance shapes in one transformer sequence.
Uses control tokens and a persistent object workspace to alternate between language generation and geometric scene updates.
An attention mask forces answers to be derived from the settled workspace rather than earlier prose.
In 2D tests, the model constructs and transforms multi-object scenes, transfers shapes to unseen nouns, and causally uses the workspace for spatial questions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the spatial workspace paradigm. Words and continuous objects share a single sequence through the language model (treated as a black box). Each object combines a 5-element pose (𝑥, 𝑦, cos 𝜃, sin 𝜃, 𝑠) with a 32-element signed-distance shape embedding ®𝑧32 compressed from its 128-point outline [13], projected by𝑊in into object embeddings ®𝑒obj alongside word embeddings ®𝑒𝑤 projected by𝑊emb. Control tokens switch between natural language (Word Head) and object representation (Object Head). Emitting the <LOOK> token masks the entire prior sequence so the model can only read the current geometry from the object workspace.

Figure 6. Coordinate-free scene layout. The user prompt contains only relative natural-language statements with no coordinates or sizes; the model constructs a 2 × 2 workspace layout across four held-out nouns and answers from <LOOK>.

Figure 2. Parallel spatial stream and attention mask on Qwen3-1.7B [12]. (a) Across each of the 28 pretrained layers, a 256-dimensional parallel spatial block runs alongside the 2048-dimensional language stream (+4.4% added parameters). Language features are down-projected from 2048 to 256 dimensions so language and geometry enter each spatial block at equal width, and spatial updates are projected back into upper language layers (ℓ ≥ 6) through zero-initialized cross-projections (𝐵 = 0). (b) Attention visibility across the sequence: text tokens attend causally, object tokens within the same <STEP> or <LOOK> block attend to each other bidirectionally, and <LOOK> blocks all earlier text and intermediate steps.

papers.abstract: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.
authors: Nannan Zhang, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yanjie Zhu, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses limited structured relational modeling in existing 3D vision-language methods.
Uses a Pyramid Vision Encoder, a language-model decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention, and MSG-based relational descriptions.
Introduces City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset containing geometric observations, captions, and scene graphs.
On City-3DQA, reaches 88.35% sentence-wise and 64.79% city-wise top-1 accuracy, improving over 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points.
Achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, indicating strong urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.

papers.abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.
authors: Gautham Krishnan P, Shrisharanyan Vasu, Aniketh Vijesh, Rajagopalan Rameshbabu, Harikrishnan Anil Maya, Sarin Xavier, Mahesh Kappanayil, Gilad Gressel
bullets: Introduces a multi-label interactive CHD diagnosis benchmark spanning 247 CT/MRI scans, three cohorts, and 38 CHD types.
Provides CHD-Harness, open-source software connecting VLMs to 3D Slicer through 22 examination tools and recording diagnostic evidence.
Compares medical, open-weight, and closed-weight VLMs with a 3D CNN and rule-based methods.
Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest reported macro F1 across cohorts: 0.63, 0.63, and 0.43.
Interactive examination improves macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views; broader clinical generalization remains outside the reported scope.

papers.abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.
authors: Chengyi Sun, Deyuan Liu, Lei Zhao, Jungang Li, Qi Jia
bullets: Covers 114 conditions across image editing, video reconstruction with full or partial starter assets, and from-scratch tasks.
Uses independently reopened projects and 228 archived scores to assess scene quality against native reference states.
On 24 from-scratch tasks, all models received full dynamics credit on 14 tasks, but some reconstructions still had zero relation points.
Relation errors accounted for most of the reported mean-fidelity gap between GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra under the fixed scoring weights.
Archived execution and recovery differences prevent causal conclusions about the effect of starter assets.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Figure retrieval from reference atlases in expert domains like forensic pathology, dentistry and geology must work without labels or training pairs, on content that often cannot leave local hardware, and on images outside the training data of image-text encoders. This work proposes a structure-aware pipeline that satisfies all three, retrieving figures through the page structure recovered by layout geometry and a local open-weight 8B VLM. Methods: A geometry-based pairing method is introduced, in which the model receives a schematic of the detected boxes and selects each picture's caption without access to pixels or text. Caption retrieval is evaluated on three private corpora (29 books, 10,421 figures, 218 queries) with blind human grading, against a lexical baseline, generated descriptions and five image-text encoders. Results: Geometric pairing was correct for 96%, 92% and 77% of pictures in the three domains, against 76%, 45% and 53% for the better of two document parsers. A hosted model given the schematic was equally accurate, while coordinates as text lost 22 points. Caption retrieval obtained an nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87 and 0.76, against 0.54, 0.51 and 0.27 for the best cross-modal encoder and 0.41, 0.28 and 0.30 for generated descriptions. Pairing errors carried over to retrieval. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves accurate figure retrieval with small local models and no in-domain training, where general and biomedical image-text encoders fall far behind. Its geometry-only pairing is the most accurate of five methods and exposes no content, even to a hosted model. Code and prompts are released.
authors: Argyrios Zafeiriou, Dionysios Koulouris, Ilias Maglogiannis
bullets: Targets expert-domain figure retrieval under label scarcity, privacy constraints, and out-of-domain content.
Pairs figures with captions from layout-box schematics, without exposing image pixels or text to the model.
Evaluated on three private corpora spanning 29 books, 10,421 figures, and 218 queries, with blind human grading.
Geometry-based pairing reached 96%, 92%, and 77% accuracy across domains, outperforming document parsers.
Caption retrieval achieved nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87, and 0.76, substantially above the best cross-modal encoders; pairing errors limited retrieval.

Fig. 5 Number of kept figures per topic in the three corpora The retrieval queries used to benchmark the system were drafted by a large language model (GPT-5.4-pro [45]) using only the topic names as context. The model drafted 100 short English queries for each domain naming one finding that an expert might look for, such as "contact gunshot wound of the head with muzzle imprint", "squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue" or "peridotite in thin section". Subsequently, near-duplicate drafts were removed on the query text alone, with no image, caption or retrieval result in view, leaving 58 queries in forensic pathology, 80 in dental and oral medicine and 80 in geology, spread over the topics of each domain. These queries are in English in every domain, providing cross-lingual evaluation in the dental corpus where they meet captions in Spanish and Portuguese. papers.abstract: Composing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) skills under an agentic planner promises scalable long-horizon manipulation without long-horizon demonstrations, yet strong atomic skills routinely fail at seams even under a correct plan. Standard remedies reset the robot's pose or draft entry conditions in language, missing the physical cause we uncover via causal interventions: even after re-homing, a frozen VLA rigidly retraces its habitual trajectory and collides with displaced scene residue, whether or not it can see it. We propose the Skill Envelope, a policy-measured 3D geometric precondition capturing the volume a frozen skill sweeps during successful executions. Exploiting the insight that the rigidity making a frozen skill fragile at seams also makes its trajectory predictable in advance, we expose each envelope as two classical 3D tools (CHECK to detect blocking residue and FREE to locate safe placement regions), establishing a division of labor where VLAs execute in-distribution manipulation and code repairs out-of-distribution states. On LIBERO-Goal with frozen $π_{0.5}$, our zero-failure envelope predicts collisions at 0.946 AUROC (0.944 from one RGB-D view) and beats frontier VLMs on seam readiness (0.902 vs. 0.793); using it for skill ordering and code repair lifts success from 82.8% to 92.3% on two-step seams and from 29.7% to 93.8% on drawer-bearing 3-4 step chains, matching privileged world reset. Together, these results show that reliable VLA composition hinges on measuring a policy's physical workspace rather than guessing preconditions in language. Ongoing work closes the loop with autonomous LLM orchestration, synthesized free-object recovery, and cross-policy evaluation on cluttered benchmarks and real hardware.
bullets: Frozen VLAs can collide with residual objects because they rigidly retrace habitual trajectories, even after re-homing or when residue is not visible.
The method models each skill’s swept volume as a 3D geometric precondition and exposes it through CHECK for collision detection and FREE for safe placement.
On LIBERO-Goal with frozen π₀.₅, envelope-based collision prediction achieved 0.946 AUROC, or 0.944 from one RGB-D view.
Using envelope-guided ordering and code repair improved two-step seam success from 82.8% to 92.3% and 3–4-step drawer chains from 29.7% to 93.8%.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and remains limited by ongoing work on autonomous orchestration, cluttered benchmarks, and real hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Geometric tools detect collisions from depth, outperform VLMs, and repair multi-step chains. (a) Real handoff (push the plate→ cheese in the bowl): top, CHECK flags the displaced plate (red) intersecting the next skill’s 3D envelope Ek (teal); bottom, FREE marks a safe zone outside both Ek and the following skill’s envelope Ek+1 (indigo: wine to rack) so moving the plate will not block the upcoming step (amber arrow illustrates planned free-object repair, Q2, Table II). (b) Pre-execution collision detection across 640 handoffs using only nominal-rollout overlap (no failure data): geometry detects collisions with both drawers (0.986) and free objects (0.847), and a single RGB-D camera nearly matches simulator state (0.944 vs. 0.946 AUROC). (c) Top: predicting whether the next skill will succeed on 429 handoffs, our envelope-based readiness model (0.902 AUROC) beats frontier VLMs prompted with images (Img) or BATON-style text rules (Text) by at least +0.110. Bottom: on 128 drawer-bearing 3–4 step chains, envelope-guided skill ordering and code repair (Plan+Fix) lifts full-chain success from 29.7% (Random+Home) to 93.8% (+64.1 pts), matching simulator World Reset (90.6%).

Fig. 2. Seam failures are primarily physical and policy-specific. (a) Comparing three interventions on the exact same transition and random seed of open middle drawer → push the plate (totals over 10 trials): returning the arm home (Re-homed) still collides 10 of 10 times; erasing the drawer from the policy’s camera input (View Reset, inset) leaves the physical collision unchanged (0/10 success, 10 of 10 collisions); only physically closing the drawer (World Reset) succeeds (10/10). (b) Top: on the same open drawer, push the plate’s 3D envelope intersects the drawer (red, 0/10), whereas turn on the stove sweeps clear (no overlap, 10/10). Bottom: across all nine skills that can follow open middle drawer (dashed green line: World Reset 9–10/10), our 3D overlap cleanly separates the six colliding skills (breaking five) from the three clear ones, whereas frontier VLM Qwen4-Max flags nearly every skill as blocked across 7 held-out trials per pair, even the completely unaffected turn on the stove.

papers.title: VLAs Execute, Code Recovers: 3D Skill Envelopes Bridge the Compositional Gap in Agentic Manipulation

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and stale points caused by append-only mapping in dynamic scenes.
Updates each point’s confidence using multi-view temporal evidence from segmentation, depth, and visibility consistency.
Combines point refinement with object tracking and re-identification to maintain identities through motion and relocation.
Improves mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet.
Supports downstream object navigation and embodied question-answering, with reported success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed dynamic semantic mapping framework. Given posed RGB-D observations, openvocabulary detections are generated and associated with object instances in the 3D semantic map. For each association, we perform a visibility-based point confidence update. Points supported by current detections, such as the green points on the table, receive higher confidence. In contrast, inconsistent outlier points, such as red points mistakenly fused into a bed instance due to previous segmentation errors, are down-weighted when later observations identify them as pillows. Points belonging to removed objects are identified through visibility reasoning, assigned lower confidence, and eventually pruned. Unobserved points in the current frame, shown in gray, remain unchanged until more evidence is collected in later frames. The semantic map is updated online in this frame-by-frame manner, while periodic instance-fragment merging reduces duplicate instances and re-identification preserves object identities when objects are relocated and re-observed at new locations.

Fig. 6: Example of handling under-segmentation. A pillow is initially fused into the chair instance due to undersegmentation. Once the pillow is correctly segmented in later frames, our method adds it as a separate instance and gradually removes the corresponding points from the chair instance through confidence updates.
Fig. 7: Example of in-view object tracking. Our method tracks the moving bowl in images and updates its location in the semantic map while preserving the same instance ID.

Fig. 5: Example of object fragment merging. A table is initially reconstructed as two separate instances due to temporally disconnected partial observations at 1s and 10s. As more observations become available at 12s, our method merges the fragments into a complete object instance.

Fig. 1: Dynamic open-vocabulary semantic mapping. Our method maintains a refinable object-centric 3D semantic map through point-level probabilistic updates. It handles dynamic objects that newly appear, move within the robot’s view, or are relocated out of view and later re-identified.

Fig. 9: Examples of object navigation and EQA tasks executed on the Spot robot. Our semantic map serves as an online memory that helps the LLM localize target objects, plan embodied skills, and answer questions.

Fig. 4: Example of handling incorrect detections. A plastic bag is mistakenly detected as a pillow, creating a false instance in the map. Our confidence update mechanism accumulates positive evidence for consistently detected objects and negative evidence for unsupported instances, eventually removing the false pillow while preserving the true one.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D-consistent novel views from 2D diffusion models remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. In this work, we introduce a framework that enhances geometric alignment for monocular view synthesis under drastic camera changes by jointly generating a target view and its corresponding depth map. By conditioning the diffusion pipeline on the single source image, source depth, and target camera rays, our approach forces the model to inherently reason in 3D space even under extreme viewpoint shifts. To guarantee spatial fidelity, we propose a novel per-pixel depth consistency constraint, which verifies and enforces 3D consistency across generated views. Our framework establishes a robust pipeline for geometrically consistent view synthesis, yielding superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared to current state-of-the-art methods. With this work, we pave the road towards robust 3D world models capable of understanding complex environments from a single view image.
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in 2D diffusion models under large camera viewpoint changes.
Conditions diffusion on a source image, source depth, and target camera rays to encourage 3D reasoning.
Introduces a per-pixel depth consistency constraint to preserve spatial fidelity across views.
Reports superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.
Targets robust single-image understanding for future 3D world models.

papers.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.

papers.abstract: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.

papers.abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
authors: Yu Chen, Haosen Yang, Su Ee Tan, Zhensong Zhang, Jifei Song, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Existing results are difficult to compare because papers use different sampling, resolutions, test splits, and alignment procedures.
The arena evaluates five tasks—including monocular depth, 3D/4D reconstruction, and SLAM—on 23 public datasets plus new captures spanning indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes.
Its deterministic alignment and common metrics address evaluation failures that can substantially distort reported errors.
Across 52 models, single-image depth is near saturation on public benchmarks but remains challenging in large, uncontrolled scenes.
Progress increasingly depends on cross-frame and cross-view consistency: feed-forward 3D/4D models match or exceed monocular specialists and outperform video depth models.
