papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.
authors: Yan Zheng, ShengYun Peng, Xuyao Liang, Xiaoyan Cong, Nuo Chen, Bangya Liu, Zihan Wang, Wenyan Cong, Zhiwen Fan, Zhangyang Wang
bullets: Targets failures in navigation and manipulation where models must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input.
Compares matched visual, structured, and combined inputs on identical instances, environments, and verifiers when possible.
Finds a recurring gap: models perform better when object identity, state, or target location is provided explicitly than when inferred from rendered scenes.
Shows that action-space and interaction-harness design can alter results, making protocol a confounding factor.
Open-sourced for reproducible, fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the 11 tasks in VERIWORLD, spanning four families. Interactive Control (closedloop, multi-round): MazeNavFPS (first-person grid maze navigation), Billiards (2D pool trajectory planning), TunnelNav3D (curved-tunnel flythrough), PlaceOnBottom (object stacking). Trial-and-Error Prediction (submit-and-check): BoxFold (predict the folded shape), MovingShooter (aim at a moving target), LightWar (aim and launch a projectile at a distant beacon across a large outdoor terrain). Photoreal Grounding (photorealistic 3D scenes): SceneGrounding (recover the camera pose of a given screenshot in two photoreal interior levels), ObjectGrounding (localize named kitchen objects with 3D markers in a photoreal apartment scene). Computational Physics (Slang/CUDA simulation): CurvyBilliards (ball dynamics on a parametric surface), DropToTarget (surface design for target landing). Family colours match the row banners in Table 2; Sec. 5 reports these tasks using separate core, specialized, and harness-diagnostic tracks.

Figure 1: Batch control improves performance under both evaluated information channels at an equal move budget. Same task (MazeNavFPS, 30 mazes), same model (Gemini-3.1-Pro), and the same budget of primitive moves for both protocols (125/170/210 moves for 3×3/4×4/5×5 grids): switching the action interface from Single (one move per call) to Batch (3–6 moves per call) lifts Pass@1 from 0.57 to 0.93 under VP (vision + position log) and from 0.57 to 0.97 under VRP (VP + raycast), while Batch uses fewer moves on average. Under an equal budget of 50 model calls, Batch also outperforms Single for every evaluated model (Sec. 5.3 and Table 10). This motivates VERIWORLD’s three-axis design — task, information channel, and action harness — in which the harness is treated as a first-class experimental variable rather than a fixed implementation detail.

Figure 2: VERIWORLD evaluation pipeline. A Python generator maps a seed to task parameters and instantiates the scene in Unreal Engine 5 (rendering + game-runtime bridge for in-process code execution). A VLM agent runs a closed step loop: screenshot + action log → thoughts / actions / updated knowledge → execute in UE5; the new screenshot and log feed back for up to T rounds. A deterministic Python verifier checks pass / fail at runtime for every task; some families additionally have a solvability certificate (Lean 4 or deterministic simulation, depending on the task; §3.3).

Figure 4: LightWar successful arc, V+Telemetry condition. A 2×3 stack of arc replay frames sampled at t = 0.51, 1.53, 2.54, 3.56, 4.58, 5.59 s after launch, taken from a Gemini 3.1 Pro Pass@1 episode on seed=0 (hit_forest_hilltop_beacon). The agent fires a glowing projectile from a low-elevation forest clearing (frame 1) and tracks the ballistic arc until it intersects a hilltop beacon (frame 6, bright impact flare). Each frame is the harness’s per-tick render passed back to the agent at the next round; together they form the visual evidence the agent uses to plan the next shot. Per-round screenshots like these are part of the V condition; V+Telemetry additionally reports the scalar miss distance of each shot. Without the miss distance (V-only), the mid-tier panel models (Sonnet, Opus, Kimi, Qwen3-VL-30B) drop from 0.33 to 0.00 Pass@1.

Figure 5: Six rendering variants of the ObjectGrounding harness. The main-table V/C contrast (grid-marker family, fourth column) compares 9 bboxes with small index labels inside the boxes vs. the same bboxes with enlarged, camera-facing labels under an offcenter camera; the harness-diagnostic V/C contrast (single-marker family, second column) repeats the same label-rendering ablation under a sparser, single-bbox scaffold. Auxiliary numbered-ball variants (first and third columns) are the original baselines from which the bbox variants were derived; they are not used for the V/C tables but are the scene context the seed sampler draws from. Within each family, V and C differ only in how the index labels are rendered; both include the marker-to-world-coordinate table.

Prior benchmarks typically capture only subsets of these capabilities—focusing on perception, interaction, or evaluation in isolation—while VERIWORLD integrates all components within a unified and verifiable framework. ✓ = supported, ✗ = not supported, ∼ = partial.
Table 2: Task families in VERIWORLD. We organize 11 tasks into four families by interaction paradigm and the type of spatial reasoning required. Family colours match the row banners of Table 3.

Table 4: Grid mazes under an equal primitive-move budget: batch outperforms single-step control under both information variants. Pass@1 over 30 mazes per cell (grids 3, 4, 5 × 10 seeds). Batch and single share a budget of 125, 170 and 210 primitive moves for 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 grids; the batch prompt asks for 3–6 commands per model call and single sends one. VP = rendered observation + position history; VRP = VP + a 4-direction raycast scan. These are auxiliary harness variants, not core V/S/C conditions.

Table 8: MazeNavFPS auxiliary information-channel sweep, 5×5 grids, 9-seed extension. Maze navigation does not cleanly fit the core V/S/C taxonomy: a closed-loop ReAct agent inevitably accumulates an action-history memory across rounds, so even the rendered-observation-only condition retains an implicit structured channel. We sweep four auxiliary information channels (all under batched action control, Bf ), holding the model lineup fixed at four frontier VLMs: V – rendered observation only; no harness-tracked position log; RP – 4-direction raycast wall distances + harness-tracked position log; no rendered observation; VP – rendered observation + position log; VRP – rendered observation + raycast + position log. We restrict to the hardest 5×5 grid for an apples-to-apples shape comparison and use nine seeds {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 42} that produce different maze topologies. Each per-model cell reports Pass@1 over valid episodes; Avg pools them across the four models. Each cell has n = 9 except RP (Gemini 7, Opus 4, GPT-5.2 5), VP (Opus 7) and VRP (Opus 4, GPT-5.2 8).

Table 10: Grid mazes under an equal budget of 50 model calls. Each cell shows Pass@1, with average rounds (model calls) in parentheses. The batch prompt asks for 3–6 commands per call and single executes one, so batch can execute more primitive moves. VP = rendered observation + position history; VRP = VP + a 4-direction raycast scan.

Table 3: Core V/S/C information-condition results. We include tasks for which visual (V), structured-only (S), and combined (C) conditions are defined on seed-generated task instances with the same action interface and verifier; ObjectGrounding has no structured-only condition and is reported with V and C. V provides rendered observations and task-specific metadata describing the scene setup and action interface, while retaining task-specific demands for visual identification or state estimation. S provides explicit information such as object attributes, current or target coordinates, and physical parameters without images. The S−V gap measures the resulting change in task performance (Appendix A.1). The C−max(V,S) column measures whether simply combining rendered and structured inputs improves over the better single channel. Positive S−V indicates a benefit from explicit task information, which can reduce demands on visual identification and state estimation; negative C−max(V,S) means that the combined condition, including its task-specific instructions, underperforms the better single channel, and does not by itself isolate a fusion deficit.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with VLMs; fits spatial intelligence and embodied AI.
papers.title: VeriWorld: A Verifiable Visual SWE-Bench for Spatial Reasoning in 3D Environments
papers.tldr: VeriWorld benchmarks VLM spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments by separating visual perception, structured reasoning, and interaction effects with executable, deterministically verified actions.

papers.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Defines a task combining speech understanding, object retrieval, speaker localization, and delivery.
Provides a dataset with three query types, eight subtypes, and varied object-selection and delivery requirements.
Integrates motion-aware spatial audio into an audio-visual large language model to track spatial cues during movement.
Uses multitask instruction tuning for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding.
Reports baseline results in seen and unseen environments; code is planned for public release.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our baseline framework. Details of the Motion-Aware Spatial (MAS) Audio Encoder are shown in the left panel. The original audio encoder preserves speech understanding, while the parallel MAS Audio Encoder extracts binaural spatial cues and updates them according to the agent’s motion. A lightweight projector maps these features into the language model’s token space, where they are combined with speech, visual, and textual tokens to predict executable skills. The action executor interacts with the environment and returns execution feedback for closed-loop decision making.

Figure 1. Overview of Audio-Visual Rearrangement. Given a spoken request, an agent must (1) search for and pick up a suitable object and (2) navigate to the requesting speaker and hand it over. This requires understanding what to retrieve from speech, visually grounding the target object, and acoustically localizing the speaker among multiple people, as well as navigation and manipulation.

Figure 4. AVR trajectories in unseen environments. The top and bottom examples correspond to explicit and implicit requests. Each example shows a top-down scene view, an occupancy map, and egocentric observations during exploration (1), target acquisition (2), and approach to the speaker (3). Blue and orange paths indicate object search and sound-source search. Paths connect recorded decision locations along the navigation mesh. Selected views include a simulator-rendered snapshot for illustration.

Figure 3. Distributions of initial speaker azimuths and sourceagent Euclidean distances across AVR episodes. papers.abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
authors: Zehao Liu, Huashuo Lei, Xi Lin, Haoang Li, Yuliang Chen, Huarui Zhang, Yifan Wang
bullets: Problem: Embodied agents may be vulnerable to environment-only attacks even when models and instructions are unchanged.
Method: EnvTrap creates paired safe, trap, and benign null-trap scenarios to test action safety and consequence prediction.
Finding: Environment rearrangements produced hazardous actions at an average rate of 83.4% across five evaluated action policies.
Finding: Models performed near chance at predicting consequences, whereas human evaluators achieved high accuracy; similar vulnerabilities appeared in world models.

Defense and scope: A consequence-aware defense reduced trap triggers by 76.3 percentage points in simulation and 62.9 points across physical backends, while targeting a broader physical-reasoning deficit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the EnvTrap attack pipeline. The diagnostic pipeline systematically constructs matched safe, null-trap, and trap embodied scenarios without modifying instructions or models. Through Semantic-Spatial Alignment, Spatial Constraint Sampling, and rigorous Plausibility Verification, it reveals how subtle physical layout changes cause consequence-blind embodied agents to execute hazardous actions in both simulation and real-world deployments.

Figure 3: The consequence-aware defense framework. A VLM is fine-tuned on the EnvTrap dataset to predict physical action outcomes. At inference, an asynchronous safety gate evaluates VLA actions in parallel, blocking hazardous actions and prompting replanning while allowing safe actions to proceed to the action buffer.

papers.title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution

papers.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.
authors: Xiaoqian Hu, Ruihong Qiu, Yanran Tang, Sen Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of supervised imitation and outcome-only rewards for embodied 3D reasoning.
Uses SFT to establish valid tool interactions, then applies GRPO while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen.
Introduces Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence-sensitive credit assignment.
Uses Group Coverage Sampling to maintain exploration across grounding tools.
On MSQA and Beacon3D, improves over SFT and answer/format-reward-only GRPO, particularly in spatial reasoning and grounding-answer coherence.

papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces \method, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, \method achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
authors: Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, Ye Shi, Yuxiang Gao, Jiayuan Gu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning where objects are and how they move from action demonstrations without costly dense 4D supervision.
Attaches a query-based decoder to a pretrained policy and unifies tasks such as depth, point motion, correspondence, and hand–eye relations.
Learns rich spatiotemporal structure from a small number of sampled queries during training.
The decoder can be removed at inference, adding zero runtime overhead.
Achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance across simulated and real-world settings, with training up to 5× faster; probing shows the policy retains recoverable 4D structure.

papers.abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.
bullets: Addresses object rotation, translation, and rescaling when unseen surfaces, shadows, and reflections must be generated consistently.
Introduces counterfactual state supervision with controlled conflicts between photographs and 3D states to teach source selection.
Adds symmetric counterfactual correction using photo-side and state-side twins to preserve conditioning responsiveness during sampling.
Training-only strategies require no architectural changes or extra inference steps.
Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench report strong spatial editing and content preservation, with ablations showing improved source selection.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

papers.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contactless physiological monitoring from facial videos, but facial motion, particularly mouth and jaw movements during cognitive and communicative tasks, can severely degrade signal reconstruction. We present SKIA, a lightweight, mask-guided framework that suppresses motion-prone lower-face regions while preserving physiological cues from the forehead and cheeks. Using the UBFC-rPPG benchmark, we first investigate static lower-face suppression in the classical CHROM pipeline. Static masking improves waveform Pearson correlation from 0.3507 to 0.4166 (p < 0.001) and reduces heart-rate mean absolute error (MAE) from 33.50 to 23.44 bpm. Building on this finding, we introduce SKIA-Net, a compact spatiotemporal architecture that combines raw facial frames, statically masked representations, and temporal motion differences to reconstruct blood volume pulse (BVP) waveforms. The full model achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.7522 and a heart-rate MAE of 3.73 bpm on UBFC-rPPG, outperforming single-stream variants. Ablation studies show that the static mask provides complementary information to raw appearance and that static anatomical priors outperform the tested dynamic optical-flow-based masking strategy. These results suggest that spatially informed, temporally stable masking can improve motion-robust rPPG estimation. Code: https://github.com/lee-vtruong/SKIA-rPPG

On UBFC-rPPG, the full model achieved 0.7522 Pearson correlation and 3.73 bpm heart-rate MAE.

papers.abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to locate an object indicated by a click point in a ground or drone query image within a satellite reference image. Through a quantitative prompt-sensitivity evaluation, we find that existing CVOGL methods suffer from a prompt-disobeying overfitting problem: when the click point is moved or removed, their predictions barely respond, indicating that the models rely on spurious feature correlations rather than genuinely following the prompt semantics. We trace this behavior to the limited scale of the benchmark dataset, which contains only 4,343 prompt-object pairs per task, so that the models simply memorize the object associated with each scene instead of learning the true prompt-to-object correspondence. To address this, we propose two plug-and-play components. First, we construct the CVOGL-MO dataset by expanding the existing training and test sets with diverse multi-object annotations, mitigating the memorization that induces shortcut learning. Second, we propose the Cross-View Co-Scene Multi-Object Contrastive Loss (CVMCL), which enforces distinct feature representations for different click points within the same scene, compelling the model to follow prompt instructions. We further design a prompt-sensitivity evaluation protocol with prediction-shift metrics, providing the first quantitative measurement of prompt-following capability for CVOGL. Both components are architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into existing methods without any architectural modification. Experiments on three representative backbones show that our components substantially improve prompt-following accuracy on the new multi-object test sets and markedly increase prompt sensitivity. Our dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/Sunny-Fresher/CVOGL-MO.
authors: Lingyun Xing, Wenning Hao, Kai Jiang, Dawei Jin, Xiaohan Zhang, Xiaoxiong Zhang
bullets: Existing methods overfit to scene-object correlations, so moving or removing the click point barely changes predictions.

A prediction-shift evaluation protocol quantitatively measures prompt sensitivity.
Both plug-and-play components improve prompt-following accuracy and sensitivity across three representative backbones.

papers.abstract: Geometry-aware rotary positional encodings, such as RayRoPE, help attention reason about the 3D spatial relationships between tokens and the query camera. However, they implicitly assume a static scene, encoding each key at its observed position regardless of when it was captured. For dynamic scenes with temporally separated input views, this mismatch places the same moving object at a different position in each input frame, so it can be rendered at an inaccurate position. While temporal encodings inform attention when a token was observed, they do not resolve where its content should be at the query time. We introduce a simple and general approach that aligns positional encodings with dynamic scene geometry through Galilean transport. Before positional encoding, each key's 3D position is transported to the query time using its estimated velocity and the temporal offset. By modifying only key positions, our method integrates directly with existing encodings, including RayRoPE and URoPE, without altering their formulations. Velocities can be obtained from arbitrary sources. By default, we estimate them from token correspondences within the network. Integrated into LVSM, our method improves dynamic view synthesis on Syn4D, dynamic Objaverse, and real-world Stereo4D videos over baselines. Ablations show that encoding velocities as token features yields smaller gains, while attention visualizations reveal that our method attends to query-time locations of moving content, unlike RayRoPE. Beyond view synthesis, our method also reduces tracking errors on dynamic objects in a pretrained 3D point tracker and improves moving-vehicle generation in a video generator.
authors: Youngmin Kim, Seonghyun Jin, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Static geometry-aware positional encodings can misplace moving content when input views were captured at different times.
GALILEO applies Galilean transport to each key’s 3D position using its estimated velocity and temporal offset before positional encoding.
The approach modifies only key positions and integrates with existing encodings such as RayRoPE and URoPE.
Integrated into LVSM, it improves dynamic view synthesis across synthetic and real-world benchmarks and also benefits tracking and video generation.
Velocity estimates can come from arbitrary sources; the default uses token correspondences within the network.],

papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware positional encodings with 3D spatial reasoning and velocity transport; directly fits spatial intelligence and is transferable to embodied/world-model settings.
papers.title: GALILEO: Geometric RoPE with Galilean Key Transport for Dynamic Scenes
papers.tldr: GALILEO transports key positions to the query time using estimated motion, improving attention to moving objects in dynamic 3D scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) tokenize images using fixed spatial grids, so visual token count grows with pixel area rather than scene content. We propose to group neighboring patches based on their visual appearance, allowing tokens to represent coherent image regions rather than fixed spatial windows. We introduce RVLM, a VLM trained to use regions rather than patches as its visual units. Analyzing region construction for general-purpose VLMs, we find that regions must cover the full image, stay spatially connected during end-to-end training, and preserve fine structure such as small text, while semantic grouping adds little. RVLM therefore partitions images using training-free Felzenszwalb-Huttenlocher segmentation, assigns each ViT patch to a region, and pools patches within each region into a variable-length sequence of visual tokens. The patch-to-region assignment is retained to support spatially precise prediction through coarse-to-fine decoding. Across tasks spanning VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation, RVLM matches or improves example-weighted task performance while using 21.5% fewer visual tokens than an identically trained patch baseline. The advantage grows with image resolution, reaching a 5.3-point gain while using 51.8% fewer visual tokens at the highest-resolution setting. The gains are largest on spatially demanding tasks, where prior token-reduction methods degrade most sharply. RVLM adds no model parameters and improves inference throughput by up to 35.9%. On unseen pathology and satellite images and on video benchmarks without any video training, RVLM performs on par with the patch baseline while using 2-3$\times$ fewer visual tokens. These results establish regions as a scalable alternative to patch-based visual representations while preserving the spatial precision required for grounded prediction.
authors: Savya Khosla, Chris Dongjoo Kim, Alex Schwing, Derek Hoiem, Christopher Clark, Sangho Lee
bullets: Uses training-free Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher segmentation to group patches into variable-length, spatially connected regions.
Preserves full-image coverage and fine structure, including small text; semantic grouping is not essential.
Retains patch-to-region mappings for coarse-to-fine spatial prediction.
Matches or improves performance across VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation while using 21.5% fewer tokens overall.
At higher resolutions, gains reach 5.3 points with 51.8% fewer tokens; inference throughput improves by up to 35.9%, with strong transfer to pathology, satellite, and video benchmarks.

The retained patch-to-region correspondence enables coarse-to-fine spatial grounding, where the LLM selects a region, then a patch within it, and finally a precise point within the patch.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces RVLM, a VLM that uses region-based tokenization instead of fixed patches, improving spatial grounding and efficiency, which is highly relevant to spatial intelligence and token efficiency.
papers.title: RVLM: Fewer Tokens, Better Resolution Scaling, Fine-Grained Spatial Grounding
papers.tldr: RVLM replaces fixed-grid image patches with connected visual regions, reducing visual tokens while preserving fine-grained spatial grounding and improving high-resolution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves multimodal reasoning, but response-level feedback provides limited guidance on which intermediate decisions to correct. Visual interventions reveal sensitivity to image content, yet this sensitivity alone does not establish reward alignment or support across questions. We introduce RAVEC (Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction), which selects visual corrections using local and cross-question reward support and jointly determines their strengths within each response. Paired Visual Evidence Contrast (PVEC) compares predictions from an exponential moving average teacher at the same sampled response prefix under the original image and a version with its annotated evidence region suppressed, yielding signed correction directions. Credit-Risk Allocation (CRA) screens these directions using local reward alignment and reward support from other questions, excluding all responses to the source question. It then solves a response-level budgeted allocation problem, assigning additional cost to directions that locally reduce predictive entropy. The resulting signed visual loss augments Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) during training. Inference uses only the original image and question. Across ten multimodal benchmarks, RAVEC achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared methods with both 3B and 7B Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct models, outperforming GRPO by 2.67 and 1.39 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations support the combined design of evidence alignment, credit qualification, and risk-aware allocation. The project is available at https://yangjj007.github.io/ravec/.
authors: Junjie Yang, Rui Qian, Xutao Mao, Yuhe Wu, Mingda Zhang, Jiaxuan Luo, Yang Tan, Qiang Huang, Zhisheng Chen, Yanfeng Li, Dawen Tian, Changmiao Wang, Tao Tan
bullets: Addresses the weak guidance of response-level rewards for correcting intermediate visual reasoning decisions.
Uses PVEC to derive signed visual correction directions by contrasting original images with evidence-suppressed versions.
Uses CRA to filter corrections by local and cross-question reward support, then allocates correction strength under a response-level budget.
Augments GRPO with the resulting signed visual loss; inference uses only the original image and question.
Achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods across ten benchmarks, improving over GRPO by 2.67 points for 3B and 1.39 points for 7B models; ablations support the combined design.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces RAVEC for reward-aligned visual evidence correction in multimodal reasoning, providing a mechanism for improving multimodal model alignment through visual interventions.
papers.title: RAVEC: Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction
papers.tldr: RAVEC improves multimodal reasoning by training models to correct visual evidence with reward-aligned, risk-aware interventions while requiring no extra inputs at inference.

papers.abstract: A pretrained image representation helps train a diffusion transformer in several roles, including as an alignment target, which the model's hidden states learn to match, as in representation alignment (REPA), and as a condition, an extra input describing the image to be generated. Combined, they would give the model an input and a target, but whether they conflict is unknown. To test this, we let the condition carry only part of REPA's target: we split the representation of each image patch into an image-level (global) part, shared by all patches of the image, and a within-image (local) part, the patch's difference from the image-level part, and use one token carrying the image-level part as the condition. Then, the two roles overlap on the image-level part, where they could conflict, while only REPA supervises the within-image part, where we can see whether the token helps REPA. We find that the token and REPA together teach both the image-level part and the within-image part, the main source of REPA's FID improvement, far more than the sum of what each teaches alone, so they cooperate rather than conflict. These findings give one design rule for combining REPA with an image-level condition, supply the global, supervise the local, which we implement as Global-Condition REPA (GC-REPA): REPA with the token as an extra input; the token carries no information beyond REPA's target and is drawn at sampling from a separately trained token prior. GC-REPA greatly accelerates convergence: on ImageNet 256*256, SiT-XL/2 + GC-REPA reaches REPA's 4M- and SiT-XL/2's 7M-iteration FIDs within 200K and 100K iterations (20 and 70 fewer).
authors: Chaojie Ji, Sergio Quiroga-Sandoval, Ruxin Wang, Zheju Zheng, Yankai Cao
bullets: REPA uses pretrained image representations as alignment targets, while conditioning provides them as model inputs; their interaction was previously unclear.
The method separates each patch representation into a shared global component and a patch-specific local component, then supplies the global component as a single conditioning token.
The condition and REPA cooperate: together they teach both global and local features far more effectively than either alone, rather than conflicting.
This leads to Global-Condition REPA (GC-REPA), where the token is an extra input and is sampled from a separately trained prior at generation time.
On ImageNet 256×256, GC-REPA reaches REPA’s 4M-iteration and baseline SiT-XL/2’s 7M-iteration FIDs within 200K and 100K iterations, respectively.

papers.title: Supply the Global, Supervise the Local: Combining Representation Conditioning and Alignment in Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: Combining a global image-level condition with local representation alignment makes diffusion transformers learn more effectively and converge much faster than either role alone.

papers.abstract: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.
bullets: Studies N agents with partial, distinct views that exchange budget-limited natural-language messages to answer spatial queries.
Introduces a benchmark targeting queries requiring non-trivial integration across multiple viewpoints.
Finds that limited-language communication is less damaging than prior two-agent results suggest, but substantial reasoning headroom remains.
Shows a significant gap between current decentralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling.
Reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially improves decentralized reasoning and closes the gap with the centralized baseline.

papers.title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
papers.tldr: This work formalizes decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning and shows that credit-assigned reinforcement learning can bring language-constrained multi-agent collaboration close to centralized performance.

papers.abstract: Conventional geometric measures of visual representations are symmetric, assigning equal costs to forward and reverse motion along the same path. We propose DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over frozen visual representations. Grounded in Randers geometry, DiRGeo learns a state-dependent directional field from ordered image trajectories through self-supervised contrast, without semantic labels. Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition distinguish learned directional structure from normalization artifacts and common convergence. Experiments across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple representation depths demonstrate consistent directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry beyond simple attractor-based explanations. The learned fields become increasingly process-specific in deeper representations, while natural-video experiments reveal event-dependent directional preferences. As functional validation, DiRGeo guides restoration selection. These results establish directional geometry as a useful complement to symmetric representation analysis.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of symmetric geometric measures, which treat forward and reverse paths identically.
Uses Randers geometry, self-supervised contrast, and state-dependent directional fields to model visual-process directionality.
Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition separate directional structure from normalization artifacts and shared convergence.
Across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple depths, it finds consistent whole-path asymmetry that becomes more process-specific in deeper representations.
Event-dependent directional preferences in natural videos and restoration-selection guidance demonstrate practical functional value.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over visual representations using Randers geometry. This contributes to geometry-aware multimodal models and spatial reasoning, relevant to Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: DiRGeo: Learning Directional Geometry of Visual Representations
papers.tldr: DiRGeo learns asymmetric, direction-sensitive geometry in frozen visual representations from ordered image trajectories without semantic labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.
authors: Qihang Chen, Tengjie Li, Hongwei Lu, Jason Wu, Chyna Qu, Shikui Tu, Lei Xu
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-aware perception and predictive action selection in precise manipulation.
Distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens using a frozen spatial teacher.
Learns a compact, current-conditioned latent representing actionable near-future information without future observations at inference.
Fuses the predicted latent into the Action Expert through zero-initialized residual connections.
Shows improvements across LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Planning in a visual world means reading the layout, foreseeing how the state will change, and following the task rules all at once. When a plan fails, a model should also use what went wrong to fix it. We call these two abilities spatiotemporal planning and plan repair, and test them with Railbound-Bench. A model sees a railway puzzle, adds tracks under a budget, and submits one complete layout; a simulator then moves all cars at once and decides whether the layout works. After a failure, the model sees what happened and may submit a new layout, up to five attempts in total. On the 200-puzzle main set, the best of nine models solves 59.5% within five attempts, the next 39.5%, and the other seven at most 10.0%; a 1,000-puzzle extended set with a wider range of difficulty is far easier, at 90.9% for the best model. Controlled studies on 180 fixed puzzles show that knowing the task is not the same as using it. GPT-6.1 Terra copies 97.2% of boards exactly and, given a correct layout as text, predicts all four requested future states in 91.3% of cases, yet only 22.8% of its first layouts work. Planning fails more often as the cars' routes interact, even among puzzles that a search solver finds equally easy. Visual feedback removes the reported fault in 175 of 417 first revisions, but only 43 of these revisions solve the puzzle, and at an equal budget of 40k tokens it does no better than fresh retries. The code and data are open-sourced on GitHub at https://github.com/liaoyanqing666/Railbound_Bench.

bullets: Railbound-Bench evaluates visual spatiotemporal planning and iterative plan repair under a track budget and up to five attempts.
Performance varies sharply: the best model solves 59.5% of 200 main-set puzzles, while seven of nine models solve at most 10.0%.
Strong board copying and state prediction do not translate into reliable planning: one model achieves 97.2% board copying and 91.3% future-state prediction but only 22.8% valid first layouts.
Planning becomes harder when car routes interact, even when a search solver considers the puzzles equally difficult.
Visual feedback often removes the reported fault but rarely yields a solution and performs no better than fresh retries at equal token budget.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark probing spatiotemporal planning and plan repair in multimodal LLMs; relevant to spatial reasoning in visual environments.
papers.title: Seeing Is Not Planning: Spatiotemporal Planning and Plan Repair in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Multimodal LLMs can perceive railway puzzles and predict outcomes, but still struggle to construct valid plans and effectively repair failures.

papers.abstract: 3D scene understanding tasks are often approached by building explicit 3D scene representations or by training specialized multi-modal models over point clouds, voxels, or scene graphs. We take a complementary view: for many queries, the main bottleneck is not the absence of a stronger 3D representation but the selection of a small subset of multi-view RGB views that actually makes the query answerable. We present a training-free, query-conditioned multi-view pipeline that performs diverse tasks using only 2D images and a set of tools used purely for inference. Our method first decomposes each query into a set of concepts that identify unique attributes that assist with reasoning. This drives a coarse-to-fine evidence selection process: a coarse retrieval selects and scores all views, a diversity-aware selector reduces redundancy, and a reranking stage helps shortlist views by target visibility or answerability. The resulting evidence is optionally grounded for queries that benefit from explicit localization, and a self-verification step helps refine the final response, especially for open-ended cases. Despite using no task-specific training and no explicit 3D representations at inference time, our approach provides approximately 10% gain on 3D VQA and 5% gain on dense captioning and Embodied QA while being applicable across different scenarios. We further propose a unique judge-based evaluation system, motivating a judge who takes into account many semantically correct or partially correct answers, thereby improving holistic scene understanding.
authors: Sarosij Bose, Arindam Dutta, Konstantinos Karydis, Amit K. Roy Chowdhury
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of identifying which views make a query answerable, rather than constructing stronger 3D scene representations.
Decomposes queries into concepts and uses coarse-to-fine retrieval, diversity selection, and reranking based on visibility or answerability.
Optionally grounds evidence spatially and applies self-verification to refine responses, particularly for open-ended queries.
Reports approximately 10% gains on 3D VQA and 5% gains on dense captioning and Embodied QA.
Introduces a judge-based evaluation approach that accommodates semantically correct or partially correct answers.

papers.abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.
bullets: CoT turns spatial perception into transcription: once a relation is written, the model tends to follow the text rather than re-checking the image.
Writing can weaken useful visual shortcuts and produce false spatial relations; the final sentence can also invert a correct relation, especially for converse questions.
These two failure modes explain about four in five CoT losses across tested open VLMs, including larger models.
Frontier closed models avoid the harm when they re-ground their answer in the image after writing; models without re-grounding show the open-model pattern.
A pilot suggests fine-tuning with fixed rationales and image-determined labels can restore re-grounding on natural photographs.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and repairs chain-of-thought failures in spatial VQA; directly about spatial reasoning in VLMs.
papers.title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
papers.tldr: Short chain-of-thought often worsens spatial VQA because VLMs trust their written spatial relation over the image, with false relations and conclusion-mapping errors causing most losses.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.
authors: Muxin Fu, Peike Yu, Guibin Zhang, Wenrui Zhou, Runze Liu, Lang Feng, Fuchao Yang, Feng Chen, Yixuan Li, Mengao Zhang, Shiying Zhang, Wen Shen, Ling Pan, Shuicheng Yan, Bo An

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.
authors: Xinyu Cao, Tianjie Ju, Zhuosheng Zhang

papers.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $\delta_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $\delta_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $\delta_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $\rho\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
authors: Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, Pu Miao, Chonghan Liu
bullets: Adapts Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and referring segmentation.

Geometry is learned early, but absolute depth scale remains unstable; ensembling predictions improves unaligned depth accuracy without retraining.
Depth and 2D segmentation compete for adapter capacity, and weight merging does not remove this trade-off.
Lower validation flow loss correlates with worse Cityscapes mIoU, making the loss unreliable for checkpoint selection; code, data, contracts, and evaluations are released.

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
authors: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets the long visual token sequences created by multi-view 3D inputs.

papers.abstract: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
authors: Yiyang Zhu, Xin Li, Guangyuan Liu, Ziheng Liu, Jiayi Zhang, Chau Yuen
bullets: Creates a label-free benchmark and training dataset using ray-traced cities, exact fields, and matched single-factor counterfactuals.
Evaluates both field-level prediction and fine-grained reasoning about direct or one-wall paths across six continents.
Frontier VLMs judge field strength well but fail at identifying whether individual paths exist; open models often fail at field prediction itself.
Fine-tuning a 9B open model improves field inference on unseen cities but does not improve path tracing.
Results suggest that learning final field answers does not produce the underlying single-path geometric reasoning.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity. We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.
bullets: Introduces StateBind-200: 200 real images with refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces.
Physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a +15.30-point source-image-balanced gain.
Calibration and extra reasoning do not close the remaining gap; localization can succeed while value-lattice binding fails, especially for two-endpoint ruler spans.
Proposes Factorial StateBind, a training-free verifier that independently checks target and lattice evidence before deterministic resolution.
Its high-precision mode achieves 91.67% candidate precision on 36/128 held-out images, covering 28.12% of images and 9.68% of ordered cells.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
authors: Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge, Yanning Zhou, Dan Xu
bullets: Existing VLMs struggle with metric 3D inference because uncalibrated views leave geometry ambiguous.
StereoVLM learns from binocular observations through correspondence, disparity, calibration-conditioned depth, and semantic spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Nautical charts encode safety-critical maritime information through standardized symbols, attributes, text, and heterogeneous geometries. Interpreting these charts and assessing the navigational significance of successive chart updates requires recognizing nautical features, determining their spatial relationships, and applying navigational knowledge. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising approach to nautical-chart interpretation, yet systematic evaluation of their fine-grained nautical feature recognition, chart-based spatial reasoning, and application of navigational knowledge to assessing chart changes remains limited. We introduce ENC-QA, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 77,312 questions derived from 6,612 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs). The benchmark evaluates four complementary capabilities: ENC Perception, Spatial Reasoning, Joint Perception and Spatial Reasoning, and Application. Of these, 8,227 questions form a progressive subset that decomposes selected chart-change cases into linked questions progressing from change detection to criticality assessment, enabling case-level analysis of how models use perceptual and spatial evidence to determine the navigational significance of chart changes. Evaluations of 10 open-weight VLMs reveal substantial limitations in fine-grained nautical feature recognition and feature-grounded spatial reasoning. Controlled evidence interventions show that relevant perceptual and spatial information improves change-criticality accuracy. Our findings establish ENC-QA as a diagnostic resource for nautical-chart understanding and safety-critical navigational decisions. We will release the benchmark and evaluation code upon publication.
authors: Jiyoon Pyo, Jacob Arndt, Yao-Yi Chiang, Dalton Lunga

papers.abstract: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.
authors: Hongyi Yang, Jinao Wu, Yanwei Zhang, Shengwen Fu, Haibin Ling, Bingyao Huang, Jingwei Qu
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage of existing layout metrics and viewpoint-dependent occlusion or clutter.
Fine-tunes a compact MLLM with structured human-rating supervision to predict five quality dimensions per view.
Aggregates dimension ratings into view-level and overall sample-level quality scores.
Introduces ALQA: 3,216 layouts from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories, rendered from five viewpoints and rated by three humans per view.
Reports closer agreement with human reference scores than evaluated MLLM baselines and strong agreement with human layout preferences in a user study.

papers.abstract: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each new base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.
authors: Yajun Liu, Jinxi Wu, Juan Pablo Mill\'an Raya, Xuesong Zhou
bullets: Addresses manual or unreliable open-map extraction of lane and junction data for transportation models.

At signalised intersections, exact lane-layout accuracy improves from 49–64% with a single request to 86–91% for two VLMs.
For planning-driven network edits, 16 of 18 edits pass all network checks; model-written code produces none that pass every check.
Scope: evaluated on 44 approaches and 18 edits, with remaining errors involving design or coding mistakes.
