papers.abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.
authors: Yalin Yang, Xiao Huang, Yanan Wu, Hao Yang, Ryan Zhenqi Zhou
bullets: Weight-space programming improved reference-frame accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% and StepGame accuracy from 19.2% to 33.7%; permuting the edit removed the gain.
A rank-1 LoRA trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8% on the two target tasks using 0.09% trainable parameters.
Without worked-solution supervision, the adapter failed the learning gate; generalization was partial across templates, difficulty levels, and heading-answer combinations.
Adaptation reduced distance-task accuracy from 94% and 92% to 0–2% and caused outputs to apply the StepGame solution pattern to distance questions.
The comparison exposes a trade-off between larger target-task gains and preservation of neighboring skills.

papers.abstract: Many questions about videos ask for a number, such as how tall a person is, how far a cart travels, or how fast a ball leaves a ramp. We study this task, quantitative physical reasoning from video, where the inputs are a video, a question, and a prior of known facts such as object sizes, speeds, and distances from the camera to named objects. End-to-end video-language models lack an explicit metric scale and physical consistency, and their errors cannot be inspected. We present SceneRuler, which instead recovers a measurable physical scene and answers with that scene as evidence. Its central principle, Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction, builds, for each question, only the smallest scene that suffices to measure the asked quantity, and tests sufficiency on measurements rather than assuming it. The scene is written as a program whose structure a vision-language model writes and whose magnitudes are left to measurement. Physics-guided Fitting measures them through physical motion laws, so that gravity itself can anchor the metric scale, and marks every parameter, and the read-out of the asked quantity, as determined or undetermined. Each question receives a read-out and an answer. The read-out is the asked quantity evaluated on the scene, and it is empty when the scene does not fix that quantity. The answer is always given by a model that takes the scene as evidence. We evaluate on QuantiPhy and also apply the method to 27 in-the-wild videos that we collected, which have no ground-truth answers. On its validation split, the final answer reaches a mean relative accuracy of 0.709 against 0.624 for the strongest baseline, and the reconstruction determines the asked quantity on 47 of 158 questions, where the final answer reaches 0.781. Because every intermediate quantity is explicit, each answer can be traced to the objects, scale, and motion behind it.
authors: Yumeng He, Gezheng Kang, Fanlian Zeng, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
bullets: Targets questions requiring physical quantities such as height, distance, and speed from video plus known prior facts.
Uses Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction to build the smallest question-specific scene that can determine the requested measurement.
Represents scene structure as a program, estimates magnitudes with physics-guided fitting, and can use gravity to establish metric scale.
Marks parameters and outputs as determined or undetermined; answers are generated with the reconstructed scene as evidence.
On QuantiPhy validation, achieves 0.709 mean relative accuracy versus 0.624 for the strongest baseline; fully determined cases reach 0.781 on 47 of 158 questions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents can reconstruct rooms from video as editable 3D scenes, but convincing renders do not establish geometric accuracy. We introduce a scan-referenced evaluation and use controlled experiments to study reconstruction accuracy, the role of geometric inputs, and agents' ability to verify and correct their scenes. Our geometric score measures surface, depth, and furniture placement agreement with laser scans of 30 real rooms on a 0-100 scale. The strongest tested agent, GPT-6 Astra, scores 51.4 from video alone, while a dense reconstruction from the same video scores 75.9. Given the point cloud used for that reconstruction, Astra produces an editable scene that scores within three points of it. Agents also inherit input errors: rescaling the supplied geometry changes scene scale almost proportionally. During revision, viewing renders improves appearance more consistently than geometry. Logs of their tool calls show that agents repeatedly measure their inputs but rarely compare them with the scenes they build. To provide this missing check, we introduce a geometric error report that compares each saved scene with the agent's input points and lists the largest discrepancies. Without new geometric evidence, the report raises the revision gains of GPT-6.1 Terra and Sol by 3.9 and 5.5 points over concurrent controls.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain unreliable on spatial reasoning problems that require composing grounded relations across multiple objects. Yet, scaling reasoning supervision is challenging since human-annotated visual datasets often rely on fixed relational annotations and coarse object localization, making it difficult to obtain precise intermediate reasoning states across diverse spatial configurations and complexities. We introduce FARON (Fully Automated Reasoning Over spatial relatioNs), a framework that executes spatial queries to provide both execution-grounded reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards. Rather than relying on existing annotated data, FARON constructs synthetic 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries, enabling configurable object arrangements, spatial relations, and multi-step compositions. Deterministic query execution yields intermediate sets and final answers, providing precise supervision without manual relation annotation. Our pipeline converts intermediate states into natural-language reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the execution-derived answers provide verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Controlled experiments show that trace-based SFT improves multi-step spatial reasoning over final-answer supervision and that subsequent group relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides further gains. The resulting models also demonstrate transfer across external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning. These results show the potential of using spatial query execution as a unified, flexible source of reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards for multimodal spatial reasoning.
authors: Jiyoon Pyo, Dongwon Jung, Zekun Li, Nayeon Kim, Muhao Chen, Yao-Yi Chiang

Controlled experiments find trace-based SFT improves over final-answer supervision, with GRPO providing further gains.
Shows transfer to external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding enables web agents to translate natural-language instructions into actionable interface locations. However, dense layouts and small, visually similar controls can lead models toward plausible but incorrect elements, while refinement around a single prediction may leave alternative targets unexplored. We propose the Multi-Hypothesis Verification Framework (MHVF) for training-free GUI grounding. It combines multi-hypothesis exploration with local visual verification using a single pretrained vision-language model. To explore alternative targets, MHVF constructs spatial hypotheses from multiple full-screen predictions and examines the corresponding regions through zoomed re-localization. To resolve ambiguity among the resulting candidates, it verifies their agreement with the instruction in marked local views. Verification scores then guide a second round of local search and rank candidates retained from both search levels for final selection. Experiments with five general-purpose and GUI-specific models across eight benchmark settings demonstrate improvements in grounding accuracy in most settings. MHVF improves UI-Venus-Ground-7B by 4.3 and 2.1 percentage points on Mind2Web and VisualWebBench, respectively, and raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B's accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro from 23.6% to 53.6%.
bullets: Addresses errors from dense layouts and visually similar controls, where single-prediction refinement can miss the correct target.
Uses one pretrained vision-language model to generate full-screen hypotheses, zoom into candidate regions, and verify instruction–region agreement.
Verification scores guide a second local-search round and rank candidates from both search stages.

Across five models and eight benchmark settings, MHVF improves accuracy in most settings; examples include +4.3 and +2.1 points for UI-Venus-Ground-7B and 23.6% to 53.6% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B on ScreenSpot-Pro.

papers.abstract: Multi-step visual reasoning suffers when early visual misinterpretations persist as incorrect premises in subsequent reasoning. We argue that how visual evidence is represented during reasoning matters as much as how much of it is gathered. Rather than appending observations and inferences to an ever-growing dialogue, we introduce a Visual Board-centered harness that separates visual observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning within a structured, capacity-bounded, and revisable workspace. This separation makes each premise explicit and auditable, so that conflicts between what is seen and what is derived become detectable even by a text-only critic and can trigger targeted reinspection of the original image. Without task-specific training, our harness consistently outperforms standalone models across 4B, 8B, Qwen3-VL-Flash, and 32B configurations on Euclid30K, SolidGeo, and ChartQA bar charts, with gains of up to 11.68, 18.42, and 24.82 percentage points, respectively. Under identical tools, critic, and interaction limits, the structured Board outperforms shared free-form notes by 6.67 to 13.00 points and no-Board retries by 7.35 to 18.80 points while using 7.9\% to 38.2\% fewer tokens. Supervised fine-tuning on harness trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with positive transfer to chart reasoning.
bullets: Addresses error propagation from treating uncertain visual interpretations as established premises.
Separates observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning in a capacity-bounded, auditable workspace.
Enables text-only critics to detect conflicts and trigger targeted reinspection of the original image.
Without task-specific training, outperforms standalone models and free-form or no-Board alternatives across geometry and chart tasks.
Supervised fine-tuning on Board trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with transfer to chart reasoning.

papers.abstract: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.

papers.title: ACE-Brain-0.7: Learning Execution-Grounded Reasoning for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: ACE-Brain-0.7 is a 9B vision–language model trained on execution-supervised data to improve spatially and temporally grounded reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks.

papers.abstract: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.
authors: V\'ictor Rodrigo Gonz\'alez, Pablo M. Olmos, Ignacio Peis, Alejandro Lancho
bullets: Targets quadratic attention, variable-resolution compilation breaks, and VAE throughput bottlenecks in single-GPU DiT pretraining.
Uses an AdaLN-free dual-stream backbone, SPRINT sequence sparsification, continuous aspect-normalized RoPE, and shifted square crops.
Adds a lightweight Patch Detailer Head for pixel adaptation with velocity regression.
Pretrains an approximately 206M-parameter model in about 160 GPU hours for under $55 on consumer hardware.
Reports GenEval scores of 0.588 at 256px and 0.609 at 512px, with DPG scores of 78.96 and 78.51, respectively, without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Asuka-FM system-architectural co-design pipeline. Top Row (Stage 1): Raw images Iorig undergo shifted square cropping to enforce static tensor dimensions (X × X) and eliminate JIT recompilations, while continuous aspect-normalized RoPE prevents phase collapse. Precomputed FLUX.2 VAE latents zt receive prepended in-context temporal conditioning (ztime) alongside text representations from a 2-layer adapter without per-block AdaLN parameters. Bottom Row (Stage 2): The 13-layer dual-stream DiT executes SPRINT sequence sparsification: shallow blocks (fθ) supply high-frequency dense skips ft, deep middle blocks (gθ) process macro-semantics over a 75%-sparse grid, and dense decoder blocks (hθ) fuse representations to predict flow trajectories. Finally, the lightweight 10.09M Patch Detailer Head (PDH) transfers representations directly to RGB pixels under native v-prediction.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects move in dynamic scenes requires recovering their 3D motion from visual observations and predicting their positions at unobserved times. Existing methods either optimize scene-specific velocity fields or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions. We instead study learning a continuous-time dynamics operator across scenes, mapping multi-view visual observations to 3D object kinematics. We introduce Adaptive Pixel Flows (\ours{}), which learns this operator from multi-view RGB-D observations without per-scene optimization or predefined motion models. The method fuses observations from all cameras into a shared voxel grid in world coordinates, from which the network predicts a continuous-time velocity field. Because the operator is trained across scenes, it learns motion priors that carry over to unseen scenes. The field can then be integrated from observed states to predict object positions between observations and beyond the observed sequence. On held-out PhysInOne scenes, \ours{} improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5\% for in-between prediction and 15\% for future prediction. Compared with per-scene velocity-field methods, the improvements are 30\% and 85\%, respectively. Applied zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, it improves future-prediction F1 by 12\%.
bullets: Addresses 3D motion recovery and temporal prediction without per-scene optimization or predefined physical assumptions.
Fuses all camera observations into a shared world-coordinate voxel grid and predicts a continuous-time velocity field.
Integrates the learned field from observed states to estimate intermediate and future object positions.
Improves F1 on held-out PhysInOne scenes by 2.5% for in-between and 15% for future prediction over the strongest competitor.
Transfers zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, achieving a 12% future-prediction F1 improvement.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.

Across seven frontier VLMs, six score below 20% all-target mean IoU; the best model reaches 22.52% mean IoU, with 18.36% of targets above IoU 0.5.

papers.abstract: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $\pi_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
authors: Jinxi Liu, Ruifeng Zhai, Hao Liu, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Addresses viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts in multi-view vision-language-action models.

papers.abstract: A corridor, its mirror reflection, and its image on a display can look identical, yet their physical surfaces lie at different depths. We test whether bounded camera motions distinguish these explanations. Intervene3D takes an image and an initial geometry estimate, predicts the view under each hypothesis and candidate motion, and selects a motion by maximin separability. It reports the mechanism and first physical surface only if the available motions separate the hypotheses still in contention. Otherwise it abstains. An adequacy test also rejects observations that no hypothesis explains. On a matched synthetic benchmark with exact landmarks, disabling abstention gives confident answers on 76.4% of unresolvable scenes. With abstention, none receives a confident answer under exact or noisy landmarks. At 100% accuracy on answered scenes, maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes and summed selection 43.1%. The adequacy test lowers wrong answers on strongly curved mirror scenes from 56.8% to 12.4%. Real display experiments compare two hypotheses using one frozen depth-network estimate. The second image supplies photometric evidence and is never passed through the depth network. One executed motion reduces the pooled median surface error of twelve networks by 31.5%. These networks have larger error inside the annotated panel than outside on 33.4% of illusion-benchmark images. They place the first physical surface behind the glass on 36.9% of Mirror3D frames.
authors: Reshad Ul Karim, Abrar Samin, Sammam Mahdi, Syeda Maliha Tabassum, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
bullets: Visual observations can be identical for real corridors, mirror reflections, and displays despite different physical surface depths.
The system predicts views under competing hypotheses and candidate motions, choosing the motion that maximizes worst-case separability.
It reports a mechanism and first physical surface only when the available motion distinguishes the remaining hypotheses; an adequacy test rejects unexplained observations.
On synthetic scenes, maximin selection answered 61.0% with 100% accuracy, while disabling abstention produced confident answers for 76.4% of unresolvable scenes.
In real display experiments, one motion reduced pooled median surface error by 31.5% across twelve depth networks; substantial errors remained on illusion images.

papers.title: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry

papers.abstract: Flat color-block drafts specify layout and regional color while leaving interior detail unspecified, yet pretrained flow-based generators can preserve their flat appearance even under photorealistic prompts. We trace this behavior to a cross-scale mechanism linking fine pixel variation to regional means in variational autoencoder (VAE) latent space. Flattening photo regions systematically shifts their latent means, with offsets concentrated along a shared channel direction within each backbone. Controlled field exchanges in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image establish the effect of this displacement on texture generation: adding the photo-derived regional mean field to a flat latent restores texture, whereas adding its complementary field alone largely preserves flatness. A second-order encoding expansion explains how encoder curvature can convert zero-mean perturbations into mean shifts. An analytically solvable conditional Gaussian flow shows how regional noise averaging enables near-unit endpoint sensitivity at high signal-to-noise ratios. This mechanism motivates training-free rendering through pixel dither before encoding, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding. Paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with draft conditioning improves content recovery and produces photo-like regional means under the standard velocity objective. Explicit regional mean guidance remains effective after adaptation, continuously controlling texture and improving color fidelity. These findings connect encoding shifts to persistent generation behavior and support interventions evaluated for texture, spatial fidelity, and semantic recovery.
authors: Zihan Gu, Jiangcan Jia, Hua Zhang, Lulu Zhao
bullets: Flattening image regions changes their latent means along backbone-specific channel directions, linking fine detail to regional statistics.
Controlled latent-field swaps in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that restoring photo-derived regional means restores texture, while complementary fields mostly preserve flatness.
A second-order encoder analysis and a conditional Gaussian-flow model explain how zero-mean detail and regional averaging can produce persistent mean shifts and high endpoint sensitivity.
Training-free interventions—pixel dithering, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding—enable texture control without retraining.
Draft-conditioned LoRA improves content recovery and photo-like regional means; explicit regional mean guidance remains effective and improves texture and color fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the mechanism of texture generation in flow-based models, revealing how regional mean latents govern spatial fidelity, which is relevant to geometry-aware generation.
papers.title: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents Govern Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation
papers.tldr: Regional mean shifts in VAE latents largely determine whether flat drafts remain textureless or recover photorealistic detail in flow-based image generators.

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in qualitative spatial reasoning, but remain limited in quantitative spatial reasoning. Current work leverages the VLM agent to invoke external vision tools to perform computation. However, these methods usually bind each functional requirement to a single predefined vision specialist, implicitly resulting in fixed and rigid tool pipelines. In practice, addressing diverse spatial scenarios and tasks demands a broader diversity in pipeline orchestration and vision specialist selection to achieve robust spatial reasoning. However, such diversity leads to a combinatorial execution space, making it challenging for the agent to orchestrate the optimal pipelines and specialists for different scenarios. In this work, we propose SpatialMem, a memory framework that enables a VLM agent to accumulate tool-use experience and leverage that memory to orchestrate vision specialists to solve the spatial reasoning problem. SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure, with task memory capturing tool orchestration and scene memory capturing tool selection. It further introduces a dual-state trajectory optimization process to preserve successful tool experiences and refine suboptimal ones. Moreover, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited coverage of scene types and tasks. To address these gap, we propose MetricBench, a benchmark covering both indoor and outdoor scenes and three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench. Additionally, the memory design yields a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent on MetricBench.
authors: Zinan Zheng, Nuo Chen, Jia Li
bullets: Targets VLMs’ limitations in quantitative, rather than qualitative, spatial reasoning.
Uses task memory for tool orchestration and scene memory for selecting vision specialists.
Applies dual-state trajectory optimization to retain successful tool-use experiences and refine weaker ones.
Introduces MetricBench, covering indoor and outdoor scenes across three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks.
Reports state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, with a 32% improvement over the best VLM baseline on MetricBench and a 9.1-point gain over a memory-free agent.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.
bullets: Studies 20-class tree-species mapping in 0.2 m aerial imagery from TreeSatAI.
Compares a frozen DINOv3 encoder with a linear classifier against end-to-end fine-tuned ImageNet ResNet-50s.
On the official split, fine-tuning scores higher, but substantial patch overlap may inflate performance.
On a spatial split with held-out 2 km squares and buffers, performance is statistically inconclusive and learning curves overlap across label budgets.
Frozen features perform better on the rarest classes but mainly confuse closely related species; validation-based input/layer selection improves them.

(c) Over all 20 classes, the clear lead of the fine-tuned ResNet-50 on the official split becomes inconclusive on the spatial split. (d) On the five rarest classes, the fine-tuned model loses much more than the frozen DINOv3 model; the remaining difference on the spatial split has a confidence interval that includes zero. papers.selection_reason: Empirically compares frozen foundation model features against fine-tuned CNNs for tree species mapping, highlighting the efficiency and data leakage issues in current evaluation splits.
papers.title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
papers.tldr: Fine-tuned CNNs outperform frozen satellite features on the official split, but geographically separated evaluation makes the difference inconclusive and favors frozen features for rare species.

papers.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
authors: Linjia Kang, Binhan Jiang, Juan Yang, Zhiqin Song, Xiangsen Wu, Qionglin Ren, Jiang Liu, Zhongjiang He, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses limited guidance for intermediate decisions and the cost of repeated planning in tool-augmented VLMs.
Uses policy learning and experience evolution, including RSPO for process-aware training and WDL for weakness-targeted demonstrations.
At inference, LAWR reuses suitable workflows for a fast path, while a ReAct-based path handles novel tasks.
Label-free feedback from execution, workflow adoption, and cost savings updates workflow memory.

papers.abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.
authors: Junyoung Hong, Minsu Kim, Jaehyun Kim, Jeonghwan Cho, Jiwoo Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Studies proactive spatial reasoning: answering whether and when a queried spatial condition becomes true as video unfolds.
Introduces ProSpace-Bench with nine object-, camera-, and scene-level reasoning tasks, plus ProSpace-Train for supervised learning.
Injects causal geometric encodings into intermediate VLM layers, uses the KV cache as spatial memory, and selects spatial tokens for efficient streaming.
Experiments show a substantial VLM–human gap, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines.
Analyzes how the model retains previously observed spatial information across viewpoint changes.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA
authors: Jiaming Liu, Linghe Kong, Guixu Zhang, Huaxi Huang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and poor failure recovery in pipeline-style 3D visual grounding agents.
Uses a semantic anchor for optical-flow tracking and VLM-based local verification.
Uses a geometric anchor for voxelization and multi-keypoint projection to reason over 3D space.
The two anchors exchange information in a closed-loop tool-calling process to select subsequent perception-action steps.
Achieves 73.6% Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer and 70.4% overall accuracy on Nr3D in zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.
authors: Jingning Tian, Hao Zhang, Yumin Huang, Zizhuo Li, Xingyu Jiang, Erdun Zhao, Jiayi Ma
bullets: Addresses the limitations of single-view fusion by supporting coherent fusion across continuously varying viewpoints.

Introduces the Multi-View Language-Supervision dataset with language instructions, calibrated viewpoints, and corresponding fused images.
Experiments show accurate target localization and consistent regional fusion control under diverse instructions.

papers.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
authors: Yanjing Li, Sheng Xu, Baochang Zhang, Xianbin Cao, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets the storage and computation costs of full-precision latent reasoning in VLMs.
Dynamics-Guided Quantization preserves rotary-key structure to reduce distortions in vision-language information retrieval.
Dynamics-Preserving Distillation aligns latent thoughts, readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher.
On ScienceQA-IMG using Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM reaches 90.43% accuracy.
Reports 16.64× fewer bit-operations and 6.40× lower measured latency than explicit chain-of-thought.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

papers.abstract: We study how to obtain a task-specific Vision-Language Model (VLM) for language-guided path generation between start and end points on remote sensing images. We explore this question from three aspects. First, we implement three widely used architectural approaches and compare their performance. Second, we design a scalable method for constructing pre-training data and build an effective pre-training dataset with a degree of diversity. Methods trained on this dataset achieve promising zero-shot performance. Third, we construct three benchmarks that support stratified evaluation and design three metrics for path generation. We investigate this problem through extensive experiments. The results show that the zero-shot performance of methods trained on the constructed pre-training dataset can exceed that of some advanced commercial VLMs. Code and Dataset can be available at https://github.com/jzdang/RemoteVLPG
authors: Junzhe Dang, Mengmeng Zhang, Yuxiang Zhang, Wei Li
bullets: Compares three widely used VLM architectural approaches for the task.
Introduces a scalable method for constructing diverse pre-training data.

Reports that trained methods can outperform some advanced commercial VLMs in zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that closes this gap via a schema-guided mechanism. Upon code execution, a structured schema captures the correspondence between each code-level instance and its geometric attributes, establishing a bidirectional link between code space and geometry space. Emulating engineer review practices, SGLayout evaluates layouts along two complementary dimensions: intent compliance through quantitative structural checking and qualitative vision-language assessment, and rule compliance through DRC. All identified violations are then back-projected through the schema onto precise code targets, enabling surgical repair. This closed-loop process iterates until layout convergence. On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.

bullets: Addresses unreliable one-shot layout generation caused by LLMs’ limited spatial awareness.
Uses a schema to bidirectionally map code instances to geometric attributes.

papers.abstract: Panoramas can serve as shared scene backgrounds for multi-shot video generation, but most existing panorama generators take text alone or a single input image. We present a single model that generates a full equirectangular panorama from a text caption and K in {0,...,4} perspective conditioning views taken by a four-camera rig at one viewpoint. We fine-tune a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer in two stages. In the first stage, each conditioning view is appended to the token sequence together with the ID of its camera slot, and the number of views varies during training, so one set of weights serves every input setting. In the second stage, we improve the region not covered by any conditioning view. Supervised training computes its loss on noisy latents of the ground truth and never scores a panorama the model has generated and decoded, so we propose Uncovered-Region GRPO (UR-GRPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that rewards the candidates a vision-language model prefers in pairwise comparisons on crops around this region. Because the slot ID alone does not tell the model which way the rig points, we also offer an optional variant that writes each view's camera direction into its position encoding, which lets the user decide where each view appears in the output. With one conditioning view, our model outperforms the previous state of the art, 360Anything, trained on the same data and evaluated with the same code, on Laval Indoor and gives mixed results on an indoor subset of SUN360; the second stage improves the results for every number of conditioning views.
authors: Rui Hong, Xugang Ye, Jana Ko\v{s}eck\'a, Kai Fan
bullets: Addresses panorama generation for multi-shot video by combining captions with up to four views from a four-camera rig.
Fine-tunes a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer with camera-slot-aware view tokens and variable numbers of inputs.
Introduces Uncovered-Region GRPO, using vision-language-model preferences on crops of regions not covered by conditioning views.
An optional direction-aware positional encoding lets users control where each view appears in the panorama.
With one view, it outperforms 360Anything on Laval Indoor, shows mixed results on SUN360, and the second stage improves results for all view counts.

papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
authors: Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng, Dongqi Fu, Huajun Xi, Junnan Li, Jingcheng Liang, Jieyu Zhao, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Jian Kang

papers.abstract: Existing weakly supervised image manipulation localization (IML) methods typically rely on annotation-specific training strategies, hindering the joint use of diverse annotations within a single model. This limits the scale of usable training data and constrains further progress. We propose UniIML, a teacher-student framework that maps diverse weak annotations into a unified representation to guide the Segment Anything Model (SAM) in generating multiple candidate masks. However, SAM is designed for general-purpose segmentation and has limited sensitivity to manipulation traces; its predicted quality scores alone may therefore fail to reliably identify the candidate that best delineates the manipulated region. We introduce Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which first filters candidates using trusted weak-annotation constraints encoded in the unified representation. It then ranks the remaining candidates separately by consistency with weak annotations, SAM-predicted quality scores, and cross-view stability, aggregating these rankings for an initial selection. To assess how changes in the evaluation criteria affect candidate selection, OSC repeats ranking and selection while omitting one criterion at a time. The most frequently selected candidate is adopted as the final mask, and its relative selection frequency quantifies selection stability. We construct soft pseudo-labels from the selected candidate's predicted probabilities and estimate pixel-level supervision weights based on selection stability, pixel-level agreement among candidates, and predictive certainty. The student receives direct supervision in regions defined by weak annotations and learns from soft pseudo-labels elsewhere through reliability-weighted distillation, enabling unified training across weak annotation types. Experiments show that UniIML achieves superior average performance compared with state-of-the-art IML methods.
authors: Songlin Li, Hui Ma, Zhiqing Guo, Dan Ma, Gaobo Yang, Xin Liao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing weakly supervised IML methods use annotation-specific training strategies.
Uses a teacher–student framework to convert diverse weak annotations into a shared representation that guides SAM to generate candidate masks.
Introduces Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which filters and ranks candidates using annotation consistency, SAM quality, and cross-view stability.
Builds soft pseudo-labels and pixel-level supervision weights from selection stability, candidate agreement, and predictive certainty.
Experiments report superior average performance over state-of-the-art IML methods, without specifying numerical results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1--11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/YenanLiu/ScaleDiag.
authors: Chen Liu, Zhen Fang, Xin Yu, Dadong Wang, Ling Chen
bullets: Visual scaling depends on target occupancy, not a fixed crop ratio; zooming too far can hurt.
Instruction scaling benefits mainly from appearance and spatial cues, while added attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful.
Repeated sampling often generates correct coordinates but fails to select them, leaving 5.1–11.0 points of oracle headroom.
Geometric consensus provides almost no improvement, indicating that sampling and selection have distinct bottlenecks.
Findings are based on five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our controlled diagnostic framework for GUI grounding. (a) Controlled visual interventions vary the visual evidence while keeping the instruction fixed. We construct target-centered, aspect-ratio-preserving crops at different area ratios, and separately add resized distractor screenshots while preserving the target screenshot at its native resolution. (b) Controlled instruction interventions keep the screenshot and target fixed while modifying the instruction. Rule-based attribute injection appends ground-truth-derived position, color, size, or shape cues, whereas an LLM generates natural descriptions from appearance, spatial, functional, and goal-oriented views. (c) Repeated sampling keeps both the screenshot and instruction fixed and generates multiple coordinate predictions, allowing us to compare greedy decoding, coordinate-medoid consensus, and oracle candidate coverage. Together, these interventions isolate the effects of visual evidence, instruction information, and candidate selection.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.
authors: Anima Singh, Suhas Yogin, Weicheng Kuo, Ivor Rendulic, Ivan Jurin, Antoine Yang, Oran Kelly, Rohan Doshi, Hammad Ayyubi, Ioana Bica, Sergi Caelles, Matthew Conniff, Dan Graur, Anastasija Ili\'c, Ahmet Iscen, Chao Jia, Tomasz K\k{e}pa, Chunyuan Li, Noah \'O Donnaile, Filip Pavetic, Goran Petrovic, Khalid Salama, Zhicheng Wang, Polina Zablotskaia, Yiqian Zhang, Ming Zhao, Benjamin Caine, Mario Lu\v{c}i\'c, Melvin Johnson, Radu Soricut, Jean-Baptiste Alayrac

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.
authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna, Julia Richter, Julian Nubert, Joonho Lee, Matthias M\"uller, Marco Hutter
bullets: Targets robust autonomous navigation in diverse, unstructured real-world terrain.
Uses a VLM to interpret scenes, assess risks, understand signs, and assign navigation costs.
Converts semantic outputs into a real-time dense risk map through open-vocabulary segmentation.
Conditions pre-trained RL policies for agile locomotion and local navigation.
Real-world trials achieved kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, while exposing limits in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the ROAM pipeline. The proposed system bridges high-level reasoning from vision-language models (VLMs) with low-level actuator commands for autonomous robot control. It processes RGB images and robot descriptions through a VLM to generate object labels enriched with risk, preferred area, and steppable values. These labels are converted into semantic images using open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, which operates at a higher frequency than the VLM analysis. The semantic images are then fused with elevation maps to create an environmental representation that reinforcement learning (RL) policies utilize for fast and robust robot control.

Fig. 2. Deployment of ROAM across diverse environments. These include natural outdoor settings such as mountain trails (A to E), forests (F), and grassy areas (G), as well as urban environments such as university campuses (H) and roads (I). The system was also tested in indoor settings (J to L). Additionally, we evaluated its performance in the presence of various challenges, such as smoke (M), train tracks (N), and signage (O).

Fig. 4. Comparison of ROAM with baselines on a course with semantic and contextual challenges. The experiment covered a 1.2 km path with challenges such as an inaccurate global path deviating into bushes or grass, a mannequin lying on the path as an obstacle, and a construction zone with warning signs. (A) Robust pathfinding. The global path was offset into bushes [(i) and (ii)] and into grass [(iii) and (iv)]; (i) and (iii) show ROAM, and (ii) and (iv) show the geometry-only baseline. (B) Semantic hazard avoidance with a mannequin lying on the path for ROAM, the geometry-only baseline, and ViNT. (C) Contextual awareness with construction signs. The map shows the paths of the three methods and the global path. The remaining panels show the robot views, the risk and preferred-area images, and the VLM responses before and after ROAM read the “ROAD WORK AHEAD” sign (r1) and the “END ROAD WORK” sign (r2), followed by snapshots of the geometry-only baseline (g1 to g3) and ViNT (v1 to v3). Information icons mark the ViNT interventions.

Fig. 5. ROAM brings world knowledge to locomotion, local navigation, and exploration. (A) ROAM reads signs and uses this information in locomotion: (i) metal cans with a “WARNING: EXPLOSIVE CANS” sign and (ii) wooden pallets on grass without a sign, with a sign on the pallet, and with signs on the grass. The table in (i) lists the VLM labels and their values, the boxes in (ii) show the VLM responses, and the map in (ii) shows the wooden pallet (orange outline) and the foot trajectories for the three sign conditions. (B) Comparison of ROAM with a geometry-only baseline on (i) a campus route, (ii) a route next to a railroad, and (iii) a snow-covered path. In (i), images 1 to 4 correspond to the numbered points along the paths taken by the two methods, highlighting the different terrains encountered, such as paved areas, gravel, and grass. (C) Exploration behavior in the presence of an obstacle blocking the path: (i) the blocked path, (ii) the alternative route along the path, (iii) the shortcut through the grass, and (iv) the return to the global path. The robot explored along the path after encountering the obstacle and took a shortcut through the grass to merge back to the global path.

Fig. 6. Comparison of VLM output abstractions for navigation. (A) Comparison of VLM-based navigation methods by output type. ROAM outputs semantic labels and values, avoiding the need for spatial understanding. Methods outputting directions or coordinates require spatial reasoning; those generating direct commands (such as velocity) additionally require embodiment understanding. (B) Example trajectories from different methods, including three “select label” variants. ROAM information can augment label placement on ground regions. (C) Quantitative evaluation of the safety and preferred ratios, defined as the fraction of all trajectory pixels, pooled over the scenes (N = 27 scenes; see Statistical analysis), that lie within the hand-labeled “safe” and “preferred” regions. Error bars, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Fig. 3. Long-distance hiking experiments in the Swiss Alps. (A) Zermatt experiment. This experiment covered a total distance of 10.1 km with an elevation change of 1220 m. The route encompassed diverse terrains, including gravel paths, rocky sections, grassy areas, and segments near a lake and train tracks. The steepest segment of the hike had a gradient of approximately 30%, posing a substantial challenge for locomotion. (B) Seealpsee experiment. This experiment covered a total distance of 2.38 km with an elevation change of 20 m, following a path around the lake. The route included a narrow trail close to the water, encounters with cows, gravel sections, and a forest area near the goal. In (A) and (B), photographs (i) to (vi) show the robot at the correspondingly labeled locations on the map.

Table 1. Safety and preferred ratios of VLM-based path generation methods. Values are fractions of trajectory pixels pooled across N = 27 hand-labeled scenes (see Statistical analysis). Goal reached denotes scenes ending within 20% of the start-to-goal distance from the goal; P, Holm-corrected two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against ROAM A*.

papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

Fig. 5. Positional generalization. Every rollout is plotted at the Mahalanobis distance of its measured cable position (dots near 100 are successes, near 0 failures), with per-zone success rates and 95% Wilson intervals (squares) and a per-method logistic fit, crossing 50% at 2.8σ (base) and 3.4σ (VG-Steer).

Fig. 9. Visual-geometric guidance via VLM-selected distance pairs. Offline (a–c): the demonstration is segmented (Gemini 3 Flash + SAM2) and split into sub-trajectory phases (STRAP); the VLM selects each phase’s entity pairs, projections, and sub-goal constraints. Online (d–e): the live scene is matched to the demonstration, and the guidance steers the frozen policy so the selected projected distances track the reference.

Fig. 4. Positional sweep on cable bagging, in the camera view. (a) Training distribution of the 110 cable grasps in the demonstrations. (b) The single reference rollout, with its end-effector path split into sub-trajectories. (c, d) Per-cell outcomes: dots mark the measured cable position of every trial, filled green for success, red rings for failure.

Fig. 2. Differentiable guidance injection. At each denoising step, the candidate chunk is rolled out by forward kinematics, and the guidance loss (position, orientation, gripper) is differentiated; a golden-section line search sets the step size, and the correction is applied to the policy’s velocity field, steering the trajectory without modifying weights.
Fig. 8. Real-world outcome breakdown (share of rollouts, counts on bars). Residual failures concentrate in grasp and transport, which the guidance does not address.

Fig. 7. Task variation on cable bagging. Left: the single reference rollout above the new setting in which cable, banana and spoon share the workspace. Center, right: confusion matrices (instructed object in rows, reached object in columns) for the base and the guided policy.
Fig. 6. Disambiguating the target object in a cluttered scene. In red and blue, the distance pairs used per sub-trajectory (ST0 approach, ST1 transport).

Fig. 3. Per-action-chunk inference overhead on π0.5 (mean over the four suites, CUDA-synchronized). With VG-Steer a chunk takes ∼73 ms in total (1.2× the base’s ∼61 ms), comparable to gradient-only VLS (∼70 ms total); full VLS costs ∼20× more, scaling with its particle count (20 here).

Fig. 10. The three images provided to the reasoning VLM for the worked example of Appendix O: (a) the raw RGB observation, (b) the segmentation overlay that labels every object with its instance ID, and (c) the end-effector path split into color-coded numbered sub-trajectories.
