papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with accurately capturing camera-object relations, especially for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots. This stems from the fact that existing MLLMs are trained on images with limited diverse camera-object relations and corresponding textual descriptions. To address this, we propose a synthetic generation pipeline to create large-scale 3D visual instruction datasets. Our framework takes 3D assets as input and uses rendering and diffusion-based image generation models to create photorealistic images preserving precise camera-object relations. Additionally, large language models (LLMs) are used to generate text prompts for guiding visual instruction tuning and controlling image generation. We create Ultimate3D, a large-scale 3D-grounded 2D visual instruction dataset. Ultimate3D consists of 240K VQAs with precise camera-object annotations, and corresponding benchmark. MLLMs fine-tuned on our proposed dataset outperform commercial models by a large margin, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 29.7% on camera-object relation recognition tasks. Our code, dataset, and benchmark will contribute to broad MLLM applications.
authors: Liu He, Yizhi Song, Ruiqi Xu, Baris Sarper Tezcan, Xiao Zeng, Albert Y. C. Chen, Lu Xia, Shashwat Verma, Sankalp Dayal, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Daniel Aliaga
bullets: Targets weaknesses in recognizing object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots.
Uses 3D assets, rendering, diffusion-based image generation, and LLM-generated prompts to produce photorealistic training images with precise relations.
Provides 240K visual question-answer pairs with camera-object annotations and a corresponding benchmark.
MLLMs fine-tuned on Ultimate3D achieve a reported 29.7% average accuracy improvement over commercial models on camera-object relation tasks.
Scope is focused on 3D-grounded camera-object relation recognition.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Generating Synthetic Visual Instruction Dataset. Our framework uses open-sourced 3D assets to generate photo-realistic images with precisely controlled camera-object relation. Corresponding text instructions are also generated by Large Language Model (LLM). The generated Ultimate3D dataset (240K) and benchmark (8K) advance baseline MLLM models (Gemma-4, Qwen3-VL, etc.) to outperform commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5, etc.) on camera-object relation recognition tasks. The left panel illustrates representative MLLM failures, while the right panel provides a direct same-image comparison between base and Ultimate3D-fine-tuned models.

Fig. 5: Ablations on Image Generation Pipeline. Our framework shows superior performance by using multi-ControlNet with SDXL backbones, and introducing both Canny edges and depth maps as visual priors. It consistently delivers better robustness and quality compared to text-only SDXL and [80]. When these visual priors are removed (top-right: removing all visual priors; bottom-right: removing depth prior), the generator often fails to produce good results and brings lower generation success rate (see Sec 4.6, [80] only achieves 55.11% success rate v.s. ours 93.07%)

Fig. 2: Our Framework. Each shade box corresponds to a section in Sec. 3. Given open-sourced 3D assets, our approach leverages a 3D Renderer to generate 3D visual priors (Iβ) preserving ground truth camera-object relation (β). Meanwhile, LLMs take 3D asset category to generate diverse image descriptions (Timg) as conditional guidance. Both the 3D visual priors and diverse text prompts are used to generate synthetic images (Isyn) by multiple ControlNet-based networks. Corresponding text QA instructions (Tqa) are generated by LLMs given the ground truth camera-object relation. Our Ultimate3D dataset and benchmark (i.e. pairs of Tqa and Isyn) contribute to fine-tuning and evaluation of MLLMs.

Fig. 3: 3D Visual Prior Rendering. With a general camera model, our method utilizes a 3D Renderer (e.g., Blender) to render multiple 3D visual priors given arbitrary camera-object relations. O: camera center; A: object center; D: camera-object distance.

Fig. 4: Qualitative Results. We show responses by GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5-Flash with high thinking, Gemma-4-31B-it, and finetuned Gemma-4-31B-it on the Ultimate3D benchmark. Each model is asked questions (in gray boxes) regarding object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera-shot type, together with the input images on the left. The model responses illustrate that the Gemma-4-31B-it model finetuned on Ultimate3D can precisely recognize camera-object relations on synthetic images. GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.5-Flash with high thinking sometimes provide correct answers, but also exhibit inconsistent predictions across relation types. The original Gemma-4-31B-it frequently fails to produce the correct camera-object relation labels, while the finetuned model provides substantially more accurate and taskrelevant answers.

Table 1: Quantitative Comparisons. We evaluate open-source and closed-source MLLMs on the Ultimate3D and MMVP benchmarks. LLaVA and Llama models are fine-tuned using their original full fine-tuning recipes, while Gemma-4 and Qwen models are fine-tuned with LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning (for Qwen, the vision-language merger is also fully trained). Results report MLLM response accuracy (%) for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera-shot recognition. Superscripts indicate the fine-tuning setup: F full fine-tuning and L LoRA fine-tuning.

Table 2: Generalization. We finetune LLaVA1.6-13B model using a mixture of both general VQA and camera-object relation VQA datasets. Without degradation on general VQA tasks, finetuned model improves its ability on camera-object relation recognition and beats SOTA (i.e. GPT4o) by 28.42% accuracy on Ultimate3D benchmark. ∗ denotes the average accuracy (%) across all 3 types of camera-object relation VQAs in Tab. 1.

papers.abstract: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.
bullets: Vision foundation models struggle with semantic prediction in natural, unstructured offroad scenes.
The method fits a sphericity–elevation distribution for each semantic class using only high-confidence vision predictions.
These class-specific geometric priors are fused with vision foundation model outputs to produce the final 3D semantic map.
The approach improves the SAM3 baseline on RELLIS-3D by 6.3 mIoU points and 8.9 accuracy points, and on WildScenes by 1.7 and 2.1 points, respectively.
The work focuses on offroad semantic mapping and plans to release its source code upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Targets appearance and geometric defects in unseen categories without target-specific training data.
Uses Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation to refine 3D point features with density-adaptive neighborhoods.
Uses Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation to smooth multi-scale CLIP patch embeddings with a trainable adapter.
Introduces Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive loss to align normality and abnormality concepts across modalities.
Reports state-of-the-art results on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies, with up to 2.9% higher pixel-level AUPRO than competing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Paradigm comparison for zero-shot multimodal anomaly detection. (a) Existing ZSMAD pipelines typically suffer from three fundamental limitations: Geometric Loss during 3D-to-2D rendering, Spatial Noise and Weak Integration due to raw CLIP embeddings and simplistic late-fusion, and Semantic Misalignment between prompts and multimodal features. (b) The proposed AggCLIP framework effectively addresses these gaps. It refines noisy back-projected point features via the Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module, suppresses 2D spatial noise using Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) paired with a learnable Adapter, and directly enforces deep cross-modal semantic interaction via the Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson, Ferdinando Fioretto, Sandeep Madireddy
bullets: MatterChat uses a large bridge and separate contrastive alignment; this work instead learns representation selection jointly on downstream tasks.
Different target properties benefit from representations at different depths of Zatom-1, while CHGNet and Zatom-1 provide complementary information.
Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations.
Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, including up to 47.8% lower RMSE, with fewer trainable parameters and half the training time.
Adding UMA-S shows flexibility across encoder combinations; the three-encoder setup reaches 89.61% macro-average classification accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our proposed Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) methodology. (a) Frozen domain encoders (Zatom-1 and CHGNet) extract complementary atom-level representations from a crystal structure. Here, features from all 16 Zatom-1 layers are retained, and CHGNet features are projected from 64 to 512 dimensions. (b) The property requested by the prompt selects a learned task residual, which is added to 32 latent queries. Two Perceiver blocks apply cross-attention to the structural features, followed by latent self-attention and a feed-forward network. These taskconditioned queries allow the bridge to weight encoder sources and layer depths differently for each property. (c) The fused latents are projected into the language-model embedding space and combined with prompt embeddings. A frozen language model then generates the response. The trainable components are optimized jointly using a downstream language-modeling objective.

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.
authors: Rong Zou, Haiqing Hao, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses feature staleness when visual content changes between image observations.
Uses events to incrementally transport and correct multi-layer DINOv3 features from an anchor image.
Trains a lightweight updater end-to-end on synthetic data without downstream-task supervision and transfers to real event streams without adaptation.
Across three real-world datasets and five task settings, it outperforms evaluated event-based methods for detection, segmentation, and depth estimation.
On DSEC with a 200 ms-old anchor, it improves anchor predictions by 30.9 mAP, 11.6 mIoU, and 15.9% AbsRel, while reducing FLOPs by 82.4% and latency 2.5× versus image re-encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ALIVE. (a) Training uses synthetic RGB–event sequences. A frozen DINOv3 encodes every RGB frame: F0 initializes the feature state (with memory h0 = 0), and later frames provide teacher features Ft. For each event packet E(t−,t], the ALIVE updater Uθ predicts a displacement dt that transports both the features and the memory, a residual correction ∆t that yields Ut, and a signed, zero-sum 3× 3 kernel kt per token that refines Ut into F̂t. The ConvGRU memory ht conditions the residual and the refinement. All modules are trained jointly with feature-level losses only, without task labels or task heads. (b) The trained updater is applied without adaptation to real event streams. Moment matching aligns the per-channel statistics of F̂t with the anchor moments to produce the updated features F̄t, and frozen task heads trained on DINOv3 features of real RGB images read F̄t directly. Predictions are shown 200 ms after the anchor on DSEC, and detections are drawn on the RGB frame at that time for visualization only (C: car, P: person).

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on test samples. Each column shows one sample at its target time, and each view is followed by a zoom of the framed region. The top four rows show the anchor frame, the events between the anchor and the target time (red: positive, blue: negative), the target frame, and the ground truth. The other rows show the predictions of the frozen heads from the features of each method. Detection: predictions in orange and ground truth dashed in green. Depth: red (near) to blue (far), with one range per sample. Apart from Current RGB, no method receives the target frame, and the ground truth is shown for reference only.

Figure 3. Accuracy versus update cost (top) and versus anchor age (bottom). Each column is one task–dataset setting, evaluated with a frozen task head shared by all methods. Top: accuracy pooled over all anchor ages against the time per feature update. The dashed line marks the stale anchor features, the dotted line marks the 5 ms limit for updates at 200 Hz, and the star marks the goal of reaching the accuracy of Current RGB within this limit. Current RGB encodes the target frame itself, which is unavailable between frames. Bottom: accuracy at each anchor age. The blue line connects the best baseline at each age, and its markers identify the method as in the top row. Arrows give the gain of ALIVE over the stale features at the longest age (for AbsRel, the relative decrease).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an event-based method to incrementally update foundation model features (DINOv3) at inference time, addressing feature staleness and efficiency.

papers.tldr: ALIVE efficiently keeps frozen visual foundation-model features current between image frames by using event streams, improving downstream vision tasks while avoiding repeated image encoding.

papers.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.
authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limits of appearance-only guidance for diagnosing geometry, material, and illumination errors.
Combines geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues during iterative scene refinement.
Uses Lighting Reasoning Memory to track light-source hypotheses, evidence, and revision history, including partially visible or unseen sources.
Requires no additional training or differentiable rendering.
Reports improved reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, with benefits for editing, object insertion, and relighting.

papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism to achieve deep feature complementarity between image and point cloud features, mitigating projection bias through channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration. Besides, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy is adopted to preserve multi-modal structural consistency while optimizing local feature combination. Finally, dual-path collaborative reconstruction is implemented to recover original modal features from the fused representations, where cross-modal consistency constraints effectively eliminate mapping ambiguities. Extensive experiments show that FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Qiyu Chen, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Addresses weaknesses of intra-modal reconstruction and cross-modal reconstruction, including missed complementary information, projection bias, and ambiguous mappings.
Uses bidirectional cross-modal attention with channel alignment and dynamic spatial priors to combine image and point-cloud features.
Applies learnable pixel-wise gated fusion to preserve structural consistency and optimize local multimodal feature combinations.
Uses dual-path collaborative reconstruction with cross-modal consistency constraints to recover the original modalities.
Reports 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% on Eyecandies, improvements of 2.9 and 4.1 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art methods, respectively.

The framework of FBR, comprising (a) Bidirectional Cross-Modal Attention (BiCMA), (b) Spatial-Gated Adaptive Fusion (SGAF), and (c) Multi-Modal Collaborative Reconstruction (MMCR). Given an image I2D and its corresponding point cloud P3D, we first extract modality-specific features to obtain image features F2D and point cloud features F3D, respectively. These features undergo initial fusion through the BiCMA, followed by gated fusion refinement via the SGAF to produce the final fused representation Ffinal. The fused features are then fed into two modality-specific reconstruction networks ϕ2D and ϕ3D to generate reconstructed features F̂2D and F̂3D. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a fusion-reconstruction paradigm for multimodal (image/point cloud) anomaly detection, utilizing spatial priors and geometric features.

papers.abstract: Text prompted 3D computed tomography (CT) segmentation requires both full slice context and fine boundary precision across volumes where over $80\%$ of organ prompted slices lack the queried target. Existing medical vision language models (VLMs) are largely non native segmenters: they delegate pixel delineation outside the VLM by compressing reasoning into a 1D [SEG] vector for an external Segment Anything Model (SAM) decoder, quantizing masks into lossy discrete codebooks, or issuing box prompts to stateless external SAM tools without empty slice screening or spatial state memory. We introduce NativeSeg, a native vision language segmentation framework on Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapted Qwen3.8-27B that performs dense mask decoding, volumetric triage, spatial error self diagnosis, and multiround local zoom directly over the VLM's 2D spatial visual tokens without external SAM decoders. NativeSeg decodes confidence maps from upper layer 2D spatial tokens fused with a five slice U-Net pathway, halts at zero zooms on $>91\%$ of standalone evaluations via a native presence gate ( ), localizes uncertain boundaries via a 20 cell multiscale error gate ( ), and accepts zoomed updates only when predicted error decreases. Trained solely on adult CT, NativeSeg improves Round $0$ DSC by $+19.81$ and $+7.04$ points over discrete codebook and 1D [SEG] readouts on the identical backbone, reaches $86.81\%$ adult and $87.04\%$ zero shot pediatric DSC, and safely refines 2D nnU-Net ($89.52\%$ adult; $86.86\%$ pediatric), 3D SegVol ($86.81\%$), and 3D VoxTell ($89.85\%$).
authors: Chengqian Ma, Gaole Dai, Zijie Meng, Weixuan Jin, Yijie Du, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
bullets: Addresses missing-target slices and boundary imprecision in text-prompted 3D CT segmentation.
Uses a LoRA-adapted Qwen3.8-27B with dense mask decoding from 2D spatial visual tokens plus a five-slice U-Net pathway.
Performs volumetric triage, spatial error diagnosis, and multiround zooming, accepting refinements only when predicted error decreases.
On adult CT, achieves 86.81% DSC and 87.04% zero-shot pediatric DSC; it also safely refines several existing segmentation systems.
Scope is limited by training solely on adult CT, despite the reported pediatric zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.
authors: Zijian Zhang, Wenqing Tian, Qiang Liu, Liang Wang
bullets: Addresses tool-augmented agents’ inconsistent object/reference-frame semantics and poor judgment of evidence sufficiency.
Uses an Execution Agent to acquire, associate, and assess evidence with role-specific memory.
Uses a Control Agent to diagnose evidence-chain failures and revise tools, interfaces, skills, memory, and decision rules.
Across multiple benchmarks and four base models, it reports substantial accuracy gains on ViewSpatial and MMSI.
Provides a unified approach for deriving answers from spatial evidence rather than simply increasing tool calls.

papers.abstract: People often understand the world by comparing different views of it. Vision-language models (VLMs), however, receive these views as separate images and still struggle to relate them. One problem is data. Training on these tasks requires groups of images with a known relationship: the same object from different viewpoints, or the same scene before and after a change. Such examples are hard to collect at scale from existing photo collections. We introduce ReSynth, which turns single-image perception and controllable image generation into cross-image relational supervision. Localized editing produces before-and-after pairs, viewpoint generation produces multiple views of the same instance, and verified scene contents support comparisons of counts and attributes. ReSynth combines Qwen3-VL-8B's captioning, grounding, and counting capabilities with Qwen-Image-2.1's generation and editing capabilities. It verifies single-image facts such as object counts and attributes, then combines these facts to construct multi-image QA. Using GRPO on approximately 440K ReSynth questions, with no real images during training, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B improve by 17.73 and 6.10 average points on BLINK, MUIRBench, and VLM2-Bench, while single-image performance is broadly preserved on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and improves across all four evaluated benchmarks on Qwen3-VL-8B. Notably, this supervision enables the 8B perception model itself to outperform Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench.
authors: Yilin Wang, Xin Yu, Xinyi Guo, Xiangxi Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Alex Jinpeng Wang

papers.abstract: Inferring the unseen side of a 3D assembly requires reasoning about part placement and occlusion. Different assemblies can match the observed views while producing different hidden views, leaving the target ambiguous. We introduce SixthView, a benchmark in which models predict a sixth orthographic view from five observed views and information about the component shapes. The benchmark contains 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2--10 parts and requires a dense grid of part labels for the missing view, allowing both exact-view and cell-level evaluation. For each item, we exhaustively verify that all legal assemblies consistent with the exact component geometry and observed label grids yield the same target view. With these inputs, the task tests symbolic assembly and coordinate reasoning. The image-only variants additionally require shape recovery from rendered views, where occlusion can make different 3D shapes look identical. We evaluate three vision-language models under four input conditions. Across 552 items with complete evaluations, exact-grid accuracy with images plus exact text ranges from 33.2% to 85.4%. Adding exact text to separate images improves accuracy by 19.7--63.0 percentage points, whereas adding images to exact text changes it by only $-0.5$ to $+2.1$ points. Separate image panels outperform a merged sheet by 6.7--11.1 points. The results show that performance depends strongly on access to exact symbolic information, with little further improvement from images once the geometry is specified. GitHub: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sixthview_benchmark
authors: Pooya Khosravi, Jen-Feng Chang, Fnu Pramono
bullets: The task predicts a sixth view from five observed views plus component-shape information, requiring part-placement, occlusion, and coordinate reasoning.

Across three vision-language models, exact-grid accuracy ranges from 33.2% to 85.4% across evaluated conditions.
Adding exact text geometry substantially improves image-based performance, while adding images to exact text provides little benefit; separate image panels also outperform merged sheets.

papers.abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.

papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.
authors: Jiawei Shen, Jie Feng, Junpeng Zhang, Guanbin Li, Wanyi Chen, Weisheng Dong, Guangming Shi

Distills MLLM feedback about candidate corrections into a lightweight reward predictor for efficient correction decisions.
Integrates selected object-level corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection during denoising.
On 3D-FRONT, improves functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive quality and diversity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ReflectScene. ReflectScene integrates hierarchical scene understanding and MLLM-guided decisions into objectcentric diffusion. At each denoising step, intermediate clean estimates are assessed to select object-level actions, providing transient conditioning, while buffered non-STOP actions are executed every 50 steps to update a persistent correction state. This state is projected onto subsequent clean estimates before DDPM posterior sampling, with decision-effect consistency learning promoting target recovery and non-target preservation.

papers.abstract: Accurately matching human intentions in 3D space is an important goal of artificial intelligence. Recently, 3D Intention Grounding (3D-IG) has emerged, aiming to localize target 3D objects given a natural-language intent. Unlike conventional visual grounding with descriptive referring expressions, 3D-IG intents are abstract and non-descriptive, making object localization substantially more challenging. This requires inferring latent functional requirements from non-descriptive intents and aligning them with object-level 3D representations. However, existing methods largely rely on implicit intent-object matching, leading to logical gaps and limited interpretability, robustness, and generalization. To address these challenges, we propose Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a causality-inspired functional dependency reasoning framework that explicitly bridges abstract intentions and candidate objects through intermediate functional requirements. Specifically, CoCR progressively decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, thereby forming an explicit intent-function-object reasoning chain that links abstract intentions to object suitability. Building on this chain, we construct a causality-inspired functional dependency graph to model requirement-attribute relationships and introduce a causal-visual alignment module that aligns function-aware representations with the geometric-semantic features of 3D point clouds, enabling bidirectional verification between structured functional reasoning and visual evidence. Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding demonstrate that our method enhances intent-aware object localization. Our code is available at https://2490o.github.io/CoCR.
authors: Zihao Zhang, Aming Wu, Yang Li, Yahong Han
bullets: 3D intent grounding must localize objects from abstract, non-descriptive language, which is harder than conventional visual grounding.
CoCR decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, forming an intent–function–object reasoning chain.
A functional dependency graph models requirement–attribute relationships, while causal-visual alignment connects functional reasoning with 3D geometric and semantic features.
Bidirectional verification links structured functional reasoning with visual evidence for more interpretable and robust localization.
Experiments on 3D intention and visual grounding show improved intent-aware object localization; the abstract gives no specific numerical results.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The overall architecture. First, point cloud data and intent text are encoded by the model. The intent text is processed by the Intent Causal Parsing module for step-wise decomposition, transforming the natural language intent into functional requirements. Subsequently, Intent Causal Grounding is performed through the construction of a causal graph, defining the causal relationships between functional requirements and object attributes. The graph is iteratively updated via causal–visual feature alignment and causal pruning. Finally, causal reasoning is conducted based on the updated graph to achieve object selection and localization.

Figure 1: (a) Existing methods rely on direct semantic matching, leading to logical leaps. Our method performs step-by-step functional causal reasoning by explicitly parsing intents into functional requirements. (b) The workflow of Chain-of-Causal Reasoning builds explicit intent–function–object dependency paths for object reasoning and localization.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).

bullets: Problem: 2D visual encoders and unreliable monocular depth struggle with long-range distances, altitude selection, and coordinating forward/downward views.
Method: Lift depth from both cameras into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame, while aligning visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training.
The two components address complementary failure modes: explicit 3D lifting reduces collisions, while implicit geometry alignment improves target completion.
GRID raises target-reaching from 61.5% to 69.5% and task completion after reaching the target from 57.7% to 61.4%, with reported statistical significance.
On TravelUAV, GRID achieves the best success rate across all splits, with relative gains of 9.5%–25.4% over the prior state of the art.

papers.abstract: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.
authors: Haisheng Fu, Gexin Huang, Haikai Zhao, Jie Liang, Zhenman Fang, Jingning Han, Xiaoxiao Li
bullets: Attention sinks make raw attention unreliable for visual localization.
Question-induced changes in attention amount and spatial focus separate; the spatial effect, measured in bits, identifies useful layers.
WhereBits combines this unlabeled layer prior with per-head contrastive scores.

Across eight VLMs, it matches box-tuned pointing accuracy on COCO and RefCOCO, generalizes to held-out models and higher resolutions, and reaches 0.72 COCO pointing accuracy versus 0.22 for mean attention.
Its training-free zoom-in crops improve V* forced-choice accuracy by 6.0 points.

papers.abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.
bullets: Introduces 10,000 simulated two-port planar RF layouts with editable geometry, raster images, occupancy grids, complex S-parameters, structural categories, and response labels.

Defines seven tasks covering layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator validation, diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification.
Benchmarks seven multimodal language models and finds systematic weaknesses in structurally valid generation and electromagnetically faithful response prediction.
RF-specific fine-tuning improves structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the within-2-dB response rate from 17.7% to 62.8%.
The benchmark supports evaluation of models that link RF design intent, layout representations, and physical behavior, but substantial challenges remain.

papers.abstract: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.
bullets: Contains 32,040 corresponding RGB-infrared frame pairs from 115 surveillance videos, with 35,952 bird and drone annotations at 320×256 resolution.
Targets are extremely small: 68.1% have geometric-mean box sides of 8–16 pixels, and 99.0% qualify as COCO small objects.
Introduces an object-relative alignment ratio and alignment burden curve to quantify cross-modal geometric difficulty.
AVID-C provides seven degradation families at five severity levels, applied independently to RGB, infrared, or both modalities.
In a fixed-feature analysis, combined RGB-infrared features showed lower Bhattacharyya error bounds than either modality alone at 12–16 pixels; this is not detector accuracy.

papers.abstract: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.
authors: Gabriel Sarch, Declan Campbell, Nicholas Budny, Kia Ghods, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Jonathan D. Cohen, Brenden M. Lake, Taylor W. Webb
bullets: Collects 7,109 human gaze trials across challenging visual reasoning tasks.
Tests gaze guidance for chart understanding, visual search, and counting.
Gaze-prior supervision consistently outperforms supervision from full gaze sequences.
Introduces GGR, improving human alignment and visual grounding while matching or outperforming grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy.
Reinforcement learning further improves accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding without gaze supervision.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.
authors: Haoyang Liu, Kecheng Liang, Xinyu Li, Weixing Chen, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses premise errors caused by applying physical constraints beyond their valid states or conditions.
Uses an inference-time visual harness that links scopes to observations and creates derived views for reasoning.
Maintains scope-aware working memory by checking revisions against sources and invalidating dependent conclusions.
Outperforms direct solving across six VLMs on PhysAlign; with Gemini-3.8-flash, it exceeds Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points.
Improves OOD performance on PhysUniBench, with ablations supporting explicit scope and dependency management.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhysScope. The shared VLM performs Call 1 (Draft) and Call 2 (Solve & Decision-making). The deterministic harness manages three connected components: (a) Scope-Aware Working Memory associates premises with entities, states, conditions, sources, and versioned dependencies. (b) Grounded Visual Feedback presents the same registered physical content in text and graphics. A Delivered Snapshot records the memory, source evidence, check feedback, and views supplied to a model call. (c) Source-Grounded Memory Revision checks proposed changes, commits accepted replacements, and invalidates registered dependents. Pending or rejected revisions leave active versions unchanged. Dashed arrows mark the optional Repair path (Call 3). Semantic repair and protocol recovery share one additional call.

Figure 3. Scope distinctions in physical reasoning. Examples from PhysAlign [8] (left) and PhysUniBench [21] (right). Each example compares recorded PhysScope and Canvas-CoT [18] trajectories, intermediate diagrams are explanatory redraws. In the impact example, the Canvas-CoT trajectory carries the pre-impact rolling relation across the collision, while the PhysScope trajectory separates impact dynamics from climbing energy. In the gas example, the Canvas-CoT [18] trajectory treats the adiabatic leg as isothermal and reuses ∆UAB for the full process, the PhysScope trajectory uses TC = TA to obtain ∆UAC = 0. Red boxes mark scope mismatches, green boxes highlight the relevant state or endpoint evidence.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.
authors: Tianci Xie, Li Chen, Pinxue Guo, Rui Zheng
bullets: Targets counting actions, ordering events, and locating state changes scattered across long videos.

The strongest model scores 54.52% unaided versus 79.35% with annotated evidence, revealing a substantial search gap.
With fewer than 6K examples, Sight-35B improves interactive accuracy from 21.29% to 42.26% and gains over 8 points on two external benchmarks.

papers.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.
authors: Enhan Li, Jinghao Zhou, Jiaze Zhang, Hongyang Du
bullets: Introduces three tasks: checking scene–shadow consistency, predicting shadow changes after interventions, and inferring physical changes from visual transitions.
Includes 21,000 synthetic questions across scene and geometry splits, plus 200 real-world questions from 20 photographed scenes.
Closed-source MLLMs outperform open-weight and spatial-reasoning models, but strong models still struggle with shadow length and light height.
GRPO post-training with SpatialCast data improves open-weight model performance and transfers to several external spatial benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Generalised referring expression comprehension (GREC) aims to identify and localise the zero, one or multiple objects referred to by a language expression. In robotic manipulation, grounding also needs to remain accurate when requests for the same objects are paraphrased or embedded in additional context in robotics. However, grounding expert models are sensitive to instruction variation, while generative vision--language models (VLMs) struggle with complete target recovery and rejection of absent targets. These complementary limitations motivate combining the contextual representations of VLMs with the direct spatial prediction capabilities of grounding experts. We therefore introduce VLM-guided Grounding Expert (VGE), which combines a frozen VLM with a trainable grounding expert through layerwise joint attention and text-conditioned instance scoring. These interfaces leverage multimodal understanding of the VLM to guide object-query refinement and candidate selection while retaining direct bounding-box prediction. Across three datasets, VGE achieves the highest averaged F1 score among the evaluated methods on all five test splits, with differences of at most 1.2 percentage points across instruction conditions within each split. On the dataset with robotic scenes, VGE also achieves the highest F1 across instruction variants and no-target, single-target and multiple-target cases. VGE provides a $5.3$--$13.0\times$ inference speedup over the baseline with the same VLM base model. These results support combining VLM context with specialised spatial prediction to address both grounding challenges, with particularly strong performance in robotic scenes. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Mingcheng Zhu, Wentian Xu, Tao Lin, Shiying Duan, Ziyun Liang, Xuecheng Qi, Junyang Chen, Kuo Li, Zhifan Wan, Dong Wang, Richard Wang, Yang Gao

Achieves the highest average F1 across all five test splits on three datasets, with up to 1.2-point variation across instruction conditions.
On robotic scenes, leads across instruction variants and target-count settings, while providing a 5.3–13.0× inference speedup over the matched baseline.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.
authors: Zhaojie Chen, Junyan Yang, Le Yang, Qi Dang, Yucheng Huang, Qianyi Che, Zhaoqiang Chen, Xinqi Zhu, Qiang Zhao
bullets: Autoregressive coordinate generation is costly because each box requires multiple sequential decoding steps.
SemGeo uses a single grid token for coarse instance localization, then a geometric decoder recovers precise discrete box coordinates in parallel.
Gaussian soft labels encode coordinate distances to jointly train proposal generation and localization.
Reinforcement post-training uses model-generated proposals with box-set rewards and coordinate supervision to reduce the teacher-forcing mismatch.
Across eight benchmarks, SemGeo leads in F1@mIoU on six and achieves higher accuracy with 2.07× and 1.25× the mean throughput of representative baselines under vLLM and Transformers.

papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
authors: Oleg Pavlov, Nikita Gavrilov, Soslan Kabisov, Gennadii Savrasov, Andrey Kuznetsov, Anton Konushin, Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov
bullets: Targets privacy and affordability challenges for practitioners handling proprietary CAD parts.
Decomposes reconstruction into sequential visual decisions about what to build and correct.

papers.selection_reason: Local agent for editable CAD reconstruction from meshes via visual reasoning and geometric tools; relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
papers.tldr: CADMAGEDDON is an open-source, locally runnable agent that reconstructs editable CAD models from meshes by combining visual reasoning with precise geometric tools.

papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
authors: Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, Jialin Yu, Boyu Ning, Pietro Li\`o, Fan Mo
bullets: Addresses recursive drift in entity poses and spatial relations during long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control.
Rolls out a scene graph alongside the visual model, couples graph and visual changes, and applies a bounded residual using graph-motion context and node positions.
Acts as a plug-in for DINO-WM and DreamerV3 without backpropagating graph-learning or correction gradients into the original visual dynamics.
Across 32-step rollouts, reduces joint-position error by 11–28%; on real inverted-pendulum sequences, lowers DINO-WM pole-angle error from 12.56° to 6.69°.
In simulated inverted-pendulum control, JointGV-corrected rollouts enable 46/50 successful episodes versus none with original rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of JointGV. Given the current RGB observation and action, the original visual world model (yellow) predicts the uncorrected next visual state Zt+1 and its change ∆Zt. In parallel, JointGV (blue) uses Relation Transformer (RelTR) features to construct a task-conditioned scene graph and predicts the node-feature change ∆N̂t. For the spatial-token case shown here, learned projections map the visual-token and graph-node changes into a shared space, where a change-alignment adapter produces the graph-motion context. The predicted node positions provide a complementary position context. A bounded, gated correction combines these contexts with the original visual prediction to produce Ẑt+1 = Zt+1 + Ct. Setting Ct = 0 recovers the original prediction. Decoded images are shown only for visualization; the global-state adapter is described in Sec. 3.4.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of DINO-WM and JointGV on a held-out DMC Cheetah Run sequence. Columns show rollout steps 2, 8, 16, 24, and 32; adjacent maps show absolute RGB error amplified by four using the shared decoder. Red arrows mark representative structural differences. Kv denotes the self-fed visual training horizon and ω the propagated correction-gradient fraction. Additional episodes and videos are provided in Sec. S8.

Figure 1. Motivation. (a) DINO-WM open-loop predictions initialized from real-robot inverted-pendulum observations increasingly deviate from the observed pole. (b) Pole-angle error rises with rollout horizon for all three models, while JointGV reduces this structural drift.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on a held-out DMC Walker Walk validation sequence. Columns show rollout steps 2, 8, 16, 24, and 32, with absolute RGB error amplified by a factor of four. JointGV uses the DreamerV3 global-state change to pool the graph-node changes and applies the result as a bounded global correction. The corrected rollout better preserves the articulated pose at later steps.

Figure 6. Preliminary physical RM65-B control trial. The two actors start from comparable pole angles. At 1.27 seconds, the pole controlled using the original visual-world-model rollout has fallen to −83.3◦, whereas the actor using the JointGV-corrected rollout keeps it near upright at −2.7◦. This trial demonstrates short-duration physical deployment rather than stable six-second balancing.

Figure 5. Per-window effect across four model–task pairings. Each value is the relative change in 32-step average joint-position error from the original prediction to JointGV; values below zero indicate improvement. JointGV improves 99%, 66%, 89%, and 83% of the respective test windows, showing that the aggregate gains are not produced by a small subset of rollouts.

Table 1. DINO-WM results on 280 matched DMC Cheetah Run test windows. Values at horizon H average steps 1 through H; Token MSE denotes DINOv2-token MSE. Rows are single runs and are compared only within matched blocks. ∗The visual-residual controls adapt residual-correction principles rather than reproduce the cited methods. §The annotation-matched control uses the same auxiliary node targets but receives no predicted graph states or graph features. †The cosine run has its own matched backbone. Three-seed results and additional ablations are provided in Sec. S6.

Table 2. JointGV across visual states and control tasks. Values are average joint-position errors over rollout steps 1–32, reported as mean and standard deviation across three independently trained seeds. Every model–task pairing improves in all three seeds. Per-horizon and visual metrics are provided in Sec. S6.
Table 3. DINO-WM on 280 DMC Finger Turn Hard test windows. Values at H average steps 1 through H; additional metrics are provided in Sec. S6.
Table 4. MuJoCo inverted-pendulum control. Actors are trained with original or JointGV-corrected DINO-WM rollouts; rewardhead MSE is a diagnostic.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses recursive errors in visual world models for long-horizon robot planning by correcting entity poses and spatial relations using scene graphs. This fits Video World Models (predicting future states) and Spatial Intelligence (spatial relations).
papers.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
papers.tldr: JointGV improves long-horizon visual world-model predictions by correcting visual dynamics with parallel, task-conditioned scene-graph predictions.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.
authors: Jiachun Li, Zhuoran Jin, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces MentalGrid, a benchmark for spatial reasoning without intermediate visual feedback.
Finds that simple simulations are limited by perception, while complex ones suffer from weak multi-step reasoning.
Proposes a three-stage curriculum trained on 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples.
SpatialWalker achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model and outperforms Gemini-3-Flash on spatial simulation.
Generalizes to out-of-domain benchmarks with a 4.9% average gain.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.
authors: Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang, Jinqiao Wang
bullets: Fixed or single-level geometric fusion cannot meet the differing representation needs of tasks such as distance estimation and route planning.
GeoFus uses a gating network conditioned on text, visual semantics, and geometry to combine shallow, intermediate, and deep features across LLM decoder layers.
Negative-entropy regularization helps prevent gate collapse during adaptive fusion.
Gate visualizations suggest that the framework adjusts geometric granularity according to task requirements.
SpatialMind achieves competitive spatial-benchmark performance, including a 72.3 score on VSI-Bench.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the SpatialMind architecture. Our framework adopts a decoupled fusion design and introduces GeoFus for taskadaptive integration of multi-level geometric features with visual tokens. By jointly conditioning on textual, visual, and geometric contexts, GeoFus dynamically adjusts the contributions of geometric representations at different LLM injection layers according to task requirements.

Figure 8: Per-Task Adaptive Gating Distributions on VSI-Bench. Softmax-normalized gating weights assigned to shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric representations at the three LLM injection positions, L0, L1, and L2. Each row reports the average gating distribution over 50 randomly sampled examples from the corresponding VSI-Bench subtask. The upper five rows correspond to low-level perception tasks, while the lower three rows correspond to high-level reasoning tasks.

Figure 2: Visualization of Multi-Level Geometric Attention across 2D Views and 3D Point Clouds. Features at different levels capture spatial information at distinct scales, progressing from fine-grained details to global layouts.

Figure 3: Effects of Multi-Level Geometric Features. Shallow features contribute more to low-level tasks, while deep features are more important for high-level tasks, demonstrating hierarchical specialization and cross-level complementarity.

Figure 9: Task-Dependent Geometric Response Visualization on VSI-Bench. The low-level absolute-distance task emphasizes finegrained local geometry, whereas the high-level route-planning task produces broader responses over global scene structures.

Figure 10: Qualitative Results on Low-Level VSI-Bench Tasks. Representative comparisons on absolute-distance estimation, relativedirection reasoning, and room-size estimation. SpatialMind produces predictions consistent with or closer to the ground truth, whereas the baseline exhibits substantial metric and directional errors.
Figure 7: VSI-Bench Task Taxonomy. The eight VSI-Bench subtasks are grouped into low-level perception and high-level reasoning according to their dominant spatial operations

Figure 11: Qualitative Results on High-Level VSI-Bench Tasks. Representative comparisons on appearance-order reasoning, cross-view object counting, and route planning.
