papers.tldr: SpatialMind improves 3D spatial reasoning in multimodal LLMs by dynamically selecting the geometric feature granularity suited to each task.

papers.abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.
bullets: Rendered scenes isolate five 3-D relations, with the image cue correct for half of the statements and wrong for the other half.
At low reasoning effort, three frontier models show shortcut gaps of +18 to +37 percentage points, or +7 to +29 when confounded relations are excluded.
When given ground coordinates and relation definitions, the models reach 99–100% accuracy, locating the main failure in image-to-layout reasoning.
Top-down scene maps usually preserve depth order but compress depth; GPT-5.5 largely copies the image, while Opus 5.5 and Gemini partially undo the compression.
The models also lose accuracy on photographs when reliable 2-D cues conflict with the true relation; pixel measurements with camera depths reduce the gap for objects fitting through openings.

figures.caption: Figure 5: One scene drawn from above by each model. The statement “The yellow sphere would fit through the gap between the orange sphere and the pink cylinder” is true. (a) In the picture the gap is 16 px and the sphere 164 px. (b) On the ground the gap is 2.10 units and the sphere 1.67. (c) The picture-plane copy. (d–f) Each frontier model’s drawn map from the image alone. Every layout is aligned to the truth by a similarity transform and drawn with the true footprint sizes, with dashed circles at the true positions. Panel titles give each layout’s depth-to-width ratio and gap width in units. Each map compresses depth and narrows the gap below the sphere’s width.

Figure 3: The perspective form of the running example. Equal cells in the picture cover very different areas of ground. (a) The picture with a 64-pixel grid and the prompts’ visible box, ground-contact pixel and camera depth for the three objects in the statement. (b) The grid carried to the ground plane through the exact image-to-ground homography, the projective map from pixels to ground points. The two shaded cells are equal in the picture, but the far cell covers 2.94 square units of ground and the near cell 0.32. The gap, farther from the camera than the cube and seen at a slant, spans 60 px against the cube’s 132 px although it is wider on the ground.

Figure 2: One cue-right (top) and one cue-wrong (bottom) true item per relation from the medium tier. In the bottom row the named 2-D cue gives the wrong answer, which is what the shortcut gap tests. The cues are pixel area for closer, pixel height for taller, masks within 3 px for touching, the angle test on mask centroids for between and pixel gap against pixel width for fits.

Figure 1: The same fits item read in the picture plane and on the ground plane. (a) In the image the gap spans 60 px and the nearer cube 132 px. (b) On the ground plane the gap is 1.85 units and the cube 1.12, so the cube fits. (c) Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini at low reasoning effort answer False from the picture and True from the ground plane. Given pixel measurements and camera depths, which nearly determine the answer, only Gemini still answers False. Only the input changes between the rows. Over the 600 medium items their pooled gaps are +21.3, +35.0 and +24.7 points from the picture and +4.0, +5.3 and +4.7 from the top-down map (Table 6).

Figure 4: The shortcut gap by relation (points, image condition) for the frontier models and Grok 4.7, one row per model and tier. The gap is concentrated in fits, between and touching. Each cell prints its gap, and darker red marks a larger positive gap. Each cell has 120 items and one run, the frontier models at low reasoning effort and Grok 4.7 at the provider default. The relation closer is the control.
Figure 7: Cue-wrong items answered wrongly by Claude Opus 5.5 with chain of thought (medium tier). From left to right, fits, between and touching.

Figure 6: Linear probes on Qwen3-VL-4B’s object representations, by decoder layer. Ground-plane depth (red) and lateral position (blue) are decodable at every layer and peak in the middle of the network. Picture-plane position (grey) is decoded better still. Horizontal lines give the same ridge readout applied to the exact 2-D measurements, and to the visible boxes alone. R2 is within scene and cross-validated over 1,252 scenes.

With numeric definitions, ground coordinates give 99.0, 100.0 and 99.5% accuracy. Pixel measurements narrow the gap in the point estimates, with several intervals reaching zero.

The ground-plane form (top-down map, coordinates) brings the frontier models to gaps of +4 to +6 and Grok 4.7 to +5 to +18, while the five others stay at low accuracy. Frontier models used low reasoning effort, others the provider default. Columns marked + add that input to the image. Text only and coordinates only drop it. The constancy index puts GPT-5.5 lowest, Opus 5.5 highest. The picture-plane copy’s ratio is 0.61 (medium) and 0.30 (hard). RMSE is the median position error after alignment. Relation columns re-derive the statements from the map with true sizes, scoring those inside a reject band as wrong (accuracy in %, map gaps in points). Heights are not mapped, so taller is left out. % compressed counts scenes with a ratio below 1.

The last rows give how often each cue is right and on how many items it is wrong. Where the lower box is the farther one, every frontier model loses accuracy, and the Qwen intervals end within half a point of zero. The size of the box carries no reliable gap, with no interval above zero, as for closer in the rendered scenes. Where the object nearer the reference in the picture is farther from it in the scene, every model loses accuracy on Distance too. Intervals are 95% item-bootstrap intervals.

Table 4: Accuracy (%) on the four fits cells of each tier, split by whether the pixel-width cue is right and whether the object fits (30 items per cell, one run at low reasoning effort). The size-constancy reader of Section 4 scales each pixel width and gap by its image distance below the horizon and makes no correction for foreshortening. It fails where the object fits but looks too wide, because the gap then runs along the line of sight. GPT-5.5 and Gemini fall short of it on the cue-wrong items where the object does not fit, the cell that tests size scaling.

Table 34: Common support for the difficulty adjustment (medium, image). The column “% off” gives the share of items with a propensity of being cue-right outside [0.05, 0.95] under a Firth propensity model on the difficulty covariates and proposition truth. The gaps are raw, raw on items with propensity in [0.1, 0.9], and inverse-propensity weighted (weights trimmed at [0.05, 0.95]). The adjusted gaps come from a within-relation Firth outcome model without the interaction of cue status with margin, with construct membership as a binary flag or as construct type and scene-bootstrap CIs.
Table 42: Calls and tokens over every input on the rendered tiers. The total leaves out the CV-Bench calls and the calls to the two probed models, which ran locally.

Table 7: The fits and between gaps (points) under the inputs of Section 5.2 on the medium tier, 120 items per relation, one run per model at low reasoning effort. Pixel measurements and ground coordinates are given as text. Table 5 gives how far each input determines the answer.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.
authors: Thorben Prein, Elton Pan, Rafael G\'omez-Bombarelli, Santiago Miret
bullets: Motivation: Experiments provide coupled molecular and spectral measurements, but conventional models often use only one conditioning direction.
Method: Randomly masks modalities and trains a transformer on multiple denoising tasks across 3D structures, UV, IR, and Raman spectra.
Contribution: A single model supports flexible any-to-any generation and arbitrary subsets of available measurements.
Result: On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, with reported gains over spectra-to-structure and specialist structure-to-spectra baselines.
Scope: The approach also supports molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references; ablations show benefits over structure-only training across model sizes.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MOSAIC training and architecture. (a) At each training step, we perform any-to-any training by randomly selecting target modalities T and conditioning (context) modalities C. For example, IR and Raman provide conditioning for generating UV and molecular structure. (b) The pretrained encoder converts the conditioning modalities into context tokens, while each target modality is noised to xm t at timestep tm. We pass both sets of tokens to an MMDiT [7], where each of the D blocks applies joint self-attention across them. The model predicts target velocities vθ, which are used at inference to iteratively generate the target modalities from noise. The same model handles different combinations of conditioning and target modalities.

papers.title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
papers.tldr: MOSAIC uses masked multimodal flow matching to generate any subset of molecular structures and spectra from any other subset, extracting more supervision from each experiment.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
authors: Boyu Han, Qianqian Xu, Shilong Bao, Zhiyong Yang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between contrastive discrimination and generative reconstruction in visual encoders for MLLMs.
Recasts reconstruction as a ranking problem that scores matched outputs above mismatched ones.
Introduces AUCGR for AUC-based ranking and pAUCGR for focusing on reliable mismatched comparisons to reduce supervision bias.
The objectives are plug-and-play and require no architectural changes.
Experiments report improved discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation, supported by theoretical generalization analysis.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. An overview of our method. (a) A generic comparison principle for generative reconstruction. (b) AUC-oriented instantiations, including AUCGR and pAUCGR. (c) Reconstruction learning pipeline. Our method serves as a plug-and-play optimization module that replaces the original optimization strategy in existing reconstruction learning methods, thereby yielding balanced enhanced visual representations.

Fig. 10. Ablation study on different generative model structures. We evaluate our method with Stable Diffusion v1.5, Stable Diffusion v2.1, and Rectified Flow as the generative reconstruction backbone. All experiments use OpenAI CLIP ViT-L@224 as the visual backbone. The results show that our framework is not tied to a specific generative architecture and consistently improves both P-Ability and D-Ability.

Fig. 1. Motivation of our method. (a) Reconstructive learning improves P-Ability by preserving a sparser representation space. (b) Contrastive learning improves D-Ability by organizing representations into compact semantic clusters. (c) The naive method searches for a balanced representation through heuristic weight tuning between contrastive learning and reconstructive learning, but the proper weights are difficult to determine. papers.title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
authors: Katharina Winter, William Engel, Zain A. Alishammat, Fabian B. Flohr
bullets: Addresses the challenge of running autoregressive language generation alongside real-time onboard driving planning.
Uses lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception, spatially structured tokens, and frame-wise scheduling to interleave planning with asynchronous language generation.
Supports trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, navigation instructions, driving explanations, and scene question answering.
Reports 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM, 57.6% nuScenes-QA accuracy, 32.7 ms standalone planning latency, and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline.
Evaluations include public benchmarks, proprietary recordings, and open-loop operation on a research vehicle; the abstract notes both strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.
bullets: Benchmarks persistent spatial memory with 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes and 9 tasks.
Tests room association, state tracking, and downstream reasoning under viewpoint changes, distractor rooms, and changing objects.
The best evaluated zero-shot model reaches 50.5% accuracy versus 90.1% for human annotators; agentic frameworks do not improve overall results.
Key failures include omitted evidence and incorrect associations between rooms visited at different times.
Training on the separate RS-30K dataset improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 35.5% to 60.4%, especially on room association and real-life scenes.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/
authors: Rohit Gandikota, Arnab Sen Sharma, Adam Belfki, David Bau
bullets: Binding heads link text tokens and previous answers to their corresponding image regions.
A progress signal acts as a cursor marking how far through the image’s regions the model has written.
A selection step chooses the nearest unwritten region or stops generation.
Gaze heads execute the selected pointer, while language components convert the retrieved visual concept into an answer word.
Causal patching in Qwen3-VL models supports the mechanism across formats, photographs, languages, and model sizes from 2B to 32B parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Task setup: We provide an image strip with each panel containing a shape and a letter. We ask the model to retrieve the label of the panel that contains the queried shape. (b) The mechanism, with tokens across and layers down. The model solves the task early, at the shape token star, well before it answers: (1) binding heads match the request against the image and resolve a pointer to the matching panel. (2) Relay heads carry that pointer to the “:” token, where the answer has to be produced, and (3) gaze heads execute it to retrieve the letter from that panel. (4) Once T is written, binding heads bind it to its panel, and the model calculates its progress and (5) selects what answer to mention next (by repeating steps 3-5) or to stop if none is left.

Figure 3: (a) Relay heads transfer the pointer from the shape token to the colon. When each relay head may read only one token at a time, the pointer is transferred mostly when the relay heads at the colon token read the shape token. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on 500 heldout pairs. (b) A copied comma state skips a written panel at layers 20-21. When patching the source’s comma-token residual into the target’s colon-token residual, one layer at a time: at layer 20 the target skips to its next candidate, T, in 91.0± 2.4% of pairs, and in 70.0± 3.9% at layer 21. From layers 22-28 it takes the source’s next panel pointer, W, and from layer 30 the source’s letter, A. (c) A copied comma state says where the list goes on. With a more targeted setup, we find at layers 20 and 21 the model answers with the first candidate “after panel 4”, W, in 98.4± 1.1% and 97.6± 1.3% of pairs. The shaded band marks layers 20-21.

Figure 6: Only the shape token and the colon token change the answer. Each cell patches the source’s residual vector into the target at one text token and one layer, and counts the cases that answer with one outcome letter of Section 3. (a) T, the target’s own letter. (b) D, the source’s letter. (c) K, the target’s letter at the source’s panel. (d) P, the target’s letter inside the source’s shape. (e) R, the target’s letter where the source’s layout puts the asked shape. The shape token is shown in bold. The request, P, sits at the shape token up to layer 19. The pointer, K, sits at the shape token around layer 20 and at the colon token from layers 23-29. The source’s letter, D, comes through the colon token from layer 30. All panels use the 500 held-out pairs.

Figure 8: The selection rule fixes the number of heads. We patch the top K heads of each singlehead search together on the 100 validation pairs. These are the queries, image keys, and outputs at the shape token, and the values that the relay heads read at the colon token. (a) Cases whose next token is the letter the patch predicts. (b) Cases in which the published Gaze Heads look at the matching panel. The dotted line marks the 80% rule. The queries and the image keys first pass it on both readouts at 8 heads, with 83.5% and 80.5% for the queries and 85.0% and 84.5% for the image keys. The outputs and the relay values first pass it at 16 heads.

Figure 25: On comic images, the colon token holds the pointer at the same layers. We replace the target’s residual vector at the colon token with the source’s at one layer, as in Figure 2a, on cases with comic drawings under the markers and the longer prompt. (a) The target’s next letter. The pointer, K, peaks at 80.2% at layer 24, and the source’s letter, D, comes through from layer 30. (b) The panel the published Gaze Heads look at, with no head patched. At layer 23 they look at the source’s panel in 45.0% of cases.

Figure 23: Zeroing the language heads, against setting them. We patch the top K heads of the language search at every generated token, in runs asked in German, French, or Chinese on the heldout images. Solid purple: we zero the heads and the answer turns English. Dash-dot gray: zeroing breaks the output. Dotted light gray: we zero random heads. Dashed purple: we set the heads to their English average and the answer turns English, run up to 64 heads. (a) Colored shapes: 16 heads set to English give English in 100.0% of runs, and 16 heads zeroed give it in 62.7± 2.4%. (b) Objects: 100.0% and 23.7%.

Figure 10: Relay heads carry the pointer from the shape token to the colon token. (a) At the colon token, we let one attention head at a time read the source’s values from the shape token and the tokens after it, while its own query and keys stay unchanged. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on the 200 discovery pairs. The 16 relay heads that the search selects are outlined, in layers 19-35. (b) Each relay head alone reads the source’s value at one text token only, while its query, keys, and attention stay unchanged. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on the held-out pairs. When all 16 relay heads read only the shape token, the target answers K in 47.3± 3.1% of cases, and when they read only the “?”, it does so in 9.9± 1.8%.

Figure 24: Choosing the language with no source. We set the top 16 language heads to their average output under the target language (columns), in runs asked in the question language (rows). Each cell is the percent of held-out images whose answer names its own concept in the target language. (a) Colored shapes. (b) Objects. Leaving English is the hardest direction.

Figure 19: Finding the gaze heads, and how they compare with the published ranking. (a) The number of heads shared in the top K of three rankings of all 1,152 heads: our query-patch search, the Gaze score measured on our task, and the published Gaze Heads ranking. From K = 16 to 128, our ranking shares more heads with the Gaze score on this task than with the published ranking, 20 against 10 in the top 32. (b) The top K heads of the two searches, patched together at the colon token on the 100 validation pairs. Patching their queries moves the answer to the source’s panel in 68.5% of cases at K = 8, and in 73.5% to 76.5% from 16 to 256 heads. This stays below the 80% rule, so the rule takes its best size, 32 heads. Blocking up to 256 heads from the image loses the target’s answer in at most 2.5%.

Figure 22: MLPs performing translation. (a) The language shift when we patch the output of one MLP at the colon token from the source, by target language, averaged over the three source languages. (b) The top k MLPs patched together, ranked over all languages and both questions, grouped by source language and averaged over its three targets. The top 4 MLPs are layers 32-35, and the top 8 are layers 28-35.

With r2 written it also answers r2, in 75.1% at layer 19, and answers r3 from layer 23 (82.4%). Up to layer 19 the copied state says only that one letter was written. From layer 20 the target starts after the written panel. (b) The skip experiment of Section 5.1, split by the shared first matching panel. Averaged over layers 0-17, the target skips it in 80.6± 4.5% of pairs when the shared panel is panel 1, 8.6± 3.3% for panel 2, and 4.7± 2.4% for panel 3. At layer 20 it skips in 99.5± 0.8%, 97.5± 2.2%, and 74.2± 7.1%, and at layer 21 in 53.2± 6.7%, 72.0± 7.4%, and 88.4± 5.1%. (c) The standard source, which has written the target’s first letter at r2 and has its own next matching panel at r4. The target answers with a count, r2, at layer 19 (86.5%), with the panel after the written one, r3, at layer 20 (68.4%), with the source’s own choice, r4, at layer 24 (87.6%), and with the source’s letter from layer 30. The shaded band marks layers 20-21.

Figure 27: The same heads work on images with no panels. Every bar uses the head sets selected on panel images, with no new search. (a) The single-answer tests, on the held-out pairs with panels (gray) and with no panels (blue). (b) The list tests, on the held-out list cases whose unedited runs are right. (c) The Spearman correlation between the head rankings of each target language, over all 1,152 heads.

Figure 17: What the comma token’s residual holds, with no patch. (a) We train ridge probes on the residual of the last comma token on half of the held-out pairs of the list task, and read them on the other half. The written panel is named in 94.0± 2.8% of pairs at layer 12 and 100.0± 0.0% at 18. The probes read whether each panel is a matching panel with 95.9± 1.0% accuracy at layer 17 and 99.3± 0.5% at 21, from a chance level of two thirds. The next panel is named in 98.0± 1.8% at layer 18 and 100.0± 0.0% at 20. (b) Image attention of the binding heads at the comma token, by layer. At layer 21 they put 51.6± 1.9% of it on the next panel and 3.9± 0.2% on the written panel. (c) Image attention of the gaze heads at the comma token, by layer. At layer 20 they give 22.3± 0.6% to the next panel and 23.0± 0.7% to each other matching panel, and by layer 23 they give 61.9± 1.4% and 7.4± 0.4%.

Figure 4: (a) Gaze heads exist after layer 20. Pointer logit gain when one head’s query at the colon token is patched. The 32 gaze heads are outlined, all in layers 19-34. (b) Our gaze heads vs. the published Gaze Heads (Gandikota & Bau, 2026). Solid lines replace the queries and count the target’s letter at the source’s panel, K. Dashed lines let the heads read the source’s image values and count the source’s letter at the target’s panel, C. The vertical lines mark our 32 heads and the top 100 published heads. Our 32 heads beat the top 100 published heads, and random heads stay at or below 2.1± 1.0%. (c) Language heads set the language. Scoring the language change of a word when patching attention head outputs from a source in a different language. The 16 language heads are outlined, in layers 19-35. The color scale is capped at 1.6; L24H27 scores 5.03.

Figure 2: The pointer is resolved at the shape token by a few attention heads. (a) Patching the source’s residual at the colon token into the target, one layer at a time. Up to layer 20 the target keeps its own letter T; from layers 23-29 it answers K, the target’s letter at the source’s answer location, so the colon token holds a pointer to a panel; from layer 30 it copies the source’s letter D. (b) The same patch at every text token and every layer, tracking the logit of K: the pointer appears only at the shape token, around layer 20, and at the colon token, from layer 23. Each cell patches one attention head at the shape token from the source on its own, averaged over the 200 discovery pairs. papers.abstract: Structure-level wildfire vulnerability assessment is critical for reducing losses in wildland-urban interface communities, yet existing methods often fail to combine parcel-scale ignition pathways with community-scale geographic coverage. This study introduces Wildfire-SSR (Satellite and Street-view for wildfire Risk), a geolocation-aware multimodal framework that integrates macro-scale satellite context with micro-scale street-view evidence. A Vision-Language Model extracts wildfire-relevant building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and converts them into structured semantic text. These features are spatially aligned with satellite imagery through a decoupled cross-attention fusion decoder, while a frozen satellite-pretrained DINOv3 encoder captures overhead visual context. Alternative geolocation embedding strategies are evaluated to anchor text-derived features within each satellite patch. The framework is tested on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, using wildfire risk labels derived from relative post-event damage patterns to better represent inherent structural vulnerability. Rotary Positional Embedding provides the strongest spatial grounding, achieving a building localization F1 score of 0.6735 and a harmonic mean F1 score of 0.2476 for five-class pixel-level risk classification, outperforming unimodal baselines and an unanchored multimodal configuration. The model also shows a conservative bias in higher-risk classes, reducing severe-risk underestimation, and completes end-to-end assessment of the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU. Wildfire-SSR reframes cross-view fusion as localized semantic alignment and provides a scalable tool for mitigation prioritization, resilience planning, and insurance-oriented wildfire risk assessment.
authors: Yu-Hsuan Ho, Yiming Xiao, Hao-En Lai, Ali Mostafavi, Samuel D. Brody
bullets: Addresses the gap between parcel-scale ignition pathways and community-scale geographic coverage in wildfire vulnerability assessment.
A Vision-Language Model extracts building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and aligns them with satellite context using cross-attention and geolocation embeddings.
Evaluated on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, with labels based on relative post-fire damage patterns.
Rotary Positional Embedding performed best, reaching a building-localization F1 of 0.6735 and a five-class pixel-level risk harmonic mean F1 of 0.2476.
The model reduced severe-risk underestimation and assessed the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU, supporting mitigation and resilience planning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed geolocation-aware multimodal framework for structure-level wildfire risk assessment. The pipeline addresses the limitations of isolated unimodal approaches by integrating macro-scale satellite imagery with micro-scale street-view data. A Vision-Language Model first extracts semantic building vulnerabilities from street-level images into structured text descriptions. To bridge the spatial disconnect between modalities, the geographical coordinates of the street-view captures are mapped to local relative coordinates and injected into CLIPencoded text embeddings. A decoupled cross-attention multimodal fusion decoder then aligns these geolocation-aware text features with overhead visual features extracted via DINOv3. The proposed model processes these fused representations into pixel-wise risk labels, which are then transformed into a detailed, actionable community-scale wildfire risk map.

Figure 2: Overview of the model architecture. Ground-level street-view images are first processed by a Vision-Language Model to extract structured semantic attributes, which are combined with their geographic coordinates to form spatially anchored text embeddings. A multimodal fusion decoder then integrates these location-aware micro-level features with macro-level visual features extracted from pre-event satellite imagery via a frozen satellite-pretrained vision encoder to generate precise, structure-level wildfire risk maps.

Figure 6: Pixel-level wildfire vulnerability predictions from the proposed RoPE-based multimodal framework (right) compared against the ground-truth building-level risk labels (left) for representative tiles in the Eaton and Palisades study areas. Colors denote the five ordinal risk classes from minimal to extreme; the comparison illustrates the model’s capacity to capture broad spatial patterns of structural vulnerability while highlighting residual confusion between adjacent low and moderate tiers.

Figure 5: Study area: final perimeters of the 2025 Eaton and Palisades wildfires in the Los Angeles region, showing the wildland-urban interface neighborhoods used for structure-level vulnerability evaluation. Perimeter data are sourced from the City of Los Angeles GeoHub (City of Los Angeles, 2025c).

Figure 4: Schematic representation of the geometric localization algorithm. To preserve view-angle perspective, orthogonal normal vectors (ns) are cast from the street-view camera’s heading direction. The intersection of these street vectors with the heading vectors (nb) originating from adjacent building centroids determines the precise spatial anchor point on the observed facade.

Figure 3: Structure of the two-way cross-attention block utilizing a decoupled attention mechanism. Geolocation embeddings (GEs) are injected specifically into the queries (Q) and keys (K) to facilitate spatial routing, while values (V ) remain purely semantic to preserve micro-level building attributes. The block consists of three sequential steps: sparse text self-attention to capture geometric dependencies between structural, sparse-to-dense cross-attention to update textual context with overhead visual data, and dense-to-sparse cross-attention to infuse the macro-level visual map with ground-sourced semantic details.
Table 3: Ablation study results on input modalities and geolocation embeddings. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 4: Results of the label reconstruction diagnostic experiment utilizing explicit risk levels as text input. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 1: Performance comparison of geolocation embedding strategies. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 2: Quantitative evaluation of building wildfire risk classification across pixel-level and building-level aggregated metrics. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.
bullets: The failure occurs at two stages: correspondence is present in visual tokens but is not reliably read out, and cross-image attention in a small set of heads is misrouted.
Across Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, and Gemma-3, answer-position probes outperform calibrated outputs by 15–25 points, while steering does not reliably change answers.
Redistributing attention in 16–32 identified heads causes 15–32-point accuracy drops, far larger than changes from random or attention-matched heads.
Training only the query and key projections of these heads improves SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points for Qwen3-VL-8B and 25.1 points for InternVL3.5-8B, with transfer to HPatches and BLINK.

papers.title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: VLMs often locate cross-image correspondences internally but fail to route or read them into the final answer; targeted attention-head repair substantially improves this behavior.

papers.abstract: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.
authors: Vincent Li Weixin, Chen Jingkun, Vicente Grau
bullets: Addresses the high cost of annotating every frame in long echocardiography sequences.
Uses a mean-teacher architecture with frozen, pretrained DINOv3 encoders and parameter-efficient adaptation.
Combines complementary losses, including temporal consistency, to generate segmentation priors for unlabeled frames.
Experiments on CAMUS and CardiacNet show improved performance over other scribble-supervised methods.
Reduces annotation requirements independently of sequence length while targeting temporally stable segmentation.

papers.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.
authors: Yong Liu, Zhanpeng Shi, Peicong Lin, Zhenyi Zhong, Yizhou Dang, Wendi Wu, Haoling Li, Shuangjia Zheng
bullets: Addresses the separation between biomolecular structure models and language models.
Qwen3.5-9B processes sequences enriched with ESM2 residue features and invokes a pretrained SimpleFold head through a folding request.
The structure head receives protein information only through the LLM’s residue states and achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808, 0.635, and 0.900 on three evaluated sets.
Compared with an ESM2-3B/SimpleFold-3B baseline, differences were inconclusive for 100–299-residue chains and lower for 300–600-residue chains.
Protein training reduced accuracy on the evaluated 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%.

papers.abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.
authors: Ruizhe Wang, Rui Liu, Hongliang Chen, Junyi Guo, Fangyu Wu, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets assembly hierarchy inference from individual parts and target illustrations.
Fuses a dedicated SVG encoder with representations from a pretrained vision-language model.
Uses RHPO to reward hierarchy-preserving equivalent solutions rather than only matching one reference tree.
Adds repair-cost feedback to prefer decisions requiring fewer downstream corrections.
Achieves the best Equivalent-Hard F1 among evaluated methods, including a 17.69-point gain over GPT6-Astra on an IKEA-derived test set, with strong independent-dataset performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Assembly architecture and RHPO training (a–c) The indexed parts and target drawing illustrate four assembly steps. Each resulting subassembly maps to an internal node of the reference tree, also shown in nested JSON. (d) For a fixed goal or action, unassisted rollouts estimate full success (Q) and tree quality (V). Separate repair rollouts estimate the mean number of subsequent repairs (C). At the first certified downstream error, the verifier rolls back, replaces the erroneous merge using the annotated graph and reference tree, and resumes the frozen policy. GRPO uses Q and V at both decision levels and favors lower repair cost among eligible candidates with near-best quality and a certified paired cost gap. Action-only distillation transfers probability mass from verified invalid actions to verified valid actions while preserving the mass on unknown actions.
Figure 3. Ablation study of VASR. VASR-S is trained only through the supervised stages (T2–T4).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces VASR, a framework for furniture assembly planning using a vision-language model and hierarchical policy optimization, directly addressing robot manipulation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: VASR: Vector-Aware Assembly Planning with Equivalent Structures and Repair-Cost Feedback
papers.tldr: VASR improves furniture assembly planning by combining SVG geometry with visual-language features and optimizing for valid, low-repair-cost assembly hierarchies.

papers.abstract: Image generators are good at drawing scenes in which things that belong together appear next to each other. In almost every image they generate, and in almost every benchmark used to evaluate these images, "belonging to the same whole" and "adjacent to each other" go together. Therefore, we cannot know whether the model truly grasps the scene as a whole, or simply makes each part connect with its adjacent parts. We propose GJBench to disentangle the two. It requires the model to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle: an image is cut into interlocking pieces, then moved apart and rotated. Thus, the spatial plausibility of the scene exists only in how these pieces collectively point to a whole. The model may have a reference image, a target layout, both, or neither. We separately evaluate three requirements: whether the scene is broken down into a specified number of separate pieces, whether the pieces interlock, and whether the pieces can reconstruct the reference scene. While every open and closed model we evaluated could draw these scenes well as a whole, none could keep them together as scattered puzzle pieces, and the three requirements categorized failures into different patterns. The models draw separate pieces but miscount them in different ways, and unless their outlines are provided, the pieces rarely interlock, and their content does not reconstruct the reference image. We also found that the target layout helps the puzzle pieces fit together, while the reference image improves neither their count nor their fit. These findings show that keeping a scene continuous across space that the canvas no longer shows remains an open problem for image generators.
bullets: Tests whether models understand a scene as a whole rather than relying on local adjacency.
Evaluates piece count, interlocking geometry, and reconstruction of the reference scene separately.
All evaluated models produced plausible scenes globally but failed to maintain coherence across scattered pieces.
Models often miscounted pieces; without provided outlines, pieces rarely interlocked or reconstructed the reference.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark disentangling scene-wholeness from adjacency in image generators; directly tests spatial reasoning and scene-level spatial understanding.
papers.title: Can Image Generators Hold a Scene Together When Space Is Broken Apart?
papers.tldr: GJBench reveals that image generators struggle to preserve scene coherence when a scene is split into separated, rotated jigsaw pieces.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.
bullets: Introduces 854 benchmark items in 427 minimal pairs of 2D rigid-body chain-reaction scenes, with simulator-computed outcomes.
Tests 30 models across 10 families, using hint ladders from identifying the deciding step to providing the exact calculation.
Without assistance, frontier models achieve at most 72% on the deciding person and 34% on both paired cases.
Providing the deciding calculation raises frontier-model accuracy to 82–92%, while small open-weight models remain near chance.
Fluent scene descriptions or pointing to the relevant step are insufficient; models must independently derive and compute hidden quantities such as speeds.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks physical reasoning from still images for models that plan/act in the physical world, directly relevant to embodied AI and spatial reasoning in multimodal models.
papers.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
papers.tldr: DominoBench shows that leading vision-language models struggle to predict multi-step chain reactions from still images because they fail to compute the decisive physical quantity.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that are difficult to express in text. Existing approaches either rely on external drawing tools or image generators, or encode these states in latent tokens without explicit spatial correspondence to the input image. We introduce SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and use visual marks directly in their native visual feature space. By treating the visual token grid as a canvas, SelfMark establishes explicit spatial correspondence between marks and images. This is achieved through a locate-mark-read procedure, where the model identifies relevant locations, constructs task-dependent mark features, and reads the resulting visual features to guide its reasoning. We jointly train a single model on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing. Across six benchmarks, SelfMark outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM-based methods specialized for individual tasks. These improvements also persist with a stronger backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of visual marking across different model capabilities. Overall, SelfMark provides a unified approach to visual reasoning by integrating spatially grounded marks directly into the visual feature space of MLLMs.
authors: Jiazhen Liu, Yanghao Wang, Chaolei Tan, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of representing intermediate spatial states in text or latent tokens without explicit image correspondence.
Uses a locate-mark-read procedure over the visual token grid as a task-dependent reasoning canvas.
Trains one model jointly for spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing.
Outperforms specialized MLLM-based methods across six benchmarks, with gains also holding for a stronger backbone.
Provides a unified framework for integrating explicit visual marks directly into MLLM visual features.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SelfMark. (1) Locate: after reading the image and the question, the MLLM emits a type token, here <PTS>, and fills in mask placeholders, one per patch, in a single forward pass; a lightweight head turns them into the locate conditions. (2) Mark: a lightweight editor, which never sees the image, translates the conditions into mark features on the same grid as the visual tokens. (3) Read: the same MLLM reads the original visual tokens and the question, followed by the mark tokens, and answers. Dashed orange parts are used only in training: Lloc fits the conditions to position labels, Lmark aligns the mark features with the target Z∗, the frozen-ViT features of the marks drawn on a blank canvas, and the answer is trained with CE and RL; no marks are drawn as pixels at inference.

Figure 1. Four ways of thinking with an image. A simple counting task reveals how different approaches handle visual evidence. (a) Think in text translates visual structure into words, risking plausible but ungrounded descriptions such as “rows of five.” (b) Draw in pixels relies on an external vision module to annotate the image, inheriting its missed detections. (c) Latent imagination encodes intermediate visual states in a handful of latent tokens, leaving their spatial grounding implicit. (d) SelfMark takes a different route: the MLLM first locates the targets, a lightweight editor marks them in its visual feature space, and the MLLM reads the resulting marks alongside the original visual tokens. Each dot corresponds to a located object, turning counting into explicit, inspectable visual reasoning. The same locate–mark–read procedure handles the other tasks with other marks (bottom).
Figure 3. Inference cost. (a, b) Performance vs. latency on V* and FSC-147 (upper left is better). (c) Latency vs. object count.

papers.selection_reason: MLLM visual marking in native feature space for spatially grounded reasoning; fits multimodal LLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Visual Marking as a Native Reasoning Capability for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: SelfMark gives multimodal LLMs a native visual workspace for creating spatially grounded marks that support visual reasoning.

papers.abstract: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.
authors: Bart M. N. Smets, Gijs Bellaard, Pieter Wils
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between overly restrictive built-in equivariance and costly data augmentation.
Introduces an architecture that can become equivariant to selected symmetry groups based on the training data.
Provides a post-training fingerprint indicating which symmetries are relevant and to what degree.
Demonstrates the architecture and fingerprinting process on image classification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: An input image is first converted to a set of geometric tokens through splatting. GLInT processes these tokens to, in this case, classify the image. After training, the model can be inspected to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that tells us which of our candidate symmetry groups are relevant (shown are the subgroups of Aff+(2) that we used, see also Fig. 3).

Fig. 4: MNIST test errors over 20 independent training runs. We train ViT on both the original MNIST and a rasterized version of our splatted MNIST to show the fidelity of our tokenization method. We also train GLInT with and without noise to show that fingerprinting noise does not degrade performance.

Fig. 3: The set of symmetry subgroups of Aff+(2) we are interested in. Green arrows add translations. Red arrows add rotations. Blue arrows add isotropic scaling. Purple arrows add area-preserving maps.

Fig. 2: Top row: a sample from the MNIST dataset [10] (28 × 28 pixel images). papers.selection_reason: Introduces a soft-equivariant architecture that learns geometric invariance and symmetry groups, providing a mechanism for geometric reasoning and spatial understanding in neural networks.
papers.title: Symmetry Fingerprinting with Geometric Learnable Invariants Transformers
papers.tldr: A soft-equivariant transformer learns which geometric symmetries matter for a task and exposes them through an interpretable symmetry fingerprint.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.
authors: Rongxin Gao, Dongxuan Liu, Chu Li, Chengyang Ji, Jialing Huang, Runyu Chen, Kairun Wen, Chenxin Li, Jingrui Ye, Haosong Zhen, Xinghao Ding, Yue Huang, Yuzhi Huang, Xiaodong Tu, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between recognizing observed dynamics and forecasting dynamics beyond a video’s observation window.
Encodes video dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states.
Uses 4D Latent Alignment to combine visual-semantic and geometric grounding with joint language supervision.
Pros4D-Engine creates geometry-grounded training examples, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates eight dynamic spatial reasoning categories.
Experiments report consistent improvements over strong baselines on both observed-dynamics understanding and future-dynamics prediction.

papers.selection_reason: Latent 4D world modeling with future-dynamics prediction and dynamic spatial reasoning for VLMs.
papers.title: Pros4D: Modeling Evolving 4D Worlds in Latent Space for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Pros4D enables VLMs to understand observed 4D dynamics and predict future spatial changes directly in a grounded latent space.

papers.abstract: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world. Do their hidden features encode the direction from which the camera views a scene, and if so, in what form? We study the relative viewing direction $\alpha$ of two objects in rendered scenes where both object centres stay at fixed pixels while the camera moves, so that perspective, shading and shadows change but the projected layout does not. In eight pretrained models, from diffusion models to self-supervised and image-text encoders, $\alpha$ is encoded in a strikingly simple form: a single two-dimensional plane in the hidden space, shared across scenes, in which the difference between the two objects' features traces $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$. The plane keeps its orientation when lighting, colours, floors and object shapes change. This encoding is more than a summary of a few visible measurements: readouts fitted on one set of camera paths stay accurate at camera positions outside their range in seven of the eight models, whereas decoders of the measured object and shadow geometry, equally accurate within that range, fail there. In the diffusion transformer PixArt-$\alpha$, the plane forms abruptly at a single block and carries direction information to later blocks, yet editing it changes the objects rather than the generated viewpoint. We also examine how this encoding carries over to scanned real objects.
bullets: Tests viewing direction while keeping object centers fixed, isolating changes in perspective, shading, and shadows.
Across eight pretrained models, feature differences trace $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ in a scene-shared 2D plane.
The plane remains stable across lighting, colors, floors, and object shapes.
Readouts generalize to camera positions outside their training paths in seven of eight models, unlike geometry-based decoders.
In PixArt-$\alpha$, the representation appears abruptly in one block and persists later, but editing it changes objects rather than viewpoint; transfer to scanned objects is also examined.

papers.selection_reason: Probes how frozen vision models encode viewing direction and 3D geometry, contributing to spatial understanding in multimodal models.
papers.title: Beyond the Training Cameras: Coverage-Controlled Probes of Viewing Direction in Frozen Vision Models
papers.tldr: Frozen vision models consistently encode relative camera-view direction as a shared 2D circular representation in hidden features, but this representation is not a straightforward viewpoint-editing mechanism.

papers.abstract: Comprehensive audio-visual perception requires both semantic and spatial reasoning. Existing spatial models suffer from poor generalization due to data scarcity, while semantic-only models fail to capture spatial characteristics completely. We introduce a model capable of jointly reasoning over binaural audio and vision on semantic and spatial tasks with improved generalization. To overcome the shortage in real-world data, we develop an automatic pipeline that localizes the sound source in a video, estimates its relative 3D trajectory, and renders binaural audio. We then use this to spatialize VGGSound, allowing us to train at a much larger scale. We demonstrate improved performance and generalization on spatial reasoning tasks while still remaining competitive on semantic tasks compared to semantic-only models.
authors: Mengyu Yang, You Zhang, Vishnu Raj, Olha Townsend, James Hays, Andrea Fanelli, Gautam Bhattacharya
bullets: Addresses poor spatial generalization caused by limited real-world audio-visual data.
Automatically localizes sound sources, estimates relative 3D trajectories, and renders binaural audio.
Spatializes VGGSound to provide larger-scale training data.
The resulting model improves spatial reasoning and generalization while remaining competitive on semantic tasks.
Scope: performance depends on automatically estimated source locations and trajectories.

figures.caption: Figure 8. Architecture diagram of our model. We initialize the encoders for each modality from pretrained checkpoints and project the output features to a common 512-dimensional space. We mean-pool over space and time to get a single embedding vector per modality and apply our spatial and semantic losses.

Figure 1. Visualization of our automatic spatialization pipeline. Starting from a video with mono audio, we automatically detect the sound source (car in red) using SAMA-AVS [19] and estimate its relative 3D trajectory with Video Depth Anything [3] and SAM 2 [29]. We use that information to render binaural audio from the mono source. As modelled in the output frames, listening to the rendered binaural audio will give the sensation of the car swerving towards and then past the listener.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.
authors: Nhat-Quynh Le-Pham, Khoi Nguyen, Binh-Son Hua
bullets: Uses dense pixel-level CLIP features instead of mask-wise embeddings for fine-grained, proposal-free localization.

Lifts 2D tracks into 3D Gaussians using visibility voting to produce consistent segmentation masks.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups.
Supports efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.

The pivot is refined and propagated across views within a fixed frame budget using a Tracking Segmentor with our Mask Refinement module to ensure geometric consistency and coverage. The resulting masks are lifted to 3D Gaussians via visibility voting, forming an occlusion-aware 3D instance mask, which is rendered at novel views to obtain high-quality 2D instance segmentation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for autonomous driving through question-answering benchmarks, yet high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily reflect visually grounded reasoning. We present a diagnostic evaluation framework that systematically probes whether VLMs base safety-critical driving decisions on visual evidence or instead rely on language priors, answer biases, and dataset regularities. Our benchmark comprises two task categories, Adverse Weather and Junctions \& Intersections, with a nuScenes spatial reasoning extension, and evaluates open-source (general, driving, and spatial-reasoning) VLMs along four diagnostic protocols: image versus no-image evaluation, counterfactual weather sensitivity, linguistic robustness under paraphrasing and negation, and spatial reasoning. All ground-truth labels are derived programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM annotations, enabling reproducible evaluation without manual labeling. Across all models, we find that competitive overall accuracy conceals systematic failure modes, including strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance performance on negated questions despite high paraphrase consistency, and confident driving decisions even without visual input. These results demonstrate that current open-source VLMs remain insufficiently grounded for safety-critical autonomous driving and underscore the need for diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy.
authors: Shankar Gangisetty, Muskan Singh, C V Jawahar
bullets: Tests VLM reliance on visual evidence versus language priors and dataset regularities.
Covers adverse weather, junctions/intersections, and nuScenes-based spatial reasoning.
Uses four protocols: image removal, counterfactual weather changes, paraphrase/negation robustness, and spatial reasoning.
Finds affirmation bias, poor counterfactual sensitivity, near-chance negation performance, and confident answers without images.
Concludes that current open-source VLMs are not sufficiently grounded for autonomous driving decisions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.
authors: Kevin Nguyen, Ceyhun Efe Kayan, Feng Liu, Li Zhang
bullets: BW-PO is a controlled Blocksworld benchmark designed to expose failures in VLM planning under occlusion and depth ambiguity.
The proposed VLM-as-perceiver paradigm limits VLMs to local visual extraction rather than end-to-end planning.
External solvers handle cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation.
Plan success rises from near zero to 84–97% across the evaluated model-specific challenging subsets.
The approach separates failures in depth-ambiguity reconciliation from incomplete visual extraction in dense scenes.

Across (a)–(c), progressively more of the pipeline moves from stochastic to deterministic components.

papers.abstract: A robot that returns to a space must tell which objects were added, removed or moved since its last visit, while its trajectory, viewpoints and lighting differ between the two visits. We find that multi-image vision-language models (VLMs) fail at this task mainly because they cannot find the place where an object was. A VLM recognises what each frame shows but cannot check whether an object is still at its place in the other capture. It therefore reports objects that only one capture shows and misses most removed and moved objects. We propose STILL, which reformulates change detection as object verification at a registered place. 3D geometry registers the place of each change hypothesis in the other capture, and one VLM answers, from a scene view and a local place view, whether the object is still at that place, trained with supervision of the same form. Under the official SceneDiff protocol, STILL raises the main metric obj/sc AP from 24.0 to 37.8, and from 11.6 to 20.6 on the egocentric kitchen subset without any kitchen training data. It improves F1 by more than 21 points over a VLM fine-tuned on the same annotations and adds only about 11% to the runtime.
authors: Jinjie Xie, Baihua Li, Qinggang Meng
bullets: Problem: VLMs struggle to determine whether objects were added, removed, or moved when viewpoints and lighting differ between visits.
Method: Use 3D geometry to register each change hypothesis’s location across captures, then have a VLM verify the object using scene and local-place views.
Training uses supervision matching the place-verification task.
Under the official SceneDiff protocol, obj/sc AP improves from 24.0 to 37.8, and from 11.6 to 20.6 on the egocentric kitchen subset without kitchen training data.
STILL improves F1 by over 21 points versus a similarly fine-tuned VLM, with roughly 11% runtime overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of STILL. (1) A high-recall proposer, SceneDiff by default, gives change hypotheses hi, each with a frame, a box and a geometric cost ci. (2) π3 reconstructs both captures jointly. Each hypothesis is lifted to 3D and projected into the other capture, and a depth occlusion test selects the frame in which its place is best visible, which gives the registered place pi. This step relies only on the static scene, so it stays correct where the object is gone. (3) One fine-tuned VLM answers two questions. The scene view (5+5 frames) asks whether the object is still at its place in the other capture, and the place view (object crop next to place crop) asks whether it is still at this place. The fused score si is thresholded at the operating point chosen on dev. The verifier is trained on per-object questions of the same form, built from real captures with same-capture hard controls and from synthetic two-view pairs.
