papers.abstract: Single-photon LiDAR (SPL) sensors offer exceptional temporal resolution and single-photon sensitivity for depth imaging. However, cost-effective SPL arrays typically suffer from extremely low spatial resolutions (e.g. $8\times 8$ pixels), limiting their real-world utility. In this paper, we propose a novel, one-step super-resolution framework, D2ToF, Distilled Diffusion for Time-of-Flight, that bridges the gap between high-fidelity generative modeling and real-time execution. Our approach uses an amortized variational distillation strategy that allows for a measurement-based data consistency term to be incorporated directly into the one-step training objective. This encourages that the synthesized high-resolution depth maps are consistent with the captured low-resolution Time-of-Flight (ToF) histograms. To overcome the severe ill-posedness of upsampling extremely degraded inputs, we introduce a multimodal guidance strategy. By leveraging a foundational monocular depth model to extract structural priors from a high-resolution reflectivity image, our network is guided by a rich triad of the ToF histogram, reflectivity map, and relative depth estimate. Experimental results outperform evaluated baselines, achieving $16\times$ spatial super-resolution (from $8\times 8 \times 100$ histograms to $128\times 128$ depth maps) at an accelerated inference speed of approximately $83$ milliseconds.
authors: Pallabjyoti Deka, Lewis Wilson, Stephen McLaughlin, Jonathan Leach, Abderrahim Halimi
bullets: Addresses the severe spatial-resolution limitations of cost-effective single-photon LiDAR arrays.
Uses amortized variational diffusion distillation with a measurement-based data-consistency objective.
Combines ToF histograms, reflectivity images, and monocular relative-depth priors to guide reconstruction.
Achieves 16× spatial super-resolution from 8×8×100 histograms to 128×128 depth maps.
Reports approximately 83 ms inference and outperforms the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Natural-language point-cloud localization typically retrieves candidate map cells and then predicts a position inside each candidate, yet the final output is still determined by retrieval order. A retrieval score measures region-description relevance, not whether the coordinates a region yields are accurate: a relevant region may produce a displaced prediction, and a lower-ranked region may contain a successful one. We study the final selection problem after the candidate pool and Fine predictions are fixed---how to choose the coordinate most likely to localize successfully, and under which conditions the gain holds. We propose SCAR (Spatial Consistency-Aware Reranking). SCAR treats each cell--Fine-coordinate pair as a localization hypothesis, interprets directional relations as functions of position, and reads spatial support at the backbone's actual Fine point (Fine-conditioned Evidence Readout). It organizes this readout with center support, semantic presence, retrieval score, and geometric offsets into a 23-D representation, trains a shared scorer with localization-success labels, and at inference reranks existing hypotheses and returns their original coordinates. Experiments cover four public backbones and a corrected Des4Pos reimplementation across five domains. Excluding one protocol-reference configuration, exploratory TEST point estimates on the remaining 24 configurations show Top-1@5\,m above Original on 23 and Cell R@1 above Original on all 24. On development-set VAL, the Fine readout improves Top-1@5\,m by 5.77 percentage points (pp) over a center surrogate on corrected Des4Pos*KITTI, and the complete scoring scheme improves it by 13.98\,pp over FSR on MambaPlace$\times$nuScenesFull; the latter measures the complete scheme, not learned ranking alone.
authors: Shuhan Dong, Tianyi Shang, Zhenyu Li
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between retrieval relevance and coordinate-level localization success.
Represents each cell–coordinate pair with fine-point spatial evidence, center support, semantic presence, retrieval scores, and geometric offsets.
Trains a shared scorer on localization-success labels, then reranks fixed hypotheses and returns their original coordinates.
Across 24 exploratory TEST configurations, Top-1@5 m improves over the original method in 23, while Cell R@1 improves in all 24.
Validation results show gains from fine-point readout and the complete scoring scheme, though the reported gains are protocol- and configuration-dependent.

papers.abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure the likelihood the models assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it. When the wall of each object is given, they place most objects against that wall, but do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts, and by less than two thirds when both priors are spatially smoothed. These results support the use of LLMs for object-room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.
bullets: The study evaluates Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it as spatial-prior generators for object-goal navigation.
Using CubiCasa5K and ScanNet layouts, it tests likelihoods on real and perturbed rooms and examines generated layouts.
Generated rooms capture room-type object frequencies and sizes, but not room-specific wall proximity or reliable room containment.
Models use provided object and wall information to place related objects, though generated placements often need geometric validation.
Generated priors reduce search area versus uniform search, but substantially less than priors learned from real layouts, especially after smoothing.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs as spatial priors for object-goal navigation, relevant to vision-language navigation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Evaluating Language Models as Spatial Priors for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: LLMs can encode object–room associations and constrained spatial relationships, but are weaker than real-layout priors for predicting where objects are placed in rooms.

papers.abstract: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.
authors: Weiru Zhang, Yuzhong Hong, Junwei Bao, Lemao Liu, Dejing Dou
bullets: Targets real-world K-12 handwritten essays, where text-only CGEC is insufficient.
Defines image-to-grounded-edit prediction: systems must output both corrections and their character-level positions.
Introduces G-CGEC-Eval with fine-grained annotations and IoU- and center-distance-based localization metrics.
Single-pass vision-language models perform poorly; OCR/grounding pipelines and agentic workflows improve results.
An error-type-based multi-agent workflow is the strongest baseline, while error discovery and character-level grounding remain key bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Many new AI models estimate how far away things are, in metres, from a single photo. To do this they must also work out what camera took the photo. We check whether they really do with a simple test: digital zoom, that is, cropping a photo and enlarging the crop back to full size. Zooming moves nothing in the scene, so a correct model should give the same distance for every point still in the picture. The test is free, exact and needs no labels. Two numbers describe a model's reaction: its depth changes like $s^{-\alpha}$ (ideal $\alpha=0$) and its focal-length estimate like $s^{\beta}$ (ideal $\beta=1$), for zoom factor $s$. On 800 images from KITTI, NYUv2 and DIODE, the widely used Depth Anything V2 has $\alpha=0.95$: it treats a zoomed photo almost as if the camera had moved closer, because it judges distance mainly from how large things look. Models that also predict the camera remove only part of this error ($\alpha\approx0.31$-$0.36$), because their focal estimate grows too little. Given the true camera, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested keep their depth ($\alpha\approx0$), so the error lies in their camera estimate. The reason: a zoomed photo is, pixel for pixel, a normal photo of a scene squashed in depth, so size alone cannot tell the two apart, and a focal estimator trained by regression stays close to the cameras it saw in training. Undoing this needs no labels or training and makes Depth Pro pass the test ($\alpha=0.04$) at almost no cost on normal photos. Controls, including a real optical zoom lens, rule out blur and resizing artefacts. Finally, label-free fine-tuning for self-consistency lowers $\alpha$ to 0.05 on KITTI and 0.07 on NYUv2 once a "blurry means zoomed" shortcut is removed; we report what this costs on normal and unseen photos.
bullets: Digital zoom should not change scene depth, making it a simple, exact, label-free consistency test.
Depth Anything V2 strongly confuses zoom with proximity, while camera-aware models reduce but do not eliminate the error.
With the true camera parameters, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested preserve depth, locating the remaining problem in camera estimation.
A camera-correction procedure makes Depth Pro nearly zoom-consistent at little cost on ordinary images.
Label-free fine-tuning further reduces zoom sensitivity, though the abstract notes trade-offs on normal and unseen photos.

papers.abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.
authors: Shiye Su, Xiaohan Wang, Ludwig Schmidt, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Existing text-to-image reward models struggle with attribute binding, relational reasoning, and counting.
Preference fine-tuning weakens the reasoning abilities of strong vision-language backbones, creating a tradeoff with preference accuracy.
The method converts visual-reasoning data into prompt-based preference pairs sharing the same image, then mixes them with human preference data.
This produces a Pareto improvement in visual reasoning and preference prediction.
Generation improves on compositional GenEval prompts by 4.0% with best-of-n selection and 5.5% with RL post-training, outperforming HPSv3 despite using fewer preference pairs.

papers.abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io
authors: Mariana Sosa Guzm\'an, Yide Song, Amin Abyaneh, Gregory Dudek, Hsiu-Chin Lin

Integrates risk fields into obstacle avoidance to modify nominal robot motions during execution.
Evaluated in simulation and the real world on preventable hazards, rejection-required tasks, and safe task variants.

papers.abstract: We study the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow for hyperbolic multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes in hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$. Our framework accommodates general permutation invariant relative margin (PERM) losses, a class that includes cross entropy and other standard multiclass losses. Our analysis is based on a decomposition: at large radius, the distance to each prototype splits into a radial term and a direction dependent term described by the Busemann function. This yields two main results. First, we prove a radial dichotomy: the sign of a drift coefficient $μ$ determines whether the radius is pushed toward the ideal boundary or back toward the interior; if the positive drift persists, then $r(t)=\tfrac12\log t+O(1)$, while persistent negative drift returns the trajectory to the large radius threshold in finite time. Second, we show that large-radius directions can approach critical points of the Busemann risk on $\partial\mathbb H^n$, even during radial return. These results provide a rigorous large-radius perspective on two phenomena we refer to as boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering in hyperbolic representation learning.
bullets: Studies Riemannian gradient flow with fixed hyperbolic class prototypes under general permutation-invariant relative-margin losses, including cross entropy.
Decomposes prototype distances at large radius into radial and direction-dependent Busemann terms.
Shows the drift coefficient’s sign determines whether trajectories move toward the ideal boundary or return toward the interior.
Under persistent positive drift, the radius grows as one-half log time plus a bounded term; persistent negative drift causes finite-time return to a large-radius threshold.
Shows directions can approach critical points of the boundary Busemann risk, including during radial return.

papers.abstract: Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize human-object pairs and recognize their interactions. Traditional supervised methods perform strongly but rely on task-specific training. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a promising route to training-free HOI detection through their broad visual-semantic knowledge and versatile perceptual and reasoning capabilities. However, existing approaches largely invoke these capabilities through loosely coordinated inference stages. This fragmented execution restricts the role of interaction hypotheses in guiding visual exploration, leaving key participants overlooked and local ambiguities unresolved. Furthermore, propagating early semantic assumptions through subsequent visual grounding and relation prediction induces self-reinforcing semantic circularity. To resolve these challenges, we propose HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that transforms passive MLLM inference into an active interaction-centric harness. Specifically, we introduce an interaction-guided perception mechanism that projects emerging interaction hypotheses back into the visual space to discover missing participants and refine ambiguous evidence through targeted observation. Furthermore, a relation-agnostic geometric adjudication module reconciles multi-source evidence to establish a unified spatial basis for grounded interaction reasoning across multiple actions and semantic roles. Extensive experiments on HICO-DET and V-COCO demonstrate that HarnessHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed harness for complex interaction understanding. Code will be released upon publication.
bullets: Targets fragmented MLLM inference, overlooked participants, unresolved visual ambiguities, and semantic circularity in training-free HOI detection.
Uses emerging interaction hypotheses to guide targeted visual exploration and discover missing human-object participants.
Applies relation-agnostic geometric adjudication to reconcile evidence across actions and semantic roles.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods on HICO-DET and V-COCO.
Code is planned for release upon publication.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.
bullets: Combines floor plans, RGB images and panoramas, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, 3D instance boxes, and camera-trajectory video.
Uses shared scene coordinates to align visual, geometric, and temporal observations.

Supports applications including 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance perception, video generation, world modeling, and scene editing.
Scope is focused on furnished residential 3D scene configurations and controlled spatial variations.

papers.abstract: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
authors: Shengtao Wu, Zichao Dong, Weixuan Qiao, Xiaolu Liu, Xin Zhan, Junbo Chen, Jianke Zhu
bullets: General VLMs transfer well to diverse driving tasks, but precise metric depth is the main limitation.
The framework trains on automatically constructed image–depth–QA triplets using three streams: task adaptation, depth-guided geometry learning, and frozen-model KL distillation.
The auxiliary depth branch is removed at deployment, preserving the original model’s open-world reasoning capabilities.
Evaluation covers 3D perception, driving language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding.
The method reportedly surpasses existing driving VLMs, approaches expert models in 3D perception, and retains general reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}
authors: Zhuo Han, Yeqiang Wang, Xinran Wang, Hongwei Han, Yi Xiong, Zunian Wan, Jianbo Mao, Huan Peng, Yongcheng Liu, Wei Shan, Maoqing Yao
bullets: Addresses VLA policies that overlook spatial structure and task history when making action decisions.
Adds features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model to temporal memory alongside visual representations.
Uses a principled scoring rule to select history that is relevant to the current observation and complementary to existing memory.
Achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods across LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge.
Improves real-world success over π₀.₅ by 58.33, 30.00, and 35.00 percentage points on block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, respectively.

Across real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, the tasks collectively stress geometry-sensitive manipulation and progress tracking through multi-step execution. Across four simulated benchmarks and three realworld manipulation tasks, STVLA consistently outperforms strong VLA, memory-augmented, and spatially aware baselines.

papers.abstract: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Xldln/RICapBench.
authors: Xue Wang, Yubin Xu, Kun Tan
bullets: Covers general, UAV, and dense small-object remote sensing scenes with 245,466 instance annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly capable, yet their reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes can remain coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence. We propose Gravity and Flight (G&F), a framework for scene specialization with limited supervision that separates visual and reasoning verification while coupling policy updates. It combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning (EoT-SFT) and Relational Transfer Policy Optimization (RTPO). EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis, and supported conclusions. RTPO independently samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained visual differences under a shared task. Its rubric-based verification combines Gravity, which checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight, which takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgments. Their scores and task correctness yield a shared pair-level advantage that couples policy updates from both responses. Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbor specialization, G&F achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls show gains over single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Applying G&F to urban specialization also improves on the base model and supervised initialization across three evaluation subsets. Project details and updates are available at https://github.com/Z0ngL1ng/Gravity-and-Flight.
authors: Yuheng Zong, Minghua Wang, Xin Zhao, Xiaobin Liu, Yongjian Dong, Chanho Eom
bullets: Targets coarse, insufficiently grounded reasoning in complex remote-sensing scenes.
Combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning with Relational Transfer Policy Optimization.
Uses Gravity to verify visual fidelity and coverage, and Flight to assess evidence use and paired relations.
For harbor specialization, achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, outperforming the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points.
Removing either verification view reduces performance; gains also transfer to urban specialization across three evaluation subsets.

papers.abstract: Distinguishing different heat sources in low-resolution infrared (IR) images is inherently difficult, as multiple thermal emitters often collapse into ambiguous and overlapping responses. Existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structures from such ambiguous 2D evidence, leading to thermal drift, boundary merging, and unreliable restoration under infrared degradations. We propose FlowIR, a depth-driven rectified flow framework that resolves thermal ambiguity by injecting 3D geometric cues into the generation process. Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects, while cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss further enforces geometric alignment during refinement. Built upon a lightweight rectified flow backbone, FlowIR restores IR images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust, and geometrically faithful high-resolution results.
authors: Xingyue Zhu, Qinyun Mei, Zhexi Min, Yang Zou, Xingyuan Li, Zhiying Jiang, Jinyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses thermal ambiguity in low-resolution IR images, where overlapping emitters cause boundary merging and unreliable restoration.
Injects pseudo-3D depth cues through depth-guided 3D convolutions to disentangle overlapping foreground objects.
Uses cluster-wise inter-attention to reduce feature contamination between distinct thermal sources.
Applies a Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss to preserve geometric alignment during refinement.
Its lightweight rectified-flow backbone enables restoration in only a few steps and improves robustness to IR degradations.

papers.abstract: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.
authors: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha, Zaid A. El Shair, Ali Al-Bustami, Samir A. Rawashdeh
bullets: Pothole detectors locate defects but generally do not assess severity or recommend actions; single-image severity estimation is inherently ambiguous.

The five-stage offline pipeline applies perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro classification with composite risk scoring, and warning generation.

Geometric grounding substantially changes warnings: it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier, increases critical-tier assignments by 109%, and is preferred 3.5:1 over image-only warnings in a blind study.

Severity agreement is weak with both human references and measured depth, although predictions preserve the ordering of measured depths; the categories should be interpreted as visual perceptions, not depth estimates.
The system costs USD 0.105 per scene and is intended for large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; maneuver suggestions are advisory and not validated vehicle guidance.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the problem of pothole severity assessment by integrating geometric measurements with VLM reasoning, providing a modular framework for infrastructure assessment that leverages spatial understanding.
papers.title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: A geometry-grounded VLM framework produces more useful pothole severity warnings than image-only assessment, but its severity classes are not reliable measurements of physical depth.

papers.abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.
authors: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Filip Rybansky, Quoc Vuong, Frank Guerin, Andrew Gilbert
bullets: Introduces sub-action detection, requiring explicit recognition of hand roles and manipulated objects during high-level actions.
Adds FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention module that emphasizes action-relevant visual cues without changing the underlying vision or language encoders.
Uses MetaLoss, a masked object-weighted loss that prioritizes visually grounded terms.
Introduces BiScopeCap-100K, a densely captioned egocentric video dataset with hand-role, object, action, and spatial metadata.
Improves action, hand-role, and object recognition across evaluated Video-LLM backbones, with the strongest aggregate performance among tested configurations on BiScopeCap.

papers.abstract: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle
authors: Shreelekha Revankar, Mikhail Klassen, Creon Levit, Ash Hoover, Kavita Bala, Bharath Hariharan
bullets: Targets the challenge of identifying where change occurs, what it becomes, and when it finishes across diverse event types.
Represents temporal change as vector differences between vision-language model embeddings to search for semantic transformations.
Uses this approach to automate global event discovery without manual annotation.
Introduces a dataset with 21,000+ locations, 64+ event types, and approximately 2 million satellite images across six continents.
The resulting model achieves 93.5% maximum F1, 3.6× stronger predicted-event retrieval than baselines, and 3-day median completion-date error up to nine months ahead.

papers.title: Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery
papers.tldr: A vision-language embedding approach enables open-vocabulary satellite event discovery and anticipation at global scale, detecting and forecasting events months before completion.

papers.abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes' rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92-100% of in-distribution and 92-100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12-22% of targets that were present, against 1.6-3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.
bullets: Models uncertainty over both object locations and which environmental nodes may conceal them using a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP.
Plans over room and object nodes through a hierarchical transition system.
Fuses human-informed semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs to initialize location beliefs, then updates them with Bayes’ rule.
Across five simulated settings, finds 92–100% of in- and out-of-distribution targets and generally matches or outperforms comparison methods.
Can declare a target absent at a stated error level; it abandons fewer present targets than a per-step LLM policy.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMBS, a multi-modal Bayesian search method that unifies ontologies, LLMs, and VLMs to locate concealed objects in partially observable environments.
papers.title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
papers.tldr: COMBS combines Bayesian search, hierarchical environment abstractions, and multimodal priors to efficiently find concealed objects while avoiding false conclusions that objects are absent.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io
authors: Arpit Jadon, Valentinos Pariza, Jona Ruthardt, Ryousuke Yamada, A. Sophia Koepke, Andrei Bursuc, Yuki M. Asano
bullets: Identifies interacting design factors for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing.

Legend ensembling improves segmentation by up to 8.7 mIoU points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining.
Releases data-processing, training, evaluation, and checkpoint resources for reproducibility; instance segmentation remains a weaker area.

papers.selection_reason: Unified recipe for converting generative models into multi-task perception, including depth estimation, relevant to spatial understanding.
papers.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception
papers.tldr: Open Vision Banana provides a fully open recipe for adapting image generators into unified multi-task vision systems, achieving strong segmentation and depth results with reproducible resources and test-time legend ensembling.

papers.abstract: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.
authors: Ameen Izhac, Nobuko Yoshida, Ronald Clark
bullets: Addresses the limited native spatial reasoning abilities of current vision-language models.
Builds a metric scene graph using feed-forward 3D reconstruction and open-vocabulary segmentation.
Lets the VLM query distances, object positions, and camera properties, then combine them for complex spatial tasks.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and VSTI-Bench, improving its base VLM by 15–22 points per benchmark.
Scope: relies on the quality and availability of real-time 3D reconstruction and object segmentation.

papers.abstract: This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning. Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity. For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments. This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors. In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction. On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.

papers.abstract: Infographic charts communicate data through cohesive compositions of visual elements such as charts, text, and images. Existing infographic chart datasets primarily annotate individual elements with bounding boxes and category labels. Such element-level annotations do not capture hierarchical and spatial relationships, limiting their use for understanding how elements are organized and related within an infographic and for generating well-organized designs. To address this limitation, we introduce ChartGalaxy++, a richly annotated dataset of 217,195 infographic charts. At the core of this dataset is a scene graph representation, in which nodes represent visual elements and semantic groups, and edges encode their hierarchical and spatial relationships. For real infographics, we construct scene graphs by detecting and progressively grouping visual elements; for synthetic ones, we derive them directly from the generation process. We demonstrate the utility of ChartGalaxy++ through three applications: 1) image-to-scene-graph prediction, 2) scene-graph-augmented infographic question answering, and 3) evaluation of scene graph preservation in image generation. Together, these applications highlight the value of ChartGalaxy++ for advancing chart understanding and generation.

papers.abstract: Language-guided place recognition requires recovering geographic identity across visual observations beyond the image from which a description originates. However, aggregate retrieval scores often entangle observation transfer, gallery competition, and linguistic evidence, obscuring the underlying recognition capability. We introduce AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark establishing a systematic evaluation standard for bidirectional language--vision place recognition. Built upon GSV-Cities, AcrossPlace comprises 56,726 places across 23 cities, 156,800 automatically generated, rule-filtered descriptions, and 113,404 target images. Each description retains its source-image provenance, while retrieval operates on disjoint target observations. Text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval share a unified place-identity relevance criterion supporting multiple valid matches. Two geographic protocols evaluate unseen places within represented cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1). Paired observation comparisons, gallery-controlled evaluations, fixed-query scaling, and blinded annotation auditing systematically characterize retrieval performance. Across three training seeds, place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 decreases from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0. For fixed P1 queries, expanding the gallery from 500 to 8,425 places reduces Recall@1 from 14.67% to 2.87%. A 240-description audit further reveals discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence. These findings establish AcrossPlace as a reproducible evaluation standard for assessing transferable place identity across visual observations and geographic environments.

papers.abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models for global weather forecasting achieve remarkable predictive accuracy, yet they frequently produce states that violate fundamental physical laws, including conservation of mass, hydrostatic balance, or spectral energy scaling. We term these outputs physical hallucinations and propose PhysXAI, a rigorous diagnostic framework that detects, localises, and attributes such inconsistencies. Unlike existing post-hoc metric suites, PhysXAI is a learnable system that explicitly decouples forecast error from physical plausibility. We formalise the problem through a novel joint condition on numerical and physical residuals, and introduce a multi-branch encoder that extracts representations from conservation, dynamical, spectral, cross-variable, and spatiotemporal residuals. A key innovation is a physics-consistency contrastive learning objective, which we theoretically show the latent representation to be approximately isometric to the physical residual space, ensuring that diagnostic decisions remain grounded in physically meaningful deviations. We further derive an adaptive multi-objective loss with gradient-based weighting to balance competing diagnostic objectives. The framework produces spatially resolved hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty, enabling both detection and interpretable attribution of physical inconsistencies. We conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of PhysXAI across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2, using forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM, with Python-written code and a fully reproducible experimental protocol. Our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation establish PhysXAI as a principled framework for diagnosing physical hallucinations and advancing trustworthy AI for weather forecasting.

papers.abstract: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at https://rslivebench.space

papers.abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.
authors: Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun, Hanwang Zhang

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how multimodal training shapes text-only spatial reasoning, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
papers.tldr: Multimodal training can causally induce vision-shaped representations that support text-only spatial reasoning, even without visual inputs.

papers.abstract: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.
authors: J. Zach Gazak, Ryan Swindle, Justin Fletcher
bullets: Introduces an open, procedural diagnostic using colored point clouds across 1D and 2D coordinate systems and four question types.
Open-weight VLMs perform near chance (47–52%), despite much higher scores on conventional spatial benchmarks.
Probes show spatial information is recoverable in both vision and language components, while text-only controls substantially outperform visual inputs.
Attention and component-tuning analyses localize the failure to mid-stack visual-integration and reasoning workspaces, where models identify answer sets but choose randomly.
LoRA fine-tuning brings 7B-class VLMs to frontier-level aggregate accuracy on Sophon, supporting a routing-bottleneck explanation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Sample Sophon stimuli, one per (question type, coordinate system) cell: 1D linear / categorical (left), Cartesian / binary (center), polar / quantitative (right). Each panel shows its coordinate system and ground truth transform parameter. No objects, scenes, or textures appear in any stimulus (Appendix B).

Figure 5: Per-layer GT vs competitor logit gap, five LoRA conditions, four architectures. Each panel projects the answer position hidden state through the unembedding WU at every decoder layer and reports the mean gap between the ground truth direction token and its same axis competitor (e.g. “left” vs “right”). The shaded region marks the reader band. In every architecture BASE and READER sit at or below zero throughout, so reader-band training installs no contrast. The three trained conditions rise late in the stack and largely coincide, and WORKSPACE’s contrast appears despite the reader band and WU being frozen. The reader band’s contrast emerges when the workspace is reorganized to feed it (§5.3).

Figure 4: Quantitative answer distribution taxonomy. Bar height is Pearson r between parsed answer and GT magnitude (n=200). Filled = stimulus engaged: Perceiver (r≥0.5, top-1<50%), Direction perceiver (r≥0.5, top-1≥50%). Hatched/outline = engagement failure: Noisy (r<0.5), Few anchor (top-3≥50%), Constant (top-1≥85%). Labels above bars are answer uniqueness (nunique/n). Human scale r reflects rater unit ambiguity. See all models version in Appendix U.

Figure 13: Sophon diagnostic heatmap, grouped by tier. Rows are organized into four bands: Human (Prolific n=30), Frontier closed weight (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4, Grok 4.20), Open 7B base (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-32B-AWQ, LLaVA-NeXT-7B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B), and Chance (per-cell random baseline). Columns are coordinate system × question type accuracy cells (1D Linear has no comparative) plus per-coord system rotation MAE and scale MAE columns. Each cell shows mean accuracy or MAE. Quantitative cells are diagonally hatched when parse rate is below 25% (numerically unreliable). Frontier accuracy cells include the 3-seed cross seed standard deviation ±s from the variance subset. Frontier models match or exceed humans on most binary cells but trail on categorical and comparative. Open 7B models cluster near per-cell chance. Grok 4.20 collapses to a near constant token output under greedy decode (Appendix I).
Figure 7: Binary examples across all three coordinate systems.
Figure 8: Categorical examples across all three coordinate systems.

Figure 18: Qwen2.5-VL-7B training volume curve, plus 1k points for the two other architectures. Error bars on the Qwen 1k point are 1σ across seeds 42/43/44, and other points are single seed. Sophon saturates at 5k, What’sUp is stable, and BLINK transfer peaks at 1k and regresses at higher volumes.

Figure 3: The readout-routing bottleneck: spatial content traverses encoder and decoder, then collapses at the readout. (a) Linear probe accuracy on Sophon direction classification at each encoder layer. Five frozen encoders cluster at 83−85% in mid-to-late layers regardless of pretraining objective (Appendix C). (b) Probe accuracy at the answer emission position across four open architectures, sampled at five depths each: 80−86% at every layer, including the final one. (c) Final layer probe accuracy (solid) vs. end-to-end Sophon categorical accuracy (hatched) across the same four decoders. Figure 14: Decoding temperature partially releases Grok-4.20’s constant token attractor on categorical cells but not on binary cells, and does not improve the per-model mean accuracy of any frontier VLM. Top panel: constant token rate (fraction of samples assigned the most common parsed answer) versus decode temperature for the 15 (model, cell) combinations that collapse at temp=0 (const ≥ 85%). Lines staying above the 85% threshold indicate a persistent attractor, and lines dropping below indicate a decode induced artifact. All three GPT-4o (purple) cells release, as does the single Sonnet 4.6 (orange) cell. Of Grok-4.20’s 11 collapsed cells, 4 release (the categorical cells on Cartesian trans x, Cartesian trans y, Cartesian rotation, plus the rotation quantitative cell) while the 7 binary and comparative cells stay ≥ 88% at every temperature. Bottom panel: per-model mean accuracy across all 11 scoreable cells in the 5-spec subset, plotted against decode temperature. Frontier models that succeed at greedy decode (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) remain approximately flat (∆ ≤ +5 pp from τ=0 to τ=1.0). GPT-4o degrades ∼ 11 pp. Grok-4.20 stays at chance across the entire sweep. The full per-cell breakdown backing both panels is reported in Table 5.

Figure 22: Opus 4.6. Quantitative answer distribution vs. ground truth on the four (coordinate system, transform) cells. Each panel overlays the ground truth histogram (gray fill) with no hint predictions (red, solid edge) and range hint predictions (blue, hatched). The two horizontal range bars at the top show the no hint stimulus support (red dashed) and the explicit range supplied by the hint (blue solid), and mode of response annotations point at the dominant text anchor in each condition. The polar scale panel is the only cell where Opus 4.6 tracks the stimulus continuously (r=0.80, perceiver class). The other three panels collapse to a single mode near 90◦ or ∼1.0 regardless of GT (canonical few anchor). Range hints shrink the support of the predicted distribution but do not move the mode toward GT, which is the basis for our claim that hints constrain the answer set rather than reveal perception.
Figure 19: Cross-coordinate transfer asymmetry across three open architectures we test.

Figure 24: GPT-5.4. Same layout as Fig. 22 (no range hint condition was run for GPT-5.4, so the blue series is absent). Both scale cells reach perceiver (r=0.79 each), the only frontier model in our suite that does so on Cartesian scale. Rotation distributions remain noisy (r=0.37 Cartesian, r=0.47 polar). Rotation values spread but are not strongly correlated with GT.

Figure 23: GPT-4o. Same layout as Fig. 22. Polar scale is the lone non degenerate cell (r=0.62, direction perceiver, meaning the model tracks scale direction up vs. down but does not produce continuous magnitude). Cartesian scale collapses to a single anchor (r=0.09, constant), and both rotation cells are few anchor at ∼45◦.

Figure 21: All models version of the quant response taxonomy (Fig. 4 shows only Human plus the four current/recent closed weight flagships). Adds Grok 4.20 and four open 7B–32B models. The five classes and the color scheme match the main-paper figure: Perceiver, Direction perceiver, Noisy, Few anchor, Constant (neutral grey). Numerical labels are the percentage of responses that are unique values. None of the additional models reaches the perceiver or direction perceiver class on any cell. Qwen2.5-VL-7B Cartesian rotation (u=1%, top-1=98%) and Grok 4.20 polar-rotation (u=5%, top1=97%) are canonical Constant cells. LLaVA-NeXT polar rotation (u=11%, top-1∼37%, r=−0.11) is the noisiest entry, with many distinct guesses and none correlated with GT.

Figure 20: Vocabulary distractor effect across five categorical specs. Each dumbbell connects random restricted accuracy (open marker, 2 transform appropriate direction words offered) to random full accuracy (filled marker, all 6 direction words offered, order randomized in both conditions). The translation (Cartesian Translation X / Translation Y) and polar Radial (radial translation, answer choices inward / outward) cells plunge toward the 6-way chance floor under the full vocabulary across both open (Qwen-7B, NeXT-7B) and frontier (GPT-4o, Opus 4.6) tiers. The extra rotation tokens (clockwise, counterclockwise) draw probability mass away from the correct translation answer even though the underlying transform is not rotational. The Cartesian Rotation control stays flat because rotation vocabulary is already among the choices in both conditions, so widening the option set adds no novel distractors. The pattern is consistent across capability tiers, supporting the claim that the failure is at the answer set interface rather than at perception.

Figure 17: Qwen-VL ViT probes after 10k Sophon fine tuning (LoRA 10k). The shift in Sophon direction peak from L14 to L31 relative to the base (Fig. 15) is small relative to the decoder side end-to-end gain.
