papers.selection_reason: Procedural diagnostic for spatial reasoning in VLMs, identifies routing bottleneck and shows fine-tuning improves spatial intelligence, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Sophon reveals that open-weight VLMs often contain spatial information but fail to route it through their reasoning circuitry, a bottleneck that targeted LoRA fine-tuning can repair.

papers.abstract: Radar systems can recover scene geometry and recognize predefined categories, but these outputs do not provide a persistent spatial representation for open-ended language queries. Such queries require linking observations from different viewpoints to the same physical locations. We present TextRadar, a framework that constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from panoramic radar observations. The field combines occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations, allowing the reconstructed scene to be queried with new descriptions. A single-frame radar distillation model predicts aligned ranges and language features from each radar observation. Using radar-estimated poses, we register these predictions to reconstruct the field from radar alone in a new scene. Experiments on approximately 20k synchronized observations across seven buildings demonstrate scene-level natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization. Analysis of camera-to-radar concept transferability shows stronger agreement for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.
bullets: Addresses the lack of spatially persistent, language-queryable representations in radar-based scene understanding.
Distills each radar observation into aligned geometry and language features, then registers them using radar-estimated poses.
Constructs a scene-level field combining occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations.
Demonstrates natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization across seven buildings and about 20k synchronized observations.
Concept transfer is stronger for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

figures.caption: Fig. 13 Overview of the TextRadar framework. A rotating mmWave radar provides high-resolution panoramic RF measurements, while a front-facing camera supplies multiscale language supervision during data collection. Building on these inputs, TextRadar jointly learns geometry and language-aligned embedding from RF measurements and builds a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field, which supports several tasks.

Fig. 3 Scene-level natural-language querying of small structures and objects. The field localizes architectural structures, including (a) “Stairs” and (b) “Windows,” as well as compact objects, including (c) “Trash bin” and (d) “Human.” The RGB images provide representative observations of the queried regions, with dashed boxes indicating the corresponding targets. For categories with multiple instances, such as stairs and windows, the system simultaneously highlights geometrically separated regions throughout the scene.

Fig. 2 Scene-level natural-language querying of large building structures. The reconstructed geometry is colored according to the cosine similarity between the scene-level feature at each surface point and the CLIP text embedding of the query. Warmer colors indicate higher semantic relevance. The queries (a) “Ceiling” and (b) “Floor” activate complementary upper and lower surfaces across multiple corridors and room regions. The spatially coherent responses over distant parts of the environment show how the persistent occupancy-language field associates related structures across a common 3D coordinate system.

Fig. 5 Natural-language querying of high-level concepts. The prompts describe human configuration, affordances, and functional regions: (a) “Standing” localizes a standing person, (b) “Going down” highlights a descending staircase, (c) “Things to sit” retrieves a bench and other seating, (d) “Taking a rest” identifies a shared seating area, (e) “Entrance to other places” highlights doorways and passages, and (f) “Working region” identifies the occupied workspace in a laboratory office. These examples show responses to contextual prompts beyond direct object and material names.

Fig. 9 Radar-camera feature disagreement. The top row highlights concepts dominated by visual content: (a) televisions and monitors, (b) information signs, and (c) exhibition boards. The bottom row highlights appearance-dependent concepts: (d) ribbed texture, (e) yellow color, and (f) roughness and grid patterns. Dashed boxes mark the relevant regions in the RGB observations. While the camera-derived features clearly distinguish these regions by displayed content, color, or fine surface appearance, the radar-predicted features often assign them similar embeddings and thus fail to distinguish them.

Fig. 1 TextRadar constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from radar observations. A robot collects panoramic mmWave measurements along a trajectory (left). Surface geometry and language features predicted from these measurements are integrated in shared 3D coordinates (center). The right panels illustrate natural-language querying, prompt-free semantic visualization, and camera-to-radar concept transferability. The query “Things to sit” highlights a bench, while the feature visualization reveals semantic organization without specifying a prompt. Comparisons of radarpredicted and camera-derived features show stronger agreement for structures, objects, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

Fig. 8 Prompt-free semantic visualization of material-related regions. The examples show (a) wood doors, (b) a glass window, and (c) a metal cabinet. The highlighted material regions occupy distinct portions of the projected feature space and therefore appear with colors different from their surrounding walls and structures. The agreement between the radar-predicted and camera-derived PCA images indicates material-related information being retained beyond range geometry alone.

Fig. 6 Prompt-free semantic visualization of general indoor structures. For each example, the rows from top to bottom present the rendered panoramic RGB image, the predicted range image, the three-component PCA projection of the radar-predicted CLIP features, and the corresponding camera-derived reference projection. The predicted and reference features are projected using a shared PCA basis, and the three principal components are mapped to RGB channels. Similar colors therefore indicate nearby positions in the projected semantic feature space, rather than predefined semantic classes. Large structural regions, including ceilings, floors, walls, corridor openings, and wall-mounted structures, form spatially coherent groups in the radar-predicted visualization and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference.

Fig. 4 Geometry and natural-language queries. Each example shows, from top to bottom, the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the range image predicted from the radar measurement, the query-relevancy map obtained from the radarpredicted CLIP-aligned features, and the corresponding map obtained from the camera-derived reference features. Warmer colors indicate higher cosine similarity to the text query. The queries cover materials, including (a) “Glass,” (b) “Metal,” and (c) “Marble”; objects, including (d) “Trash bin,” (e) “Chairs,” and (f) “Human”; and structures, including (g) “Stairs,” (h) “Floor,” and (i) “Ceiling.” The radar-predicted maps localize both compact objects and extended structural regions, remain spatially consistent with the recovered geometry, and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference maps.

Fig. 7 Prompt-free semantic visualization of structures and objects. The examples examine (a) stairs, (b) humans, and (c) chairs, with two scenes shown for each concept. The dashed boxes in the rendered RGB image indicate the structures or objects of interest. A shared PCA projection is used for each prediction-reference comparison, allowing their color organization to be compared directly. Stairs, human silhouettes, and individual chairs emerge as coherent regions whose boundaries follow the corresponding geometry, despite some differences in their sizes, shapes, and spatial extents.

Fig. 11 Example scenarios in our dataset. The dataset spans common indoor environments, including hallways, lounges, offices, classrooms, and open floor areas. These examples are captured by the front-facing camera on the robot and illustrate the visual context used to generate language supervision.

Fig. 12 Radar-camera feature disagreement around glass. Each column presents one example, and the rows show the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the radar-predicted range image, and the pixelwise cosine similarity between radarpredicted and camera-derived CLIP features. Dashed orange boxes indicate glass windows. Warmer colors represent stronger feature agreement, and cooler colors represent weaker agreement. Similarity decreases around the indicated glass regions, where the two sensors observe different scene content.

Fig. 10 Hardware platform for data collection. The mobile robot carries a rotating mmWave MIMO radar, a 3D LiDAR, and a front-facing camera. A stepper motor rotates the radar, while the battery and WiFi router rotate with the radar to prevent cable twisting and are placed behind it for weight balancing. Radar commands are sent through the wireless router. (a) Front view. (b) Rear view.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TextRadar, a framework for constructing 3D occupancy-language fields from mmWave radar, enabling natural language querying of 3D scenes.
papers.title: 3D Occupancy-Language Fields from mmWave Radar
papers.tldr: TextRadar builds a persistent 3D occupancy-language representation from panoramic mmWave radar, enabling open-ended natural-language scene queries without cameras.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems need geometric perception that exploits available observations beyond images alone. Recent feed-forward 3D models incorporate geometric priors, including camera poses, intrinsics, and depth. However, handling noisy poses, preserving accurate priors, and recovering physical scale require more than simply accepting these inputs. We introduce \emph{Vision-Prior Geometry Grounded Transformer} (VPGGT), a VGGT-based framework that extends OmniVGGT for prior-aware embodied perception. We formulate sensor-motivated pose corruptions from ground-truth trajectories for training and introduce a parameter-free \emph{prior residual connection} (PRC) to mitigate \emph{prior dilution}, where predictions are less accurate than their supplied pose priors. Our noise formulation targets camera poses; supplied intrinsics and depth receive no additional corruption. We further introduce \emph{Metric Global Attention}, which conditions a global scale token on available pose and depth scales and predicts a shared metric scaling factor for the geometric outputs. Experiments across four datasets show that \emph{PRC} improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC over a matched training baseline when camera priors are provided for all views, under both exact and corrupted poses. These results support explicit prior access during refinement as a useful addition to feature-level conditioning.
bullets: Addresses noisy camera poses, prior dilution, and missing physical scale in prior-aware geometric perception.
Introduces sensor-motivated camera-pose corruption for training while leaving supplied intrinsics and depth uncorrupted.
Adds a parameter-free Prior Residual Connection to retain and refine pose priors explicitly.
Uses Metric Global Attention to predict a shared scale factor from available pose and depth scales.
Across four datasets, PRC improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC with exact or corrupted pose priors.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VPGGT. Images and optional camera or depth priors are encoded and processed by a shared alternating-attention backbone. PRC places available camera priors in the camera head’s refinement state after its initial prediction. A Scale Encoder conditions a global token on available metric-scale statistics, using learned placeholders when they are absent. The camera, depth, and pointmap heads predict geometry, and a scale head supplies a shared factor that converts translations, depths, and points to metric units.

Figure 5: Pose-prior corruption in the training data. Two examples are shown for each dataset. Within each panel, the left plot displays the complete trajectory, while the right plot displays a selected segment of the same ground-truth and corrupted trajectories. Colors identify the ground truth and corruption realizations, as indicated by the plot legends. Ground-truth and corrupted poses share a coordinate system, without independently fitted trajectory or scale alignment. Spatial units and segment information are provided in the plots.

Figure 2: Prior dilution during camera refinement. A0 is released OmniVGGT; A1 uses the same checkpoint with PRC enabled, without additional training. All views receive camera priors; no depth is supplied. Colors distinguish methods and markers distinguish datasets. Dashed lines show input-prior scores. Reset is a state intervention, not a learned iteration.
Figure 4: Prior Residual Connection. PRC retains feature-level conditioning and supplies aligned camera priors as the state from which subsequent residual updates are predicted.

Table 1: Ablation of auxiliary information guidance. Depth and pose accuracy with varying prior coverage. Bold identifies the better score between the matched-training OmniVGGT-trained and PRC-only models at identical input settings; released-model and input-prior references are not ranked. Blue parentheses report PRC-only gains over OmniVGGT-trained, in percentage points, with full camera priors and no depth input. Depth is median-aligned per frame; RTA and AUC use sign-free translation errors.
Table 6: Base pose-corruption parameters before severity scaling. Time-scaled white increments use a reference interval of 0.1 s.

ATE is in millimeters for C3VD and meters for the other datasets. All three metrics are lower-is-better; different input settings are not ranked against one another.

papers.selection_reason: Explicitly targets prior-aware geometric perception for embodied systems, with direct relevance to spatial intelligence and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Deep Prior Learning for Embodied Perception
papers.tldr: VPGGT improves embodied 3D perception by explicitly preserving camera-pose priors and recovering metric scale under noisy pose inputs.

papers.abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.
authors: Enhao Cui, Junzhi Yang, Yaoshun Lin, Yuhan Feng, Zijian Chen
bullets: The study tests whether left/right judgments come from image content, ViT position codes, or language-model token positions.
Mirroring ViT width positions reproduces flipped-image answers on 84.3–93.2% of CV-Bench left/right questions across several Qwen and InternVL models.
The effect is concentrated in global-attention ViT blocks, especially the final block in Qwen2.5-VL-7B; shifting the position grid also changes many answers.
Mirroring LLM-side token IDs or order produces few left/right changes, whereas reversing object order substantially affects some CV-Bench answers.
What'sUp results qualify the finding: many errors appear tied to relation binding, object localization, or use of the reference object.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes spatial reasoning in VLMs via position-code counterfactuals, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3
papers.tldr: Mirroring a ViT’s horizontal position code often flips vision-language models’ left/right answers, while language-side position changes have little effect, though object order and relation binding also influence errors.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.
authors: Kim Alexander Christensen, Dina Zimmermann, Martin Steinert, Eleni Kelasidi
bullets: A representative outdoor 3D scene-graph method transfers reasonably to maritime environments for many geometry-supported objects, but produces substantial physical-entity fragmentation.
The method preserves the underlying mapper and post-processes accumulated evidence to consolidate fragments using metric-semantic cues and geometry-grounded multi-view VLM reasoning.
Consolidated entities are grouped into local places, while maritime macro regions are built from map priors and onboard water and structure observations.
The resulting representation reduces fragmentation, supports matching fixed local places across repeated traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on reviewed queries over tested baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the maritime scene-memory pipeline. It first accumulates persistent map fragments and their observation histories, followed by a conservative geometricsemantic consolidation. Selected geometrically grounded multi-view observations are then processed by a visionlanguage model (VLM) at two abstraction levels: physicalentity reconciliation decides which fragments belong to the same object, while place formation groups persistent entities and observations into meaningful local places. In parallel, coarse maritime regions are derived from geographic topology and onboard water/structure evidence. Local places are associated with these regions and corresponding places are related across repeated traversals, forming a persistent scene memory for contextual retrieval.
Fig. 3: Macro regions compared. The first is defined by [39] while P00 and P03 are from our method. The regions are largely consistent, with one small extra region in P03.

Fig. 4: Place persistence and retrieval at the Northern port quay. The same fixed setting is matched despite different vessel occupancy and reconstructed geometry. Place relations retrieve 6/6 reviewed vessel records across P00 and P03, compared with 3/6 for the 50m radius baseline centered at the P00 anchor location in both surveys.
Fig. 2: Representative view of the MUT north bank showing (a) B0 fragmentation, (b) C050+VLM objects, and (c) local places.
TABLE I: Physical-entity evaluation on MUT dataset. Each bank reports recovered vessels, nodes per recovered vessel, and fragmented recovered vessels.
TABLE II: Contextual retrieval on Pohang.

papers.selection_reason: Adapts open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs into persistent maritime metric-semantic scene memory with geometry-grounded VLM reasoning; directly fits embodied memory and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Persistent Metric-Semantic Maritime Scene Memory from Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graphs
papers.tldr: Adapting open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs with geometry-semantic consolidation and maritime spatial abstractions enables more persistent, coherent scene memory for robots operating across repeated maritime traversals.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.
authors: Lorenzo Cirillo, Irene Amerini, Andrea Cavallaro
bullets: Deep neural networks are difficult to interpret because their layered activations encode complex, interdependent relationships.
Individual neurons may represent multiple concepts, complicating direct interpretation.
Mechanistic interpretability analyzes components whose activations are causally responsible for model behaviors.
The article reviews advances, methods, and frameworks for causal analysis across image, audio, and language-processing systems.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Categorization of mechanistic interpretability, along with representative methods under each category.

Fig. 6. Combining mechanistic interpretability categories at neuron granularity: activations are observed through visualization, isolated through disentanglement, tested for behavioral impact through causal intervention, and are part of the circuit responsible for the model behavior if the causal intervention on that activation changes the prediction.

Fig. 3. Sparse autoencoder applied to the linear module activation of a transformer block at module granularity. Each monosemantic feature in the hidden space of the sparse autoencoder reacts to the input concept it is associated with.

Fig. 4. Activation patching for ViT-B/16 audio spectrogram classification at module granularity. (a) Interchange ablation on the feed forward module of the first transformer block. Injecting the base run activation into the target run alters the logits and restores the vacuum cleaner prediction. (b) Logits for vacuum cleaner ( ) and rain ( ) during activation patching applied to every feed forward module separately. Patching any of the first three feed forward modules raises the vacuum cleaner logit, reverting the prediction from rain.

Fig. 5. Edge attribution patching with zero ablation for the convolutional autoencoder at layer granularity. (a) Estimation of ∆M for the first encoder layer. The performance metric M is the Mean Squared Error (MSE). A scalar ∆M score is obtained by summing all elements of the resulting ∆M tensor. (b) ∆M for each layer. The top-k layers ( ) with the highest ∆M scores (k = 3 is chosen for this implementation) constitute the circuit responsible for reconstructing the input image. The remaining layers ( ) are excluded from the circuit.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a comprehensive overview of mechanistic interpretability for deep neural networks. This review is relevant to understanding the internal mechanisms of Language Foundation Models and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
papers.tldr: This article surveys mechanistic interpretability methods for uncovering how internal neural-network components causally produce specific behaviors.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.
authors: Sandarbh Agrawal, Rakshith Sathish, Ashwathi Nambiar
bullets: Compares five architecture- and objective-matched EO/generic encoder pairs among 14 frozen encoders across five RGB scene-classification datasets and six low-label splits.
Tests k-NN, linear and attentive probes, and image retrieval using native preprocessing and paired per-image significance tests.
EO pretraining significantly helps some pairs but hurts others—even for MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery.
Effects are strongest with 1–5% labels, concentrate on small man-made objects, and persist across token pooling and attentive probing.
Frozen-embedding silhouette score strongly predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval performance on four of five datasets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.
authors: Xianping Ma, Yu Zhang, Mingzhe Jiang, Wanxin Xie, Qing Zhu, Nan Xu, Xiaokang Zhang, Yuanxin Ye
bullets: Reframes cross-modal pairing from exact instance alignment to class-consistent semantic alignment.
Uses a latent-factor analysis to show semantic structure is preserved while instance-specific correlations are averaged out.
Introduces MixPair to continuously control the degree of exact versus semantic pairing.
Experiments find SemPair performs comparably to exact pairing, while transfer varies non-monotonically with the exact-pair ratio.
Suggests reducing reliance on costly instance-aligned multimodal data for scalable pretraining.

papers.title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
papers.tldr: SemPair shows that multimodal remote sensing pretraining can learn transferable representations from semantically matched, non-identical cross-modal pairs rather than requiring exact instance correspondence.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
authors: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren, Yidan Zhang, Peijin Wang, Xian Sun, Kun Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of verifiable evidence in report-level disaster assessment using vision-language models and agents.
Uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow over bitemporal optical imagery.
Builds a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph to organize disaster-related changes across space and time.
Extracts graph evidence and attaches inline citations, creating a link from each report statement to supporting imagery.
Outperforms compared baselines on DisasterM3 and RSCC, with reported gains of 13.5% and 15.34% on the respective metrics.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of DisasterAgent. The framework processes multimodal inputs through two primary stages. (2) Skill-Guided Workflow: Guided by the registered skills, the framework sequentially executes a three-step pipeline comprising Perception, Evidence-based Augmentation, and Generation.

papers.title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
papers.tldr: DisasterAgent generates disaster reports from before-and-after satellite imagery with structured, citation-linked visual evidence for verifiability.

papers.abstract: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
authors: Boyan Han, Xiaoyan Wang, Zhe Sun, Ziqi Wang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Liang An
bullets: A general-audio codec retains spatial information despite being trained without spatial supervision, with lateral cues encoded in the left–right channel difference.
Naively using these features fails in dual-source scenes because audio describes both sources while the answer refers to only the queried one.
A controlled 2×2 study finds that complete scene descriptions or exposing inter-channel differences improves left/right accuracy; both are needed for source-direction binding.

AURA freezes both the codec and language model, yet surpasses the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy with about 40% of its trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 5: AURA architecture. (a) Existing dedicated spatial pathways and general-audio pathways are separate and rely on different feature spaces, so features cannot be shared for unified perception. (b) AURA provides a shared, frozen general-audio codec representation that unifies perception in a single audio feature space. (c) Details of the AURA pipeline: for each ear, RVQ layers L0–L2 and L3–L7 are summed into content-oriented (S) and acoustic-oriented (A) bands, and adding the band-wise interaural difference yields six slots. A shared projector maps these slots to audio tokens for the language model, which generates a scene description and, for relation questions, a geometric analysis before the final answer.

papers.selection_reason: Develops AURA, a unified audio-language model for auditory spatial intelligence, focusing on spatial reasoning and understanding spatial relationships in audio.
papers.title: AURA: Auditory Spatial Intelligence via a Unified Representation from a General-Audio Encoder through Complete Alignment
papers.tldr: AURA shows that a frozen general-audio codec can support spatial question answering when inter-channel cues and queried-source binding are properly aligned.

papers.abstract: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. To address these challenges, we propose RaRe, a reasoning-aware relational representation learning framework that transforms MLLM-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales into structured relation embeddings. Rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace for final prediction, RaRe directly optimizes the rationale-derived representation space to improve inter-relation discriminability. Specifically, RaRe first aligns rationale embeddings with textualized relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning, and then refines rationale generation with a specificity-oriented reinforcement learning objective that encourages semantically object-pair-specific relational evidence. Experiments on VG150 and PSG demonstrate improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines, while the additional gains from learning vary across datasets and proposal settings. Code available at: https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe.
authors: Jiawei Xiao, Boya Wang, Longtian Qiu, Shan Ning, Xuming He
bullets: Targets bias and entanglement caused by object–predicate co-occurrence patterns, long-tailed data, and noisy localization.
Aligns rationale embeddings with textual relation descriptions using self-supervised contrastive learning.
Uses specificity-oriented reinforcement learning to encourage relation evidence tailored to each object pair.
Experiments on VG150 and PSG show improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines.
Additional gains vary across datasets and proposal settings.

papers.abstract: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. Extensive experiments on a large-scale internal dataset (seen during training) and held-out evaluation on three external datasets demonstrate that P2Echo matches or exceeds both view-specific specialists and state-of-the-art universal models at a fraction of their computational cost, offering an efficient, controllable solution for multi-plane cardiac analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/P2Echo.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.
authors: Zhaoyi Liu, Haichuan Zhang, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Bowei Tian, Wanghao Ye, Yufan Zhang, Ang Li
bullets: MRoPE assigns spatial coordinates to both visual and text tokens, potentially affecting text–vision attention.
The work separates intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to study their distinct roles.
It identifies a limitation of shared coordinate layouts that prevents removing cross-modal effects without also losing visual spatial encoding.
Controlled experiments across model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks find that spatial references for text tokens provide little benefit and can impair performance.
Intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.
authors: Hao-Chih Lee, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
bullets: Addresses the challenge of clinically meaningful 3D pathology localization from weak, scan-level supervision.
Generates pathology predictions and localization maps from pathology-conditioned query–image feature similarities.
Uses token-to-voxel upsampling for high-resolution maps and gradient-guided thresholding without extra learned parameters.
Across five tasks and 355 annotated CT scans, achieves 96.1% voxel-level AUROC and 34.5% AUPR, outperforming the compared saliency methods.
Reports classification AUROCs of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline.

papers.abstract: Accurate and timely identification of road closures is critical for large-scale navigation and logistics systems, yet remains challenging due to the need to jointly reason over visual evidence, spatial context, and road network topology. Existing approaches either rely on manual map updates or focus on detecting closure-related objects without resolving which road segment is affected. In this work, we introduce a unified multimodal and multitask framework that jointly performs road closure classification (no, partial, complete) and road segment association within a single learning architecture. Our model integrates graph-structured map data, satellite imagery augmented with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention, enabling explicit reasoning over visual cues and network topology. Evaluated on nearly 20K real-world scenarios collected from a large-scale commercial vehicle fleet, our approach achieves 72.7% closure classification accuracy and 60% road segment association accuracy, outperforming frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on closure classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster at inference. Extensive ablations demonstrate the importance of cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing for accurate geospatial reasoning. This work establishes the first benchmark for joint road closure classification and segment-level attribution, and shows that task-specific architectural inductive biases substantially outperform general-purpose multimodal models for structured geospatial understanding.
authors: Izzeddin Teeti, Vaibhav Kango, Nidhi Sridhar, Mohamed Moustafa
bullets: Targets timely, segment-level road-closure mapping for navigation and logistics.
Fuses map graphs, satellite imagery with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention.
Performs joint classification of no, partial, or complete closure and road-segment association.
Evaluated on nearly 20K fleet-collected real-world scenarios, achieving 72.7% classification accuracy and 60% segment-association accuracy.

Outperforms frontier vision-language models on classification while using substantially fewer parameters and faster inference; results highlight the value of graph reasoning and cross-modal attention.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding maps a screenshot and a natural-language instruction to the screen location where an agent should act. Zoomed views can reveal small targets but may lose the context needed to identify them. We introduce GroundCascade, a training-free controller that uses agreement between a grounder's full-screen and zoomed predictions to decide when to consult a complementary model. It selects between zoomed predictions while preserving corroborated full-screen locations. An optional Finalizer predicts from an unmarked joint crop when disagreement remains (Full); omitting it yields the two-stage Selective variant. GroundCascade reaches 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro with Indeed-UI-32B/8B/32B and 88.43% on the visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined subset with Qwen3.6-27B/3.8-27B/3.8-27B, gains of 2.66 and 2.35 percentage points over the stronger standalone two-pass grounder. On UI-Vision, GroundCascade reaches 72.20% category-balanced accuracy, with Selective slightly higher at 72.28%. Across these three evaluations, GroundCascade in Full mode uses 2.42-2.73 calls per request, 31-39% fewer than unconditionally acquiring both models' two-pass predictions. At matched second-model call budgets, selective acquisition gains 1.52-2.56 points over standalone Two-pass, compared with 0.22-0.69 points from stratified random acquisition. GroundCascade leads the official ScreenSpot-Pro leaderboard and exceeds reported GUI-specialist comparisons on OSWorld-G-Refined and UI-Vision, subject to differences in external evaluation protocols.
bullets: GUI grounding must balance zoomed detail against full-screen context, which can cause incorrect target selection.
The training-free controller compares full-screen and zoomed predictions, preserving corroborated locations and consulting a complementary model selectively.
An optional Finalizer resolves remaining disagreements from an unmarked joint crop; the Selective variant omits it.
It achieves 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 88.43% on visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined, and 72.20–72.28% on UI-Vision.
Full mode uses 31–39% fewer model calls than unconditional two-model, two-pass acquisition; results depend on external evaluation protocols.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can render a photorealistic analog clock but cannot control the time it displays. Across four pretrained models, fewer than 1% of generated clocks place both hands within 6 degrees of the requested time; the models instead collapse onto visually dominant configurations such as the canonical 10:10 pose. The same failure appears when a specific fraction of a circular object is requested, where models return complete or conventionally sliced objects. We observe that these two failures share a geometric structure: both target quantities can be parameterized by angular variables. We introduce a geometric token encoding framework that conditions generation directly on these angles. Each angular component is encoded as a periodic sine-cosine feature and projected into a role-specific token embedding that is injected into the prompt before a frozen text encoder. To spatially ground these tokens without requiring localization input at inference, we introduce Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR), which stochastically relaxes attention supervision from component-level to object-level to unconstrained localization during training. For clocks, we additionally introduce a hand-swap preference objective that discourages assigning the correct angles to the wrong hand roles. On analog clocks our method reaches 63-78% Acc@6 degrees across evaluation methods, compared with below 1% for the baselines. On circular-fraction generation, it achieves 89.5% Acc@0.10, while maintaining 88.8% on unseen object categories and 84.9% on unseen target values, compared with roughly 20% for pretrained baselines.
authors: Furkan G\"uzelant, Basavaraj Sunagad, Aysegul Dundar, Adam Kortylewski
bullets: Problem: Text-to-image models struggle to generate objects with precisely requested angular configurations, often defaulting to common visual patterns.
Method: Encode target angles with periodic sine-cosine features as role-specific prompt tokens, using Stochastic Localization Relaxation to ground them spatially.
Clock generation adds a hand-swap preference objective to preserve the roles of the hour and minute hands.
The method achieves 63–78% clock accuracy within 6° versus below 1% for baselines, and 89.5% accuracy for circular fractions versus roughly 20%.
It generalizes to unseen object categories and target values, reaching 88.8% and 84.9% accuracy, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Left: Overview of our geometric token encoding framework, illustrated for clock-time control. The target clock time (h,m) or fraction-sector boundaries are encoded as sinusoidal pairs and mapped through the projection network P to produce role-specific geometric tokens eh, em (or es, ee) injected into the prompt before the frozen text encoder. Both tasks share the same MLP architecture and condition a LoRA-adapted SD 2.1 denoising U-Net. Right: Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR). Training samples one of three localization regimes (55/30/15%): component-level CALL using component boxes, object-level CALL using a shared object box, and unconstrained standard cross-attention. No localization input is required at inference.

Figure 5. Fraction generation. Base models frequently produce complete objects or conventional slices, whereas our model accurately follows the requested fraction for both pizza and pie across five target values.
Figure 4. Clock generation. Under the same random seeds, baseline models often produce common clock configurations instead of the requested time, whereas our model accurately follows the target time.

Figure 9. In-scene generation with no bounding-box supervision at inference. (a) Clock time control across diverse room scenes. (b) Food-fraction control in top-down food settings. In both domains the model accurately tracks the requested geometric quantity (time / fraction) while maintaining scene coherence and object placement.

Figure 8. Qualitative comparison of the original periodic encoding and the augmented encoding with the scalar fraction f near the angular boundaries. The periodic encoding produces small sectors near 0◦ but may generate narrow slices even for complete-sector targets (360◦), reflecting its endpoint ambiguity. Adding f distinguishes the endpoints and enables complete-object generation, but can produce oversized sectors for small target angles (1◦–5◦). Results are shown for pizza, pie, and cake.

papers.abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.
authors: Shanwen Wang, Sirui Wang, Xin Sun, Jungong Han
bullets: Addresses the limited labeled data and weak scene-understanding capabilities of existing landslide detection models.
Uses Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning to support multiple visual tasks with labeled and unlabeled data.
Feeds predicted landslide regions as explicit spatial guidance to a parameter-efficiently adapted vision-language model for reasoning and analysis.
Introduces LandslideVL, a benchmark combining landslide imagery with textual prompts for intelligent landslide analysis.
Experiments on public datasets and LandslideVL report strong quantitative and qualitative performance, including better specialized reasoning than general-purpose VLMs.

papers.abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.
authors: Haoran Zhang, Huizhen Sun, Hanbin Wen, Jie Leng, Jiaxin Zhu, Zhaohua Sun
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering 56 sites, four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 imagery, and 238 questions across ten land-change tasks.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.
bullets: Addresses missed relevant memories and fixed representations in semantic-retrieval memory systems.
Builds a relational graph of memory episodes using textual and visual anchors, then expands retrieved seeds with neighbors.
For each memory, selects among summaries, captions, grounded views, raw images, and interaction history based on the query.
Across three multimodal memory benchmarks, improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90% versus efficient multimodal baselines.

papers.abstract: In ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, the objects that questions count in a region or relate by direction often span only a few pixels. Existing methods mainly decide where a vision-language model (VLM) should look and trust its answer in the chosen view. We show that this assumption fails for counting, and measure VLMs as one calibrates a sensor. All eight open VLMs tested fall increasingly short once a view holds more than a certain number of objects, about five for most on DOTA aerial images. This counting horizon narrows as views grow and objects appear smaller. An empirical power-law response model predicts the undercount a split recovers and the spurious counts it adds, and supports the rule of splitting only views beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a text-only language model parses the question into a typed spatial program that fixes the region and its resolution. The VLM only grounds and counts within its operating range, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. To our knowledge, it is the first UHR method to split views by a measured limit of the VLM. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 on spatial relations in XLRS-Bench, and has the highest reported accuracy, trained methods included, on regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points, 15.6 of the former from splitting. On MME-RealWorld counting it gains 11.4 points, and we show that an option that is almost never correct yet often chosen distorts comparisons there. Project page: https://avalon-s.github.io/GeoScope/
bullets: VLM counting accuracy degrades sharply beyond a view-dependent horizon of roughly five objects, especially as objects become smaller.
A text-only language model converts questions into typed spatial programs that specify regions and resolution.
GeoScope splits only views exceeding the measured counting horizon, while the VLM grounds and counts within its reliable range.
It computes directional relations explicitly from grounded object boxes rather than relying solely on VLM judgments.
Without training, it reports substantial gains across XLRS-Bench, UHR-Micro, and MME-RealWorld counting tasks.

papers.abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.
bullets: Targets sparse data and nonlinear traffic shifts during rare adverse weather events.
Converts weather, points of interest, and holiday descriptions into semantic embeddings using an LLM.
Fuses heterogeneous inputs with multimodal attention and calibrates predictions through a gated residual head.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by an average 11.82% MAE across three cities, with stable performance under sparse, non-stationary conditions.

papers.abstract: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.

Combines VGGT-SLAM 2.0 geometric estimates with SAM3 open-vocabulary semantic observations.

Maps persistent instances via class-constrained 3D connectivity in a globally optimized coordinate system, avoiding temporal ID propagation.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
bullets: Targets gaps in existing benchmarks, including shortcut visual cues and predominantly static scenes.
Covers 54 task variants spanning spatial reasoning and spatial memory.
Uses an automated pipeline to generate and annotate tasks with verified targets and executable interactions.
Evaluations show consistent weaknesses in tracking object identities after spatial changes and translating relational or geometric constraints into actions.
The benchmark is publicly released on GitHub.

papers.abstract: General-purpose vision-language models struggle with crisis imagery due to its inherent noise, ambiguity, and high variability across disaster events - yet timely, accurate scene understanding is critical for humanitarian response. To address this, we introduce DisasterVLG, a large-scale multi-task dataset containing 1.24 million disaster images from 142 countries paired with 33 million structured annotations spanning dense captioning with localization, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded visual question answering (VQA) across diverse hazard types and scene contexts worldwide. Unlike prior disaster benchmarks that focus narrowly on classification, DisasterVLG unifies recognition, grounded reasoning, and uncertainty-aware interpretation. A distinguishing feature is its evidence-grounded annotation design: each VQA instance includes supporting evidence text that links visual observations to answers, alongside positive and negative question pairs, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Visual grounding layer links caption phrases to image regions and relationship statements to subject-object boxes, with explicit labels for visual supports and clues. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct a human-verified test set of 38K images (1.15M annotations) spanning broad geographic regions and disaster types. Experiments with domain-adapted vision-language models demonstrate strong performance across disaster captioning, incident recognition, and grounded VQA, while also exposing the limitations of general-purpose models in crisis-specific reasoning. DisasterVLG establishes a scalable, reproducible benchmark for vision-language models that must reason reliably under real-world uncertainty. We will publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.
bullets: Introduces 1.24M disaster images from 142 countries with 33M structured annotations.
Covers localized dense captioning, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded VQA.
Links answers and descriptions to visual regions, supporting evidence, clues, negative pairs, answer formats, and difficulty labels.
Provides a human-verified test set spanning diverse geographic regions and disaster types.
Experiments show domain-adapted models perform strongly but reveal persistent limitations of general-purpose models in crisis reasoning.

papers.abstract: In modular grounding a frozen detector proposes regions and a vision-language model (VLM) selects one, at lower cost than letting the VLM decode a box, but it is unclear where such systems fail. We hold perception fixed---every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, which contain the referent for at least $99.8\%$ of RefCOCO/+/g queries---and vary the selection interface one factor at a time for two VLMs of one family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B). On RefCOCOg, what the selector reads matters more than how it is built: the VLM's image-conditioned query encodes the referent's location and beats a text-only query by $0.15$--$0.18$ with every head tested (by less for InternVL3-8B, whose vision encoder differs; one head tested). The remaining errors are rankings among a few top candidates; a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding on RefCOCOg, and with Qwen2.5-VL on RefCOCO/+ when also trained on their data. Beyond that distribution it does not: on Ref-L4's Objects365 images, mostly of categories outside training, every trained head falls to $0.19$--$0.28$ while Qwen decoding keeps about $0.8$ (InternVL3's drops too), neither a wider detector prompt nor a class-agnostic proposer closes the gap, and on public reasoning benchmarks Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO full-budget heads trail decoding by $0.19$--$0.37$ although proposals cover most referents. A trained verifier reduces to an existence probe on the VLM's query state and does not beat the VLM's yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.
bullets: Frozen detector proposals contain the referent for at least 99.8% of RefCOCO/+/g queries, isolating proposal selection as the main bottleneck.
Image-conditioned VLM queries encode location and outperform text-only queries by 0.15–0.18 on RefCOCOg across tested selection heads.
Cross-attention selection can match coordinate decoding in-distribution, especially with supervision on the target data.
Out of distribution, selection accuracy drops to 0.19–0.28 on Ref-L4, while coordinate decoding remains about 0.8; broader proposals and prompts do not fix the gap.
Verifier training mainly probes whether a target exists and does not outperform the VLM’s direct yes/no answers on no-target benchmarks.

Right: accuracy of heads trained on all of RefCOCOg and of coordinate decoding (bars: Qwen2.5-VL-7B; ticks: Qwen3-VL-8B; gray: proposal recall). A frozen detector, prompted with one fixed text independent of the request, supplies proposals and region features; the frozen VLM reads image and request and returns the query u. Only the orange components are trained: the hook selects a proposal and the verifier decides whether to answer. papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses VLM proposal selection in grounded referring tasks; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Where Does Proposal Selection Fail? Diagnosing Frozen Vision-Language Queries over Detector Proposals
papers.tldr: Frozen-proposal grounding usually fails at selecting among candidate regions—not at detecting the referent—and selection generalizes poorly beyond training distributions.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced through large-scale pretraining and strong visual backbones, yet metric depth remains sensitive to scene-level scale. Indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges, but most depth decoders infer this global structure implicitly from visual features. We ask whether scene-level semantic structure can instead act as an upstream prior that shapes the metric output space before dense prediction. We present LangDepth (SemanticBins), a monocular depth architecture that couples strong visual features with a scene-conditioned output space. A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of scene- and geometry-oriented concept keys convert image features into a compact scene descriptor, without requiring per-image text or an external captioner. A Scene Prior Module (SPM) maps this descriptor to a scene-conditioned metric depth interval, providing a global range anchor before dense decoding. In parallel, a DINOv2-L backbone with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features, and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network (PPAN) assigns pixels to the scene-prescribed bin structure. A confidence gate fuses the dense visual estimate with the SPM prior. We train LangDepth jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI under a modest supervised depth budget, without web-scale depth supervision or pseudo-labelled depth data. A single model achieves delta_1 = 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1, and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, the gate becomes SPM-dominant on outdoor scenes, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1. These results support scene-conditioned output spaces as a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.
bullets: Addresses scene-scale variation between indoor and outdoor environments, which can make metric depth estimation sensitive to global range.
Uses a frozen CLIP encoder and learned scene/geometry concept keys to form a compact scene descriptor without per-image text or captioning.
A Scene Prior Module predicts a scene-conditioned depth interval, while DINOv2-L, an FPN, and PPAN perform dense depth decoding with confidence-gated fusion.
Trained jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI with modest supervised depth data, the single model reports strong results across NYU, KITTI, DIODE, iBims-1, and SUN RGB-D.
Scene priors adapt to compact indoor versus wider outdoor ranges; disrupting routed scene context substantially harms performance on KITTI and iBims-1.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: LangDepth (SemanticBins) pipeline. The input image is encoded by a frozen CLIP ViT-B/32, whose image features are routed through learnable scene and geometry concept keys to produce a compact scene descriptor z. The Scene Prior Module (SPM) uses only z to predict a scene-conditioned range (dmin, dmax), ordered bin centres {ck}Kk=1, and a global prior over those centres. In parallel, DINOv2-L with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features. PPAN conditions these features on z and predicts per-pixel bin weights {Wk}Kk=1 and a gate map g. Depth fusion forms the visual estimate dvis = ∑ k Wkck and the SPM prior dSPM = ∑ k πkck, then outputs d̂ = g ⊙ dvis + (1− g)⊙ dSPM.

Table 3: SPM range statistics. The SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and a much wider outdoor range for KITTI. The learned prior over bin centres is highly concentrated across datasets, indicating that the SPM primarily acts as a sceneconditioned range predictor and global scale anchor.
Table 4: Confidence gate statistics. KITTI is strongly SPM-dominant, while indoor datasets are more balanced or slightly vision-dominant.

Table 2: Component ablation study. All variants use the same matched ablation protocol and are intended for relative component comparison. w/o gate fusion bypasses the confidence-gated SPM blend but still uses CLIP concept routing and the SPMdefined bin structure; it is not a no-text baseline. The ablation protocol applies perimage median scaling uniformly on all benchmarks, including KITTI, which accounts for the difference in KITTI AbsRel relative to Tab. 1 (0.054 vs. 0.064); the latter follows the benchmark-standard direct metric evaluation for KITTI.

Table 5: Eval-time scene-context perturbation. Perturbing the routed scene descriptor at evaluation time causes large accuracy drops on KITTI and iBims-1. ∆ denotes the change in δ1 relative to the original prediction.

papers.selection_reason: Vision-language scene priors for monocular depth estimation; combines multimodal and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: LangDepth: Vision-Language Scene Priors for Semantic Binning and Cross-Domain Monocular Depth Estimation
papers.tldr: LangDepth improves cross-domain monocular depth estimation by using vision-language scene priors to set a global metric depth range before dense pixel-level prediction.

papers.abstract: Textured 3D meshes specify object geometry and appearance, making them a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image. We introduce LocateAnyMesh, a vision-language model that uses the mesh itself as part of its prompt. A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence, which a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens. We evaluate two grounding models with PPAT mesh tokens: LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, while LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly. Neither requires rendered query views or view-template matching. New objects require a single encoder pass and no object-specific fine-tuning. LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation. Secondary experiments compare mesh encoders, and a LAM-Direct study isolates surface color. A single-seed LAM-Select continuation supplies pointing and mesh-only description evidence without replacing the reported localization model. The results support mesh tokens as a query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.
bullets: Uses a frozen 3D encoder and learned connector to combine colored mesh tokens with image and instruction tokens.
Introduces LAM-Select for selecting image-region proposals and LAM-Direct for directly predicting coordinates.
Avoids rendered query views and view-template matching; new objects need only one encoder pass without object-specific fine-tuning.
LAM-Select improves localization on reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation.
Limitations include presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.
