papers.abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.
bullets: SurgKnowBench harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks to evaluate proprietary and open-source multimodal models.
Current models show partial visual knowledge but weak relational, procedural, and workflow understanding.
SurgAgentGym enables agents to use bounded SurgWiki searches and general-purpose visual grounding without additional surgical training.
Tool-mediated inference mainly improves perception-heavy tasks; fine-grained localization and expert assessment remain bottlenecks.
The framework supports future research on agentic approaches to surgical understanding.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness
bullets: VLMs can fail when they misinterpret scenes or mentally simulate transformations that violate spatial constraints.
A Perceiver combines question-derived constraints with visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame.
A physics engine executes viewpoint changes and provides measurements and rendered views to guide a Reasoner.
Evaluated on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs.
On MindCube, it improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%; with identical annotated poses, it achieves 98.25% versus 71.81% for internal reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of Spatial Harness. The Perceiver combines question-derived constraints with specialized visual estimates, aligning camera frames and fusing observations into a JSON world state s = (L,Ω, C): a shared layout, per-view observations, and stated constraints. The Reasoner instantiates L in MuJoCo and issues Python tool calls for viewpoint control, measurement, and rendering. Computed measurements and rendered views update its context and guide subsequent operations and the final answer. The JSON and code are illustrative excerpts.

This makes both the estimated layout and the consequences of the transformation available for inspection. papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.
bullets: Targets the gap between static indoor 3D visual grounding and dynamic outdoor autonomous-driving scenarios.
Provides 850 nuScenes scenarios, 31,128 frames, and 144,568 temporally evolving motion-aware prompts.
DynaVG uses the SLIDE module to capture both short-term local motion and long-term temporal context before language–point cloud alignment.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG and support the value of motion-aware encoding.
The benchmark also highlights open challenges for future outdoor 3D visual grounding research.

papers.abstract: We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision-language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing physics-augmented text-to-3D systems to handle deformable objects with invalid meshes, missing rest shapes, and absent material models.
Constructs rest shapes, collision meshes, material parameters, and admissible placements from information available in the generation pipeline.
Uses unified differentiable contact simulation to bring multi-body scenes to static equilibrium, with grid search and adjoint optimization for placement and material refinement.
Verifies prompt compliance and geometric validity using checks and a vision-language model.
Across 65 prompts, reports no undesired interpenetration, while every compared system exhibits some; the approach also supports prompt-only scene generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SoftPAT3D. Each card shows the state of one prompt at that point of the pipeline, and its label names the step that produced it. (a) The prompt is expanded into a reference image, segmented and lifted as in PAT3D, and the support hidden under each deformable object is inpainted, regenerated and converted into a collision mesh (Sec. 3.4). (b) Each deformable object receives a rest shape from its manufacturing process under a size prior (Sec. 3.2), a material from the material library and a placement above the part the prompt names (Sec. 3.4). (c) One simulation brings the scene to equilibrium under a single contact barrier (Sec. 3.3), and the result passes the geometric checks and the prompt check (Sec. 3.5); a scene that fails enters placement optimization (Sec. 3.6).

Figure 6. Scene editing and manipulation on equilibrated scenes. Top: the five stuffed toys of the messy bed are set on the floor in turn while the quilt and pillows keep settling. Middle: a cloth pulled off a stool by one corner. Bottom: the throw is lifted off the armchair, the rabbit carried to the floor and a pillow placed on the seat, every body simulated; the arm is posed for visualization.

Figure 3. Generated scenes. Top two rows: single-object scenes from the main run, development and held-out, each a generated support with a sewn cloth at equilibrium on the part the prompt specifies. Bottom: multi-body scenes with two to eight deformable objects, quilts, pillows, garments and stuffed toys, brought to equilibrium in one simulation. papers.abstract: Multi-task scene understanding models typically rely on modified vision encoders or complex decoders for cross-task interaction, which limits their flexibility and compatibility with off-the-shelf vision foundation models (VFMs). We introduce Virtual Task Prompting (VTP), which frames multi-task prompting as retrieving task-adaptive compositions from a shared virtual state, where both the state and routing process are optimized in an end-to-end manner. Concretely, VTP maintains an expanded set of virtual tasks alongside the backbone. At each layer, learnable routing matrices read task-specific compositions as input to interact with image tokens and write the processed results back, forming explicit pathways that capture the intricacies among tasks outside the encoder. Since VTP keeps the backbone clean, it integrates seamlessly with pretrained VFMs, advancing the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2. Stress test on Taskonomy with 13 heterogeneous tasks further shows VTP's robustness in extreme settings. Ablations and analysis indicate that VTP's gains stem from adaptive routing rather than increased capacity. The project page is available at https://jacky1128.github.io/VTP/.
bullets: Addresses the rigidity and incompatibility of conventional modified encoders or complex decoders for multi-task interaction.
Maintains shared virtual tasks and uses learnable routing matrices to compose task-specific prompts at each layer.
Keeps the vision backbone unchanged, allowing seamless integration with pretrained vision foundation models.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2, with robustness across 13 heterogeneous Taskonomy tasks.
Ablations suggest improvements come from adaptive routing rather than simply increasing model capacity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Qualitative results on Pascal-Context [9]. Figure 6: Additional qualitative results on Pascal-Context (Set 1). Two multi-person outdoor scenes that stress-test inter-individual disambiguation. Left: a man holding an infant against a cluttered natural background. TaskPrompter [71] (red circles) lets semantic labels bleed across the person with background contour in segmentation, fragments body-part assignments at the overlapping arms in parsing, and over-highlights background clutter in boundary. Right: a crowded group where closely spaced individuals share similar appearance. TaskPrompter’s parsing labels entangle across adjacent persons, with leg assignments bleeding from one individual into the next. In both scenes, VTPtimm recovers coherent per-person segmentation masks, disentangled body-part labels, and tighter saliency focus. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 [57, 52] further resolve fine-grained inter-person boundaries, saliency, and produce geometrically smoother surface normals, approaching the ground-truth.

Figure 7: Additional qualitative results (Set 2). A challenging street scene that stress-tests two orthogonal challenges simultaneously: extremely small and thin semantic objects (distant poles, a tiny person occupying only a handful of pixels) and dense edge structures from road markings, building contours, and lampposts. TaskPrompter [71] (red circles) drops these tiny objects entirely from its segmentation and parsing maps, and produces a large spurious saliency blob on the background sky. VTPtimm begins to recover the thin structures in segmentation and parsing while suppressing the false saliency response. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 further sharpen the objects (the blue and green masks in Semseg) and produce boundaries that capture both macro building contours and micro pole edges.

Figure 8: Qualitative results on Taskonomy [77]. An indoor scene with 9 dense prediction tasks under the extreme 13-task joint training regime. From top to bottom, predictions become progressively finer and more accurate. TaskPrompter [71] produces over-smoothed depth maps, flat curvature, and imprecise edges, while VTPtimm through VTPdinov3 successively recover depth discontinuities, surface details, and region coherence, converging toward the ground truth. This progressive improvement requires no additional computational cost. Only the backbone weights are swapped among VFMs.

Although it shares similar technical formation with those PEFT methods, their goals are different. papers.abstract: Despite world-class snow monitoring by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI) and Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI), no station-anchored, multi-parameter snow benchmark dataset exists for the Nordic boreal domain. We present Hydro-Dataset v1.1, a reproducible open-source pipeline that harmonizes 582 SMHI meteorological observation stations across nine hydrological winters (2015/16-2023/24) into a CF-1.9 NetCDF product with 1.8~million annotated station-days. Six derived snow parameters, such as Snow Water Equivalent (SWE), snow phenology, melt rates, degree-day melt factor, rain-on-snow flags, and freeze-thaw cycles, supply benchmark-ready labels for hydrological foundation model training. ERA5-Land cross-validation (Pearson R=0.78, bias=-262mm) confirms observation-anchored SWE provides a more reliable benchmark than reanalysis for machine learning training.

Produces a CF-1.9 NetCDF dataset with 1.8 million annotated station-days.
Includes six derived snow labels, including SWE, snow phenology, melt rates, rain-on-snow events, and freeze-thaw cycles.
ERA5-Land cross-validation supports observation-anchored SWE as a more reliable ML benchmark than reanalysis.
Scope is the Nordic boreal domain and the dataset version is Hydro-Dataset v1.1.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observations remain a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{\Ours{}}, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, \Ours{} robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, \Ours{} generates a single asset per instance, estimates its metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it across frames for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from \Ours{} improve performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). Our project page is available at: \href{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}
bullets: Addresses box mislocalization and missed objects caused by sparse, partial LiDAR observations in driving scenes.
Aligns canonical amodal 3D asset geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR using image-to-rendered-view correspondences.
Improves consistency and efficiency by estimating each instance’s scale once, propagating it across dynamic-object frames, and aggregating observations for static objects.
Detectors trained on AmodalBox annotations improve by 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for vehicles on Waymo Open Dataset.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AmodalBox. Given time-synchronized images and LiDAR scans, we first extract instance-level cues and estimate the motion state of each instance using VFMs [18, 20], scene flow [44], and PP scores [16]. We then align the amodal 3D prior [23] with the partial LiDAR point cloud across their coordinate spaces using correspondences obtained from image-level matching. Finally, we generate a 3D bounding box annotation from the aligned amodal asset.

(A) We generate a 3D asset from the anchor-frame image using [23], render Irender and Drender, and obtain 3D–3D correspondences via image matching and depth unprojection. (B) Using the anchor-rendered Irender and Drender, we aggregate neighboringframe correspondences and estimate the alignment (Eq. (9)). (C) We estimate the anchor scale s⋆ (Eq. papers.abstract: Lane-level map updating requires temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state together with the current observation. We introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior to improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary effectiveness of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. A cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models while reserving complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Since its deployment in March 2025, RoadState has supported lane-level map updating across more than 360 cities and reduced overall production costs by 30%. Together with human-in-the-loop auditing, the system maintains robust performance under stress-test conditions. These results demonstrate how domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing, and human quality control can bridge the gap between VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent and physically invalid road semantics caused by occlusions, ambiguous markings, obstacles, and viewpoint changes.
RoadState-VLM predicts the current structured road state from prior observations, symbolic state, and the current image.
Geo-CoT uses a dependency graph as a domain prior to improve consistency across interdependent road-state dimensions.
Reports 94.33% mean accuracy across six dimensions and complementary benefits from Geo-CoT and temporal context.
Deployed across 360+ cities, the cascaded system reduced production costs by 30% while retaining human-in-the-loop quality control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the RoadState-VLM framework. The pipeline consists of three main stages covering input and preprocessing for Geo-CoT data construction, the RoadState-VLM training architecture with symbolic feedback injection and a latent reasoning buffer, and autoregressive inference with state evolution for temporally consistent road state estimation.

Figure 2: The RoadState production system. Crowd-sourced and survey imagery is assembled into clips, triaged by complexity, and routed to either lightweight models (∼85% of frames) or RoadState-VLM (∼15%). Both branches emit the same structured road state, which must pass a deterministic constraint check before entering map change fusion; violations and low-confidence outputs are escalated to human auditors, whose corrections are recycled as Geo-CoT training data. Section 3 details the RoadState-VLM component.

Figure 4: Qualitative Case Studies. Representative visualization cases highlighting the complexity of real-world driving scenarios. Red text denotes prediction errors, underscoring the superior reasoning capabilities of our method.

Figure 5: Qualitative Case Studies of Geo-CoT Reasoning. Representative samples illustrating the hierarchical reasoning process of RoadState-VLM across diverse driving environments. Each case demonstrates the model’s logic through Global Observation of static road geometry, Temporal Analysis of ego-motion, and Logical Deduction enforcing axiomatic constraints.
Figure 1: An example of structured road information generated from a crowdsourced front-view image sequence.

M1 does not output the three feasibility dimensions; therefore, its aggregate mean is omitted and should not be compared directly with M2–M4. M4 represents our full proposed RoadState-VLM framework.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.
bullets: Introduces FoundationChain, which asks VLMs to infer a crochet pattern from an object image.
Uses hand-crocheting as a tangible, low-cost way to verify whether generated procedures work.
Evaluates 40 patterns from four VLMs through physical execution.
Only four generated patterns are error-free.
Failures reveal weaknesses in visual, geometric, and procedural reasoning that automated checks may miss.

Yarn is wrapped over the hook (A), the hook is inserted into the target stitch and yarn is drawn back through (B), then through two of the loops on the hook (C), and finally through the last two loops (D), completing the stitch and returning to the state in A. papers.abstract: Cinematic composition questions depend on in-frame geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) use inconsistently. External perception tools can expose this geometry, but naive prompt injection can overwrite useful visual predictions. On ShotBench composition, pre-question geometry reduces Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 49.5% to 46.3%; corrupted measurements lower it to 33.6%. CompositionEvidence derives nine reproducible features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts and supplies their shared 24-dimensional representation through two interfaces. A training-free channel appends gated neutral evidence after the question, reaching 56.2% (+6.7, exact McNemar p=0.0018) and 48.4% under corrupted evidence. A minimal-training channel maps the same representation to four soft tokens with a 7.37M-parameter projector while leaving the VLM frozen; it reaches 61.0% (+11.5). Across nine VLMs, including five commercial models queried through official provider APIs, zero-shot accuracy ranges from 43.8% to 63.0%, and the text channel changes it by +6.7 to -6.9 points; the highest baseline is among the regressions. The effect of explicit geometry depends on measurement reliability and on how the receiving model integrates it.
bullets: Composition questions rely on in-frame geometry that VLMs use inconsistently, while naive geometry prompting can hurt performance.
It derives nine features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts into a shared 24-dimensional representation.
A training-free gated text interface reaches 56.2% accuracy and remains more robust to corrupted evidence than pre-question prompting.
A minimally trained four-token projector reaches 61.0% while keeping the VLM frozen.
Across nine VLMs, geometry changes performance from −6.9 to +6.7 points, showing that reliability and model integration are critical.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CompositionEvidence architecture. Frozen detection, depth, and line experts feed deterministic synthesis and nine geometric functions, which yield the shared vector z. Channel A gates and appends selected measurements as post-question text; Channel B maps z into four evidence tokens. Only the fitted thresholds and the projector reach inference.
Figure 4: The training-free recipe applied unchanged to nine VLMs on ShotBench composition. The five commercial models are queried through official provider APIs.

Figure 3: A Before/After Q&A demo (shotbench-2638), drawn from the pool of items that C0 answers incorrectly and Channel A answers correctly. The supplementary material adds two further demos and a counterexample in which Channel A breaks a correct answer.

Figure 2: Confusion matrices for zero-shot (left), Channel A (middle), and Channel B (right). Calibrated evidence recovers directional classes while preserving much of the baseline diagonal; Short side remains nearly absent.

Table 2: ShotBench composition results with Qwen2.5-VL-7B (n=479). Both calibrated channels improve the same zero-shot model; reasoning or raw evidence alone does not. ShotBench reference scores: GPT-4o 55.2, ShotVL-3B 57.4, fine-tuned ShotVL-7B v1.1 62.2.
Table 1: The nine geometric features and the Channel-A gates. Channel B always receives the corresponding continuous values and the presence flags.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.
bullets: Identifies a modality reasoning-access gap: models can read rendered text in images but struggle to reason over the images directly.
Mines synthetic cases where a model succeeds on text but fails on the equivalent rendered image.
Post-trains on these image inputs using GRPO, with SFT and DPO variants also explored.
Training only on synthetic rendered-text images improves performance across diagrams, science, charts, and embodied spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Activation analyses suggest TIGER aligns visual-to-reasoning pathways with text-reasoning states and complements existing visual RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: The task of visual reasoning relative pose identification (VRRPI) has exposed critical weaknesses in the multi-view 3D spatial reasoning capabilities of modern vision-language models (VLMs). We present a systematic analysis of VLMs' behavior in VRRPI, uncovering stable output biases where VLMs disproportionately predict specific motion patterns regardless of visual evidence. To mitigate these inherent biases, we propose self knowledge re-expression with iterative debiasing (SKR-ID), an annotation-free pipeline that adapts VLMs for VRRPI using only randomly extracted unannotated image pairs. SKR-ID transitions VLMs' output mechanism from generic next-token prediction to task-optimized classification heads. The pipeline proceeds in two stages: (1) a cold-start initialization using debiasing object-centric prompts to anchor motion inference in 2D visual evidence; and (2) a recursive logit-ranking mechanism that enforces statistical parity by using the median logit value as a dynamic threshold. Experimental evaluation across frontier VLMs on standard benchmarks demonstrates that SKR-ID significantly mitigates systematic biases. Our method improves open-source VLMs' Macro-F1 scores from 35.0-45.4% to 53.7-58.0%, without using any annotated data. These results show that SKR-ID can effectively improve 3D reasoning performance from a severely collapsed baseline. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/astudentuser/Codes_of_SKR-ID.
bullets: VLMs show stable, evidence-insensitive output biases in multi-view 3D relative-pose reasoning.
SKR-ID adapts VLMs using only randomly selected unannotated image pairs.

Across frontier VLMs and standard benchmarks, open-source models’ Macro-F1 improves from 35.0–45.4% to 53.7–58.0%.
The approach targets severely collapsed baselines and does not require annotated data.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.
bullets: Targets the combined challenges of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction.
Uses high-fidelity 3D shopping environments, including supermarkets and home-furnishing stores.
Assistants must elicit preferences, recommend visible or nearby items, and guide users through dialogue.
Evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness with one interactive protocol.

papers.abstract: Pose awareness characterizes the extent to which a learned feature space aligns with the underlying object-pose manifold, such that observations with similar poses exhibit greater feature similarity than those with increasingly different poses. While such structure is desirable for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks, visual foundation models pre-trained on individual 2D images typically lack explicit 3D or pose supervision. This raises a fundamental question: Do 2D visual foundation models exhibit pose awareness after large-scale pretraining? To answer this question, we introduce PoseBench, a systematic benchmark to probe pose awareness in pretrained visual features. Our evaluation follows a progressive design: held-out rendered views probe intrinsic pose-aware structure under controlled conditions, while real-image queries evaluate how robustly this structure remains accessible under real-world variations. We further introduce pose-graph-based refinement as a complementary probe of compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold. Across 31 publicly available checkpoints from 10 pretraining families, PoseBench reveals that pose awareness is an implicit but non-uniform property of 2D visual foundation models, and consistent gains from pose-graph refinement suggest that feature spaces retain structure compatible with the underlying pose manifold. PoseBench therefore provides a systematic basis for understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks.
bullets: Benchmarks pose awareness through progressively harder probes, from controlled rendered views to real-image queries.
Introduces pose-graph refinement to test compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold.
Evaluates 31 publicly available checkpoints spanning 10 pretraining families.
Finds pose awareness is present but varies across models, while refinement consistently reveals additional pose-compatible structure.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong visual perception capabilities, but existing evaluations largely focus on single-view or multi-view settings with shared camera parameters, leaving the challenge of multi-agent collaborative scenarios underexplored. In such settings, multiple agents observe a shared environment from independent viewpoints, and reliable decisions require reasoning across these independent observations of the same environment. To study this problem, we introduce MaRiO, a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaborative reasoning, and evaluate 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs on it. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) tasks governed by static perception are generally easier than tasks that require transformational event sequences; (2) most models struggle to resolve cross-agent correspondences, with errors increasing with scene complexity; and (3) models show limited ability to leverage geometric cues present in the scene. As an initial step toward addressing these challenges, we explore geometry-guided synthetic view augmentation that generates intermediate transition frames between agent observations, providing auxiliary spatial context that improves performance in certain categories. Overall, our results highlight that multi-agent collaborative reasoning remains an open challenge and an important direction for multimodal embodied systems. The code is available on the project page: https://omarftt.github.io/MaRiO-page/.
bullets: Introduces MaRiO, a benchmark for multi-agent collaborative reasoning in shared environments.

papers.abstract: A phone screen can be wrong in ways that need no reference: a label that runs off the screen, letters that touch, a line that breaks one character before its end, one button with sharp corners among round ones. We ask whether a model can box every such fault on a screenshot, given no target design and no reference image. Such a critic could serve as a cheap first pass over generated pages before a designer reviews them, but only if it stays silent on clean pages. ScreenProof poses this target-free critique over three families of faults: general faults, local style faults (one element breaks the style its page sets) and text layout faults (letter spacing, line height, line breaks). A data engine makes each fault in page code and records the changed element's box, and hard negatives change every sibling alike. No frontier judge is reliable: frontier models flag 18-62% of clean real screenshots and 18-82% of clean generated pages, find 47-72% of text layout faults, and rarely find a foreign icon (5-19%). Our small critic ProofJudge (Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA), trained on code-made pages with one to four faults each and keeping a finding only when it is confident, reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 even without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated), the property such a first pass needs, at about a hundredth of Argon's cost. It finds the most general faults (59%) but fewer local style faults than Argon (25% against 41%) and fewer text layout faults than the API judges (43%; Gemini 4 Argon 47%). Against a named brand the task is harder still: models know a design language about as well as its public documentation states it.
bullets: Targets three fault families: general UI errors, local style inconsistencies, and text-layout problems.
Generates faults directly in page code, records the altered element’s box, and uses hard negatives where all siblings change consistently.
ProofJudge, a Qwen3.5-9B model with LoRA, reaches F1 0.48 and limits false alarms to 2% on real clean pages and 9% on generated ones.
It detects general faults best (59%), but is weaker on local style faults (25%) and text-layout faults (43%).
Named-brand critique remains difficult; models largely know a design language only as well as its public documentation describes it.

papers.selection_reason: A vision-language critic that localizes UI faults requires spatial and layout reasoning over screenshots, fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: ScreenProof: Where Is This Screen Wrong? Finding UI Faults Without a Reference
papers.tldr: ScreenProof evaluates whether AI can detect UI faults in screenshots without a reference, with a small confidence-filtered critic offering the best balance of fault detection and low false alarms.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving. We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space. In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving). The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model. Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference. This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning. These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual driving information and sparse language or trajectory supervision in VLA models.
Introduces a progressive chain of task-specific latent expert tokens within the VLA model.
Distills visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from DINOv3, SAM3, and DepthAnything3.
Uses curriculum-style supervision that progresses from representation to semantics and geometry while targeting efficient inference.
Experiments across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks report consistent improvements in object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning.

For trajectory planning, LECDrive combines discrete motion primitives with continuous offset refinement to improve robustness and precision.

papers.abstract: 3D spatial reasoning from video remains challenging for VLMs because videos provide sequential, view-local observations rather than persistent metric scene records. Many questions must be answered in a query-specified perspective rather than the observed camera viewpoint, and prompting with a fixed set of RGB views may miss sparse or occluded visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce BEV3SR, a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework for RGB-D videos with camera parameters. BEV3SR turns video observations into queryable metric bird's-eye-view (BEV) scene memory and formalizes each query into an evidence-aware spatial task. The Spatial Task Formalizer specifies the query's reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and evidence requirement. The evidence requirement determines the appropriate reasoning pathway. A query treated as requiring geometric evidence is handled by the Geometric Reasoner, which deterministically computes the answer using the metric BEV records in the query-specified reference frame. Otherwise, a query treated as requiring visual evidence is passed to the Visual Evidence Aligner, which uses BEV-indexed object records and their associated supporting views to retrieve object-consistent and scene-context RGB frames for VLM grounding. Within a standard 16-frame budget, BEV3SR consistently improves different VLM backbones across multiple 3D scene QA benchmarks, delivering large gains on spatially intensive questions and significant improvements on open-ended scene QA. These results demonstrate that BEV3SR offers an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for explicit 3D spatial reasoning from video.
bullets: Addresses view-local, sequential video observations, query-specific viewpoints, and sparse or occluded evidence.
Formalizes each query’s reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and required evidence.
Computes geometry-based answers deterministically from metric BEV records in the requested reference frame.
Retrieves object-consistent and contextual RGB frames for VLM grounding when visual evidence is needed.
Improves multiple VLM backbones across 3D scene QA benchmarks, especially spatially intensive and open-ended questions, within a 16-frame budget.

papers.abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.
bullets: Evaluates task-conditioned actionable spatial belief across coffee, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance domains.
Includes 860 frozen cases and over 115,000 evaluator episodes using closed-loop actionability and functional-OOD protocols.
A diagnostic belief-state pipeline ranks views by missing functional evidence and achieves 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success.
Seven vision-language models achieve only 26–43% on the same cases.
Ablations show that command binding, functional reasoning, and image content are essential to performance.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a benchmark for task-conditioned spatial belief in manipulation, evaluating view selection policies that acquire specific evidence for manipulation commands, directly relevant to embodied AI and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation

papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common kidney cancer in adults. We present a region-aware architecture for CT-based ccRCC classification. Tumor and 0--10 mm peritumoral context are pooled separately from shared frozen DINOv3 feature maps. A shared position-aware slice aggregator precedes fixed training-only principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting representations are fused with radiomics using two scalar feature gates. Evaluation on KiTS23 and 111 external cases yields internal test and external AUCs of 0.8078\pm0.0154 and 0.9094\pm0.0015. Compared with matched single-tumor readout, mean AUC increases by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points, respectively. Early-PCA and reconstruction controls yield lower internal mean AUCs, while external AUC is similar for early and late PCA. These findings highlight the joint role of regional readout and slice aggregation in adapting frozen visual features to renal CT.
authors: Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
bullets: Separately pools tumor and 0–10 mm peritumoral regions from shared frozen DINOv3 features.
Uses position-aware slice aggregation, training-only PCA, and gated fusion with radiomics.
Achieves internal and external AUCs of 0.8078±0.0154 and 0.9094±0.0015 on KiTS23 and 111 external cases.
Outperforms matched single-tumor readout by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points in mean AUC.
Results support combining regional readout with slice aggregation; external performance is similar for early versus late PCA.

The encoder receives unmasked CT slices. T and C pass separately through the same trainable position-aware slice aggregator (PSA), followed by fixed PCA32. papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) classification from computed tomography (CT) may benefit from representations that capture different aspects of tumour phenotype. However, simply concatenating reconstruction-derived features, image--text embeddings, and radiomic descriptors may not fully exploit their complementary information. We propose MSR-ABC, a global--local framework integrating MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics. Spatially matched local image descriptors interact through cross-representation attention, while radiomic auxiliary supervision encourages the pooled local representation to retain quantitative tumour attributes. A gated residual mechanism integrates local information with global summaries. Area-aware pooling and visual and soft-text prompting complete the framework. We evaluate discrimination using a patient-level split of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases, reporting mean AUROC over three training seeds with 95% patient-bootstrap confidence intervals. MSR-ABC achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally. Internally, it exceeds global MedVAE--radiomics and three-source concatenation by 3.35 and 3.61 AUROC percentage points, respectively. Removing any source lowers mean AUROC in both cohorts, with the largest decreases following radiomics removal. Individual removal of cross-representation attention, auxiliary supervision, or gated fusion also lowers internal mean AUROC. These findings are consistent with complementary contributions within the integrated architecture and support further investigation of structured representation fusion for non-invasive renal tumour characterisation.
authors: Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
bullets: Addresses the limited benefit of simply concatenating reconstruction, image–text, and radiomic features.
Uses MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics in a global–local framework with cross-representation attention, radiomic auxiliary supervision, gated residual fusion, area-aware pooling, and prompting.
Evaluated on patient-level splits of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases.
Achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally, outperforming specified internal baselines by 3.35–3.61 percentage points.
Ablations indicate that all feature sources and key fusion components contribute, with radiomics removal causing the largest drop.

papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
bullets: Addresses MLLMs’ difficulty composing precise temporal and spatial evidence into coherent multi-step reasoning.
Represents videos as Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded reasoning chains from validated evidence paths.
Introduces a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark with grounded chain-of-thought annotations.
Finds that MLLMs often localize relevant evidence but struggle to compose it correctly, a weakness hidden by answer-only evaluation.
Fine-tuning with V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.abstract: The main challenge of multi-modal image registration is shared structural feature extraction with higher accuracy and lower computational complexity. Compared with a State Space Model (SSM), the State Space Principles (SSP) formulation of Mamba-3 uses a more accurate discretization with lower truncation error while maintaining linear complexity. However, vanilla SSP is designed for natural language processing (NLP) and is not directly suitable for images. To address this issue, we propose a novel non-causal SSP (NC-SSP) with shared structure awareness and develop a coarse-to-fine registration method named RegNC-Mamba3. First, NC-SSP is designed to eliminate the dependence of the integral computation on the scanning path. By combining relative-weight normalization with aggregation over all circular scan paths, NC-SSP constructs a globally hidden state without long-range decay, which provides a wider receptive field and higher efficiency than the original Mamba-3. Second, NC-SSP is modified to strengthen the extraction of cross-modal structural features. When computing hidden states and feature interactions, we construct complex-valued sequences in NC-SSP by applying learnable Log-Gabor kernels, with different orientations to each head for frequency-domain modulation. This improves the perception of shared structural information across modalities and increases both registration accuracy and quality. Experiments on VIS-SAR and VIS-IR demonstrate that RegNC-Mamba3 outperforms the compared detector-based and semi-dense multi-modal registration methods.
authors: Zhikang Li, Yan Wu, Xin Hu, Yi Dai, Ming Li
bullets: Addresses accurate, efficient shared-structure extraction for multi-modal image registration.
Introduces non-causal SSP (NC-SSP), which removes scan-path dependence and aggregates circular paths for a global hidden state without long-range decay.
Uses relative-weight normalization to provide a wider receptive field while retaining linear-complexity processing.
Applies learnable, orientation-specific Log-Gabor kernels to construct complex-valued sequences for stronger cross-modal structural perception.
A coarse-to-fine RegNC-Mamba3 method outperforms compared detector-based and semi-dense methods on VIS-SAR and VIS-IR registration tasks.

papers.abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.
authors: Xinyi Niu, Lingfeng Chen, Jiehua Zhang, Panhe Hu, Li Liu, Zhen Liu, Yongxiang Liu
bullets: Addresses inefficient and poorly targeted region exploration in multimodal understanding of ultra-high-resolution imagery.
Uses a frozen JeV model to score candidate regions and coordinate search decisions.
Region Rank selects priorities, Sparse Branch adapts branching width, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth.
Achieves 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32% accuracy on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA, respectively.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B’s average accuracy by 5.32 percentage points with 1.12 seconds of added latency, and is 7.8× faster than a recent method.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
authors: Zanting Ye, Yunrui Lin, Shengyuan Liu, Jing Hao, Chen Hu, Yefeng Zheng, Lijun Lu
bullets: Addresses the high cost and redundancy of processing hundreds of volume slices in medical vision–language models.
Separates visual-content selection from token-budget allocation instead of coupling them.
Groups contiguous slices into ordered units and uses Lorentz distance for token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement.
Uses visual-encoder attention entropy to assign more tokens where attention is more dispersed.
Across nine settings, retains 22.78% of tokens on average while achieving 121.68% mean relative quality and robust performance at a 10% budget.

papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
authors: Zuhao Liu, Melih Darcan, Zhengdi Yu, Riza Alp Guler, Tolga Birdal
bullets: Addresses the need for hand-pose priors that account for the interacted object, beyond unconditional pose models.

Evaluations show utility for pose refinement, occluded-hand reconstruction, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.
authors: Hengwei Zhao, Qirui Wang, Zhuo Zheng, Xiaoyan Lu, Rusty Feagin, Wenzhe Jiao

Experiments on global disaster benchmarks show effectiveness and robustness; a 2025 Los Angeles wildfire application demonstrates practical potential under limited supervision.

papers.abstract: Data-driven Riemannian geometry provides nonlinear interpolation and geometric representations of high-dimensional data. For these operations to be statistically meaningful, paths between observations should preferentially traverse high-likelihood regions. Existing scalable pullback constructions typically use a unimodal Gaussian latent distribution, assuming that the data reside close to a single manifold. For multimodal data, mapping separated modes or local structures into one Gaussian region can require substantial transport deformation and compromise the resulting geometry. We introduce a pullback geometry for data supported on mixtures of manifolds. Using a latent Gaussian mixture, we define its Riemannian metric as the matrix square of the responsibility-weighted expected component precision. The metric is smooth and positive definite and recovers the existing Gaussian construction in the single-component limit. For structured overlapping mixtures, we establish conditions under which the log-density is concave along geodesics, providing a formal connection between the proposed geometry and paths through high-likelihood regions, and derive the corresponding local curvature relations. We instantiate this geometry in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, allowing the number of active components to emerge from the data and supporting component-wise reconstruction and local effective-dimension estimation. Experiments on synthetic geometric data, a controlled multi-view image setting with a known reference trajectory, and MNIST show reduced transport distortion, competitive path support, close reference-trajectory recovery, and improved interpolation realism. These results extend scalable pullback geometry beyond datasets that reside close to a single manifold while retaining tractable and interpretable local structure.
bullets: Addresses distortion caused by forcing separated modes or local structures into a single Gaussian latent space.
Defines a smooth positive-definite metric from responsibility-weighted component precisions, recovering the Gaussian case with one component.
Provides conditions linking geodesics to high-likelihood paths and derives associated local curvature relations.
Implements the geometry in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, enabling component-wise reconstruction and local effective-dimension estimation.
Experiments on synthetic data, multi-view images, and MNIST report reduced transport distortion, strong trajectory recovery, and more realistic interpolations.

papers.abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.
bullets: Studies when and why models benefit from outputting coordinate-based visual grounding in chain-of-thought reasoning.
Introduces an analysis method to measure whether models actually use their predicted grounding in reasoning traces, plus an ablation of the training recipe.
Finds improvements for counting but no significant gains over non-grounded baselines across broad spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks.
Synthetic tasks show grounding is most useful for undescribable visual references that are difficult to express in language.
Introduces BrickVision, a benchmark designed to require such undescribable visual references.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 2D vision-language pre-training and reliable 3D robotic manipulation.
Jointly trains action prediction with alignment between VLA visual features and a frozen 3D perception model.
Unifies heterogeneous robot datasets across embodiments, tasks, scenes, and geometric annotations.
Uses feature-dependent layer aggregation, partial depth/calibration, and probabilistic state dropout to improve spatial supervision and visual reliance.
Training-only auxiliary components enable direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights without changing inference.

papers.abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.
bullets: Addresses the need to manually engineer proposition-grounding functions for reward machines.
An LLM generates the reward machine from a natural-language task description.
A VLM grounds reward-machine propositions in image observations during policy learning.
A VLM-based value estimator provides dense rewards based on progress toward reward-machine transitions.
Across grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, it achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods.

papers.abstract: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.
bullets: Targets PCB routing, which requires coordinating connectivity strategy, geometry, and strict design rules.
Uses board images plus electrical and geometric data to plan topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions.
Executes plans through KiCad’s native router with bounded local recovery and structured feedback for guide revision.
Achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% across four PCBWorld-Bench splits.
Outperforms the evaluated baseline on three real-world subsets, while performance drops substantially on D3-C.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are a widely adopted starting point for remote sensing tasks. Most are pretrained on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery at a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. Many applications instead rely on very high resolution (VHR) imagery, where individual buildings, roads, and amenities are resolved. We study which pretraining regimes transfer well to this scale. We introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark suite of ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer spanning five task families, eight application domains, and both satellite and aerial platforms. We evaluate twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions. We find that both pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining transfer effectively to VHR tasks, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce; at the full label fraction the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead, with the two close together there. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. Guided by these complementary results, we continue the self-supervised pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluate the resulting encoder without changing the downstream protocol. The continued model gives a clear improvement over the released backbone when labels are scarce and a modest one at the full fraction, at no increase in inference parameters or compute. These findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: already strong, broad natural-image pretraining can be further improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.
bullets: Introduces VHR-Bench: ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer, covering five task families, eight domains, and satellite and aerial imagery.
Evaluates twelve frozen encoders across three pretraining tiers and two labeled-data fractions.
SkySense performs best with scarce labels; at the full label fraction, DINOv3 ViT-L is slightly ahead, with both closely matched.
Continuing DINOv3 ViT-L pretraining on 1.02 million VHR tiles improves performance, especially when labels are scarce, without increasing inference parameters or compute.
Findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: broad natural-image pretraining followed by VHR adaptation.

papers.title: When GeoFMs Meet VHR: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Very High Resolution Earth Observation Imagery
