papers.abstract: Text-guided image editing with diffusion models struggles with spatial edits (e.g. manipulating objects, changing viewpoints, manipulating occlusions) that depend on the 3D structure understanding of a scene. Marigold and follow-up work demonstrate that a pretrained diffusion backbone already harbors strong geometric priors that can be activated for depth estimation, yet how to redirect these priors toward editing remains unresolved. Through per-layer gradient probing, we discover that the editing and depth objectives are compatible in early transformer layers but actively conflict in late layers, explaining why naive depth-conditioned editing either ignores geometry or degrades visual quality. We present StitchEdit, which first activates the backbone's geometric capability via a lightweight depth-denoising adapter, then selectively fine-tunes this adapter for editing using a probe-guided per-layer learning rate schedule that preserves depth knowledge where it helps and prunes it where it conflicts. On the proposed StitchEditBench, a benchmark of 150 geometry-dependent edits spanning spatial transformation, occlusion manipulation, and viewpoint change, StitchEdit consistently surpasses both instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines on perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.
bullets: Geometry-dependent edits such as viewpoint changes, spatial transformations, and occlusion manipulation remain challenging for text-guided diffusion editors.
Per-layer gradient probing finds that editing and depth objectives align in early layers but conflict in late layers.
A lightweight depth-denoising adapter activates geometric knowledge before probe-guided, layer-specific fine-tuning for editing.
On StitchEditBench, StitchEdit consistently outperforms instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines in perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of STITCHEDIT. Stage 1: Depth activation via a frozen-backbone LoRA adapter. Per-layer gradient probing reveals the layer-wise compatibility between the depth and editing objectives. Stage 2: The probing profile fundamentally determines both the LoRA pruning boundary and the per-layer learning rate schedule for the editing fine-tuning.

Figure 1: Top: Challenging 3D-aware edits generated by STITCHEDIT conditioned on text instructions. The model accurately handles complex object repositions and occlusions while strictly preserving visual quality. Bottom: Qualitative comparison against baselines. Nano-Banana [4] manipulates 2D appearance without explicit scene geometry, while uniformly fine-tuning the depth adapter (Depth-Init) leads to catastrophic forgetting, causing structural failures.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. STITCHEDIT maintains strict geometric consistency while preserving exceptional visual quality. Instruction-based editors frequently fail to respect 3D spatial structures, and Uniform FT suffers from depth degradation.

Figure 3: Per-layer gradient probing profile ρ(l). The probe value saturates near 1 in early layers, decays through the intermediate layers, and drops below zero in late layers, indicating that the editing gradient actively interferes with depth knowledge. The shaded band denotes ±1 standard deviation across the calibration set. This empirical profile directly dictates the pruning boundary le and explicitly guides the per-layer learning rate schedule in Stage 2.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically using a single global scale-and-shift alignment. Crucially, we discover a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This discovery invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which warp scene geometry by enforcing a single transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Across diverse experimental settings, our sensor-free method shows strong photometric quality of Gaussian Splatting while substantially improving geometric accuracy and outperforming state-of-the art geometry-focused methods.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 3DGS’s strong visual quality and weaker geometric accuracy.
Identifies that monocular depth errors are piecewise-linear and vary across regions, making global scale-and-shift alignment inadequate.
Models depth correction with regionally smooth, edge-aware affine fields.
Uses spatial gradients in a normal-aware regularizer to align rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals.
Reports strong photometric quality alongside substantially improved geometry across diverse settings, without sensor data.

figures.caption: Figure 8: We compare the raw disparity predictions of (a) Metric3D-V2 and (b) MoGe against groundtruth sensor depth on the exact same scene. While the distinct network architectures allocate their local scale-and-shift parameters differently, both fundamentally exhibit the same region-dependent, piecewise-linear fragmentation. This confirms that spatial affine distortion is a systemic property of modern foundation depth models.

Figure 2: Method overview. (a) 3DGS renders depth D and normals n, and Depth-Anything-V2 predicts the disparity d. (b) The affine fields α and β are estimated from disparity and depth gradients and smoothed by a guided filter (Sec. 3.1). (c) They supervise the losses of Secs. 3.2 and 3.3. All fields are re-estimated at every iteration.

Figure 1: Robust 3DGS geometry via spatially varying affine rectification. (a-c) Standard 3DGS overfits appearance, producing noisy underlying geometry. In contrast, our method extracts clean, highly accurate meshes while maintaining photorealism. (d) Monocular disparity exhibits piecewise-linear distortions, proving that a single global scale-and-shift alignment is fundamentally insufficient (scatter plot). (e) We overcome this by estimating an edge-aware spatial scale field (αsmooth) to rectify the monocular depth prior, yielding geometrically consistent 3D representations.

Figure 9: Additional qualitative comparison on NeRF-LLFF dataset. Visualized across the Flower, Fern, and Horns scenes under extreme view sparsity (rendered RGB, depth, and surface normal maps). (a) Unconstrained 3DGS severely overfits to the limited training views, resulting in massive floating artifacts and chaotic underlying geometry. (b) DRGS mitigates some artifacts via global depth alignment, but still suffers from noisy surface normals and blurred geometric details. (c) DropGaussian struggles to properly initialize in this sparse setting, leading to heavily corrupted backgrounds and incomplete structures. (d) In contrast, our proposed method leverages spatially rectified monocular priors to extract clean, highly accurate geometry with sharp object boundaries, smooth backgrounds, and highly consistent surface normals, all while preserving photorealistic appearance.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative mesh comparison on ScanNet++ dataset. (a) The DN-Splatter baseline exhibits high-frequency noise and artifacts across large planar surfaces like walls and ceilings. (b) Our proposed method successfully suppresses this noise to reconstruct much smoother, flatter surfaces that better approximate (c) the ground-truth geometry.

Figure 7: Piecewise-linear disparity fragmentation across diverse indoor topologies. Across various scenes, the monocular depth prior consistently fractures into distinct, spatially coherent affine regimes (visualized in red, orange, and grey). The accompanying scatter plots demonstrate that fitting a single global scale-and-shift transform (K = 1) is mathematically ill-posed, as the optimizer would be forced to average errors across fundamentally incompatible linear clusters.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on Mushroom dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.2). (a) The globally aligned DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline suffers from degraded geometries due to structural warping. (c) By rectifying the exact same monocular prior, our method better recovers crisp planar surfaces and sharp complex object boundaries than (b) the sensor-supervised DN-Splatter.

Figure 12: Qualitative comparisons of our proposed geometric regularization on MuSHRoom dataset. Visualized via rendered normals (top row) and depth maps (bottom row). (a) The unconstrained baseline (All off) exhibits severe geometric drift, yielding highly chaotic and noisy surface normals. (b-d) Applying individual loss terms in isolation yields incomplete geometry: while Ldepth anchors global scale, it fails to resolve high-frequency structural noise, and while Lgrad or Lnormal improve local structure, they struggle without an absolute metric anchor. (h) Our full formulation combines these constraints. By anchoring the global metric scale while explicitly enforcing local spatial gradients and physical orientations, the complete approach reconstructs exceptionally clean planar surfaces (e.g.,, the walls and ceiling), sharp structural boundaries, and globally consistent depth.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on ScanNet++ dataset. We show rendered RGB and depth with red bounding boxes highlighting areas where we generate visually sharper depth, particularly along boundaries of furniture and complex geometry, compared to the DN-Splatter baseline.
Figure 6: Qualitative mesh comparison on ScanNet++ dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.3). Interestingly, we are able to recover window geometries which are absent from ground-truth mesh.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons on NeRF-LLFF dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.1).

Figure 10: Additional qualitative comparison of rendered RGB, normals and depths on MuSHRoom dataset. While (a) the globally aligned DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline suffers from severe surface rippling and rendering artifacts, (c) our spatially rectified approach successfully recovers sharp, clean geometry that closely matches (b) the ground-truth sensor-supervised DN-Splatter.

Table 1: Empirical analysis of disparity distortions. Evaluated at a 0.02 residual threshold. A single global transform (K = 1) leaves a significant percentage of the scene misaligned. We report photometric (novel-view synthesis), depth estimation, and 3D mesh reconstruction metrics against the unconstrained Splatfacto baseline. Best results in each column are indicated in bold.

Novel-view synthesis and depth metrics are reported on the right (disjoint-trajectory) split, whereas Tables 6 and 14 report the left split. Removing the filter results in severe geometric degradation due to raw monocular noise. While a standard Gaussian filter mitigates some noise, it indiscriminately blurs across physical boundaries. Table 18: Comprehensive scene-wise evaluation of the DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline. Evaluated across the MuSHRoom dataset test split. Because this baseline relies on a single global scale-and-shift transform to align monocular depth, it is highly susceptible to piecewise-linear distortions. This results in severe structural collapse on complex scenes (e.g., computer and kokko), validating the necessity of our proposed spatially varying affine rectification.

Table 16: Ablation on gradient matching formulation. Evaluated on the coffee_room scene. Novelview synthesis and depth metrics are reported on the right (disjoint-trajectory) split. Relying solely on MSE fails to capture sharp orientational changes, leading to degraded Normal Consistency. While Cosine similarity provides excellent directional cues, combining both magnitude (MSE) and directional (Cosine) alignment yields the highest overall surface extraction F-score and best novel view synthesis.

papers.title: AffineGS: Unlocking Accurate Geometry in 3DGS via Spatially Varying Affine Rectification
papers.tldr: AffineGS improves 3D Gaussian Splatting geometry by correcting region-dependent monocular depth distortions with spatially varying affine rectification and normal-aware regularization.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.
bullets: Targets a gap in static spatial benchmarks: reasoning about object moves, swaps, and resulting scene-state changes.
Provides 7,082 examples spanning 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators.
Includes dense causal annotations covering intervention sources, affected and invariant relations, expected effects, and metric changes.
Introduces CT-OPSD, which teaches a teacher model causal state-transition chains and distills them into a student using real observations.
Experiments show standard spatial-reasoning methods can fail under counterfactual interventions, while CT-OPSD offers initial model improvements.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the CST-Bench transition taxonomy. CST-Bench contains 7,082 counterfactual spatial QA samples across six intervention families and twelve transition operators. Figure 4: Overview of CT-OPSD with CST-Bench supervision. Privileged transition annotations from CST-Bench train a causal teacher but are never provided as student inputs. The frozen teacher aligns with the observation-only student on student-generated prefixes, and only the updated student is retained for inference.

Figure 3: Overview of CST-Bench construction. Constraint-aware generation jointly derives counterfactual states and annotations, answer-blind VLM consensus filters ambiguous candidates, and uncertainty-guided human verification resolves uncertain cases and audits all transformation operators.

papers.abstract: To serve a request in a human environment, a robot system must find an object that satisfies a functional requirement and a robot that can feasibly reach it. Scene graphs record which objects exist and where, but they often omit capabilities documented only in product manuals. Retrieval-augmented generation methods can read such manuals, yet they rarely reason jointly over object capabilities, physical instances, robot states, and dynamic connectivity. We introduce E2W-Bench, the Exists-to-Works Benchmark, which links dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals to evaluate capability-grounded robot--object assignment under availability, mobility, vertical-reach, and connector constraints. We also present Embodied RAG++, a spatially grounded retrieval framework that scopes retrieval to the manuals linked to candidate objects, caches extracted capabilities per product model, and resolves robot--object feasibility through deterministic spatial reasoning. On E2W-Bench, Embodied RAG++ reaches a pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, compared with at most 0.30 and 0.55 for the baselines, while requiring the shortest preprocessing time among the retrieval-based methods and tying for the lowest total token count.
bullets: Addresses the gap between knowing which objects exist and determining which can fulfill a requested function.
Introduces E2W-Bench, linking dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals under availability, mobility, reach, and connector constraints.
Scopes retrieval to candidate-object manuals, caches product capabilities, and uses deterministic spatial feasibility checks.
Achieves pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, outperforming reported baselines.
Uses the shortest preprocessing time among retrieval-based methods and ties for the lowest total token count.

papers.abstract: Scaling has become a primary driver of progress in language and vision foundation models, yet its role in precise correspondence matching remains underexplored. In this work, we present Flow Any Scene Transformer (FAST), a scalable correspondence model driven by two key insights. First, we reveal that the query-key projections inside single-view vision foundation models encode a coarse yet reusable prior for cross-view matching. Second, reusing these pretrained projections in cross-attention form yields a highly effective initialization for a ViT-based matcher built from a single-view encoder. Guided by these insights, we build FAST upon a vanilla single-view foundation model, utilizing a zero-parameter rewiring strategy to convert selected self-attention layers into cross-attention for cross-view interaction. This design allows ViT-based matchers to scale with advances in single-view foundation models, bypassing the need for a dedicated pair-centric pretraining stage. To fully unlock the scaling potential of this formulation, we assemble a 6-million-pair training corpus for general-purpose dense 2D displacement estimation across diverse co-visible image pairs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FAST achieves state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks, while scaling favorably with both backbone size and training data.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored role of scaling in precise correspondence matching.
Reuses query-key projections from single-view vision foundation models as a coarse, transferable cross-view matching prior.
Uses zero-parameter rewiring to convert selected self-attention layers into cross-attention, avoiding pair-centric pretraining.
Trains on a 6-million-pair corpus for general-purpose dense 2D displacement estimation across diverse co-visible images.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across many benchmarks, with favorable scaling by backbone size and training data.

papers.abstract: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.
authors: Chibueze Praise Onyenweaku, Toyibat Adele, Sikirulahi Opeyemi Abdulkareem, Obed Honour Eje
bullets: Apparent pedestrian height remains relatively stable under occlusion, while monocular depth shifts toward the nearer occluding surface.
The method uses only the ordering of these cues, avoiding focal-length, body-height, and depth-scale calibration when depth errors are approximately a gain.
It requires no training or occlusion annotations and can check the depth-model assumption without labels.
It detects heavy occlusion with AUC 0.909 on KITTI, 0.819 in synthetic CARLA scenes, and remains effective within fixed distance ranges.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method to detect occlusion in monocular depth/height estimates without training labels, which is crucial for robust robot navigation and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Occlusion for Free: Detecting Occlusion from the Disagreement Between Two Monocular Distance Cues
papers.tldr: Occlusion can be detected without occlusion labels by comparing two monocular distance cues whose disagreement reveals when depth is pulled toward an occluder.

papers.abstract: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.
bullets: Raw integer-grid serialization obscures spatial structure and causes excessive exploratory actions.
A zero-parameter, linear-time perception engine builds object inventories, tracks changes over time, distinguishes invariants from hypotheses, and annotates frames.
Combined with code-as-action execution, grounded perception improved the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 and reduced token use by 89.4%.
Geometric invariants generalized perfectly on 23 held-out games, while single-frame affordance guesses were unreliable, motivating active verification.
On the public set, briefing improved single-pass efficiency from 59.4% to 63.5%; the system scored 16.53 on the hidden evaluation within nine hours.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SARBLOH, an agent that prioritizes spatial perception (geometric invariants, object inventory) over planning to solve visual puzzles, directly addressing spatial intuition and geometry-aware reasoning.
papers.title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
papers.tldr: SARBLOH shows that grounded spatial perception, rather than planning alone, is the main bottleneck for efficient ARC-AGI-3 reasoning.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection offers a low-cost route to 3D perception, but it remains fundamentally ill-posed, since depth must be inferred from a single view. Recent transformer-based detectors learn geometry purely from image features and 3D box annotations, lacking the high-level semantic priors that vision-language models (VLMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining. VLMs offer such priors, but deploying one directly as a detector is impractical due to its heavy inference cost. We propose MonoLaDN, a language-guided denoising framework that transfers the geometric reasoning of a VLM into a monocular 3D detector while keeping the deployed model purely vision-based. During training, a frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle from the image and its ground-truth boxes. We encode this reasoning into queries, perturb them with noise, and train the detector to reconstruct the clean reasoning. Reconstructing the corrupted reasoning forces the detector's depth-guided features to internalize the VLM's geometric priors, so this knowledge remains available even after the reasoning path is discarded at inference, adding no latency or parameters to the deployed model. Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes show that MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and generalizes well to new domains.
authors: Kiet Dang Vu, Cao Le Minh Khoa, Nguyen Viet Tri Pham, An Nguyen Gia, Tam Le Thuc Ho, Duc Dung Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed depth estimation problem in monocular 3D detection.
Uses a frozen VLM during training to reason about object occlusion, depth, dimensions, and angles.
Encodes and noise-perturbs this reasoning, training the detector to reconstruct the clean version and absorb geometric priors.
Discards the reasoning pathway at inference, so the deployed detector remains purely vision-based with no added latency or parameters.
Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art detectors and strong cross-domain generalization.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MonoLaDN. During training, a 3D Reasoning Generation stage queries a frozen VLM with the image and ground-truth 3D boxes to produce structured reasoning about each object’s occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle. A text encoder and noise injector turn this reasoning into perturbed queries, decoded jointly with the N learnable object queries under a Language-Guided Mask and trained to reconstruct the clean attributes, alongside the detection loss. At inference, the reasoning path is discarded, leaving a purely vision-based detector with no added cost.

Fig. 1: Comparison of paradigms for monocular 3D detection. (a) VLM-based methods carry rich semantic and geometric priors but are too costly for real-time inference. (b) Traditional vision-only detectors are efficient yet lack such priors, learning geometry only from image features and box annotations. (c) Our MonoLaDN injects VLM-derived 3D reasoning into a depth-guided detector during training, so it gains these priors while keeping a vision-only, efficient model at inference.

The occlusion output Êocc has no box target of its own and is broadcast as shared visibility context (dashed) to the dimension, depth, and angle heads. When a head takes more than one embedding, the inputs are averaged before the head; the 2D center head uses the mean of all four outputs. The reconstructed components are supervised by the same 2D and 3D objectives as the detection loss.

Fig. 3: 3D Reasoning Generation. The object-centric visual input and a geometryto-language mapping are fed to a frozen VLM. The mapping discretizes each attribute into an ordinal label: depth by distance binning, angle by viewpoint sectoring, dimension by shape-archetype matching, and occlusion by combining truncation and occlusion flags. The VLM then produces structured reasoning per attribute.

Fig. 2: Decoder self-attention under the Language-Guided Mask on the KITTI val set. Each row is one scene. The left column shows the image with all projected ground-truth 3D boxes (the target object in orange, others in green) and the generated reasoning for its four attributes. The right column shows the decoder self-attention matrix over the W = 4M + N queries, ordered as the 4M reasoning queries followed by the N = 50 learnable queries; the red lines separate the two groups and the thin gray lines delimit the four-attribute block of each object.

Fig. 1: Deformable cross-attention of the reasoning queries on the KITTI val set. Each row is one object, and the four columns show the occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle reasoning queries. For each query, we accumulate its deformable sampling locations at the final decoder layer, weighted by the corresponding attention weights, into a Gaussian heatmap overlaid on the image (red high, blue low). The target object is marked in green, and the generated reasoning for each attribute is shown beneath its column.

Fig. 3: Designs of the language-guided attention mask. Black entries are blocked and white entries are permitted. The leakage-prevention mask Alp stops the learnable queries from attending to any reasoning query. The separated-reasoning mask Asr lets each reasoning query attend to all reasoning queries of the same object and to those of the same attribute across objects. The attribute-isolated mask Aai is a stricter variant that additionally blocks different attributes of the same object from attending to each other.

Fig. 4: Strategies for forming the perturbed queries. All three start from the ground-truth 3D boxes and end with perturbed queries, but inject noise at different stages. BBox perturbation perturbs the boxes before the VLM, so the reasoning is generated from corrupted geometry. Reasoning perturbation generates clean reasoning and then applies text augmentation to the reasoning text before encoding. Embedding perturbation (ours) encodes the clean reasoning and injects learned noise in the embedding space.

papers.title: MonoLaDN: Language-Guided DeNoising for Monocular 3D Object Detection

papers.abstract: Existing reasoning segmentation frameworks typically employ multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with broad world knowledge to extract semantics in a human-like manner and generate corresponding segmentation masks. Nevertheless, these frameworks lack the necessary scene-specific awareness. This paper introduces driving scene reasoning segmentation (DSRS), a scene-specific task that requires models to interpret implicit instructions, infer spatial relations, detect potential risks, handle challenging conditions, and comprehend underlying traffic rules, ultimately generating accurate segmentation masks. Meanwhile, we establish a benchmark dataset to facilitate future research on the DSRS task. To pioneer this task, we propose DSRS-Net, a novel architecture with advanced reasoning segmentation capability for automated driving. Specifically, DSRS-Net seamlessly infuses geometric features for deeper reasoning segmentation, without compromising the original multimodal fusion mechanism. This strategy effectively mitigates the modality representation mismatch in MLLMs caused by RGB-only pretraining, while enhancing the integration of geometric, contextual, and linguistic features. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of DSRS-Net in both driving scene reasoning segmentation and other language-driven segmentation tasks across various public datasets. The source code and dataset will be released upon publication.

papers.abstract: Underwater spatial reasoning depends on object boundaries and geometric cues that are obscured by scattering, color distortion, and low visibility. Existing underwater resources capture these cues through images, annotations, and depth maps, but provide fragmented supervision for vision-language models. We present a spatial data engine that connects visual appearance with object-level geometry through enhancement, 2D and geometry-assisted question generation, and expert filtering. It produces 4.27M QA pairs across five capability groups. We use this corpus to train USI-Brain and introduce an Underwater Prior-guided Rectifier (UPR) that applies gated corrections to visual features. USI-Bench evaluates the resulting capabilities with 6,525 held-out QA pairs. On its 15 task metrics, USI-Brain and USI-Brain + UPR improve over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct by 5.76 and 7.63 points on average, respectively, using signed differences on 100-point scales. Ablations show that geometry-assisted supervision improves depth and ordering by 4.8 and 6.1 points with UPR disabled, while UPR adds 18.0 points in scene description under matched training data. Both variants use raw images at evaluation. Across NautData, UWBench, and MarineEval, USI-Brain achieves the best or joint-best score on 28 of 32 metrics. Model weights and USI-Bench will be released at https://github.com/SKY-Zhu-91/USI-Brain.
authors: Zhiliang Zhu, Zhiqiang Zhao, Xie'an Jiang, Yingxin Lai, Kangye Zheng, Dawei Zhao
bullets: Underwater scattering, color distortion, and low visibility obscure object boundaries and geometric cues needed for spatial reasoning.
A spatial data engine generates and filters 4.27M QA pairs covering five capability groups, including geometry-assisted supervision.
USI-Brain uses this corpus, while the Underwater Prior-guided Rectifier (UPR) applies gated corrections to visual features.
On USI-Bench, USI-Brain and USI-Brain + UPR improve over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct by 5.76 and 7.63 average points across 15 metrics.
Across three external benchmarks, USI-Brain obtains the best or joint-best result on 28 of 32 metrics; evaluation uses raw images.

papers.abstract: Humans can easily recognize the same objects across different viewpoints of a 3D scene, whereas teaching models such multi-view-consistent perception typically requires videos or calibrated multi-view captures, which are considerably more expensive and less diverse than large-scale monocular data.~In this paper, we introduce Feature Puzzles, a novel framework for learning multi-view-consistent segmentation using only single-image semantic segmentation supervision. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective pipeline that constructs multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations. We further introduce a lightweight, plug-and-play network that leverages the multi-view-consistent image features learned by existing pretrained 3D foundation models and the generated pseudo-labels to perform multi-view-consistent segmentation. Importantly, our flexible framework supports various types of prompts provided from one or multiple views and can be readily extended to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Under this single-image supervision, our feed-forward model achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++ against baselines using per-scene optimization or in-domain multi-view training, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Visual comparisons are available on our project page: https://featurepuzzles.github.io/
authors: Jiahao Ma, Qiang Zhang, Miaomiao Liu, David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Chuong Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited diversity of video or calibrated multi-view supervision.
Builds multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations.
Adds a lightweight, plug-and-play feed-forward network using pretrained 3D foundation-model features.
Supports prompts from one or multiple views and can extend to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.
Achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++, and transfers zero-shot to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.

papers.abstract: Recent LLM-centric advances can generate attractive furnished rooms by selecting and arranging assets. Yet evaluation remains limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, failing to reflect overall scene quality. To address this pressing need, we introduce GREP. Its core is a focus shift from defining specific questions to establishing a three-tier evaluation philosophy: basic physical validity checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints; visual coherence concerns compatibility in object scale, style, and composition; and, at the highest level, human-use logic requires object arrangements to align with everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent autonomously and adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. This supports scene-specific issue discovery and reliable judgments. Experiments show that (1) GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. (2) GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. (3) GREP suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. Stronger models are therefore expected not only to plan well, but also to adapt to external guidance and constraints more flexibly. Project page: https://han-808.github.io/GREP/
authors: Mohan Cao, Yongsen Mao, Chucheng Xiang, Zhongyuan Liu, Zhihang Zhong, Haiping Wang, Yuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of viewpoint- or question-specific room evaluation by assessing overall scene quality.

Achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences and outperforms baseline evaluators.
Feedback from GREP improves scene quality, while score-only and no-feedback approaches slightly reduce it; evaluation remains focused on generated room scenes.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance, but the symptom has two causes that call for opposite repairs: the relation may survive in the pooled embedding yet be unreachable by native image-text similarity, or pooling may discard it while the dense features retain it. On clean two object photographs, across ten encoders, the lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet a search over a million captions leaves nine of the ten at chance under native scoring: an access failure. On controlled C4 orbits, where the relation is the only thing that varies, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 and loses its polarity, which the patch grid retains: a pooling failure. Both sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both. Our zero parameter, query conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding. On a 118,287 image index it raises left/right pairwise accuracy against reversed geometry negatives from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96 and conditional R@1 among 21 category matched candidates from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query, while reproducing the native ranking exactly for queries that name no relation.
bullets: Across ten encoders, left/right polarity is often linearly decodable from pooled embeddings (0.77–0.99) but remains inaccessible to native image–text scoring.
Controlled experiments show pooling can preserve arrangement while discarding polarity, which remains available in patch-grid features.
A query-conditioned spatial moment recomputes geometry from patch features and stores it alongside the native embedding.
On a 118,287-image index, pairwise accuracy improves from 0.51–0.53 to 0.81–0.96, and conditional R@1 from 0.05 to 0.37–0.75.
The method adds under 1 ms per batched query and exactly preserves native rankings for queries without spatial relations.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and repairs spatial relation failure in VLMs, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Discarded or Unreachable? Diagnosing and Repairing Spatial Relation Failure in Vision--Language Similarity

papers.abstract: In biodiversity monitoring, a single image raises several questions: which taxon, how many, which trait, and whether the individual has been seen before. Vision-language models (VLMs) could answer all of these from the image, but their ability is largely untested in biology, as existing benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups. We present Bio-VQA, the largest biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark and the only one to span four aspects of biological visual understanding: hierarchical taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and individual re-identification. Bio-VQA contains 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, and extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring, so a near-miss counts for more than a distant one. Evaluating 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, we find that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms: the best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls to one sixth, from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name, and scaling helps mostly at coarse ranks. The gap to a domain specialist widens accordingly, from 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 at class (1.2x) to 0.269 against 0.544 at scientific name (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of the 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline that predicts one fixed number for every specimen, and on re-identification, 17 of the 18 models fall below chance under adversarial conditions. These failures persist across a tenfold range of model size. We hope Bio-VQA becomes a standard test of how well VLM capabilities transfer to the biological domain.

bullets: Introduces a benchmark spanning four biological reasoning tasks: hierarchical taxonomy, attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and re-identification.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support construction hazard monitoring, yet their frequent false alarms remain poorly understood. This study investigates whether false struck-by hazard warnings arise from failures in object recognition, spatial relation encoding, or hazard decisions dominated by learned co-occurrence priors. We evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B using 355 counterfactual worker-excavator scene pairs with controlled spatial proximity and worker-removal variants, combining behavioral analysis, internal representation probing, causal interventions, and decision correction. Both models recognized the entities and encoded their spatial relations (out-of-fold AUROC: 0.82 and 0.91), assigning higher hazard scores to near than far scenes in 79% and 73% of pairs. Nevertheless, 74% and 100% of far scenes were falsely classified as hazardous. Removing the worker reduced Qwen's hazard rate to 11%, while worker presence exerted 2.4- and 3.2-times greater influence on hazard scores than spatial proximity in the respective models. Attention-head interventions, neuron-level interventions, and activation steering failed to eliminate this co-occurrence bias. However, conditioning hazard decisions on the model's own spatial-relation representation improved Qwen's specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity, outperforming threshold recalibration. These findings reveal that VLM struck-by false alarms stem primarily from decision-making failures rather than deficiencies in object recognition or spatial encoding, suggesting that future efforts should prioritize conditioning hazard decisions on encoded spatial evidence rather than further improving visual recognition alone.

papers.abstract: Satellite-ground localization estimates the planar position and yaw orientation of a ground camera within a geo-referenced satellite image. Most recent methods map ground and satellite features into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) space and establish spatial correspondences. However, insufficient depth constraints can assign one ground feature to different distances along a viewing direction, creating geometric ambiguity in BEV feature placement. Similar appearances at different locations can also create descriptor matching ambiguity, while existing descriptor learning lacks explicit semantic supervision to distinguish them. We propose GeoSem-BEV, a geometry-semantic constrained BEV representation learning method. Radial depth supervision constrains distance assignment, and vertical height supervision constrains height aggregation. Shared explicit semantic supervision promotes consistent semantic predictions across views and helps distinguish locations with similar semantics. These constraints improve feature placement and descriptor discriminability, enhancing state-of-the-art BEV localization models. On VIGOR with unknown orientation, GeoSem-BEV reduces mean orientation error by 37.2% and 38.1% in the cross-area and same-area settings, respectively. The corresponding errors are reduced by 10.8% and 15.6% on DReSS-D. On KITTI-CVL, it reduces same-area mean orientation error by 26.8% under 10 degree orientation noise.
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity in BEV feature placement and descriptor ambiguity between visually similar locations.

Applies shared explicit semantic supervision to produce consistent predictions across satellite and ground views.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.

papers.abstract: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.

Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution assigns local evidence-based credit to the observation actions responsible for each branch’s outcome.
Experiments show consistent improvements across Qwen3-VL model scales, with competitive performance versus larger and tool-augmented models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.
authors: ZhengXian Wu, Qianhao Nie, Zhuohong Chen, Junjie Gao, Yuyao Zhang, Yunyao Yu, Hangrui Xu, Cheng Cheng, Guiyu Ma, Jin Zhang, Xingzhong Xu, Kai Yang, Haoqian Wang

Covers set-wise, sequential, hybrid wide-deep, competitive disambiguation, and visual-structure-guided search.
Each task includes a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules for overall success and intermediate results.
Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solved 26.47% of tasks.
Findings highlight challenges in linking visual evidence with retrieved information to produce complete answers.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained cross-view localization aims to precisely localize a ground camera against geo-referenced aerial imagery, but current methods typically assume a narrow geographic prior, substantially limiting their applicability when upstream localization remains coarse. To bridge this gap, we study this task over much larger aerial regions. However, this seemingly simple extension fundamentally changes the localization problem: the growing disparity in spatial extent between ground and aerial views makes reliable cross-view matching difficult to establish directly, while the increasing number of look-alike locations in larger regions introduces substantial visual ambiguity. To address these challenges, we propose RingMatch, a search-and-verification framework for wide-area cross-view localization. RingMatch first leverages predictive uncertainty to uncover plausible locations and progressively zooms into their surroundings to obtain increasingly fine-grained evidence, yielding a compact set of promising candidates. We then introduce the depth ring, a novel geometric representation that reveals subtle variations in the spatial layout around a location and serves as a view-shared spatial signature for an LVLM verifier to resolve residual ambiguity. To benchmark this setting, we construct VIGOR-Pro by composing VIGOR aerial tiles into contiguous regions with spatial extents of up to 400 m. Experiments show that RingMatch maintains strong localization performance as the aerial region expands, consistently outperforming representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods.
authors: Qingguo Hu, Xinyu Ma, Yujie Lin, Yaoxiang Wang, Qi Shi, Zonghao Guo, Chi Chen, Jinsong Su
bullets: Addresses the limited geographic priors and visual ambiguity that hinder fine-grained cross-view localization over large aerial areas.
Uses predictive uncertainty to propose plausible locations, then progressively zooms in to gather finer-grained matching evidence.
Introduces depth ring, a view-shared spatial representation used by an LVLM verifier to distinguish look-alike candidates.
Constructs VIGOR-Pro with contiguous aerial regions spanning up to 400 m to benchmark wide-area localization.
Experiments show strong performance as region size grows, outperforming representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RingMatch. RingMatch first performs multi-hypothesis branch-and-zoom search over the aerial region, using predictive uncertainty to expose plausible hypotheses and recursively zoom into them to produce a compact candidate shortlist. It then resolves the remaining ambiguity with depth-ring-grounded verification. Ground observations and candidate aerial patches are mapped to depth rings that capture subtle details of the surrounding spatial layout. The correct candidate exhibits strong consistency with the ground observation, whereas a look-alike candidate does not. An LVLM verifier leverages this evidence to select the final location.

Figure 1: (a) Existing fine-grained cross-view localization methods incur substantially larger errors as the aerial region expands from 35 × 35m to 400 × 400m. (b) A large aerial region can contain multiple look-alike locations compatible with the same ground observation (inset). In this example, locations • A and • B share similar appearance with the true location (⋆). The main differences lie in subtle spatial details, such as building outlines and the arrangement of surrounding vegetation.

Figure 7: Architecture of the aerial-to-ring predictor. DINOv2 and DPT encode the local aerial patch into a dense feature map. The candidate location p conditions the A azimuth queries through FiLM modulation. For each azimuth, a directional beam is sampled from p, and the corresponding query attends only to features along that beam. Each updated query predicts a metric-depth class, producing the aerial depth ring over all azimuths. During training, the predictor is supervised by the ground depth ring extracted from the corresponding panorama.

papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.
bullets: Addresses persistent AR assistance when historical questions require visual evidence from earlier encounters.
Uses hierarchical acquisition: quality, novelty, and temporal cues select monochrome observations for detailed RGB capture.
Links semantic observations to source images and separates capture acceptance, interpretation, and question-specific support.
Introduces bounded reassessment of familiar views and source-dependency-guided retention.
In replay, six RGB views were selected from 648 observations, while feature extraction covered 97.7%; frequent local inference remains costly.

papers.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.

bullets: Targets robot understanding of object references from a 3D scene, pointing gesture, and language description.
Uses an Embodied Fusion module to jointly represent language, gesture, and vision in a shared embedding space.
Applies foveation to focus point-cloud processing on a coarse region near the estimated pointing direction.
Reports approximately 8% higher accuracy and 2.95× faster execution with comparable accuracy when foveation is used, relative to prior models.

papers.abstract: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, respectively, substantially outperforming the strong training-based baseline UniTranslator. On the more challenging and realistic whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1\% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which only address the text-rendering stage rather than the complete IIMT task. These results establish flow-based editing as a strong, fully training-free baseline for IIMT.
authors: Zhixian Li, Xingsong Ye, Yongkun Du, Yunyan Xiao, Yanglin Huang, Pinxuan Chen, Jiyu Zhuang, Cong Xu, Zhineng Chen
bullets: Addresses IIMT without requiring paired before-and-after translation images.
Uses OCR to identify text and an LLM to create translation prompts for a text-to-image diffusion model.
Introduces Region Coupling Release and Coupling Expansion to improve translated-text accuracy and naturalness during editing.
Achieves 20.6 PRIM BLEU and 57.2 COMET under EasyOCR read-back, outperforming UniTranslator.
Reaches 40.1% exact-match accuracy on whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese; results establish a training-free baseline for IIMT.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of the IIMT framework and editor paradigms. (a) The pipeline: OCR extracts text → a translator produces the translation → a scene text editor generates the output image. (b) Rule-based: remove, render, and paste separately. (c) Training-based: a learned GAN or diffusion editor (requires extra training). (d) FlowTranslator (ours): training-free flow editing with trajectory controls (CE and RCR) for text translation with background preservation.

Figure 2 Overview of FlowTranslator. OCR extracts the source text and forms a source caption, while a frozen LLM translates it to obtain the target caption. A frozen VAE encodes the source image into 𝑍src 0 , from which noise initialization produces 𝑍FE 𝑇 . At each editing step, the same frozen DiT predicts source- and target-conditioned velocities. Their difference updates the flow-editing latent. RCR perturbs the target-branch noise within the detected text region, and CE amplifies the accumulated displacement before it is fed back to the target branch. The final latent 𝑍FE 0 is decoded to produce the translated image.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparison on whole-image ScenePair En→Zh translation. For each example, we show the source image (with red boxes marking text to be translated), the requested target text, and outputs of existing open-source methods, followed by FlowTranslator. FlowTranslator renders the requested Chinese text within the original region. It preserves both the surrounding scene and the local text appearance.

papers.abstract: Promptable perception, from GroundingDINO to Rex-Omni, puts one model behind one prompt interface and returns coordinates for any localisation task. Every model in that line was built for photographs; none has been given a sketch. We present Sketch-Omni, to our knowledge the first perception MLLM built to work on sketches and from them. On a sketch, the sketch is the image, and text prompts detect, point, resolve object and spatial referring expressions, and ground affordances in it. From a sketch, the sketch is the prompt, and a drawing of one object localises that object in a photograph, even among several of the same category, a query that neither a category name nor a photo exemplar can pose. Two obstacles stand in the way. A photo-trained model's attention is tuned to colour and texture, which a sketch does not have, and no dataset pairs a drawing with the one instance it depicts among others of its kind. We build the training data instead of collecting it. An edge detector turns every labelled photograph into a sketch-like drawing that keeps the photograph's labels, and two constructions produce sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing data. On top of this, photo-guided relation alignment passes each photograph and its edge sketch through the same model and trains the sketch pass to reproduce how the photograph pass relates phrases to patches and patches to each other. Not one training label is drawn by hand. Sketch-Omni reaches 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation against 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with a lead that doubles when the photograph holds several instances of the queried category, and it is best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks. Code, model, and a hand-annotated benchmark of 2754 sketch-to-photo links will be released.
authors: Dongyu Wang, Dar-Yen Chen, Zhiming Hong, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of sketch-capable perception models and the difficulty of identifying one instance among multiple same-category objects.
Builds training data automatically by converting labelled photos into edge sketches and constructing sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing datasets.
Uses photo-guided relation alignment to transfer phrase–patch and patch–patch relationships from photographs to sketches.
Achieves 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation versus 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with larger gains in multi-instance scenes.
Performs best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks; a hand-annotated benchmark of 2,754 sketch-to-photo links is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.

bullets: Targets embodied and web agents’ difficulty with multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints.

Finds a gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning: agents miss optimal task sequences and produce infeasible grounded actions.
Shows that perception and topology understanding alone do not reliably support constrained planning.
Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is pivotal for computer-assisted intervention, yet demands compositional reasoning across instruments, anatomy, and workflow. Existing surgical vision-language models rely on instruction tuning with large-scale question-answer pairs, entailing laborious data curation and costly retraining. To bridge this gap, we propose SurgEye, a perception-reasoning framework that grounds reasoning in a vision foundation model without instruction tuning. Specifically, we devise Routed Multi-Task Perception (RMP) that routes the vision foundation model through task-specific pathways learned from public perception labels, producing spatial and temporal evidence. We further introduce Agentic Compositional Reasoning (ACR) that employs a frozen large language model to coordinate RMP specialists and temporal memory as callable tools, composing evidence across tasks and time into grounded answers. Moreover, we construct SurgEye-Bench spanning eight surgical procedures, pairing each question with perception labels for verifiable evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SurgEye outperforms state-of-the-arts in surgical reasoning. The source code will be available.

papers.abstract: Humans imagine scene changes under hypothetical motions, an ability central to spatial reasoning and robotic planning. However, this capability remains underexplored in vision-language models and world models. We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) and introduce FlowBench, a resource for training and evaluating both, with 428K training examples spanning simulated and real-world scenes, household environments and tabletop manipulation, and diverse question types. A scalable, fully automatic pipeline pairs each hypothetical motion with spatial questions and, in simulation, exact outcome frames and optical flow. For VLMs, proprietary models exhibit an imagination gap, performing worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when observed, and open-source models perform near chance; fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train raises its accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, a strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for all four model families we test, raising the accuracy of Psi-0.6 from 52.1% to 61.7%. FlowBench thus serves as a training and evaluation resource for both. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/liuyifan22/FlowBench.

bullets: Introduces Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) as a benchmarkable capability for spatial reasoning and robotic planning.

FlowBench training improves text-to-flow prediction across four tested world-model families, including Psi-0.6.

papers.abstract: Earth observation (EO) workflows require selecting among known outcomes, estimating confidence, and processing large volumes of imagery. Generative vision-language models can address these tasks, but autoregressive decoding is computationally costly and their confidence estimates are unreliable. Decision models offer an alternative, returning probabilities over candidate answers in a single forward pass. However, their accuracy, calibration, and transfer across EO tasks remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these properties through a diagnostic study of d3-flash (8.4B parameters) across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks. We find that compositional reasoning transfers well and calibration improves over its Qwen3.5-9B backbone on 24 settings, while counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain challenging. To address these limitations, we adapt d3-flash through low-rank fine-tuning on public EO training splits, producing EO-Jev. EO-Jev improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28. It also achieves an average gain of 8.0 points across 12 held-out settings and lower expected calibration error than specialists on 21 of 28 settings. These improvements come at a modest cost of 1.8 points in general decision performance. Our results demonstrate the potential of adapting general decision models into competitive EO generalists while highlighting persistent challenges in quantitative perception, option-order consistency, and calibration under distribution shift.
bullets: Decision models provide single-pass probabilities over candidate answers, avoiding the costly decoding and unreliable confidence of generative vision-language models.
A diagnostic study evaluates d3-flash across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks.
Compositional reasoning transfers well, but counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain difficult.
Low-rank fine-tuning yields EO-Jev, which improves over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28.
EO-Jev gains 8.0 average points on 12 held-out settings and improves calibration, with a modest 1.8-point decline in general decision performance.

papers.abstract: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.
bullets: Addresses interoperator variability caused by manual caliper placement in ultrasound biometry.
Uses clinical measurement questions and language-model decision representations to query shared dense ultrasound features.
Generates endpoint probability maps rather than directly predicting coordinates, capturing localization uncertainty.
Trains jointly with landmark-localization and clinical-measurement losses.
On the FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, reports 22.50-pixel MRE and 15.38 measurement MAE, outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Geospatial text spotting involves locating and transcribing geographic labels, such as road names, district names, and landmarks, in raster maps. These labels are often small, densely arranged, and arbitrarily oriented. Although Arabic text recognition has been studied extensively in documents and natural scenes, Arabic geospatial text spotting remains underexplored. We introduce ARABGEOTEXT, an Arabic-centric benchmark covering 970 geographic locations in Riyadh and Jeddah, with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type. For each location, we pair an OpenStreetMap (OSM) rendering with a composite created by overlaying that rendering on the corresponding remote sensing (RS) imagery. The paired views preserve label content and pixel geometry, allowing evaluation across different backgrounds. Geographic partitions support in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting. Experiments with direct Qwen3.5-4B spotting show difficulties in recovering all labels within a tile. We therefore propose a tool-augmented vision-language framework that combines YOLO26 localization and crop rectification with Qwen3.5-4B recognition adapted through low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting across both image views and test cities. With localization held fixed, reader adaptation further improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ArabGeoText.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored task of locating and transcribing small, dense, arbitrarily oriented Arabic geographic labels.
Provides 970 locations in Riyadh and Jeddah with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type, pairing OpenStreetMap renderings with remote-sensing composites.
Supports in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting across different visual backgrounds.
Combines YOLO26 localization, crop rectification, and LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B recognition.
The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting, while reader adaptation improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader.
