papers.abstract: Many manipulation goals are easier to visualize than to specify numerically through explicit geometric constraints. We present VerifLM, a framework that converts image-edited goal configurations into physically verified 6-DoF object poses for planning. Using an edited image, VerifLM recovers an initial relative pose between an active object and a passive object, then prompts a vision-language model to generate axis-wise sampling constraints and a task-specific validation program. Candidate poses are evaluated in a physics simulator, and the VLM selects the most task-consistent retained candidate. To operate without predefined object meshes or physical parameters, VerifLM reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs multiple hypothetical simulations with varying physics and geometry. Parallel-world validation evaluates candidates across geometry--physics variations and ranks them by the number of worlds in which they satisfy the validation program. We evaluate VerifLM on nine manipulation tasks. VerifLM achieves the highest task success on eight of nine tasks, with the largest performance gain on goals requiring precise orientation and contact relationships.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying manipulation goals with explicit geometric constraints.
Uses a vision-language model to generate axis-wise pose constraints and task-specific validation programs from edited images.
Reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D data and tests candidate poses across simulations with varied geometry and physics.
Ranks candidates by how consistently they satisfy the validation program across parallel simulated worlds.
Evaluated on nine tasks, achieving the highest task success on eight, with the largest gains for precise orientation and contact goals.

papers.abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of dense scaling for complex, multi-request video editing.
Introduces MoE-Attention, which routes key–value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens.
Scales from a 5B initialization to 14B and 56B parameters, activating approximately 8B parameters per token in both variants.
Analysis finds routing responds more to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories, with sensitivity to object-level semantics.
Identifies decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling; evaluations compare against existing methods and complementary MoE baselines.

papers.abstract: Two machines can each recognize an object well and still fail together. We study classifiers that see different parts of one object and send short messages to a receiver that identifies its class. Coordination asks how to design messages together; cooperation asks whether the team outperforms one sender given the whole budget. On three digit datasets, messages designed together beat messages designed apart by 18.07 to 22.68 percentage points on average with two-bit messages, with gains in all 24 configurations. A fixed agreement, you report the row and I the column, recovers about half this gain, with only the receiver learned. Senders that draw the same distinctions waste a narrow vocabulary, and senders whose distinctions cross multiply it. A team has no more possible messages than one sender with the same budget, so a partner must bring evidence the first lacks. A solvable model shows individual statistics alone cannot determine whether a partnership helps. On MNIST digits, six shared bits remove 49.54 percent of the strongest tested solo's errors on average. Paired measurements correctly predicted most sensor teams would reduce average accuracy on new participants. Who should speak is a property of the pair, and must be measured in pairs.
bullets: The study examines classifiers that observe different parts of an object and send short messages to a receiver.
Jointly designed messages outperform separately designed ones by 18.07–22.68 percentage points across 24 two-bit configurations on three digit datasets.
A fixed row/column communication scheme recovers about half the coordination gain while learning only the receiver.
Senders should make complementary distinctions: overlapping distinctions waste limited message capacity, while cross-cutting distinctions expand useful information.
Pairwise measurements predicted that most tested sensor teams would improve average accuracy on new participants.

papers.title: The Tower of Babel in artificial intelligence: who should speak, and when it pays to listen
papers.tldr: Effective AI teams depend on complementary, jointly designed communication between partial observers—not merely on strong individual classifiers.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects and their spatial relationships evolve in 3D space over time remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), particularly under changing viewpoints. Recent approaches incorporate geometric information into reasoning, but explicit supervision for temporally ordered 4D state evolution and its use as intermediate evidence remains limited. We introduce \textbf{Trace4D}, which trains VLMs to predict 4D state sequences and reason over their inter-timestep changes alongside temporal visual observations. Its 4D-grounded chain-of-thought (CoT) explicitly represents 4D states, analyzes temporal visual context, and connects both as evidence for the answer. We construct Trace4D-Train from in-the-wild videos with 600K 4D perception examples and approximately 70K grounded QA examples, and train with joint supervised fine-tuning followed by geometry-aware GRPO. At inference, Trace4D predicts 4D states and reasoning directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model. Experiments on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D show improved QA accuracy over the base VLMs and benefits from reasoning over 4D state changes and temporal visual observations.
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty in tracking object states and spatial relationships over time under changing viewpoints.
Predicts temporally ordered 4D states, analyzes their changes, and combines them with temporal visual observations in grounded chain-of-thought reasoning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.
bullets: Introduces 282 offline Street View tasks involving panorama rotation, zooming, and movement, plus 42 expert-referenced GeoGuessr championship rounds.
Tests three task types: coordinate localization, place naming, and finding, reading, or counting nearby objects.
Evaluates 23 VLMs; best reported accuracy is 62.5% for place naming and 35.0% for object finding, while the strongest agent approaches expert GeoGuessr performance.
Finds only weak correlation between localization and exploration ability, with errors categorized as vision, navigation, or tool-use failures.
Shows that environment difficulty can be adjusted through view limits and that a Planner-Worker-Compressor harness reduces planner tokens by 57–61%.

papers.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
bullets: Introduces drawing-to-render correspondence: deciding whether an orthographic drawing and shaded render depict the same part.
Builds BlueCAD-30K from 29,925 CAD models with aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings across six viewpoints, and surface metadata.
Frozen encoders achieve up to 65% Recall@1 with known viewpoints, falling to 43% when viewpoints are unknown.
Zero-shot vision-language models reach 0.52–0.67 verification accuracy and exhibit model-specific Yes/No biases.
LoRA fine-tuning slightly improves accuracy but does not solve viewpoint failures and intensifies bias.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent target-related responses from different camera viewpoints in MLLMs.
Uses geometry tokens to predict local SO(3) rotations and channel-wise routing coefficients in learned feature subspaces.
Applies a closed-form Padé–Cayley transformation and gates identity-relative corrections into visual and geometry features.
Improves 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning across training scales and backbones compared with additive fusion.
View analyses show changing routing states, more localized target responses, and stronger performance across viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.
bullets: Motivation: Strong single-image benchmark performance does not guarantee coherent 3D structure over video or viewpoint changes.
Method: Evaluate predictions on real-world video sequences with moving cameras and use structure from motion to anchor affine-invariant depth to metric values.
Findings: The evaluation exposes challenges in achieving temporal consistency over long time periods.
Scope: It also reveals limitations in directly using structure from motion for metric grounding of monocular depth.
Contribution: A viewpoint-sequence benchmark methodology for assessing consistency and metric applicability of monocular depth models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, such as saying an object that is not present in an image. We ask a more fundamental question: whether a VLM is even aware of where it is looking before understanding the semantic meaning in the image. We formulate this question as a LOOK task: identifying which parts of its visual input were available to the model. We construct the task in a self-supervised way without manually labeling the available region to the model. Our experiments show that existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region. We further show that fine-tuning VLMs on the proposed LOOK task improves a model's awareness of visual input.
bullets: Targets visual hallucination and the more basic issue of visual-input awareness.
Defines LOOK as identifying the portions of an image available to the model before semantic interpretation.
Constructs the task without manually labeling visible regions.
Finds that existing VLMs struggle to localize their visible input.
Shows that fine-tuning on LOOK improves visual-input awareness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Where does a hallucination originate? In this example, we ask what animal is grazing in a photograph of a dog on grassland, a model answers “a sheep”. papers.abstract: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.
bullets: Benchmarks joint prediction of oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor scenes.
Separates evaluation into Structure, measuring relative layout, and Metric, measuring physical scale and camera-anchored placement.
Includes nine atomic spatial QA tasks and offline navigation to connect reconstruction quality with spatial reasoning and path planning.
Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs finds a consistent Structure–Metric gap; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure versus 58.7% on Metric.
Diagnostic studies show relational consistency does not guarantee metric accuracy, while spatial fine-tuning transfers across spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
bullets: Reframes floodwater-level detection as an explicit visual reasoning task to address weak interpretability and poor cross-scene generalization.
Uses Qwen2.5-VL with Group Relative Policy Optimization and a HydroKG-based path reward to supervise reasoning without requiring extensive reasoning annotations.
Introduces HydroLevel, a 3,000-image floodwater benchmark for training and evaluation.
Outperforms conventional vision baselines by 4.0 percentage points in-domain and 13.6 percentage points out-of-domain; out-of-domain performance drops 4.4 points.
4-bit quantization reduces GPU memory usage by 57% and latency by 43%, while confidence-based routing improves safety and reduces cloud computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed collaborative edge-cloud traffic monitoring network. The system leverages 5G technology to aggregate multi-source floodwater imagery from Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), vehicles (dashcams), and Roadside Units (RSUs). These diverse data streams, captured from heterogeneous viewpoints, are transmitted to the cloud server or processed locally, where the proposed HydroReasoner framework performs efficient and interpretable floodwater level reasoning.

Fig. 2. The overall framework of HydroReasoner. The pipeline comprises three stages: (I) Reasoning Path Generation: the policy model performs explicit reasoning on the input floodwater image and outputs a structured reasoning path. (II) HydroKG Path Verification: the reasoning path is parsed into candidate triples and verified against HydroKG for structural completeness and consistency with domain grading rules. (III) Reward Shaping and GRPO Update: the verification result, together with format and accuracy signals, forms a composite reward that drives the policy update.

Fig. 7. Comprehensive performance analysis of HydroReasoner versus baseline models. The subfigures illustrate: (a) the relationship between in-domain/outof-domain four-class accuracy and safety; (b) the relationship among parameter scale, generalization gap, and accuracy; (c) the trade-offs among coarse-/finegrained task performance, safety, and model size; and (d) an overall assessment that integrates out-of-domain accuracy, safety, and robustness (note that all metrics in the figure are normalized).

papers.abstract: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.
bullets: Targets semantic lifting methods that rely on local 2D mask evidence and lack holistic object-level structure.
Uses vision-language models to provide object-level semantic priors alongside mask-based lifting.
Builds an object-group scene graph with intra-group refinement to reduce semantic noise.
Uses inter-group acquisition to expand object support with structurally relevant neighboring candidates.
Experiments on indoor scene datasets show improved semantic consistency and structural completeness of object categories.

Throughout 3D Gaussian optimization, the semantic representation and scene graph are iteratively updated, allowing object-centric reasoning over Gaussian groups. The scene graph further guides language-based intra-group refinement and inter-group acquisition, improving semantic consistency and structural completeness.

papers.abstract: Geometry is the very form that connects space, time, and matter, serving as the fundamental fabric of the physical world, from continuous fields to discrete structures. Despite its importance, deep learning is inherently blind to geometry. Riemannian geometry stands as a well-established mathematical foundation for studying geometry, yet it remains largely incompatible with deep learning architectures. To bridge this gap, we establish a new learning framework--Geometric Morphology Learning--that learns geometric or topological structures, shapes or conformations for representation learning, reasoning and action modeling. Moving beyond early attempts limited to specific geometric priors, this theory centers on modeling the intrinsic geometry of objects and learning from such geometric or topological knowledge. Specifically, we construct a neural bundle, a unified scaffolding linking local and global structures, and formulate differentiable operators, including connection and curvature, thereby enabling the study of geometry with advanced geometric concepts such as holonomy and cohomology. Consequently, Geometric Morphology Learning opens new horizons in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDE systems, and dynamics, marking a fundamental shift toward instilling systematic geometry in artificial intelligence.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between geometry’s role in physical systems and deep learning’s limited geometric awareness.
Introduces a neural bundle to connect local and global structures in a unified scaffold.
Defines differentiable geometric operators, including connections and curvature, and supports concepts such as holonomy and cohomology.
Targets applications in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDEs, and dynamical systems.
The abstract presents a broad theoretical framework but reports no specific experiments or quantitative results.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes geometry-aware learning framework for foundation models, targeting spatial reasoning and dynamics.
papers.title: Geometric Morphology Learning: Empowering Foundation Models from Structure to Spacetime Intelligence
papers.tldr: Geometric Morphology Learning proposes a framework for integrating intrinsic geometric and topological structure into deep learning, enabling more geometry-aware representation, reasoning, and action modeling.

papers.abstract: Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT$^3$, the first 3D-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object-mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. To mitigate this multi-instance ambiguity, we design an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism that uses query-guided cross-attention to fuse candidate object tokens and inject both evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning process. To better equip the model with multi-step reasoning capability, we further develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT instruction tuning dataset with approximately 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue, and planning tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D-text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding.
bullets: Addresses weak grounded multi-step reasoning and text-centric inference in 3D large language models.
Interleaves task-relevant 3D scene evidence with textual chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses query-guided cross-attention to aggregate candidate objects while preserving ambiguity cues.
Introduces PointCoT, a 176.2K-instance 3D chain-of-thought instruction-tuning dataset covering captioning, QA, dialogue, and planning.
Experiments on six benchmarks report consistent improvements and state-of-the-art performance.

These tokens are injected into the reasoning chain to form the final 3D-text interleaved multi-modal CoT.

papers.abstract: Motion language models (MoLMs) encode 3D human motion as discrete tokens for language-based understanding. Deploying them on monocular video raises two problems. Pose detection yields 2D joint sequences, leaving a dimensional gap from the 3D motion used in training. Moreover, the 2D observation changes with the camera viewpoint, while the depth lost in projection makes the 2D pose ambiguous across viewpoints. We propose MoPort, a view-aware 2D interface that enables MoLMs to take 2D observations as input. We introduce Paired View Alignment (PVA), which gives two views of the same motion a shared 3D teacher target and directly constrains the consistency of their latents, so that 2D observations from different viewpoints are mapped to a consistent semantic representation. Camera-Modulated Encoding (CME) estimates the camera extrinsics from the 2D sequence and uses them to modulate encoding, providing the 2D latents with geometric information about the viewpoint. MoPort achieves R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming all evaluated baselines. On HumanML3D, its R@1 decreases only from 0.5763 on in-distribution viewpoints to 0.5585 on out-of-distribution viewpoints. We validate portability on three downstream MoLMs. Furthermore, on the real-world RGB video dataset Fit3D, MoPort achieves 80.36\% accuracy. Code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Addresses the 2D–3D representation gap and viewpoint ambiguity when applying MoLMs to monocular video.
Uses Paired View Alignment to map different-view 2D observations of the same motion to consistent semantic latents.
Uses Camera-Modulated Encoding to estimate camera extrinsics and incorporate viewpoint geometry during encoding.
Reports R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Shows robustness across viewpoints, portability to three downstream MoLMs, and 80.36% accuracy on Fit3D.

An MLP maps the standardized R6D representation c of R̂ to multi-scale FiLM parameters. (c) At inference, YOLOv8x [11] and ViTPose-H [37] extract 2D tracks, which MoPort maps to the native tokens of a pretrained MoLM. Dashed arrows indicate training supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MoPort, a view-aware interface for Motion Language Models to handle 2D observations of 3D motion, addressing spatial understanding and geometric consistency.
papers.title: MoPort: A View-Aware 2D Interface for Motion Language Models
papers.tldr: MoPort lets motion language models interpret monocular 2D pose sequences by aligning views and encoding camera geometry, achieving strong cross-view motion-text retrieval and real-video recognition.

papers.abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
bullets: Detects meaningful scene changes with patch-embedding dissimilarity and triggers burst captures selectively.
Combines motion-based patch changes with top-down attention to focus on task-relevant regions.
Reweights, rather than removes, visual tokens during generation using a calibrated value cache.
Feeds decoder text-to-vision attention back into the next observation cycle for iterative refinement.
On a 500-video EgoSchema subset, achieves 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 calls per clip; captioning matches the best baseline with 57% fewer calls than uniform sampling.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions, requiring reasoning over semantics, spatial relationships, and multi-view observations. Training-free approaches avoid costly annotations but often rely on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which may waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions. We observe that effective grounding should prioritize observations that provide evidence for the query rather than uniformly represent the entire scene. Based on this insight, we introduce QVR3D, a query-guided visual reasoning framework that operates on RGB-D observations using off-the-shelf foundation models. QVR3D combines Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) for selecting complementary query-relevant views with Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) that integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency, and relationship consistency. The framework supports both single- and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation. Experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, while QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/jwliao1209/QVR3D.
bullets: Targets inefficient scene-level view selection that spends visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions.
Uses Query-Guided Maximum Coverage to select complementary views relevant to the language query.
Uses Grounding Probability Estimation to combine instance, attribute, and relationship consistency.
Supports both single-object and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art zero-shot results on ScanRefer and Nr3D, with improved frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks.

papers.abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to identify a query-view target in a satellite image, yet reliable instance grounding remains challenging under substantial viewpoint discrepancies. Although recent methods incorporate multimodal prompts, they insufficiently address the varying transferability of linguistic and visual evidence across views. Viewpoint-dependent descriptions (e.g., building facades visible in oblique UAV views but not in top-down satellite images) may become unreliable for satellite grounding, while visually similar instances further complicate target identification. To address these challenges, we rethink CVOGL from a visual grounding perspective and propose GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for constructing target-centered evidence and establishing discriminative cross-view correspondence. Specifically, view-aware referring reasoning mitigates viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen visual-semantic correspondence, and scene-level supervision with alignment-based verification distinguishes competing satellite instances. We further introduce CVOGL-Text, a street- and drone-to-satellite benchmark with query-derived expressions. GAV achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5 (+18.19 percentage points) and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on CVOGL-Text.
bullets: CVOGL must transfer target evidence between street/drone views and top-down satellite imagery despite major viewpoint differences.
GAV uses view-aware referring reasoning to reduce ambiguity from descriptions that are unreliable across viewpoints.
Multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen cross-view visual-semantic correspondence.
Scene-level supervision and alignment-based verification help separate competing satellite instances.
GAV reports 62.55% Acc@0.5 on MoP-UAV and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on the introduced CVOGL-Text benchmark.

papers.abstract: Digital image correlation (DIC) is a widely used non-contact technique for full-field displacement measurement. Data-driven deep-learning DIC offers rapid inference but may generalize poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels, and illumination conditions. Classical optimization-based DIC and recent image-constrained neural formulations avoid labeled displacement data, yet their convergence and accuracy remain vulnerable to initialization, large rigid-body motion, fine non-uniform deformation, and gray-value disturbances. This paper presents a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework for robust pixelwise measurement. Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement, providing a reliable initialization under large translation and rotation. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), and optimizes it using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss. The local gray-value model explicitly accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation, and degraded imaging conditions.
bullets: Addresses poor generalization of learning-based DIC and optimization failures caused by large motion, fine deformation, noise, and gray-value disturbances.
First estimates dominant rigid motion using coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement for reliable initialization.
Then models residual displacement with a hybrid KAN–MLP neural field optimized using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss.
Explicitly accounts for multiplicative and additive intensity changes through a local gray-value model.
Simulated and real experiments show accurate and stable recovery under rotation, non-uniform deformation, noise, illumination variation, and degraded imaging.

papers.abstract: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.
bullets: Targets reliable perception of UI components and synthesis of structured, executable interfaces.
Uses an 80-category, two-level taxonomy with supervision for category prediction, OCR, color recognition, and grounding.
Generates UIs progressively as DSL outputs from requirement–screenshot–JSON training tuples.
Applies online GRPO with server-side rendering and LLM-based and contrastive preference evaluation.
Reports strongest referring/dense-grounding results on its benchmark and the best composite generation score among compared compact models; finer perception also improves generation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison learned by prior within-instance self-supervised methods.
Pairs two visual instances, mixes their local elements, and trains the model to separate them by origin while restoring spatial, temporal, or geometric order.
Uses diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum to create richer automatically verifiable rewards from unlabeled data.
Applied to cross-image jigsaws, 3D depth, and video temporal ordering, with reported gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding across benchmarks.
Evaluations across model scales and families indicate broad generality, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

papers.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-only methods and language-based planners that lack spatial beliefs.
Combines VLM object-likelihood scores with geometric occupancy evidence using Bayesian log-odds filtering.
Uses high-belief voxel regions to choose viewpoints, explore unseen areas, or interact with closed cabinets.
Evaluated end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid, outperforming geometry-only and LLM-based search methods.

papers.abstract: Multi-image vision-language models (VLMs) incur substantial computation when processing long visual sequences. Compressing these sequences must preserve complementary evidence across images and keep tokens from different images separate. Global selection can underrepresent question-relevant images, and pruning in early decoder layers risks removing relevant content before sufficient multimodal processing, yet existing methods spend most of the budget on these early layers. We propose SIEVE, a training-free, single-pass framework that jointly allocates visual tokens across images and decoder depth. SIEVE first pools each image into a compact spatial grid to reduce early processing cost. It then progressively selects representatives using prompt attention under equal per-image quotas and aggregates unselected tokens into similar representatives from the same image. These operations keep every image represented and its tokens separate from other images, while refining the retained representations. A closed-form schedule sets retention counts to target a prescribed average token budget across decoder layers. Across four VLM backbones, SIEVE achieves the highest average at a 6.25% budget on five multi-image benchmarks and four single-image benchmarks, and the highest mean on two video benchmarks. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 9.96 and 9.03 points at 6.25% and 12.5% budgets, and at 12.5% it exceeds the uncompressed model by 2.01 points with 6.6x fewer prefill FLOPs.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of compressing long multi-image visual sequences without losing question-relevant or cross-image evidence.
Pools each image into a compact grid, then progressively selects prompt-relevant tokens under equal per-image quotas.
Aggregates discarded tokens only into similar representatives from the same image, keeping image-specific information separate.
Uses a closed-form depth schedule to distribute token retention across decoder layers.

Across multiple VLM backbones and image/video benchmarks, SIEVE achieves leading average performance at low budgets; on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it delivers 6.6× fewer prefill FLOPs while exceeding the uncompressed model at a 12.5% budget.

papers.abstract: We propose \emph{Déjà Vu}, a test-time decoding module for semantic correspondence. Matching semantically equivalent keypoints across images of the same object category is challenging due to variations in appearance, viewpoint, and scale. While features from large pretrained vision models carry strong zero-shot correspondence ability, existing methods reduce final matching to greedy top-$1$ nearest-neighbor selection. We show that the correct correspondence appears among the top-ranked candidates far more often than top-$1$ matching achieves: with $30$ candidates, zero-shot features exceed the top-$1$ accuracy of a supervised model. This reveals a \textit{decoding bottleneck} rather than a limit of the representation. Motivated by this observation, we formulate semantic correspondence as a \textit{recall-then-rerank} problem. Our method first nominates an adaptive candidate set, larger when the similarity distribution is ambiguous and smaller when it is confident, then re-ranks the candidates with a graded cycle-consistency score: each candidate is matched back to the source image and penalized by how far its reverse match lands from the original keypoint. The module operates entirely on the similarity matrix already computed by the base method. It consistently improves three representative baselines on SPair-71k, its geometric subset, and PF-Pascal under both unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, with gains of up to $+1.8$ PCK@0.10 on SPair-71k and $+3.4$ PCK@0.15 on PF-Pascal, and $+4.9$ under Keypoint Average Precision.
bullets: Addresses a decoding bottleneck: pretrained vision features often contain the correct match among their top candidates, even when top-1 matching fails.
Uses a recall-then-rerank strategy with candidate-set size adapted to similarity ambiguity.
Scores candidates by graded cycle consistency, penalizing reverse matches that return far from the original keypoint.
Operates entirely on the base method’s existing similarity matrix and improves three baselines across SPair-71k and PF-Pascal settings.
Reports gains of up to +1.8 PCK@0.10, +3.4 PCK@0.15, and +4.9 in Keypoint Average Precision.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Given a query source patch, we apply top-p sampling on the row of the similarity matrix to form a candidate pool (forward pass). For each candidate, we perform a reverse lookup on its column to identify the nearest source patch (backward pass). Each candidate’s final score is its forward similarity minus a penalty that grows with the distance between its reverse match and the original query.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a cycle-consistent re-ranking strategy for semantic correspondence, a core task for spatial understanding in vision-language models.
papers.title: Déjà Vu: Cycle-Consistent Re-ranking for Semantic Correspondence
papers.tldr: Déjà Vu improves semantic correspondence by adaptively reranking top candidate matches using cycle consistency instead of relying on greedy top-1 selection.

papers.abstract: Cross-view geolocalization aims to determine the geographic location of a ground-level image by retrieving its corresponding satellite image, offering a promising alternative for localization in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied or degraded environments such as urban canyons, dense forests, and disaster scenarios. Despite recent progress, existing approaches remain limited by the lack of globally diverse training datasets and benchmarks that are often geographically restricted. Furthermore, most benchmarks rely on panoramic ground views, which do not reflect the limited field-of-view imagery captured by real world cameras. To address these challenges, we introduce Cross-View World 500k (CVW500k), a large-scale globally distributed dataset containing over 500,000 ground-satellite image pairs collected across diverse geographic regions and environments. Unlike previous datasets, CVW500k uses limited field-of-view ground images, providing a more realistic and challenging setting for cross-view geolocalization. In addition, we propose GeoQueryNet, a query-based cross-view fusion transformer framework designed to bridge the viewpoint gap between ground and satellite images. The model leverages a CLIP-based visual encoder with parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation and introduces a Cross-View Alignment Module that uses learnable query tokens to extract geographically consistent features across viewpoints. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/Fahim17/Cross_View_World_Dataset.git .

papers.abstract: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.
authors: Multi-Center Cooperative Clinical Study Group for "Lesion-Phenotype Brain Mapping in Acute Stroke"
bullets: Addresses scarce, heterogeneous clinical data and the limitations of fixed, representation-based brain foundation models.
Pretrains a reusable, reconfigurable prior on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices.
Supports task-aligned synthesis for low-data prediction and post-training for image reconstruction.
Improved segmentation and classification across 48 downstream tasks and enabled high-fidelity enhancement across imaging conditions.
Multicenter stroke validation showed clinical applicability; radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy improved by 14% with AI assistance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of BrainGFM for Computational brain imaging. a. Heterogeneity in brain diseases, patient populations, clinical status, acquisition protocols, and clinical centers produces heterogeneous brain imaging distributions and limits the generalization of DL models. b. Our BrainGFM-1.3M comprises about 1.3 million axial slices spanning major MRI sequences and CT, providing a large-scale dataset for brain generative pretraining. c. Our BrainGFM learns a reusable brain-imaging prior from generative pretraining on our BrainGFM-1.3M dataset. d. Task-specific conditioning controls the pretrained generator where class labels are used for class-conditioned synthesis, segmentation masks for spatially conditioned synthesis, and source images for brain image reconstruction. These conditions are combined with task-specific adaptation as detailed in Fig. 6b,c. e. Evaluation spans 48 downstream tasks, comprising 20 segmentation, 8 classification, and 20 imageenhancement tasks. f. Clinical validation in a multicenter stroke cohort assesses BrainGFM for TOAST stroke subtyping, lesion segmentation, and MRI sequence transformation, as well as its clinical utility in reader studies and radiologist-AI collaboration.

Fig. 6 BrainGFM architecture, generative pretraining and downstream adaptation. a. BrainGFM pretraining consists of brain-domain adaptation of a multi-scale visual tokenizer and next-scale autoregressive generative pretraining. A shared encoder (E) and vector quantizer (Q) map brain images and segmentation masks into multi-scale discrete tokens using a shared visual codebook. The autoregressive Transformer learns the distribution of tokens through coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction under categorical modality and sequence conditions. The pretrained decoder (D) reconstructs brain images or segmentation masks from generated tokens. b. Task-aligned data synthesis adapts BrainGFM with limited supervision using LoRA. For classification, task-specific class conditioning enables the synthesis of class-labelled images for training ResNet50. For segmentation, BrainGFM generates task-specific masks and synthesizes corresponding images, producing image-mask pairs for training UNet. c. Task-adapted post-training adapts BrainGFM for image enhancement using paired source-target images. Source-image tokens condition autoregressive prediction of target-image tokens, while LoRA is optimized using token-level prediction and image-level reconstruction losses.

Fig. 7 Data flow and study design of BrainGFM. a. Six clinical stroke cohorts comprising 4,796 patients and 4,829 cases from two internal centers (JLH and NFH) and four external centers (NJH, WXPH, NJPH, and CZSPH) were collected. Task-eligible cases were selected according to task-specific imaging and annotation criteria for lesion segmentation, TOAST subtyping, and DWI-to-FLAIR transformation. Internal-center data were used for task-specific training, including low-data settings, while separate internal and external test sets were used for clinical validation.

papers.abstract: Converting a raster image into a resolution-independent, stroke-editable vector sketch while faithfully preserving both structural contours and tonal texture remains challenging: raster-space rendering pipelines are difficult to edit at the stroke level, while generation-from-scratch vectorization methods struggle to remain faithful to an arbitrary input image. We present SketchForge, a training-free framework that converts an input raster image into a resolution-independent SVG sketch through per-instance test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. Strokes are seeded via a contour and attention-guided initialization, then refined by a vector-native differentiable rendering pipeline that decouples structural contour strokes from free-form texture strokes under dedicated objectives, composited via multiply-blend layering. Extensive experiments show that SketchForge consistently outperforms existing vector-based baselines in structural fidelity and generation quality. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchForge
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving contours and tonal texture while producing resolution-independent, stroke-editable vectors.
Uses per-image test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning.
Initializes strokes with contour- and attention-guided seeds, then refines them using differentiable vector rendering.
Separately optimizes structural contour strokes and free-form texture strokes, combining them with multiply blending.
Experiments report improved structural fidelity and generation quality over existing vector-based baselines.],

papers.abstract: Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes. In the first version of Taurus, the model's review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than the noise between two reviews of the same case. A free-form agent running Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher on most datasets. Moving what the free-form agents did well into the automated pass then carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version smooths the label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for the large errors the automated pass tends to make, such as an aneurysm drawn to half its size. Each check that fires puts a multiple-choice question to the model, with candidate corrections drawn on the scan. It matched the surface smoothness of the human references, and in the primary metric we found no difference from the free-form Opus agent, at under half its cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case. Most of what made Taurus competitive came from the harness and its automation rather than from the language model itself. Taurus shows that this kind of annotation can be automated, so that expert time can move from drawing labels to checking them.
bullets: Dense aortic CT labeling is slow, and public datasets use inconsistent structure-labeling conventions.
Taurus combines automated segmentation with LLM review, targeted error checks, candidate corrections, and fixed surface smoothing.
It was evaluated through blind label recovery on six public datasets totaling 939 volumes, plus 38 held-out cases.
The final system matched the free-form Opus agent on the primary metric and matched human-reference surface smoothness.
The reported cost was $1.22 per case versus $2.71 for the free-form agent; most gains came from the harness and automation.

papers.abstract: Outpainting sparse sketches while preserving contour coherence and stroke style remains challenging. We present SketchBloom, a training-free framework that combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization. Given a sketch, a scene prompt, and an optional reference style, it produces an editable Scalable Vector Graphic (SVG) composed of Bezier strokes. Adaptive latent blending balances content contours and reference texture without model retraining. A reference-derived stroke vocabulary initializes contour- and DINO-attention-guided strokes, which are optimized separately for structure and texture before contour-emphasizing multiply fusion. As in prior optimization-based vector sketching, no task-specific network is trained; our contribution is the synthesis design specialized to sketch outpainting. On LineArtOut-1K, comprising 1,024 input and style combinations, SketchBloom improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over the evaluated vector baselines when all methods vectorize the same outpainted raster. This protocol evaluates vector synthesis rather than end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority. Runtime is approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchBloom/
bullets: Addresses contour coherence and stroke-style preservation in sparse sketch outpainting.
Combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization.
Initializes and separately optimizes Bezier strokes for structure and texture, then fuses them with contour emphasis.
On 1,024 LineArtOut-1K input/style combinations, it improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over evaluated vector baselines under a shared-raster protocol.
Runs in approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200; evaluation does not establish end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority.

papers.abstract: Inserting an unseen part requires sub-millimetre precision and the correct orientation of keyed features. Current zero-shot agentic manipulation methods built on vision-language models (VLMs) produce spatial outputs that are far too coarse for this. We propose to let a VLM build a sketch model of the task, i.e., a few geometric primitives and two mate frames, which a VLM agent measures with geometric tools in multi-view depth and which a standard planner and compliant controller execute. Because a sketch describes the parts independently of their placement, the robot needs to build it only once per task. A sketch memory stores each agent run and transfers the stored sketch to later placements by point-cloud registration, so that the VLM is called only for unfamiliar parts. After grasping the part, the robot inspects both mating faces at close range and corrects the sketch by shape matching. On 69 simulated insertion episodes, our method inserts 88% of the parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test, while ReKep and MOKA with the same VLM insert none. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing one stored run inserts as many parts as calling the agent in each episode, and it produces the sketch in 3.4 s instead of about 90 s.
bullets: Targets sub-millimetre insertion of keyed parts, where existing VLM-based agents produce overly coarse spatial outputs.
A VLM builds a task sketch with geometric primitives and mate frames; geometric tools, a standard planner, and compliant control execute it.
The robot refines the sketch by inspecting mating faces at close range and shape-matching them after grasping.
A sketch memory transfers prior sketches to new placements via point-cloud registration, invoking the VLM only for unfamiliar parts.
In 69 simulated episodes, SketchMate achieved 88% strict-kinematic insertion versus 0% for ReKep and MOKA; reuse matched fresh agent calls while reducing sketch creation from about 90 s to 3.4 s.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/kreshuklab/Open-Weight-MLLMs-Cannot-Compare-What-They-Cannot-Name
bullets: The study tests MLLM comparison of ant body-part sizes in synthetic images, motivated by scalable biological image analysis.
Models succeed on some parts but fail on others despite equivalent visual comparison difficulty.
In-context learning strategies and a related object-recognition task are evaluated.
Results suggest recognition-driven grounding failure: unrecognized structures are mapped to familiar concepts, impairing comparison.
Vision-encoder analysis supports the possibility that fine-grained structure is poorly preserved without semantic support.

papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.
authors: Miguel Andrade, Jos\'e Almeida, Carlos Santiago, Catarina Barata
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of high-resolution spatial and single-cell transcriptomics by leveraging widely available WSIs and bulk RNA-seq.
Extracts morphology with the UNI2-h pathology foundation model and builds hierarchical patch- and cell-level spatial graphs.
Trains with direct supervision and weakly supervised consistency losses across bulk, spatial, and single-cell biological scales.
Evaluated on TCGA, Visium, and Xenium samples from lung, kidney, and breast tissues.
Predictions support survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification using molecular signatures.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made significant progress in spatial reasoning, particularly by integrating RGB images with depth data, which is often assumed to faithfully reflect physical distances. However, mirrors violate this assumption: they distort depth readings while reproducing object appearances, making reflections difficult to distinguish from real objects. As existing benchmarks rarely consider such reflective scenarios, VLM performance in mirror scenes remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset from reflective scenes to evaluate the spatial reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art VLMs in these scenarios. Specifically, we collect 1,011 RGB-D images from 525 real-world scenes, spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, six reflective surface types, and both daytime and nighttime conditions. All images are annotated with reflective surface region masks and mask annotations for both directly observed and mirror-reflected objects. Then, we curate a benchmark named MIRA-Bench (Mirror-Induced Reasoning Ambiguity Benchmark), comprising 14,140 QA pairs across eight sub-tasks organized into three cognitive levels: Reflection-aware Perception, Spatial Reasoning, and Scene-level Decision-making. We evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on MIRA-Bench and find consistent failures across tasks: models misclassify whether objects are directly observed or reflected, fail to match reflected instances to their real-world counterparts, and produce erroneous spatial inferences. Remarkably, providing depth data actually degrades reasoning performance, implying that VLMs cannot identify incorrect depth in mirror scenes. The code and data are available at https://github.com/EvaYin-cloud/MIRA-Bench
authors: Hao Yin, Tianchen Guo, Heming Du, Yan Ke, Yanbin Liu, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset of 1,011 images from 525 real-world scenes across varied environments, reflective surfaces, and lighting conditions.
Provides annotations for reflective regions, directly observed objects, and mirror-reflected objects.
Builds MIRA-Bench with 14,140 QA pairs spanning eight tasks and three levels: reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and scene-level decision-making.
State-of-the-art VLMs often confuse reflections with real objects, fail to associate reflections with their sources, and make incorrect spatial inferences.
Depth input degrades performance, suggesting models do not recognize unreliable depth measurements in mirror scenes.

papers.title: When Depth Lies: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Mirror-Induced RGB-D Ambiguity

papers.abstract: Real-world robotic manipulation requires reasoning about cluttered scenes, partially observable or hidden objects, and semantically appropriate actions, in addition to low-level execution within those scenes. However, existing simulation benchmarks primarily test the latter and remain dominated by comparatively clean environments with limited clutter and narrowly scoped task structure, leaving many forms of commonsense reasoning untested. We address this by introducing a taxonomy of reasoning processes for robotic manipulation grounded in developmental cognitive science. We operationalize this taxonomy through a new benchmark of robot tasks, MolmoSpaces-CommonSense, that requires reasoning about occlusion, containment, support relations, semantically correct grasp points, spatial affordances, and hidden objects. These evaluations require policies not only to recognize relevant scene structure but also to execute correct actions in them. We evaluate several zero-shot generalist manipulation policies. Across model types and architectures, we observe consistent failures in commonsense reasoning: success rates in cluttered scenes drop by over 50% as distractors increase, policies act on incorrect objects in cluttered settings 30% of the time, and affordance-sensitive grasping remains unreliable even with highly specific language prompts, with correct object part selection happening only about 50% of the time. Further, VLM-based success estimation struggles to reliably evaluate rollouts in these settings, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond control to the broader perception-reasoning-action stack. Our results suggest that existing benchmarks may substantially overestimate zero-shot real-world readiness. Code and policy leaderboard link at https://github.com/allenai/molmospaces.
authors: Arjun Guru, Max Argus, Jae Sung Park, Jiafei Duan, Ali Farhadi, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Introduces a developmental-cognitive-science taxonomy for commonsense reasoning in robotic manipulation.
Benchmarks occlusion, containment, support relations, grasp-point semantics, spatial affordances, and hidden objects.
Evaluates several zero-shot generalist policies on tasks requiring both scene reasoning and physical execution.
Policies show substantial failures: cluttered-scene success drops by over 50%, incorrect-object actions occur 30% of the time, and correct grasp-part selection is about 50%.
VLM-based rollout evaluation also struggles, indicating challenges across the perception–reasoning–action stack.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.
authors: Ke Yang, Zhenyu Zhang, Jun Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of tracking evolving spatial relations while preserving scene state over time.
Transfers intermediate video-generation-model representations into a vision-language model.
Uses complementary raw and temporal-delta branches to capture holistic context and changes over time.
Task-conditioned tokenwise gates fuse these signals with the model’s native visual representation.
Achieves 67.2% on DSR-Bench, exceeding the previous best result and setting a new state of the art.
