papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.
authors: Jiahe Wu, Bing Cao, Xingyue Guo, Ruipu Zhao, Beiming Yu, Jiekang Feng, Qinghua Hu, Pengfei Zhu
bullets: Targets incomplete visual observations involving small objects, subtle attributes, changing viewpoints, and multimodal inputs.
Organizes tasks around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration across images, sequences, cross-modal images, and viewpoints.
Contains 175k training and 20k human-reviewed test samples; evaluations cover 22 general-purpose VLMs.
Finds persistent weaknesses in spatial judgment and cross-modal/cross-view reasoning, with stronger perception linked to better reasoning.
UAV-PUR models adapted from Qwen3-VL improve multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points for 4B and 8B variants, respectively.

papers.abstract: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
bullets: Problem: Vision-language encoders contain spatial information, but image generators often fail to use it for precise layout control.
Method: Evaluate spatial grounding on synthetic geometric primitives with a color-aware layout metric, then vary the training signal-to-noise-ratio distribution.
Key finding: Centered SNR training yields 25.9% layout adherence, while emphasizing high-noise stages raises it to 80.8%, near the 83.6% VAE reconstruction ceiling.
Scope: The required SNR shift grows with resolution and aspect-ratio variability; conservative schedules such as FLUX.1’s are insufficient for precise layouts.
Transfer: Distribution tuning also improves layout adherence on COCO, increasing Average Precision from 1.0 to 57.3 without architectural modifications.

papers.abstract: Chest computed tomography (CT) reports generated by large language models (LLMs) can describe positive findings that lack localized evidence in the scan. We propose EviGround-CT to verify these findings after report generation. A deterministic extractor identifies positive finding sentences, and a 3D grounding model predicts an evidence mask for each sentence. Using the full sentence retains anatomical location, laterality, and descriptive modifiers in the grounding query. We evaluate report generation on CT-RATE, and grounding and verification on a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset. Using the available annotations, sentence-grounded verification raises evidence-supported precision (ESP) from 0.263 to 0.365 across 137 extracted in-scope positives, compared with category conditioning. The corresponding unsupported positive finding rate falls from 0.737 to 0.635. The paired case-level bootstrap ESP difference is +0.102 (95% confidence interval: [0.028, 0.181]). The predicted masks associate individual report statements with spatial evidence that can be inspected alongside the CT.
bullets: Targets positive report findings that may lack localized support in the CT scan.
Extracts positive finding sentences deterministically and uses each full sentence as the grounding query.
A 3D grounding model predicts an inspectable evidence mask for every statement.
On annotated cases, evidence-supported precision increased from 0.263 to 0.365, while unsupported positives decreased from 0.737 to 0.635.
Evaluated on CT-RATE and a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset; scope is limited to available annotations and in-scope positives.

papers.abstract: Thermal-to-visible (T2V) face translation has important applications in nighttime biometric recognition, low-light surveillance, and human interpretation of thermal observations. The task remains challenging because thermal images do not directly record visible appearance, while the cross-spectral cues useful for reconstruction vary across frequency components and semantic roles. Existing spatially conditioned models tend to process these cues through a homogeneous adaptation path and do not explicitly separate local structure from global identity. We propose FreqID-Control, a parameter-efficient framework that organizes thermal guidance according to spectral reliability and semantic role while preserving the pretrained generative prior. It combines frequency-routed low-rank adaptation, which allocates separate transformation subspaces to low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail, with shared cross-spectral identity conditioning, which supplies compact global identity tokens independently of spatial thermal tokens. A controlled analysis on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces provides the empirical basis for this design, revealing stable low-frequency correspondence and edge-localized detail correspondence. Experiments on both datasets demonstrate strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation, while controlled ablations on MCXFace confirm the complementary contributions of frequency routing and shared identity conditioning.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reconstructing visible appearance from thermal images, whose useful cues differ by frequency and semantic role.
Uses frequency-routed low-rank adaptation to separately handle low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail while retaining a pretrained generative prior.
Adds shared cross-spectral identity tokens independently from spatial thermal tokens to preserve global facial identity.
Experiments on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces show strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation.
Ablations on MCXFace support complementary benefits from frequency routing and identity conditioning.

The thermal input provides a spatial condition through the frozen FLUX-based T2V pathway and a global identity condition through the shared cross-spectral encoder and trainable resampler. Spatial, identity, and noisy-latent states remain separate until multimodal attention. Frequency LoRA-MoE decomposes each current hidden state into low- and high-frequency token components, applies specialized low-rank experts, and routes their updates back to the projection. Gray modules are frozen; orange and green modules are trainable.

papers.title: Frequency Routing and Identity Conditioning for Thermal-to-Visible Face Translation

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feed-forward VLA models, which ignore long-horizon context and hierarchical visual-language representations.
Injects pretrained VLM key-value features into an adaptive mixture-of-experts action module.
Uses asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and DINOv2 historical-frame features for dynamics-aware temporal conditioning.
Applies covariance-structured flow matching on an Action Dynamic Manifold to model coupled robot actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with ablations supporting the proposed components.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PRIME W0 architecture.

Figure 2: Four-stage training pipeline. (1) VLM Pretrain: the vision–language backbone is trained on general multimodal supervision (e.g. captioning / VQA). (2) NTP / task-specific pre-training: with DAT action tokens, the VLM learns visuomotor next-token prediction over instruction–observation–action sequences. (3) DiT Pretrain: the VLM is frozen while the MoT / Adaptive MoE flow-matching action expert is trained with world-model conditioning to denoise continuous actions (and associated state tokens). (4) SFT: both the VLM and the action expert are jointly fine-tuned end-to-end, optionally with action-prefix tokens that shorten the denoising trajectory at inference. Flame / snowflake icons indicate trainable vs. frozen modules.

Figure 5: Scaling with world-model capacity. LIBERO-Long success scales monotonically with WM size; the largest gain is between 5M and 50M parameters (+5.9%). Better subgoal-image prediction directly benefits the asynchronous WM→VLM→ADM pipeline.

Figure 3: Training data mixture. Robot demonstration data used by PRIME W0 totals approximately 10,000 hours, comprising Teleop (60%, ∼6,000 h; laboratory setups, data-collection factories, and public datasets), UMI (30%, ∼3,000 h; portable UMI fisheye egocentric collection), and Simulation (10%, ∼1,000 h; reconstructed scenes with procedural objects and physics randomisation).

Attention to WMpredicted subgoal tokens peaks at contact-establishment and placement phases, confirming that forward scene predictions actively condition manifold-constrained action generation during critical moments.

papers.abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying aerial perception, language grounding, reasoning, and control without offboard computation.
Uses a shared vision-language representation, a compact waypoint-generating action expert, temporal memory, and action priors.
Trains on approximately 70,000 simulated navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction–response pairs.
Runs onboard at 10 Hz on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, producing 12-waypoint action chunks.
Transfers zero-shot to physical flight, achieving a 48% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data.

(B) Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM) compresses historical action segments and their visual anchors into compact event-level tokens. (C) The Motion-Structured Prior (MSP) selects and adjusts a data-derived motion prototype to construct the action source distribution. The action expert transforms a sample from this distribution into the final action chunk through conditional flow matching.

(B) Navigation performance in seen and unseen simulated environments, measured by success rate (SR), oracle success rate (OSR), success weighted by path length (SPL), and navigation error (NE). Success requires an explicit stop within 25 m of the goal. Blue and orange bars in (B) indicate seen and unseen environments, respectively. Arrows indicate the direction of better performance.

papers.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.
authors: Baiqiao Yin, Zhongang Cai, Ruisi Wang, Qiwei Liang, Lei Yang, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Evaluates four capabilities: spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability.

papers.abstract: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.
authors: Yue Gong, Le Zhang, Rui Chen, Song Chang, Xiaochao Qu, Luoqi Liu, Ting Liu, Yebin Liu
bullets: Addresses limitations of existing insertion methods in viewpoint variation, pose and illumination adaptation, and bidirectional object–scene interaction.

Uses Geometry-Guided Adaptation to combine geometry, image, and text features for spatially consistent insertion.
Adds 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision to model object occupancy and environmental changes using image-text attention.
PhysInsert-Bench, DreamBooth experiments, and a user study report improved fidelity, placement, lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models can both generate and understand images within a single set of weights, offering an opportunity to use image synthesis as training supervision for visual comprehension. However, existing visual chain-of-thought methods rely on human-annotated helper images during training and require slow image generation at test time. We present SelfThinker, the first self-evolving framework that turns a unified model's self-generated visual thoughts into stronger understanding without human image annotations. Given a visual problem, SelfThinker samples candidate helper images from its generation pathway and uses its frozen understanding pathway to score each candidate via conditional pointwise mutual information. High-utility visual thoughts then refine the generator via flow matching and serve as privileged teacher context for on-policy self-distillation. At inference, SelfThinker reasons directly from the original image in text without generating intermediate images. Although trained only on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, SelfThinker transfers broadly to natural-image and spatial benchmarks, raising the seven-benchmark average of ThinkMorph-7B from 52.7 to 64.0 (+11.3 points). Controlled image-perturbation probes further show that SelfThinker surpasses ThinkMorph-7B by up to 40.4 points and its pretrained BAGEL-7B backbone by up to 23.2 points across fine-grained and spatial perception tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhangquanchen/SelfThinker.
bullets: Addresses reliance on human-annotated helper images and costly image generation at test time.
Samples candidate visual thoughts and scores them with the frozen understanding pathway using conditional pointwise mutual information.
Uses high-utility thoughts for flow-matching generator refinement and on-policy self-distillation.
Trained on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, it transfers to natural-image and spatial benchmarks.
Raises ThinkMorph-7B’s seven-benchmark average from 52.7 to 64.0, while inference avoids intermediate image generation.

papers.abstract: Tumor delineation is required for radiotherapy planning, yet automatic segmentation is limited by errors, predominantly false positives, that distort dose and increase editing time. The radiology report accompanies the scan and localizes disease at the suborgan level, but existing text-promptable models condition on short referring phrases, and most operate in 2D. We present RepConTUR, a single native-3D early-fusion multimodal model that conditions volumetric abdominal tumor segmentation on the narrative report. We extend AbdomenAtlas 3.0 to a suborgan-level promptable segmentation dataset and generate report-based VQA pairs, yielding four report-derived tasks on the same annotations: referring segmentation (RES), report-grounded segmentation (GSEG), report generation (RRG), and visual question answering (VQA). We train RepConTUR, comprising a 3D CT encoder, an early-fusion language model, and a native-3D segmentation module, jointly on the four tasks. Across liver, kidney and pancreas, RepConTUR attains the highest Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), instance-wise precision, and detection F1 among the text-promptable baselines, and adding the report raises mean precision while leaving recall comparable. Against two vision-only specialists, nnU-Net and the report-supervised R-Super, RepConTUR attains the highest value on every in-domain metric for liver and pancreas and the highest mean DSC, recall, precision, and detection F1 over the four out-of-distribution public cohorts. Ablations indicate that conditioning on the narrative report raises detection F1 from 0.499 to 0.528 within the same model, that joint GSEG training raises RES F1 from 0.450 to 0.482, and that the native-3D segmentation module raises GSEG F1 from 0.139 to 0.528 over its 2D counterpart. Code is available at https://github.com/Oncosoft-Research/RepConTUR.
authors: Seunghwan Lee, Sangjoon Park, Jongmin Lee, Yoon Jo Kim, Wonyoung Cho, Jin Sung Kim, Han Joo Chae
bullets: Addresses false-positive tumor delineation errors that increase radiotherapy-planning dose distortion and editing time.
Combines a 3D CT encoder, early-fusion language model, and native-3D segmentation module, jointly trained on segmentation, report generation, and VQA-related tasks.
Extends AbdomenAtlas 3.0 with suborgan-level report-promptable annotations and four report-derived tasks: RES, GSEG, RRG, and VQA.
Outperforms text-promptable baselines on DSC, instance precision, and detection F1 across liver, kidney, and pancreas; report conditioning improves mean precision with comparable recall.
Ablations show gains from report conditioning, joint GSEG training, and native-3D segmentation; evaluation focuses on abdominal tumors and specified public cohorts.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. Project Page: https://wzlwlm13.github.io/MLLM-GS
authors: Zhiliang Wu, Xinye Zheng, Kun Li, Fei Wang, Hao Guo, Yanyan Wei, Guanghui Yue, Beier Zhu, Wei Zhou, Xun Yang
bullets: Targets NVS under diverse extreme degradations without relying on degradation-specific models.

Optimizes 3DGS rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates to reduce computation, memory use, and optimization cost.
Experiments across multiple degraded scenes show effective degradation handling, high-quality synthesis, and substantially lower reconstruction time and memory consumption.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench
authors: Khai Le-Duc, Nguyen Kim Hai Bui, An Ngo, Nam D. Hoang, Yueqi Song, Jiarui Liu, Thai Quoc Hoang, Fang Wu, Chris Ngo, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Mona T. Diab, Ran Xu, Silvio Savarese, Xiao-Ming Wu
bullets: Introduces BedBench, a controlled benchmark with 13 procedurally generated tasks covering individual and composite 3D judgments.
Per-color counting exposes a major gap: humans reach 93.3% accuracy, while the best evaluated model reaches 7.2%.
Fine-tuning improves one model from 3.0% to 68.6%, but its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own counts.
Providing counts as text improves judgments, indicating that recovering a property does not ensure its consistent use.
Probing Qwen3.5-27B finds counts recoverable at the language-model input (65.0%) despite only 3.0% model accuracy; image-removal controls also reveal image-independent successes.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) jointly support visual understanding and image generation, yet information flow between these two capabilities remains largely asymmetric: understanding representations routinely condition generation, whereas generative representations are rarely reused for multimodal reasoning. In this work, we investigate whether intermediate representations from a UMM's native diffusion branch can enhance spatial reasoning without compromising general multimodal understanding. We propose DiFuse, which selectively incorporates intermediate diffusion representations into the understanding pathway of UMMs. Through systematic layer-wise analysis, we identify which diffusion representations are most informative and where they can be integrated with minimal interference to semantic processing. Guided by these findings, DiFuse spatially aligns diffusion features with visual tokens and injects them into selected multimodal decoder layers via residual fusion. Extensive experiments on UniWorld-V1 show that, DiFuse consistently improves spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while maintaining broadly comparable performance on general multimodal benchmarks. Further analyses show that these gains depend critically on the choice of diffusion representations, injection positions, and the preservation of spatial correspondence between diffusion features and visual tokens. Results on OmniGen2 further demonstrate the transferability of DiFuse across unified multimodal architectures. Overall, our findings show that native diffusion representations can provide complementary spatial cues for multimodal reasoning when selectively integrated in a structure-preserving manner.
authors: Ruixin Fan, Weining Wang, Jiahui Sun, Tailai Chen, Jing Liu
bullets: UMMs typically use understanding features to condition generation, but rarely reuse diffusion representations for reasoning.
DiFuse identifies informative diffusion layers and injects their spatially aligned features into selected multimodal decoder layers through residual fusion.
Experiments on UniWorld-V1 show improved spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while preserving broadly comparable general multimodal performance.
Results on OmniGen2 indicate that the approach transfers across unified multimodal architectures.
Performance depends on selecting suitable diffusion representations, injection locations, and preserving visual-token spatial correspondence.

figures.caption: Figure 3: DiFuse architecture. (a) Overall pipeline. Given an input image and a question, the UMM’s understanding branch processes the visual and text tokens, while its native generation branch receives the same image and a fixed generation prompt “Generate the depth map of this image.” DiFuse extracts an intermediate spatial representation from the frozen DiT at a selected layer and denoising timestep, without decoding a final image. (b) DiFuse module. The extracted feature is spatially pooled and compressed with PCA, then normalized and projected through a convolutional adapter. Bilinear resizing aligns the resulting feature map with the visual-token grid. DiFuse adds the aligned features to visual-token states at selected decoder layers through residual connections; text-token states receive no direct residual update.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.
authors: Guizhen Chen, Weiwen Xu, Wotao Yin, Anh Tuan Luu, Hou Pong Chan
bullets: Identifies a “reference gap”: failures to link language with relevant visual entities, regions, or locations, even when objects are perceived.
Introduces ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark covering five visual reasoning tasks where only the reference varies.
Tests external visual scaffolds such as numbering, motivated by visual routines theory.
Task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25%; mismatched references offer little benefit or can reduce performance.
Shows that constructing suitable references is a training-free visual skill, distinct from perception.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the 'reference gap' in multimodal reasoning, identifying a bottleneck in binding language to visual entities. This directly addresses Multimodal Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: Task-appropriate visual references can substantially improve multimodal reasoning by helping models bind language to the correct visual entities, but mismatched references may not help and can hurt.

papers.abstract: Predicting where to grasp and how to move is fundamentally a geometry problem. Vision-language models treat it as language generation instead. They tokenize spatial coordinates into text and decode them autoregressively. This mechanism ignores spatial structure and truncates continuous precision. Errors compound across coordinate tokens during decoding. In this paper, we show that compact off-the-shelf VLMs with 0.5-2B parameters already encode rich spatial information in their intermediate hidden states. Autoregressive decoding is the dominant bottleneck for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends additionally on feature depth and decoder architecture. We expose the latent spatial information with a lightweight, geometry-compatible prediction head that attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction and refines it via cross-attention over the visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone. We evaluate on ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K. Our 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60% and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline. It approaches RoboBrain on trajectory prediction (0.251 vs 0.191 DFD) at 3.8x higher throughput. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Dimity Miller, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
bullets: Problem: Tokenizing coordinates as text loses continuous spatial precision and causes autoregressive error accumulation.
Method: Attach a lightweight head to a frozen VLM, using intermediate features, instruction-conditioned queries, and cross-attention to regress boxes and waypoints directly.
Contribution: Separates geometric prediction from language decoding without modifying the VLM backbone.

Results: On ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K, the 2B model reduces trajectory error by over 60%, improves affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline, and achieves 3.8× higher throughput than RoboBrain while approaching its trajectory performance.
Scope: Affordance prediction also depends on feature depth and decoder architecture.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture overview. A frozen VLM processes an RGB image and task instruction; hidden states from an intermediate layer are passed to a lightweight geometric prediction head. A DETR-style transformer decoder, conditioned on the instruction via the final text token hidden state, refines a learned query against the visual memory tokens. Two independent FFNs decode the query into continuous outputs: affordance boxes (L1+GIoU loss) and trajectory waypoints (L1+startpoint+endpoint loss). No gradient flows into the VLM.

Figure 1. Accuracy, efficiency, and model size. Each bubble represents a model; bubble size encodes the number of active parameters. Color denotes model family: LLaVA-OV, Qwen2-VL, RoboBrain. (Bottom) Affordance mAP (↑) vs. inference speed (FPS on H100) on AGD20K. Our method outperforms both base VLMs, approaches larger-model accuracy, and retains favorable parameter and inference efficiency.

The visualizations in the first three rows demonstrate that our geometry head effectively generates end-effector manipulation trajectories based on the observation and task instruction. The fourth row presents some failure cases arising from object-localization errors or insufficient spatial understanding.

Figure 5. Qualitative affordance predictions. Red: predicted box, green: ground truth. Top row: vanilla VLM baseline. Bottom row: with our geometry head.

Figure 6. Efficiency–performance trade-off across layers on Qwen2-VL-2B for the trajectory prediction task.

Figure 7. Predicted waypoint heatmaps over the test set, visualizing how endpoint supervision shapes the spatial distribution of trajectory predictions. (a) Ground-truth distribution: waypoints are broadly spread, reflecting the spatial diversity of manipulation trajectories in the dataset. (b) Zero-shot Qwen2-VL-2B baseline: predictions collapse to the image boundaries, confirming that vanilla autoregressive generation fails to produce spatially meaningful trajectories. (d) Geometry head with endpoint supervision: the distribution recovers spatial diversity matching the ground truth, demonstrating that boundary supervision forces input-specific localization rather than dataset-level averaging.

papers.selection_reason: Decodes geometry directly from VLM hidden states for robot affordance and trajectory prediction, avoiding autoregressive tokenization.
papers.title: Decoding Geometry, Not Tokens: Efficient VLMs for Robot Affordance and Trajectory Prediction
papers.tldr: A lightweight geometry-aware head unlocks spatial information already present in compact VLMs, enabling faster and more accurate continuous robot affordance and trajectory prediction than autoregressive coordinate decoding.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Peter Bell
bullets: Targets the cost and long execution trajectories of broad tool-based audio-visual agents.
Uses staged tool-pruning experiments and progressively consolidates audio- and visual-specific tools.
The resulting workflow retains only omni-modal captioning and omni-modal question answering.
Evaluated on three widely used AVQA benchmarks with comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent.
Scope: focuses on compacting perception workflows while maintaining performance on benchmark AVQA tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly process multiple views of the same scene, but it remains unclear whether they integrate these observations into a coherent scene-level representation. Existing multi-image evaluations do not isolate this capability, as tasks may admit correct solutions through independent per-view processing without requiring cross-view correspondence. We introduce OneScene-Bench, a controlled benchmark designed to explicitly distinguish when cross-view integration is necessary. Our benchmark evaluates three complementary capabilities on real-world multi-view scenes: unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning. For counting, we control object overlap across views to separate cases solvable by simple per-view aggregation from those requiring instance-level correspondence. For consistency, we introduce localized edits in shared and view-specific regions, testing whether models distinguish genuine scene contradictions from differences caused by viewpoint and visibility. For spatial reasoning, we construct object relations that require combining spatial evidence across viewpoints to compare physical proximity. We evaluate twelve state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs and find that counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, ranging from 4.5-50.0%, compared with 45.5-81.5% on complete-overlap examples. Moreover, cross-view consistency remains around 50% across models, including recent proprietary VLMs, despite substantially stronger performance on spatial reasoning. Our results reveal a substantial gap between processing multiple images and integrating evidence across them, highlighting the need for evaluations that explicitly test scene-level multi-view understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/swathisuhas/OneScene-Bench.
authors: Swathi Suhas, Anurag Das, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark for testing cross-view integration in real-world multi-view scenes.
Evaluates unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning.
Counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, reaching 4.5–50.0% versus 45.5–81.5% with complete overlap.
Cross-view consistency remains near 50% across models, including proprietary VLMs, while spatial reasoning is comparatively stronger.
Highlights a major gap between handling multiple images and combining evidence across views.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of OneScene-Bench. OneScene-Bench evaluates whether VLMs correctly integrate and reason across views of the same physical scene through three tasks: unique object counting under complete-overlap, subset-overlap, and complementary-view configurations; crossview consistency; and spatial reasoning. Representative image pairs, questions, and ground-truth answers are shown for each task.

Figure 3: Diagnostic analyses of reasoning and number of views. (a) Counting accuracy of instruction-tuned and reasoning-enabled variants. Reasoning generally reduces performance, indicating that explicit reasoning does not improve multi-view counting. (b) Complete-overlap counting accuracy with N = 2–6 input views. Performance initially improves with additional views but peaks before N = 6 for all models, indicating that more views do not yield monotonic gains.

Figure 7: Representative examples from the five tasks in OneScene-Bench: multi-view counting under complete-overlap, subset-overlap, and complementary-view configurations, cross-view consistency, and multi-view spatial reasoning. Questions are slightly shortened for visual presentation while preserving their original meaning. Model predictions are shown using the corresponding model logos, with green checkmarks and red crosses indicating correct and incorrect predictions, respectively.

Figure 6: Screenshot of the spatial-reasoning verification interface. The tool displays the two views, the three referenced objects (A, B, and C), the generated question, and the reviewer controls for assigning the ground-truth proximity relationship or marking the example for removal.

Figure 4: Screenshot of the manual counting review interface. The interface displays the selected multi-view image pair, target object category, reviewed scene-level count, and manually assigned overlap type. Reviewers can also skip ambiguous image pairs before finalizing the annotation.

Figure 5: Screenshot of the consistency review tool. The interface displays the original and edited views, ground-truth label, edit type, and edited object. Reviewers can confirm the example, correct an incorrect ground-truth label, or permanently remove an invalid or ambiguous example.

Table 1: VLMs on OneScene-Bench. Accuracy (%) of twelve open-weight and proprietary VLMs on OneScene-Bench. The best-performing model in each group is shown in bold for every task. Across models, counting performance drops substantially on complementary views, where object correspondence and deduplication across viewpoints are required. Cross-view consistency remains around 50%, whereas spatial reasoning is substantially stronger, revealing a marked difference in model capability across forms of multi-view integration.

Table 2: No-image bias. Accuracy (%) when models receive the task instructions but no images; performance with images is shown in gray in parentheses. Models achieve non-trivial accuracy without visual input, indicating response biases and task priors, while visual evidence substantially improves counting and spatial reasoning performance.

Table 4: Image-Order Sensitivity. Absolute difference in accuracy (percentage points) between the original and reversed input-image orders, |Accoriginal − Accreverse|. Overall, 18 of 20 model–task combinations change by at most four points, indicating broad robustness to image order, with larger sensitivity for Gemma-4 on complete-overlap counting and LLaVA-OneVision-2 on spatial reasoning.

Table 5: No-image refusal count. Number of explicit refusals in the no-image setting. A refusal is counted only when a model explicitly states that the question cannot be answered without visual input; incorrect or guessed answers are not counted.

Table 3: Aggregation Heuristics. Comparison of joint and single-view counting predictions. C1 and C2 denote individual-view predictions and C3 the joint prediction. Acc. is ground-truth accuracy, shown in gray for reference. Sum agr. and Max agr. report the percentage of questions satisfying C3 = C1 + C2 and C3 = max(C1, C2), respectively, without using ground truth. Joint predictions often agree with the maximum in complete- and subset-overlap settings; in complementary views, maximum agreement remains higher than sum agreement despite being insufficient for scene-level counting.

papers.title: OneScene-Bench: Do Vision-Language Models Integrate Evidence Across Views?
papers.tldr: OneScene-Bench shows that VLMs often process multiple views independently rather than reliably integrating them into a coherent scene-level understanding.

papers.abstract: To solve problems in 3D space rather than merely describe images, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) need 3D spatiotemporal reasoning: reconstructing 3D geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipating physical dynamics, and executing precise, closed-loop actions. Prior studies test passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, requiring no execution or supplying privileged coordinates while ignoring collision, statics, and timing. We introduce SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark evaluating 3D spatiotemporal reasoning via closed-loop physical action and active perception, with SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, it has 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, without privileged coordinates, and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind, L7 levers). In brick-bridging or aperture-threading, models rotate the camera to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback (dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames). Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8-79.1 (seven solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks); for the top three, a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap while leaving collisions at 5.2 per episode, whereas adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5; for four others, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8; and 46% of failures are collision or observation loops. SpaceAct and SAPA advance evaluation to closed-loop physical interaction, showing that even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, while offering a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.
authors: Chenglong Shi, Zekai Yuan, Yue Song, Jon Pu, Will Wu
bullets: Benchmarks 3D spatiotemporal reasoning through active perception and physical action rather than passive image question answering.
Includes 108 verified brick and mechanical-puzzle instances across 36 task families, with no privileged coordinates and diagnostic settings for planning, state access, vision, and control.
SAPA uses camera rotation, in-scene measurement, 6-DoF action output, collision/statics checks, and feedback-based self-correction.
Across 10 MLLMs, performance ranges from 4.8 to 79.1; many models solve few 6-DoF tasks, and 46% of failures involve collision or observation loops.
Providing exact 3D state greatly improves performance and reduces collisions, while reference plans help less, highlighting 3D grounding as the main bottleneck.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The SpaceAct task suite and the SAPA active-perception agent. (a) The six task categories contain 36 task families and 108 verified instances in total (44 in the main matrix). (b) At each turn, the input comprises actively acquired RGB observations with rulers, task rules, the available tools, and a dynamic memory (a bounded history window plus a persistent note). A single MLLM call per turn jointly performs 3D localization (𝒢vis), physics identification (ℐphys), multi-step planning (𝒫plan), and frame-aware control (ℰctrl), returning a JSON response with a rationale, a memory update (note), and 1–5 tool calls; the four capabilities are a diagnostic decomposition, not four separate calls. The tool calls execute sequentially in swept substeps of at most 0.05 stud or 0.5°, without a motion planner, under collision/topology and static-equilibrium checks, and the simulation clock is frozen while the model deliberates. (c) Observations are RGB images with rulers and no coordinates; dynamic tasks provide five frames from the same viewpoint at 0.25-s intervals. The first violation truncates execution and skips the remaining calls, returning a 1280 × 640 split-screen rollback view (left: the violating contact; right: the last valid state). (d) The diagnostic conditions grouped by the operator of Eq. (3) that they replace or stress.

Figure 2: SpaceAct's four design principles (conceptual illustration). Active 3D grounding: the agent reads in-scene rulers and moves the camera to resolve occlusion, with no privileged coordinates. Physics-constrained action: the full swept motion path is checked for collisions and structures for static equilibrium, without a motion planner. Controlled-time dynamics: simulation time pauses while the model deliberates and during camera actions, and advances only with timed physical actions; five sameview frames expose the motion. Controlled failure diagnosis: split-screen rollback feedback pairs the contact with the last valid state, and separately run +plan and +state conditions isolate the bottleneck.

Figure 3: Inputs of the three controlled-diagnostic conditions (schematic), each run separately on the same instances. All conditions share the RGB observation, task and rules, history, and note; the model generates every action, and all actions run under the same execution protocol. +plan adds a reference high-level plan (turns and regions; distances are left to the model). +state supplies the reference plan as well, plus the coarse layout as text and the exact 3D pose of the payload at every turn.

papers.title: SpaceAct: Benchmarking 3D Spatial and Temporal Reasoning via Closed-Loop Action and Active Perception

papers.abstract: Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.
authors: Maris Basha, Yuhang Wang, Xiaoran Chen, Longbiao Cheng, Luca Yapura, Anja T. Zai, Mathieu Salzmann, Richard Hahnloser
bullets: Addresses the lack of physically verified ground truth for vocal attribution in animal groups.
Provides 33,625 verified events with 5-channel audio, three camera views, calibrated 3D poses, and telemetry across 10 finches and three experiments.
Uses an accelerometer-derived on-body vibration signal only for label verification and a near-perfect reference ceiling, not as model input.
Evaluates session-disjoint, held-out-experiment, and leave-one-individual-out settings.
Finds that familiar-caller recognition degrades sharply on unseen birds, while candidate-aware spatial methods transfer better; releases V33DA, protocols, code, and V33DA++ context data.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal benchmark requiring spatial reasoning over 3D candidate geometry for vocal attribution.
papers.title: Who Called? V33DA: A Physically Verified Multimodal Benchmark for Vocal Attribution in Zebra Finch Groups
papers.tldr: V33DA is a physically verified multimodal benchmark for identifying which zebra finch produced a vocalization using audio, video, and 3D candidate geometry, with protocols that test generalization to new sessions, experiments, and individuals.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D maps enable robots to reason about previously unknown environments using natural language. However, existing systems typically segment every incoming image, associate detections with persistent 3D segments, and frequently perform costly Vision-Language (VL) inference. We present TRACKGRAPH, an online open-vocabulary system that maintains short-term 2D mask identity directly in the image stream before fusing segments into 3D. FastSAM masks and CLIP features are computed at sparse keyframes, while dense DINOv3 features are used to propagate masks at a high rate in between. The resulting tracked masks are fused into a class-agnostic 3D segment layer within a hierarchical scene graph, with 3D association handling tracking interruptions and long-term revisits. Compact multi-view CLIP embeddings enable open-vocabulary retrieval. Across Replica, ScanNet++, and HM3D, TRACKGRAPH achieves competitive open-vocabulary segmentation and retrieval against state-of-the-art mapping methods, including the highest synonym frequency on Replica (0.50). On the same NVIDIA A100, it is 1.7x faster and uses 3.3x less GPU memory than ViT-H OVI-MAP. Real-world quadruped deployments demonstrate onboard scene graph construction and object search at 7.5Hz, while recorded drone data is used to test the method under aerial viewpoints.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of per-frame segmentation, 3D association, and frequent vision-language inference in online mapping.
Computes FastSAM masks and CLIP features at keyframes, then propagates masks densely using DINOv3 features.
Fuses tracked masks into a class-agnostic hierarchical 3D scene graph, with 3D association supporting interruptions and revisits.
Achieves competitive segmentation and retrieval across Replica, ScanNet++, and HM3D; reports 1.7× faster runtime and 3.3× lower GPU memory than ViT-H OVI-MAP.
Demonstrates onboard scene-graph construction and object search at 7.5 Hz on a quadruped, with additional evaluation on aerial drone data.

papers.abstract: As robots transition from structured factory settings into homes, they are required to interact with an ever-increasing variety of objects. Many tasks require grasping, and often it is not sufficient to just pick up the target object. Consider a task like "pouring coffee" --- to facilitate the subsequent pouring, the robot should grasp the mug by its handle. Existing learning-based approaches for grasping either find robust and collision-free grasps that are largely agnostic to the task (e.g., picking up the mug by its rim), or leverage foundation models to propose task-appropriate grasp locations that lack fine-grained physical grounding (e.g., reaching for and missing the handle). In this work, we bridge these approaches with a real-to-sim-to-real framework. Based on a single RGB-D observation, we construct a digital twin of the environment, query a large foundation model to propose grasps that align with the object's affordances and task description, and then optimize the proposals to ensure robustness and plausibility before executing the result on the real robot. Our key insight is that the grasp proposals of the foundation model should be regarded as semantic priors that serve as seeds for local, gradient-free optimization. We leverage Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling to draw batches of nearby poses, which are subsequently evaluated in parallel under domain-randomized physics rollouts. The resulting grasp is both task-oriented and physically feasible for execution by the robot arm. Our full zero-shot real-world transfer only takes a few minutes and improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% as compared to other state-of-the-art pipelines. Our code is available here: https://github.com/VT-Collab/GraspTwin/
bullets: Addresses the gap between task-agnostic robust grasps and semantically appropriate but physically imprecise foundation-model proposals.
Builds a digital twin from a single RGB-D observation and uses the task description and object affordances to generate grasp priors.
Refines these priors with gradient-free Bayesian optimization using Thompson sampling and parallel domain-randomized physics rollouts.
Transfers the optimized grasp to a real robot in a few minutes without task-specific training.
Improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% over other state-of-the-art pipelines in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of GraspTwin. (Left) We convert from real to sim by constructing a digital twin from an RGB-D image of the robot’s environment. We estimate the scene objects θ̂ and identify θ̂1, the target object for grasping. (Middle) We then render the target object θ̂1 from multiple perspectives, and use a VLM conditioned on the task τ to select task-oriented grasp positions P(i) VLM and an approach direction RVLM. (Right) These proposals become the initial guesses for localized grasp optimization. We simulate grasp poses T in the digital twin with object perturbations ∆θ. Batch Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling enables parallel evaluations for gradient-free optimization. The minimum-cost grasp pose T∗ is executed by the real robot.

Fig. 1. We present GraspTwin, a zero-shot method for identifying grasps that are both task-oriented and physically feasible. Given a single RGBD image of the scene, GraspTwin constructs a digital twin. Within that digital twin we query foundation models to propose grasps that facilitate the downstream task. These semantically-aware grasps seed local optimization while enforcing physical constraints (e.g., unintended collisions) and domain randomization. The resulting grasp pose is then executed by the real arm.

papers.title: GraspTwin: Zero-Shot Task-Oriented Grasp Optimization via a Digital Twin

papers.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.
bullets: Introduces an annotated egocentric tennis dataset synchronized with five allocentric views, global positions, contact times, and stroke labels.
Evaluates seven tasks, including player/ball localization, trajectory forecasting, stroke anticipation, contact-time prediction, and contact-position estimation.
Best models reach 0.14 m ego-player and 0.54 m ball localization error, 0.34 m and 0.91 m forecasting error over 1.1 s, and 0.14 s contact-time error.
Auxiliary depth improves 3D ball localization; longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, suggesting reliance on scene context over motion alone.
A conditional diffusion model generates adaptive whole-body tennis motion from vision predictions at real-time rates.

papers.title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Tongkun Guan, Zhibo Yang, Mingkun Yang, Haocheng Wang, Wei Shen, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Targets perception degradation during MLLM post-training, where subjective dense captions make reliable rewards difficult.
Perception RL converts verified caption errors into fixed-label QA pairs with rule-based rewards, using chain and multiple-choice formats.
Perception Agentic RL handles unresolved dense cases through multi-turn tool use, with Coordinate Injection and grounding-aware process rewards to reduce spatial errors.
Uses shared cold-start SFT followed by single-turn and multi-turn perception RL.
Achieves 71.6% average accuracy across seven benchmarks, exceeding the same-tool base model by 15.7 points and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 5.2 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Perception RL: from perceptual errors to rewardable QA. (01) Perception tree construction: A hierarchical capability map and model probing reveal perceptual weaknesses, guiding specialized and general data-construction routes. Appendix ?? expands the displayed tree with additional skills and associated failure modes. (02) Rewardable QA construction: A multi-agent pipeline mines and verifies errors in the base model’s captions, then composes them into questions with unambiguous answers. MCQs combine unrelated errors, while chain QA connects correlated errors. (03) Rule-based reward for RL: The resulting QA pairs provide exact-match rewards for training the model’s visual perception. The error distribution and example errors are illustrative.

Fig. 1: PERCEPTRL: making real-world perception rewardable, and training it at two levels. Center: How it becomes rewardable. Open-ended captions contain useful perceptual information but are difficult to score with direct rule-based rewards. We extract and verify perceptual facts from these captions, then formulate QA pairs with fixed answer labels for rule-based training (top). The pipeline organizes tasks from multiple perception families (e.g., color, spatial position, counting, functional state, orientation), using a perception tree to guide data construction (Section 3.2). The difficulty axis is what divides the two levels. Level 1: Perception RL. A single look suffices here, so we train single-turn visual QA under a rule-based outcome reward. The left panel shows what this must fix: an error entering at the perception level is inherited by an otherwise correct reasoning chain, so the answer is wrong for a purely perceptual reason. Level 2: Perception Agentic RL. This tail, where objects are small, scenes are cluttered, or details require magnification, resists a single look, so the model inspects the image over multiple grounded turns with a code interpreter. The right panel illustrates how a grounding error, where a predicted crop or annotation misses its target, can affect subsequent observations. Its propagation and accumulation across successive tool interactions constitute coordinate drift. Coordinate Injection corrects these grounding errors during data construction, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity (Section 3.3).

Fig. 3: Perception Agentic RL: correcting and supervising spatial grounding during multi-turn visual inspection. (01) Coordinate drift. A misplaced annotation changes the visual evidence available to later turns. Subsequent spatial operations can inherit this error, leading to repeated or missed counts. (02) Coordinate Injection (CI). During trajectory construction, CI identifies the intended target of each spatial operation, corrects its coordinates using a VLM judge or the LocateAnything detector, and re-executes the code before the next turn. The corrected trajectories provide cold-start SFT data. (03) Grounding-aware process reward. During RL, a fidelity judge evaluates the predicted boxes and points against their intended targets in the original image. The resulting per-turn rewards complement the final-answer reward and supervise intermediate spatial accuracy (Equation 17).

papers.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed-length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event-driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi-Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual-stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi-agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event-aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/BAI-LAB/EMMA.
bullets: Targets noisy retrieval caused by fixed-length video chunking, which can fragment events and merge unrelated content.
Detects event boundaries using visual semantic drift and spoken transitions.
Builds a three-level memory hierarchy spanning raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory.
Uses multi-agent query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation.
Experiments on three challenging benchmarks show substantial improvements, though the abstract does not specify metrics or limitations.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is a necessary step in moving multimodal large language models (MLLMs) toward reasoning about the 3D physical world. Their visual pretraining data, however, is almost entirely 2D, so the visual tokens processed by MLLMs often lack inherent 3D structural information. A growing number of methods inject such structure by transferring representations from external vision or geometry models, and collectively establish that such transfer helps. Behind these methods lies a largely underexplored question: what makes a visual representation good for spatial understanding? To answer it, we first separate what is transferred from how it is transferred, and then trace the resulting differences back to properties of the representations themselves. What we transfer comes from 3D geometry models, self-supervised image and video models, vision-language models, and generative models, in the form of latent features or explicit depth and point maps. We transfer it either by distillation, using it as a supervision target, or by fusion, feeding it as an additional input. We find that a representation's 3D structure correlates strongly with how much it helps, measured by cross-view consistency for latent features and by depth and reconstruction accuracy for explicit geometry. We further show that the form of a representation dictates the mechanism it needs. Latent features gain as much from fusion as from distillation; explicit geometry gains little from fusion, and most of its distillation gain depends on a geometry decoding head. Guided by these findings, we distill both latent features and explicit geometry into a single MLLM. Taking only RGB video as input, it consistently improves over its base model on both static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning benchmarks.
bullets: MLLM visual tokens often lack 3D structure because pretraining is dominated by 2D data.
The study compares transferred representations from geometry, self-supervised, vision-language, and generative models, using distillation or fusion.
Representation quality correlates with spatial usefulness: cross-view consistency for latent features and depth/reconstruction accuracy for explicit geometry.
Latent features benefit similarly from fusion and distillation, while explicit geometry benefits mainly from distillation with a geometry decoding head.
Distilling both representation types into one RGB-video MLLM improves static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning over its base model.

papers.tldr: Visual representations with stronger 3D structure—and transfer mechanisms matched to their form—better enable MLLMs to understand spatial scenes.

papers.abstract: Spherical data arise in many scientific applications. Often spherical transformers disregard the geometry of the underlying spherical domain, causing distortions and coordinate singularities near the poles. We introduce SO(3)-RoPE, a relative positional embedding that incorporates spherical geometry into transformer attention through unitary SO(3) representations. Our formulation is SO(3)-equivariant and compatible with FlashAttention, retaining efficiency of vanilla transformers. On shallow water dynamics prediction over a rotating sphere, our SO3ViT outperforms an S2Transformer baseline with lower errors and reduced runtime.
bullets: Addresses distortions and polar coordinate singularities in transformers for spherical data.
Introduces a relative positional embedding based on unitary SO(3) representations.
Provides SO(3)-equivariant attention while remaining compatible with FlashAttention.
SO3ViT achieves lower errors and reduced runtime than an S2Transformer baseline on shallow-water prediction.
Scope: evaluated on shallow-water dynamics over a rotating sphere.
