papers.tldr: SO(3)-RoPE builds spherical geometry into transformer attention, improving accuracy and runtime for rotating-sphere dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.
authors: Zengqi Zhao, Zun Wang, Shoubin Yu, Mohit Bansal, Yue Zhang
bullets: ImagiRep benchmarks 922 spatial questions across seven question types and two settings using RGB and six alternative representations of the same unseen state.
Different spatial questions benefit from different representations, such as top-down geometry for global distances and panoramas for open-space context.
Accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate reasoning; estimated RGB can mislead, while alternative representations provide complementary information.
GEARS adaptively selects representations at test time and outperforms existing spatial-imagination methods.
The findings suggest that visual world models should represent unseen states beyond RGB generation.
papers.selection_reason: Studies representation choice for imagined spatial states and adaptive selection for spatial reasoning, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Representing the Unseen: Rethinking Visual Imagination for Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Spatial reasoning about unseen states improves when systems adapt the representation they use instead of relying solely on imagined RGB views.

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic graph representation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling hierarchical data. Unlike Euclidean space, which exhibits polynomial volume growth, hyperbolic space grows exponentially with radius, naturally accommodating tree-like structures without the geometric distortion known as Euclidean crowding. Despite strong empirical performance, the theoretical mechanisms underlying hyperbolic embeddings remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a geometric quantifcation research for Euclidean crowding, a generalization-theoretic explanation for the superiority of hyperbolic space on hierarchical data, and further develop an adaptive Euclidean-hyperbolic fusion learning framework toward bridging this gap. Specifically, we \textbf{first} establish a geometric quantification of Euclidean crowding by analyzing layer-wise minimum separation in node embeddings, proving that fixed-dimensional Euclidean embeddings of tree-like graphs inevitably exhibit layer-wise crowding that leads to weaker margin-based generalization bounds. \textbf{Second}, we provide a generalization-bound for the superiority of hyperbolic geometry on hierarchical data. \textbf{Third}, we propose EH-Fusion, a geometry-adaptive framework that lifts Euclidean GNN representations into hyperbolic space via exponential mapping and adaptively fuses both geometries based on node-level neighborhood expansion patterns. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical insights and demonstrate the effectiveness of EH-Fusion on benchmark datasets.
authors: Hao Chen, Jian Sun, Chuan Shi, Hongying Zhang
bullets: Quantifies Euclidean crowding through layer-wise minimum separation in embeddings of tree-like graphs.
Shows that fixed-dimensional Euclidean representations suffer increasing crowding and weaker margin-based generalization bounds.
Derives a generalization bound explaining hyperbolic geometry’s advantages for hierarchical data.
EH-Fusion maps Euclidean GNN representations into hyperbolic space and adaptively fuses both geometries using node-level neighborhood expansion.
Experiments on benchmark datasets support the theory and demonstrate EH-Fusion’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a geometry-adaptive framework (EH-Fusion) for graph learning that bridges Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. This addresses spatial reasoning and geometric priors in multimodal models.
papers.title: Euclidean Crowding-Driven Adaptive Euclidean-Hyperbolic Graph Learning
papers.tldr: This work explains why hyperbolic geometry better represents hierarchical graphs and introduces EH-Fusion, which adaptively combines Euclidean and hyperbolic representations based on local structure.

papers.abstract: This report presents the implementation and validation of two end-to-end multimodal adaptation pipelines for 3D-aware visual question answering on a custom spatial dataset. The first pipeline fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B, which augments RGB observations with metric-scale 3D point maps; the second adapts Qwen3-VL through memory-efficient QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The completed engineering stack covers dataset conversion, image-annotation alignment, monocular geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpoint management, batch inference, and automated evaluation. On the target spatial benchmark, HiSpatial adaptation increases overall accuracy from 1.73% before fine-tuning to 79.89% at 3,600 steps. On a separately collected styled split, accuracy improves from 14.9% to 55.1%, indicating transfer beyond the original training set. The Qwen3-VL pipeline is likewise implemented end-to-end for both 8B- and 32B-scale models using mixed-domain QLoRA adaptation. The resulting accuracy improves from 20.74% to 45.27% for Qwen3-VL-8B and from 30.79% to 47.60% for Qwen3-VL-32B. Together, these results establish two complementary and reproducible adaptation pipelines for geometry-aware and general-purpose multimodal spatial reasoning. These results establish a reproducible engineering foundation for subsequent work on metric 3D reasoning, spatial grounding, and domain-adapted multimodal systems, while also identifying training-data composition as a central factor in preserving general multimodal capability during specialization.
authors: Yu Zhang, Xiaogang Wang, Yuhang Cheng, Jingrui Li, Wenbo Chen
bullets: Fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B with RGB images and metric-scale 3D point maps, raising target-benchmark accuracy from 1.73% to 79.89%.
Applies memory-efficient QLoRA supervised fine-tuning to Qwen3-VL-8B and 32B, improving accuracy to 45.27% and 47.60%, respectively.
HiSpatial adaptation transfers to a separately styled split, increasing accuracy from 14.9% to 55.1%.
The engineering stack includes data conversion and alignment, geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpointing, inference, and automated evaluation.
The report highlights training-data composition as important for retaining general multimodal capabilities during spatial specialization.
papers.selection_reason: Reproducible 3D-aware VQA adaptation pipelines with metric-scale spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Zhengrong-Spatial-Aware 1.0: Advancing 3D Multimodal Intelligence
papers.tldr: The report develops and validates two end-to-end pipelines for adapting multimodal models to 3D spatial visual question answering, substantially improving benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.

Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.

papers.title: 3D-SceneQ: Empowering 3D LLM With Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning and Multi-Modal Feature Enhancement
papers.tldr: 3D-SceneQ improves 3D-language reasoning by pruning irrelevant objects according to the query and enriching 3D features with 2D multimodal information.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction represents scene geometry and semantics in a unified voxel grid, enabling recognition beyond predefined categories. One approach reconstructs scenes with 3D Gaussians and converts them into voxel occupancy. However, Gaussian scale inflation and excessive overlap can distort voxel occupancy predictions, while semantic mixing can arise within Gaussians spanning multiple categories and during 3D--2D semantic feature alignment. We propose GCSR-OCC, which combines geometry calibration and multi-mode query-conditioned semantic routing for indoor occupancy prediction from a single RGB image. The Evidence-Conserving Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator (EC-G2O) uses kernel mass normalization, $p$-norm aggregation, and a learnable gain to suppress scale inflation and excessive local evidence accumulation while calibrating occupancy responses. Multi-mode Query-First Gaussian Semantic Routing (MM-QGSR) matches multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and aggregates query-specific evidence into voxels through a learnable text-conditioned router. Fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation further refine voxel-level predictions. Without 3D semantic annotations, GCSR-OCC achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary occupancy prediction on Occ-ScanNet, with 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU. It also reduces geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Bohua Wang, Congyang Zhao, Tianxiong Lv, Chenxu Zhao, He Zheng, Hangqi Fan, Leigang Luo, Zhihao Liao, Yihong Guo, Yang Cai

Uses EC-G2O to normalize Gaussian evidence, aggregate it with a p-norm, and calibrate occupancy responses with a learnable gain.
Uses MM-QGSR to match multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and route query-specific evidence into voxels.
Adds fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation for more precise voxel semantics.

papers.title: GCSR-OCC: Geometry Calibration and Semantic Routing for Open-Vocabulary Occupancy Prediction
papers.tldr: GCSR-OCC improves single-image open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction by calibrating Gaussian geometry and routing semantic evidence with text-conditioned queries.

papers.abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
authors: Lai Wei, Yatai Li, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Renjie Gu, Linhan Cao, Junkai Lin, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Linghe Kong, Yue Wang, Zhuosheng Zhang, Weiran Huang
bullets: Targets the shared capability of connecting evidence: finding relevant visual facts, linking them to entities, recovering relations, and composing answers.
Generates comparison, aggregation, and multi-step visual questions from zoomed views of related regions within one image.
Filters data using agreement among independent VLMs and region-ablation tests to verify answer quality and evidence dependence.

Although not tailored to downstream benchmarks, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with broader gains across several multimodal reasoning settings.

papers.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
papers.tldr: EvidenceConnect synthesizes targeted visual-evidence reasoning data, and RLVR training with it produces ZwZ2, improving generalizable multimodal perception across spatial, long-context, embodied, agent, and visual-reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming in is a common training-free remedy. However, most existing zooming pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally and never revisit a wrong answer. To address these issues, we propose AdaGround, a training-free framework with three components: (1) Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming, which sets the magnification, field of view and zoom depth of each sample from the model's own estimate of the target size; (2) Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement, which uses one marked-click Yes/No verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding and, with an existence query, decide when to abstain; and (3) Compositional Structure Grounding, which composes spreadsheet cells from their headers. On Qwen3-VL models, AdaGround surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, and its gains carry over to held-out UI-Vision. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/AdaGround
authors: Bingchao Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Chengyu Wang, Jun Huang, Jie Yang, Wei Liu, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Targets zoom magnification, field of view, and depth to the model’s estimated target size.

papers.title: AdaGround: Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming with Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement for GUI Grounding
papers.tldr: AdaGround is a training-free GUI grounding framework that adaptively zooms to target size and uses verifier-guided refinement to improve small-target localization.

papers.abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.
authors: Mifu Matsumoto, Yuki Nakanishi, Tomoya Hashiguchi, Hiroaki Ohshima
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing map geometry and semantic information for landmark-based route instruction generation.
Encodes spatial features in structured SVG text while preserving alignment with rendered map images.
Evaluates landmark selection at turns and near destinations using a dataset combining human-written routes with OpenStreetMap data.
Across five LLMs, structured text performs as well as or better than PNG map inputs.
Task-specific fine-tuning allows smaller local LLMs to use map layouts effectively.
papers.selection_reason: Encodes map geometry as structured text for LLM-based landmark selection, directly relevant to spatial reasoning and navigation instruction generation.
papers.title: Structured Maps for Landmark-Based Route Instructions with LLMs
papers.tldr: An SVG-based structured text representation helps LLMs select human-preferred landmarks for navigation as effectively as, or better than, map images.

papers.abstract: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.
authors: Rui Yang, Yanwei Li, Sili Chen, Jingjia Huang, Yi Lin, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Studies how visual generation can support spatial understanding through training-time geometric supervision and inference-time geometric evidence.
Introduces GeoUG, which combines spatial understanding with depth and multi-view generation using a multi-scale depth codec.
Presents 3DCueBench to test geometric difficulty while controlling 2D visual cues.
Finds generated depth particularly helps fine-grained geometric reasoning.
Uses reinforcement-learned adaptive interleaved reasoning to decide when to generate evidence; reports 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% circular accuracy on three benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a unified model for geometric understanding and generation, explicitly targeting 'Spatial Intelligence' and improving 3D scene understanding through generative supervision.
papers.title: Learning and Reasoning with Geometry: How Generation Helps Spatial Understanding
papers.tldr: GeoUG improves spatial reasoning by generating geometric evidence only when it is useful, achieving strong accuracy with fewer generation calls than always generating.

papers.abstract: Global vision--language similarities compress an image and a caption into one vector, preserving semantics but not which word corresponds to which region or how those regions are arranged; a model can recognize every word and object yet prefer a compositionally incorrect caption. We argue that a frozen encoder retains this association structure, so the problem is to read it rather than to rebuild it beside the pretrained similarity. We introduce BindCLIP, a pairwise scorer built on one latent object: a balanced token--patch--depth optimal-transport coupling that places both candidate captions and several visual depths in a single plan. Semantic, entity, order, and spatial evidence are read as energies of this state, and exchanging the candidates permutes the plan, making the score exactly antisymmetric. A geometric refinement inside the coupling contracts moves that the candidates and the visual depths do not support. No task label, parser, relation inventory, or detector is used. One checkpoint and one inference path improve the official What'sUp, ARO, and SugarCrepe benchmarks over frozen global CLIP, with the strongest transfer on the relation splits. Controls rule out patch access and caption-length shortcuts, and an inference-time lesion localizes spatial arrangement to the coupling.
bullets: Addresses the failure of global image–caption similarity to capture word–region correspondences and spatial composition.
Builds one balanced token–patch–depth optimal-transport plan jointly over candidate captions and multiple visual depths.
Derives semantic, entity, ordering, and spatial evidence from coupling energies; candidate exchange yields an exactly antisymmetric score.
Uses no task labels, parsers, relation inventories, or detectors, and follows one checkpoint and inference path.
Improves frozen CLIP on What'sUp, ARO, and SugarCrepe, with strongest transfer on relation splits; controls identify spatial arrangement in the coupling.
papers.selection_reason: Compositional vision-language scoring with optimal transport and spatial relation reasoning; fits multimodal foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: BindCLIP: One Balanced Coupling For Compositional Vision Language Scoring
papers.tldr: BindCLIP reads compositional token–region structure from frozen vision–language encoders via a balanced optimal-transport coupling, improving relation-sensitive caption scoring without extra supervision.

papers.abstract: Monocular occupancy prediction in indoor scenes aims to recover a scene's 3D geometry and semantics from a single RGB image. Existing methods are restricted to a closed set of predefined categories, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen categories. This limitation is particularly critical in indoor scenes, where objects exhibit highly diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. We study open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes and present OVM-Occ, a Gaussian-based occupancy framework with an instance-aware vision-language teacher. Specifically, we adopt Language-Embedded Gaussians as the intermediate scene representation, propose a geometry-aware deformable attention module to refine Gaussian semantic features, and construct instance-level vision-language embeddings to provide reliable semantic supervision. We further introduce geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation to mitigate the interference between geometry learning and semantic learning. To evaluate open-vocabulary occupancy prediction performance, we introduce OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica, two extended benchmarks with more diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art approach by 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU on the Occ-ScanNet dataset, with consistent gains under new open-vocabulary evaluation protocols.
authors: Shuyang Yu, Haibo Qin, Shaohan Hu, Wei Shan, Xiaoqing Guan, You Wang, Guang Li
bullets: Addresses the limited category generalization of existing closed-set monocular occupancy methods.
Represents scenes with Language-Embedded Gaussians and refines semantic features through geometry-aware deformable attention.
Uses instance-level vision-language embeddings and geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation for semantic supervision.
Introduces OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica benchmarks with more diverse, fine-grained categories.
Reports gains of 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU over the previous state of the art on Occ-ScanNet, with consistent improvements under new protocols.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction with geometry-aware vision-language distillation directly advances 3D scene perception and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: OVM-Occ: Open-Vocabulary Monocular Occupancy Prediction via Geometry-Aware Vision-Language Distillation
papers.tldr: OVM-Occ enables open-vocabulary 3D geometry and semantic occupancy prediction from a single indoor RGB image using geometry-aware vision-language distillation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) ground a referring expression in one of two ways. They decode the box as coordinate tokens, which is precise but takes one sequential step per token, or they regress it from a hidden state with a small head, which takes one step but loses accuracy at high IoU. The two fail differently: a head usually finds the right object but places its edges loosely, while coordinate tokens place edges precisely. We therefore use the regression head as a speculative drafter for the model's own coordinate tokens. Locus writes the head's box as coordinate tokens and checks them with the same backbone by Jacobi iteration over a shared image prefix. The fixed point is the model's greedy coordinate-token answer, reached in about 5.60 sequential passes on average instead of 18.46 decoding steps; head and verifier are one set of weights, trained jointly. On the 8 RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification raises Locus-2B's Acc@0.9 from 54.87 for its own head to 59.13, and the one-pass head is ahead at Acc@0.5 of every published model with at most 3B parameters except Florence-2-L. Against Jag, the strongest open regression-head model, at its own size and training budget, Locus ties at Acc@0.5 and, with typical acceptance, gains +4.52 points at Acc@0.9, with paired significance tests. Exact answers come 1.5x faster than vLLM greedy-decoding the same coordinate tokens with the same weights; a pure regression head remains faster still.
bullets: Uses the regression head to draft a box, then verifies and refines its coordinate tokens via Jacobi iteration with the same backbone.
Reaches the model’s greedy coordinate-token answer in about 5.60 sequential passes on average, versus 18.46 decoding steps.
On RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification improves Locus-2B Acc@0.9 from 54.87 to 59.13.
The one-pass head achieves strong Acc@0.5 performance, while verified outputs provide more precise box edges.

papers.selection_reason: Draft-and-verify visual grounding improves VLM coordinate-token decoding; relevant to multimodal LLMs, spatial grounding, and inference efficiency.
papers.title: LOCUS: Locate Once, Check Until Settled. Draft-and-Verify Visual Grounding with a Box Head and Coordinate-Token Verification
papers.tldr: LOCUS combines a fast box-regression head with coordinate-token verification to improve high-IoU visual grounding while reducing sequential decoding passes.

papers.abstract: Erasing all furniture from a single room image to generate its empty counterpart is valuable for XR applications such as diminished reality and virtual staging. The challenge is twofold: inpainting the furniture regions with realistic content, and doing so without distorting the room's 3D geometry. Prompt-driven image editors, such as FLUX.2, handle realism impressively, but their structural faithfulness is inferior to explicit layout conditioned inpainting. To improve geometric consistency, we propose a training recipe for finetuning a LoRA on 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs. FLUX.2 with our LoRA adaptor significantly improves geometric consistency while retaining the high texture fidelity. This single-photo inpainter can be an effective building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.
authors: Prakhar Kulshreshtha, Brian Pugh, Zachary Nussdorfer, Salma Jiddi
bullets: Addresses single-image room defurnishing for diminished reality and virtual staging.
Targets the trade-off between realistic inpainting and structural faithfulness.
Finetunes a LoRA using 2,500 furnished–empty room pairs.
The adapted FLUX.2 significantly improves geometric consistency while retaining high texture fidelity.
Designed as a building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.
papers.selection_reason: Finetunes prompt-based image editor for geometry-consistent room defurnishing; relevant to spatial/geometric consistency in multimodal models.
papers.title: Finetuning Prompt-Based Image Editor for Geometry-Consistent Room Defurnishing
papers.tldr: A LoRA-finetuned FLUX.2 editor removes furniture from room images while better preserving the room’s geometry and realistic appearance.

papers.abstract: Training a spatial VLM to answer which side an object lies on does not require it to preserve the metric displacement that determines that answer, while supervision for a distance estimate may leave categorical relations largely unconstrained. When post-training emphasizes one readout, improvements can therefore concentrate on that interface while transfer to others remains weak or even degrades; we call this observed specialization interface lock-in. ChronoReplay addresses it by replaying heterogeneous spatial supervision as chronologically ordered episodes, retaining source-native targets, and balancing supervision across families. Under the same observation access, a single ChronoReplay checkpoint improves OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench together, including a 13.41-point gain on OST-Bench, and achieves the highest three-benchmark mean among the supervision settings compared here. Same-data controls further separate the ingredients of this transfer: answer serialization redistributes gains across OST and UCS, family-balanced learning improves over ordinary joint SFT and natural turn weighting, and chronological replay exceeds a shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points across two paired seeds. Adaptive frame selection then changes evidence access while keeping the trained model fixed, providing an additional inference-time gain at lower visual cost. Streaming spatial performance depends on what distinctions supervision preserves, how heterogeneous histories are organized during learning, and what causal evidence inference makes available at test time.
authors: Yihao Hu, Yitong Lin, Pan Wang, Zhihao Wen, Hang Wang, Yiwen Zhao, Deyuan Liu, Yutong Li, Mingda Wan, Yuchen Mao, Tao Lin
bullets: Single-interface post-training can cause interface lock-in, weakening transfer between categorical, metric, and other spatial readouts.
ChronoReplay replays heterogeneous, source-native supervision as chronologically ordered episodes with balanced spatial families.
One checkpoint improves OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench together, including a 13.41-point OST-Bench gain.
Answer serialization, family balancing, and chronological order each contribute to transfer; chronological replay beats shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points.
Adaptive frame selection adds inference-time gains while reducing visual cost, with the model unchanged.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial VLM training with heterogeneous spatial supervision and chronological replay; directly targets spatial intelligence.
papers.title: ChronoReplay: One Answer Interface Is Not Enough for Streaming Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: ChronoReplay improves streaming spatial reasoning by preserving diverse spatial distinctions and replaying their supervision in chronological, balanced episodes.

papers.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Sifna Nasar, Mariam Ahmed, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of manually annotated surgical bounding boxes.
Evaluates six MLLMs and multi-call annotation designs on laparoscopic cholecystectomy frames from Cholec80.
Shows that similar instrument recognition F1 can hide substantial localization differences, with mIoU ranging from 0.180 to 0.735.
A structured multi-stage pipeline reaches 0.784 mIoU, approaching human-human agreement of 0.814.
Releases 285,977 bounding boxes covering all 184,498 annotated frames across 80 videos.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM-based framework converting presence labels to bounding boxes; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial localization.
papers.title: From Presence Labels to Bounding Boxes: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Scale Surgical Instrument Localization?
papers.tldr: A scalable multimodal-LLM pipeline converts surgical instrument-presence labels into bounding boxes, achieving near-human localization quality and enabling a large public spatial extension of Cholec80.

papers.abstract: Modern surgical AI increasingly requires multimodal understanding rather than isolated perception, yet existing datasets remain largely limited to single-task supervision such as recognition or templated question answering. Current medical VQA resources often rely on synthetic templates, lack natural descriptive supervision, or provide sparse annotations that hinder reasoning about spatial relations and procedural context. We introduce MIS-VQA, a surgical vision-language dataset generated through an annotation-driven pipeline that converts heterogeneous surgical annotations into structured textual scene representations. Using EndoVis18 and CholecT50, we transform phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation labels into unified contexts that guide large language models to generate clinically coherent question-answer pairs. MIS-VQA supports four response types-concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning-enabling hierarchical evaluation from atomic visual grounding to compositional reasoning. To address annotation sparsity, we incorporate confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks, enabling spatially grounded supervision at scale. MIS-VQA establishes a unified benchmark for surgical vision-language understanding with spatial supervision and multi-tier reasoning evaluation. To demonstrate its utility, we introduce LLaVA-SurgXpert, a family of surgical vision-language models with visual encoders to analyze how visual representations influence multimodal reasoning. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines while revealing capability gaps between perceptual grounding and higher-level reasoning hidden in prior benchmarks.
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Iheb Zouari, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Muhammed Arsalan, Ponnuthurai Suganthan, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
bullets: Addresses limitations of existing surgical VQA datasets, including synthetic questions, sparse annotations, and weak procedural or spatial supervision.
Builds unified scene contexts from phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation annotations in EndoVis18 and CholecT50.
Provides four response types: concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning.
Uses confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks to scale spatially grounded supervision.
Introduces LLaVA-SurgXpert models and reports improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines, while exposing gaps between grounding and higher-level reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Surgical vision-language dataset and MLLM family with spatial grounding and multi-step reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial understanding.
papers.title: MIS-VQA: An Annotation-Driven Surgical Vision-Language Dataset for Complex Surgical Understanding
papers.tldr: MIS-VQA turns diverse surgical annotations into a structured vision-language benchmark for evaluating both spatial grounding and multi-step clinical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary instance segmentation (OVIS) provides a promising solution for marine perception by recognizing and segmenting categories beyond predefined label spaces. Existing OVIS methods usually rely on vision-language alignment, where visual region features are matched with textual category embeddings to recognize both seen and unseen classes. However, this alignment assumption becomes fragile in underwater environments. Color attenuation, scattering, turbidity, and low contrast distort visual appearance, causing region features to deviate from their corresponding semantic concepts. As a result, the similarity between degraded visual features and textual classifiers becomes unreliable, which particularly weakens the recognition of unseen underwater categories that cannot be corrected by category-specific supervision. To address these issues, we propose GeoPrompt, a geometry-conditioned prompt learning framework for underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation. Our key insight is that geometric structure is more stable than visual appearance in degraded underwater scenes. Specifically, GeoPrompt introduces a geometry-guided visual adaptation module (GVAM) to extract depth-derived structural priors and inject them into multi-scale visual features. It further develops a geometry-conditioned prompt learning (GCPL) that generates geometry-aware textual classifiers from structural representations. These geometry-aware classifiers are integrated with fixed and image-conditioned textual classifiers to improve open-vocabulary semantic alignment. Experiments on the MARIS-OpenIS benchmark show that GeoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance and brings consistent improvements on underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation.
authors: Shanshan Han, Yuxi Wang, Can Qin, Yujie Chen, Cong Pan, Haitao Li, Guoqiang Zhong
bullets: Underwater degradation distorts visual features, making text-based recognition—especially for unseen categories—unreliable.
The method extracts depth-derived structural priors and injects them into multi-scale visual features.
It generates geometry-aware textual classifiers and combines them with fixed and image-conditioned classifiers.
Experiments on MARIS-OpenIS report state-of-the-art performance with consistent improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-conditioned prompt learning injects depth-derived structural priors into vision-language segmentation, fitting geometry-aware multimodal models.
papers.title: GeoPrompt: Geometry-Conditioned Prompt Learning for Underwater Open-Vocabulary Instance Segmentation
papers.tldr: GeoPrompt improves underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation by using stable geometric cues to strengthen vision-language alignment.

papers.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/
authors: Tianchen Guo, Tengyue Zhang, Chen Liu, Ling Chen, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces an interactive benchmark with real-world scenes and multi-turn questions, covering passive multi-view control and active exocentric exploration.
Models must query adjacent viewpoints from severely occluded views and are scored on answer quality and exploration efficiency.
State-of-the-art MLLMs often stop too early with high confidence and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometry.
Matched-view comparisons suggest the active–passive performance gap mainly stems from insufficient evidence acquisition.
GRPO-based view-seeking increases exploration but can reduce accuracy because models over-explore and fail to integrate views across turns.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive benchmark for MLLM human-centric spatial understanding and active view exploration, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Humans in Space: Can MLLMs Construct Human-Centric Spatial Understanding via Active Exocentric Exploration?
papers.tldr: SATE-Bench evaluates whether MLLMs can actively seek informative viewpoints and build reliable human-centric spatial understanding in occluded scenes.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction is important for embodied agents operating in complex environments whose semantic categories extend beyond fixed taxonomies. While recent studies have explored open-vocabulary occupancy in outdoor driving scenarios, indoor environments remain challenging due to dense occlusions, complex geometry, and fine-grained long-tailed semantics. To reduce the need for expensive voxel-level semantic annotations, we study a geometry-only supervision setting requiring only binary occupancy labels. We build upon Language-Embedded Gaussians as a unified representation coupling 3D geometry with language-aligned semantics. For geometry learning, we introduce an opacity-aware Poisson-based Gaussian-to-Occupancy formulation that enables stable volumetric aggregation under binary occupancy supervision. For semantic learning, we render Gaussian features into images and align them with a frozen open-vocabulary model, together with Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing during Gaussian splatting. Building on this framework, we further introduce Instance-Level Semantic Consistency to alleviate fragmented object predictions, and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to provide informative and less redundant multi-view semantic supervision. We also extend our framework to outdoor driving scenarios to evaluate its generality across substantially different environments. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves strong open-vocabulary occupancy performance, validating the effectiveness and generality of our framework. Code will be available at https://github.com/JuIvyy/LegoOcc.
authors: Changqing Zhou, Yueru Luo, Han Zhang, Zeyu Jiang, Changhao Chen
bullets: Targets indoor and outdoor scenes with dense occlusions, complex geometry, and long-tailed semantics beyond fixed taxonomies.
Uses binary occupancy labels for geometry, with an opacity-aware Poisson Gaussian-to-occupancy formulation for stable volumetric aggregation.
Aligns rendered Gaussian features with a frozen open-vocabulary model and applies Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing.
Introduces Instance-Level Semantic Consistency and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to improve fragmented and redundant multi-view predictions.
Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show strong performance and cross-environment generality.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction couples geometry with language-aligned semantics, fitting 3D perception and spatial understanding.
papers.title: LegoOcc++: Towards Consistent Open-Vocabulary 3D Occupancy Prediction
papers.tldr: LegoOcc++ enables open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction from geometry-only supervision by combining language-aligned Gaussian representations with consistency-aware semantic learning.

papers.abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.
authors: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Benchmarks spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot actions on BEHAVIOR-1K.
Includes 3,256 spatial questions, 1,240 grounding queries, 14 manipulation tasks, and 10 navigation tasks.
Tests held-out scene configurations and target changes under fixed training layouts.
Baseline action success drops from 41.6% on held-out configurations to 16.1% with changed instructions; oracle visual cues improve both settings.
Shows that perception accuracy does not consistently translate into robot behavior, motivating joint evaluation of spatial understanding and task completion.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark linking VLM spatial understanding to VLA behavior in manipulation and navigation; fits spatial intelligence and embodied robotics.
papers.title: Behavior Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
papers.tldr: BEHAVIOR-Spatial evaluates whether vision-language models and robot policies truly understand and follow spatial instructions in physical scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
authors: Sagnik Anupam, Utkarsh Lal, Aneesh Edara, Botong Zhang, Yao Tang, Jiatao Gu, Dinesh Jayaraman, Osbert Bastani
bullets: Evaluates VLMs on language-conditioned frame ordering, depthwise object ordering, and left-to-right pixel-coordinate ordering.
Uses stereo and wrist-camera images from real-world robots, with task difficulty controlled by the number of items to sort.
Finds that several state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with these robotics-relevant ordering problems.
Introduces an autonomous pipeline for generating scalable training data.
Shows that supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on this data improve ordering performance and transfer to downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves VLM spatiotemporal and depth-ordering reasoning for robotics via generated data; fits spatial intelligence and embodied reasoning.
papers.title: RoboReason: Boosting Robotics-Relevant VLM Reasoning Through Scalable Data Generation
papers.tldr: RoboReason introduces scalable robot-camera ordering tasks and synthetic training data to improve VLM spatial and temporal reasoning for robotics.

papers.abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.
authors: Xiaodi Huang, Zilin Wang, Jinpeng Liu, Pengchuan Xiao, Zhenlei Shao, Zhang Zhang, Shuxiang Lu
bullets: Represents each token’s observation footprint as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times.
Uses distribution-derived rotation statistics for geometric Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O content aggregation; pointwise RoPE is recovered for single-address observations.
Pre-aggregation incorporates observation geometry without processing pairs of observation nodes or increasing sequence length.
Evaluated across four robot-policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, plus reconstruction, depth estimation, and novel-view synthesis.

Fast-WAM performance improved from 91.83% to 92.88% across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks; it also outpaced P-RoPE and RayRoPE in H20 benchmarks, with 17.4% median latency overhead over Standard RoPE.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware rotary position encoding for embodied perception and robot policies.
papers.title: POD-RoPE: Rotary Position Encoding over Physical Observation Distributions for Embodied AI
papers.tldr: POD-RoPE encodes the physical extent of embodied observations into attention rotations, improving geometry-aware perception and robot manipulation while avoiding sequence-length growth.

papers.abstract: Video spatial reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand how objects are arranged and related across viewpoints. While these models can recognize objects in individual frames, integrating these observations to solve complex spatial tasks remains challenging. We examine route planning as a representative task and observe that existing models become substantially less accurate as the number of required turns increases, with several models achieving accuracy close to random guessing on routes requiring three or more turns. This finding suggests that recognizing landmarks alone is insufficient: models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GeoLift, a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction. It then uses shared geometric regions, called superpoints, to associate observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map enables explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and provides geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift improves Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including an increase in route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and achieves 59.8% accuracy on MindCube. These results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training.
authors: Xinglin Li, TingTing Long, Jingzhi Zhou, Jiajing Chen, Jian Yang, Jin Xie
bullets: Existing MLLMs struggle to connect landmarks across viewpoints, with accuracy dropping sharply on routes requiring three or more turns.
GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained feed-forward geometry models for training-free 3D reconstruction.
Shared geometric regions called superpoints associate the same objects across views without a learned matcher.
The resulting 3D map supports explicit spatial-relation and multistep-route computation, plus distance and size estimation.
It raises Qwen3-VL-4B’s VSI-Bench average from 55.4% to 64.1% and route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, while reaching 59.8% on MindCube.
papers.selection_reason: Grounds video spatial reasoning in explicit 3D maps, improving MLLM spatial and route reasoning.
papers.title: GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps
papers.tldr: GeoLift improves video spatial reasoning by mapping frame-level object detections into an explicit shared 3D scene for multiview route planning and spatial inference.

papers.abstract: Text-to-3D solid retrieval requires aligning natural language with precise geometry despite variations in pose, scale, and recording conventions. Existing methods discretize Boundary Representation (B-rep) models into point clouds or meshes, or learn features from faces, edges, and topology, risking information loss or lacking explicit invariance guarantees. We propose a text-to-B-rep retrieval framework based on group actions and spectral geometric invariants, making invariance an explicit constraint on descriptor construction. Specifically, we use group actions to characterize equivalence transformations induced by translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour recording conventions. For sketch-extrusion solids, we construct a fixed 280-dimensional spectral geometric descriptor by integrating geometric information from three complementary levels, including cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion structures. Furthermore, we use descriptor-consistent multi-positive sets and geometric attribute supervision to promote structural alignment between text and solids. On Text-to-3D solid retrieval, our method achieves 88.6% Recall@5, exceeding the previous state of the art by 13.6 percentage points and demonstrating the effectiveness of explicit geometric invariants for precise 3D solid retrieval.
authors: Hongzhu Yi, Hao Liu, Tao Yu, Tiankun Yang, Yujia Yang, Zhenghao Zhang, Tianyu Zong, Zhenyu Guan, Bingkang Shi, Haopeng Jin, Yuanxiang Wang, Zhongtian Luo, Jungang Xu
bullets: Targets information loss and missing invariance guarantees in point-cloud, mesh, and component-based B-rep representations.
Defines equivalence transformations through group actions, covering translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour conventions.
Builds a fixed 280-dimensional descriptor from cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion structures.
Uses descriptor-consistent multi-positive sets and geometric attribute supervision to improve text–solid structural alignment.
Achieves 88.6% Recall@5, reported as 13.6 percentage points above the previous state of the art.
papers.selection_reason: Text-to-3D retrieval with explicit spectral geometric invariants is directly relevant to spatial and geometric reasoning.
papers.title: Can One Hear Geometry? Gauge-Invariant Spectral Descriptors for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval
papers.tldr: A text-to-B-rep retrieval framework uses explicit spectral geometric invariants to match language with 3D solids despite pose, scale, reflection, and recording variations.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding (VG) in visual question answering (VQA) is a fundamental capability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), enabling the detection of the most relevant region in an image to answer the question. This reflects the model's capability of multimodal comprehension, which is crucial when interacting with visually impaired people (VIP). Indeed, visual grounding, when applied to assistive scenarios, is not merely a technical feature, but rather a trust and safety requirement. In this work, we study visual grounding in VLMs for visually impaired people. To this end, we assess open-source VLMs on visual grounding using the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding dataset and challenge, which contains real-life images taken by VIP. We propose VG-SHAP, which extends an existing explainability framework to provide visual grounding explanations, allowing the evaluation of black-box VLMs. Our results on the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding challenge show that despite generating correct answers, VLMs struggle to ground in the proper region in the image. However, these results are constrained by the quality of the segmentation model of our explainability framework and further research is necessary.
authors: Fairooz Azim, Lydia Achour, Claudia Borg, Lina Rojas-Barahona
bullets: Visual grounding is framed as a trust and safety requirement for assistive VQA, not merely a technical capability.
The authors evaluate open-source VLMs on the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding dataset and challenge, built from real-life images captured by visually impaired people.
VG-SHAP extends an explainability framework to generate visual grounding explanations for evaluating black-box VLMs.
Results show a disconnect between answer correctness and grounding accuracy.
Evaluation is limited by the quality of the framework’s segmentation model, motivating further research.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and explains VLM visual grounding; relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: Evaluating Visual Language Models on Visual Grounding for Visually Impaired People
papers.tldr: The study finds that open-source vision-language models can answer questions about images from visually impaired users but often fail to identify the correct visual evidence.

papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.
authors: Minghao Zhu, Bohan Hou, Kun Xiang, Zixuan Wang, Yinzhou Tang, Yifei Yang, Zhikai Wang, Tianyi Zhang, Kehan Li, Haoyu Zhao, Siteng Huang, Leigang Qu, Sicong Leng, Dongchi Huang, Mingxiu Chen, Shijian Lu, Yue Wang, Xiaodan Liang, Zhenyu Zeng, Deli Zhao, Chengju Liu, Jianfei Yang, Xin Li
bullets: Supports spatial reasoning, physical prediction, grounding, and anticipation of evolving scenes across subtasks.
An agentic reinforcement-learning extension selectively uses video predictions to reason about unobserved states and interaction outcomes.
A world-action extension translates the model’s understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control.
The model achieves the highest average embodied-understanding score among evaluated unified multimodal models and improves Rynn-VP by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano.
Its extensions improve Rynn-GEU by 6.0 points over direct reasoning and achieve 51.5% success on selected RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7% average success across three real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified embodied model combining video-language reasoning, spatial understanding, visual planning, and robot control spans multiple configured topics.
papers.title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
papers.tldr: RynnUnify is a 16B unified embodied model that combines physical-world understanding, long-horizon visual planning, and robot control through interleaved video-language reasoning.

papers.abstract: Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.
authors: Dianye Huang, Jiamei Guo, Yue Zhou, Mingde Li, Yi Xiong, Wei Wang, Nassir Navab, Zhongliang Jiang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between continuous measurements and discrete token-based numerical prediction.
Uses a shared vision-language backbone with autoregressive text generation, visual prompt tuning, and diffusion-based prediction of caliper coordinates and measurement length.
Adds coordinate-length consistency and ensemble post-processing to refine estimates.
On four echocardiographic tasks, it reduces measurement errors by 21.4–37.6% versus a Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline and preserves medical question-answering performance.
Also improves X-ray vertebral measurement error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels; evaluation is limited to the reported ultrasound, question-answering, and X-ray tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language model with diffusion-based continuous spatial measurement prediction; fits multimodal LLMs and geometry-aware VLMs.
papers.title: Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: HAD-VLM combines language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction to improve prompt-conditioned quantitative measurements in medical images.

papers.abstract: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.
authors: Panagiotis Koromilas, Eleanna Vali, Diogenis Antonopoulos, Eleni Saka, Dimitris Christofis, Nikolaos Ioannis Bountos, Konstantin Klemmer, Ioannis Papoutsis, Yannis Panagakis, Mihalis A. Nicolaou
bullets: Standard Lipschitz location encoders have intrinsic dimension at most 2, causing low-rank embeddings and preventing optimal contrastive alignment.
Frozen image encoders act as covariance regularizers, but multimodal settings require targets that are both cross-modal aligned and high-rank.
LoCA first jointly aligns Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders, then trains location and tabular metadata adapters with multi-view contrastive learning.
Across 17 geospatial, environmental, socioeconomic, biodiversity, and climate tasks, LoCA records the most task wins and wins 68.8% of per-task comparisons.
The approach is evaluated within the scope of the five compared state-of-the-art encoders and the listed downstream tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Studies multimodal alignment of location and Earth-observation encoders, contributing to spatial-geometric representation learning.
papers.title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
papers.tldr: LoCA enables multimodal geospatial location encoding by creating a co-aligned, high-rank image target before training location and metadata adapters, achieving the strongest overall results across 17 tasks.

papers.abstract: While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent \emph{modality gap}. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $\Delta^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.
authors: Shubham Gupta, Siva Reddy, Perouz Taslakian, Valentina Zantedeschi, Cem Subakan
bullets: The modality gap persists in shared embedding spaces learned by models such as CLIP and CLAP.
The method replaces unit-sphere embeddings with probability-simplex representations.
Softmax adapters and Total Variation similarity provide a shared, calibrated coordinate system for both modalities.
Across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks, the centroid ℓ₂ gap is reduced by 97–99%.
Retrieval performance matches or exceeds that of standard unconstrained models.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the modality gap in multimodal models by using simplex-constrained representations and geometric priors, improving cross-modal alignment and retrieval.
papers.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
papers.tldr: Constraining multimodal embeddings to the probability simplex with lightweight adapters substantially closes the modality gap while preserving strong retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: Text-enhanced visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) exploits textual descriptions to compensate for appearance cues that are weak or unavailable under infrared imaging. Existing methods construct compensation from differences between modality-oriented textual representations, implicitly assuming that textual differences are visually complementary. We revisit this assumption through semantic superposition and show that dense textual residuals may entangle useful appearance variations with redundant, making direct residual fusion unreliable. We propose Superposition-Aware Residual Calibration, which transforms dense textual differences into selective and visually grounded complements. Low-Interference Sparse Residual Learning represents modality-oriented text embeddings as sparse activation strengths over a shared dictionary, selects positive strength differences, and suppresses both dictionary-level overlap and activation-weighted interference to reconstruct a compact, selectively controlled residual. Visual Complement and Counterfactual Calibration further calibrates the residual against identity-specific RGB-IR visual discrepancies, encouraging retained semantics to provide meaningful compensation while preserving the residual structure. Experiments on Tri-SYSU-MM01, Tri-RegDB, and Tri-LLCM show that SARC consistently improves the VI-ReID backbone and remains competitive with text-assisted methods. Mechanism analyses show that SARC produces more concentrated textual variations, reduces dictionary-level feature interference, and improves residual-visual-complement alignment for most samples. These results demonstrate that effective cross-modal compensation requires textual residuals to be selectively represented and explicitly calibrated, rather than directly treated as visual complements. Code and implementation details will be released upon publication.
authors: Xiaoyang Li, Mingming Lu, Wei Zhou, Hao Li, Canhui Zhang
bullets: Dense differences between modality-specific text representations can mix useful appearance cues with redundant or interfering semantics.
Low-Interference Sparse Residual Learning selects informative residual differences over a shared dictionary while suppressing overlap and activation-weighted interference.
Visual Complement and Counterfactual Calibration aligns retained textual semantics with identity-specific RGB–IR visual discrepancies.
Experiments on Tri-SYSU-MM01, Tri-RegDB, and Tri-LLCM show consistent backbone improvements and competitive performance among text-assisted methods.
Mechanism analyses report more concentrated textual variations, less feature interference, and better residual–visual-complement alignment for most samples.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses cross-modal person re-identification by reformulating textual residuals as visual complements. This contributes to spatial intelligence and multimodal fusion techniques.
papers.title: Are Textual Residuals Truly Complementary? Learning Visual Complements under Semantic Superposition for Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
papers.tldr: SARC makes textual residuals more selective and visually grounded, improving text-enhanced visible-infrared person re-identification.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) read images through visual tokens, and under the small per-image budgets that efficient deployment requires, the fine text of documents, charts and infographics becomes illegible. Zooming in recovers the evidence, but the region must be chosen before the model answers. We find that MLLMs know where the evidence is, but not in a form that can be read before they answer: the answer tokens localize it from the middle layers on, whereas the attention available before answering does so only in the top layers, at a depth that varies across models, and diffusely. Supervising the pre-answer attention to point degrades reading, and the benefit of zooming is governed by each image's information gap. Building on these findings, we introduce ours, which lets an MLLM look where its answer would.
