A dedicated look token, processed in a single prefill and kept out of the answering pass, learns in hindsight to attend as the model's own correct answers do, extracting this knowledge into a concentrated pointer before any answer exists. Its hidden state then selects how to look, from no zoom to crops, square windows, windows that adapt to the pointer and foveated warps, supervised by the counterfactual outcome of every view. ours needs no box annotations, per-model layer search, external localizers or generation before the answer. On Qwen3-VL at three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it surpasses the strongest baseline by 4.8-9.1 points at 98 visual tokens per view and attention-guided zooming by 11.1-17.0 points, while running faster than attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.
authors: Zhensheng Hu, Guanglong Xu, Guanqiang Hu
bullets: Small visual-token budgets make fine text in documents, charts, and infographics difficult to read.
Answer tokens localize relevant evidence earlier and more clearly than pre-answer attention, whose useful depth varies by model.
OURS uses a dedicated look token trained from correct-answer attention to produce a concentrated pointer before answering.
The pointer selects among no zoom, crops, adaptive windows, square windows, and foveated warps using counterfactual view outcomes.

On Qwen3-VL across three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it improves over the strongest baseline by 4.8–9.1 points and attention-guided zooming by 11.1–17.0 points at 98 visual tokens per view, while running faster than both attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a mechanism for MLLMs to intelligently zoom into images before answering, optimizing visual token usage. This addresses spatial intelligence (understanding where to look) and efficient AI (token budget management).
papers.title: The Answer Knows Where to Look: Zooming before MLLMs Answer under Visual-Token Budgets
papers.tldr: OURS lets MLLMs identify where answer-critical visual evidence lies before answering, enabling effective zooming under tight visual-token budgets.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are costly to pretrain, yet model families often repeat this process across backbone scales and sensing modalities. We investigate feature distillation as a more efficient way to reuse existing representations. First, we distill frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers through patch-level feature matching. Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind Tiny, Small, and Base outperform their scale-matched released counterparts by 2.76, 3.02, and 1.87 mean IoU points, respectively; each also matches or exceeds the next-larger released model. Distilled CROMA-Base gains 2.05 points. TerraMind-Base required only 43 A6000 GPU-hours, approximately 0.5\% of the reported cost of independent pretraining. Second, we introduce TEDI, an unpaired multi-expert approach combining TerraMind for multispectral imagery and DINOv3 for high-resolution RGB. Separate patch embeddings route unpaired inputs into a shared Transformer trunk, removing the need for co-registered data. TEDI-Large achieves the highest single-model mean in our PANGAEA-9 comparison (62.51 mIoU), outperforming both teachers overall while retaining their modality-specific strengths. TEDI-Base reaches 61.75 mIoU with 72\% fewer parameters. These results show that distillation improves the GeoFM accuracy-compute frontier while consolidating complementary experts into a single versatile backbone.
authors: Mario Hamon, Pierre Adorni, Minh-Tan Pham
bullets: Distills frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers using patch-level feature matching.
Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind and CROMA models improve over scale-matched released models and often reach the performance of larger ones.
TerraMind-Base distillation used approximately 0.5% of the reported cost of training an independent model.
TEDI combines TerraMind’s multispectral expertise with DINOv3’s high-resolution RGB features through separate patch embeddings and a shared Transformer trunk, without co-registered data.
TEDI-Large achieves the highest reported PANGAEA-9 single-model mean, while TEDI-Base offers a lower-parameter alternative with competitive performance.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates efficient feature distillation for geospatial foundation models, significantly reducing compute costs while maintaining or improving accuracy. This addresses both spatial intelligence (geospatial understanding) and efficient AI (distillation).
papers.title: Reuse, Don't Retrain: Efficient, Modality-Versatile Geospatial Foundation Models through Feature Distillation
papers.tldr: Feature distillation efficiently repurposes geospatial foundation models into smaller, multimodal models that match or outperform larger pretrained counterparts at much lower cost.

papers.abstract: Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high-power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert-intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns? We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse-design loop. PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi-modal Reasoning, Inverse-Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families. We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi-agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design. Our results reveal a striking perception-design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics-aware design actions. Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures. These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding. PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi-dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI-assisted photonic engineering. The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.
authors: Shengchao Chen, Ting Shu, Sufen Ren
bullets: Evaluates 26 tasks across six stages, from geometry perception and physics understanding to inverse-design decisions and code generation.
Built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples spanning 18 structurally diverse photonic crystal fiber families.
Tests both individual VLM capabilities and multi-agent systems across the full perception-to-design pipeline.
Models recognize fiber geometry with moderate success but often fail to convert visual understanding into physics-aware actions.
Sequential agent pipelines suffer from compounded upstream errors, indicating that physical grounding—not just scaling or agent chaining—is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating VLM perception, geometry, and physics-aware reasoning for photonic inverse design, relevant to multimodal and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: PCFBench: How Far Can Large Vision-Language Models Go in Physics-aware Photonic Inverse Design?
papers.tldr: PCFBench benchmarks whether vision-language models can move beyond recognizing photonic crystal fiber geometry to making physics-aware inverse-design decisions, finding a substantial gap between perception and design.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding with vision-language models such as CLIP typically produces a single deterministic relevance map for an image-query pair, without indicating whether the localisation is reliable or whether the referent is present at all. We introduce \textbf{PROVE} (\textbf{Pro}babilistic \textbf{V}isual Grounding via Patch-Level \textbf{E}vidence), a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions without modifying the backbone. PROVE casts grounding as per-patch membership: each patch accumulates positive and negative evidence for whether it belongs to the referent, so a query may match zero, one, or many patches. We train PROVE with an evidential objective on soft patch-coverage targets, and define a prior-pull objective that keeps absent-referent examples near an uninformative prior, so that vacuity serves as an absence signal without a dedicated presence classifier. During inference, a single forward pass yields, in closed form, a posterior-mean grounding map, a spatial vacuity map, and an image-level absence score. We evaluate PROVE on referring-expression benchmarks: it is competitive in localisation with state-of-the-art CLIP grounding methods, its uncertainty tracks localisation error and supports selective prediction under abstention, and its image-level score detects when the referent is absent altogether. Our evidential patch-membership modelling offers a simple, drop-in mechanism for probabilistic verification in frozen vision-language grounding systems.
authors: Mayank Nautiyal, Tianru Zhang, Li Ju, Ekta Vats, Prashant Singh
bullets: Addresses the limitations of deterministic relevance maps, which do not show localisation reliability or referent absence.
Uses a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions for referent membership.
Trains on soft patch-coverage targets and pulls absent-referent examples toward an uninformative prior, using vacuity as an absence signal.
A single forward pass produces a grounding map, spatial uncertainty map, and image-level absence score.
On referring-expression benchmarks, PROVE is competitive in localisation; its uncertainty tracks error, supports abstention, and detects absent referents.
papers.selection_reason: Probabilistic patch-level visual grounding with CLIP is directly relevant to spatial understanding in multimodal models.
papers.title: PROVE: Probabilistic Visual Grounding via Patch-Level Evidence for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: PROVE adds probabilistic, uncertainty-aware visual grounding to frozen CLIP by modelling patch-level evidence and detecting when a referent is absent.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved Visual Question Answering (VQA) performance, yet their reasoning over structured content such as tables remains inconsistent, often plagued by spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations. Existing approaches for improving table VQA typically rely on architectural modifications or expensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which impose high barriers to entry due to the need for large-scale, expert-annotated datasets and significant computational resources. In this work, we propose Self-RefineVQA, a training-free, inference-time self-correction framework that improves table VQA performance without additional labeled data or model updates. Inspired by human revision behavior, our method enables a single VLM to iteratively act as a generator, critic, and refiner, forming a closed self-feedback loop that corrects common reasoning errors through prompt-guided re-evaluation. Experiments on tabular VQA benchmarks demonstrate that Self-RefineVQA yields consistent accuracy gains in monolingual and cross-lingual understanding, with a particularly significant boost for small models, enabling lightweight models (e.g., 2B-7B parameters) to rival the performance of significantly larger counterparts. Furthermore, we provide a comparative complexity analysis demonstrating that while inference cost increases linearly, our framework offers superior data efficiency and a lower cumulative cost by eliminating the prohibitive annotation bottleneck of human labeling required for fine-tuning. Our results highlight the potential of prompt-based self-improvement as a scalable, accessible paradigm for reliable table reasoning in VLMs.
bullets: Targets spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations in VLM reasoning over document tables.
Uses one VLM as generator, critic, and refiner in a prompt-guided self-feedback loop.
Requires no labeled data, architectural changes, or model updates.
Improves accuracy across monolingual and cross-lingual tabular VQA, especially for small models.
Inference cost grows linearly with iterations, but avoids the annotation burden of supervised fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free self-correction framework for Table VQA using VLMs. This fits Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Spatial Intelligence (structured content reasoning).
papers.title: Cycle-of-Thought: Self-Evaluative Iterative Reasoning for Table Visual Question Answering in Document Images
papers.tldr: Self-RefineVQA improves table visual question answering through training-free, iterative self-critique and refinement at inference time.

papers.abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.
authors: Radoslaw Malek, Szymon Soltysiak, Aleksandra Kawala-Sterniuk, Piotr Szymanski
bullets: Addresses the underuse of structured map data in geospatial multimodal representation learning.
Aligns H3-indexed regions across OSM-derived graph embeddings, satellite image crops, and textual descriptions.
Uses frozen pretrained encoders with trainable residual projection heads and a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective.
Introduces chained cross-modal recall, routing image–text retrieval through the graph modality under a matched candidate budget.
Graph-mediated retrieval improves R@1@1 over direct image–text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points; downstream gains are task-dependent and largest on Airbnb and Beijing housing.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns map, image, and text modalities for geographic regions, effectively modeling spatial relationships and multimodal integration.
papers.title: GeoLEON-CLIP: Graph-Anchored Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Geographic Region Representation
papers.tldr: GeoLEON-CLIP uses OpenStreetMap graph structure to anchor contrastive alignment among satellite imagery, text, and geographic regions, improving routed cross-modal retrieval and some downstream probes.

papers.abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse $\to$ ModelNet40; XYZRGB $\to$ XYZ-only), PFIR raises zero-shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated $2.6\times$ more on geometrically ambiguous samples---supporting part-level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir-3d.
authors: Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Pattern-matching 3D MLLMs struggle to distinguish geometrically similar objects, with accuracy dropping sharply on highly ambiguous samples.
The method reverses the usual information flow: geometry → function → identity, using part-level segmentation and functional chain-of-thought supervision.
PFIR trains on 507K functional QA pairs with a progressive curriculum and combines functional reasoning with descriptive grounding through dual-objective GRPO.
Under Objaverse→ModelNet40 and XYZRGB→XYZ-only zero-shot evaluation, accuracy improves from 60.5% to 66.7%.
Improvements are concentrated 2.6× more on geometrically ambiguous samples, supporting part-level functional reasoning for recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Part-level functional reasoning in 3D MLLMs to improve generalizable 3D recognition; relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition
papers.tldr: PFIR improves generalizable 3D object recognition by inferring function from parts before identifying the object, especially in geometrically ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D scene construction is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Recent methods such as SAM-3Dfy enable end-to-end reconstruction of 3D assets and their scene layouts, but still struggle with fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality. Meanwhile, specialized 3D object generators provide detailed object geometry, while 3D foundation models offer strong and generalizable spatial understanding. We propose Easy-3Dfy, a compositional workflow that decouples object generation from scene layout estimation, allowing specialized models to fully exploit their respective strengths. An RPF-based aligner then bridges these capabilities by establishing geometric correspondence between object-local meshes and partial scene pointmaps, recovering object layout for scene composition. Without requiring complete scene-level supervision, the proposed workflow consistently outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200. Our results demonstrate that explicit geometric composition can effectively combine high-quality object generation with strong spatial understanding, while enabling the workflow to benefit independently from advances in both 3D object generation and foundation models.
authors: Ziang Zhang, Wenyou Yi, Zehan Wang, Jiachen Xu, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Targets limitations in fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality in existing end-to-end methods such as SAM-3Dfy.
Uses specialized 3D object generators for object geometry and 3D foundation models for spatial understanding.
An RPF-based aligner matches object-local meshes with partial scene pointmaps to recover object layouts.
Requires no complete scene-level supervision and outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200.
Its modular design can independently benefit from advances in object generation and foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Single-image 3D scene construction via geometric composition, linking 3D object generation with spatial understanding from foundation models.
papers.title: Easy-3Dfy: Object-Level Geometric Composition for Single-Image 3D Scene Construction
papers.tldr: Easy-3Dfy improves single-image 3D scene reconstruction by separately generating detailed objects and estimating their spatial layout, then aligning them geometrically for composition.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.
Supports counterfactual simulation, such as predicting whether moving an object would block a path.
Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language world model with geometric/spatial reasoning and counterfactual simulation directly fits world models, spatial intelligence, and 3D reasoning.
papers.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
papers.tldr: Ψ-0.6 is a unified vision-language world model that adaptively combines visual, linguistic, geometric, and simulated reasoning for flexible physical-world inference.

papers.abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read-decide-execute-check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision-language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator-selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.
authors: Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Weizhe Tang, Bofeng Cao, Sikai Chen, Xiaopeng Li, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the correct path among multiple geometrically plausible work-zone routes.
Generates candidate paths geometrically, then fuses geometric scores with agreement to a VLM-predicted trajectory.
Trains the VLM to identify lane status and hazard side before making a passage decision, with rule-based intervention for control compliance.
On 2,306 ROADWork episodes, SAGE reduces average displacement error by 8.3%, final displacement error by 12.0%, and hard-constraint violations by 37% versus the geometric ranker.
The approach improves all tested generator-selector combinations and is competitive with or better than adapted driving VLMs on reported accuracy and safety measures.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-grounded pathway prediction for work-zone driving, combining geometric candidate generation with spatial/control reasoning; relevant to robot navigation and spatial VLM grounding.
papers.title: SAGE: A hybrid vision-language and geometry framework for work-zone pathway prediction under temporary traffic control
papers.tldr: SAGE combines geometric candidate paths with vision-language reasoning to select safer, MUTCD-compliant routes through temporary work zones.

papers.abstract: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.
bullets: Addresses cooperative referring scene understanding when targets or landmarks originate from another agent’s observations.
Builds local open-vocabulary, instance-aware Gaussian maps and aligns them using geometric and semantic consistency.
Uses a view-conditioned mask relation graph to reason about spatial relationships from the querying robot’s viewpoint.
Introduces CoQuad-Ref, a real-world and simulated indoor benchmark.
Refinement reduces simulated rotation error from 2.58° to 0.15°, while real-world referring mIoU improves from 52.6% to 68.8% over ReferSplat.
papers.selection_reason: View-conditioned referring grounding over fused 3D Gaussian maps is a strong spatial-intelligence and embodied perception contribution.
papers.title: CoRef-GS: Cooperative Referring Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Agent Scene Understanding
papers.tldr: CoRef-GS enables viewpoint-aware language grounding across independently built Gaussian maps by jointly aligning their geometry and semantics.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
bullets: Exact-counting ability is model-specific, with the reported R80 range spanning 3–150 dots across 9 models.
Marking items improves counting for only 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs; it can hurt imprecise pointers and rarely outperforms simpler routines.
Tag-level audits classify errors as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, exposing whether answers are grounded in the visual trace.
Precise pointers tend to derive answers from their tags, while dense scenes primarily cause omissions and models seldom revise after tagging.
Traversal order following, order-invariant counting, and regular-versus-scattered advantages dissociate, indicating multiple underlying counting capacities.
papers.selection_reason: VLM counting evaluation based on spatial marking and ordering is directly relevant to spatial reasoning diagnostics in multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A developmental counting-inspired tagging procedure reveals that VLMs’ counting failures are mainly serial, omission-prone, and poorly self-corrected, while producing useful auditable traces rather than reliably improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: RGB-D semantic segmentation has made notable progress by fusing RGB and Depth, yet mainstream models still learn features almost exclusively from pixel-level supervision, lacking direct high-level semantic constraints. This raises a central question-can external knowledge such as language priors inject stronger semantic discriminability into mainstream RGB-D segmentation models. We present DTFormer, a novel tri-modal (RGB-D-Text) semantic segmentation framework. At its core is Text-guided Semantic Alignment Module (TSAM) that first encodes textual cues into a set of semantic prototypes and then explicitly aligns multi-modal RGB-D features with these prototypes at multiple encoder and decoder layers. This design imposes strong semantic regularization on representation learning, guiding the network toward more discriminative features. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that DTFormer delivers consistent gains while remaining simple and efficient. Our results demonstrate that explicit semantic alignment offers an effective and practical route to improving RGB-D semantic segmentation. The code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Addresses the lack of high-level semantic constraints in pixel-supervised RGB-D segmentation.
Introduces a tri-modal RGB-D-Text framework with a Text-guided Semantic Alignment Module (TSAM).
TSAM encodes text into semantic prototypes and aligns multi-modal features at multiple encoder and decoder layers.
Experiments on multiple benchmarks show consistent gains with a simple and efficient design.
The approach demonstrates that explicit language-based semantic alignment can strengthen feature discriminability.
papers.selection_reason: Tri-modal RGB-D-text segmentation with depth-aware semantic alignment, fitting spatial intelligence and multimodal modeling interests.
papers.title: DTFormer: Text-Guided Semantic Alignment for RGB-D Segmentation
papers.tldr: DTFormer improves RGB-D semantic segmentation by aligning RGB-D features with language-derived semantic prototypes across the network.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.
authors: Advait Gupta, Sachin Konan, Tom Yin, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scalability of online simulator and real-world agent evaluations.
Covers Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning using 1,000 examples from 23 source datasets.
Evaluates 22 models; the best reaches 58.5% accuracy, indicating substantial remaining challenges.
Offline model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations.

Most errors stem from visual-state grounding and tracking—such as UI localization, motion interpretation, state changes, and 3D spatial reasoning—rather than task misunderstanding or downstream logic.
papers.selection_reason: Offline benchmark for agentic VLM evaluation across embodied domains, including spatial planning and egocentric video.
papers.title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding
papers.tldr: AgentVQA is an offline benchmark for testing vision-language models’ visual understanding in realistic agentic scenarios across five domains.

papers.abstract: Vision and touch provide complementary cues for object pose and local contact geometry, but external cameras are often occluded at the contact site. We present GelSlim 5.0, a fingertip sensor that acquires visual and tactile observations with one fixed camera and a continuous UV-responsive contact layer. By switching illumination, the camera sequentially acquires through-membrane visual images and contact-sensitive tactile images from a shared viewpoint, avoiding inter-camera extrinsic calibration. To combine these observations, we introduce VisTacFusion, a multimodal transformer with separate prediction paths for planar object pose and contact geometry. Asymmetric bottleneck fusion incorporates visual context while preserving tactile spatial features for depth and surface-normal estimation. Modality dropout enables inference with paired inputs or either modality alone. On real validation data from 12 known objects, paired inputs reduce depth MSE, angular error, and translation $L_1$ by 61.2%, 72.3%, and 61.3%, respectively, relative to tactile-only inference with the same model. Relative to visual-only inference, the corresponding reductions are 93.7%, 6.1%, and 8.6%.
authors: Xiangdong Wang, I-Hsuan Huang, Xiaohao Xu, Xili Yi, Nima Fazeli, Xiaonan Huang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and calibration challenges caused by external cameras at contact sites.
Uses a fixed camera with a UV-responsive contact layer and switched illumination to capture visual and tactile images from one viewpoint.
VisTacFusion uses separate pose and contact-geometry prediction paths with asymmetric bottleneck fusion.
Modality dropout supports inference from paired inputs or either modality alone.

On 12 known objects, paired inputs substantially reduced depth, angular, and translation errors versus tactile-only and visual-only inference, with the largest gains over tactile-only depth and angular errors.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal vision-touch transformer for pose and contact geometry estimation; relevant to tactile manipulation and spatial understanding.
papers.title: GelSlim 5.0: Unifying Vision and Touch with a Single Fingertip Camera
papers.tldr: GelSlim 5.0 unifies vision and touch in one fingertip camera, using VisTacFusion to estimate object pose and contact geometry from paired or single-modality inputs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.
authors: Valentino Sacco, Saurabh Pandey, Alexander Florian Jercher, Maximilian Schilling
bullets: Introduces 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs covering spreadsheet sub-elements, character-level document targets, and mixed interfaces across 100 professional applications.
Uses pixel-exact target geometry to evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI-grounding configurations.
Character-level text grounding is the hardest setting, with substantially lower success than overall benchmark performance.
Results show substantial remaining headroom for precise GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models.
Benchmark and evaluation code are publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark for fine-grained, pixel-exact GUI grounding that probes spatial and geometric reasoning in multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: PointerBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained GUI Grounding
papers.tldr: PointerBench diagnoses fine-grained GUI grounding, revealing major weaknesses—especially in character-level text targeting—even among strong multimodal and specialist models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.
authors: Ronald Fecso, Jos\'e Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber, Virginia Mares, Andreas Pollreisz, Hrvoje Bogunovi\'c
bullets: Introduces RetinaGroundBench, the first retinal OCT benchmark for biomarker visual grounding.
Contains 815 ophthalmologist-annotated B-scans, 4,537 bounding boxes, 13 biomarkers, and 8 diseases.
Proposes AggIoU to evaluate fragmented predictions by measuring coverage of the union of overlapping boxes.
Across 27 open-source MLLMs, grounding remains weak despite stronger biomarker-presence classification.
RetGrounder raises grounding F1 from 23.7% for the best general-purpose model to 33.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and fine-tuned MLLM for visual grounding of retinal OCT biomarkers.
papers.title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: RetinaGroundBench shows that MLLMs can recognize retinal OCT biomarkers far better than they can localize them, while OCT-specific fine-tuning substantially improves grounding.

papers.abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. Across seven lifting methods and four datasets, the resulting query-time calibration consistently improves mean intersection over union in both multiclass and single-query segmentation. These gains require no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting, demonstrating the value of scene-conditioned comparison for making better use of existing lifted representations.
authors: Dominik Engel, Yousef Rajeh, Leon Sick, Ivan Viola
bullets: Addresses scene-specific directional concentration that makes raw CLIP cosine similarity unreliable for 3D segmentation.
Partially removes a shared scene direction and whitens text prototypes using a fixed vocabulary of generic terms.
Uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin for single-query prediction.
Improves class-relative feature separation across evaluated scenes and consistently raises mean IoU across seven lifting methods and four datasets.
Operates entirely at query time, requiring no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation with CLIP feature calibration.
papers.title: Query-Time Calibration of CLIP Features for Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
papers.tldr: A query-time calibration scheme improves open-vocabulary 3D segmentation from fixed CLIP-based feature fields without retraining or re-lifting features.

papers.abstract: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Jiarui Guo, Haojia Wei, Yifei Liu, Yifan Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating cinematographic intent into controllable camera motion in dynamic 3D scenes.
A Director agent composes high-level camera plans from concurrent atomic operations controlling translation, rotation, and framing.
Interpreter, Scout, and Critic agents extract intent, choose viewpoints, and iteratively refine plans using rendered visual feedback.
Introduces CinemaBench with 150 Blender scenes, 750 text-directed tasks, and 60 reference videos for evaluating 3D camera generation.
Reports the strongest performance across evaluated baselines and the highest user preference, indicating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and composition.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic system translating language into 3D camera trajectories, involving spatial reasoning and 3D-aware multimodal understanding.
papers.title: FilmFlow: Agentic System for 3D Virtual Film Cinematography
papers.tldr: FilmFlow is a multi-agent system that turns text or reference videos into executable, cinematographically coherent 3D camera trajectories.

papers.abstract: Shadows are observable consequences of latent physical causes, arising from the interaction between illumination, object geometry, and scene structure. A model that understands shadows should be able not only to read a shadow's direction, but also to infer where a shadow should fall when it is absent, and to judge whether a shadow is physically consistent with the scene. We introduce ShadowBench, built from real photographs, which poses these three questions to vision-language models (VLMs). From each scene, we build a correct-shadow, a shadow-removed, and a human-annotated wrong-direction state. Evaluating 19 open VLMs (2B to 78B) and frontier proprietary models, we find that VLMs read a visible shadow's direction well above chance and improve with scale, yet infer the absent direction only weakly and fall to chance at judging physical consistency even under a bias-free two-alternative test that removes the yes-bias of single-image naturalness questions. Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, and even then only modestly and far below humans. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) does not help. The missing ingredient is not reasoning but knowledge that image generation models (IGMs) already hold. Routing a VLM through an IGM lifts its inference well above its direct attempt and helps it flag the wrong-direction shadows it otherwise accepts. Cast-shadow direction is a single facet of illumination understanding, but the sharp gap it reveals between VLMs and IGMs suggests image-generation or reconstruction objectives as a route toward illumination-aware VLMs.
authors: Ryugo Morita, Shunsuke Kitada, Stanislav Frolov, Brian Bernhard Moser, Ko Watanabe, Riku Takahashi, Jinjia Zhou, Andreas Dengel
bullets: ShadowBench evaluates VLMs on visible-shadow direction, absent-shadow inference, and physical-consistency judgments using real photographs with correct, removed, and human-annotated wrong-direction shadows.
Across 19 open and frontier proprietary VLMs, visible-direction reading improves with scale, but absent-direction inference is weak and validity judgments are near chance.
Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, modestly and far below human performance; Chain-of-Thought does not help.
Routing VLMs through image-generation models improves missing-shadow inference and helps identify wrong-direction shadows.
The findings suggest image-generation or reconstruction objectives may provide useful illumination knowledge for VLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves VLM physical/spatial reasoning about cast shadows, fitting spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Where Did the Light Come From? Diagnosing Cast-Shadow Reasoning in VLMs and Borrowing the Missing Shadow Prior from Image Generation Models
papers.tldr: VLMs can read visible shadow directions but struggle to infer missing shadows or detect physically inconsistent ones, while routing through image-generation models substantially improves these abilities.

papers.abstract: Open-world geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) agents can transform public geospatial data into accessible decision support for real-world challenges, but must balance autonomous reasoning with reliable spatial analysis and human oversight. We present a topology-guided GeoAI agentic framework for urban flood screening that takes a place name, drawn region, or uploaded boundary and returns ranked candidate basins with an interactive map and report. A deterministic controller retrieves public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure layers, extracts terrain depressions with discrete Morse theory, and ranks basins with a relative flood-priority score. The language model acts only at recorded decision points: selecting a persistence threshold from a precomputed candidate table, drafting recommendations from computed evidence, and reviewing each recommendation against the same evidence. Three human-in-the-loop checkpoints let users revise the threshold, factor weights, or recommendation. In a College Park, Maryland case study, the selected threshold reduced 278 raw terrain minima to 70 basins, with 77% of these basins' lowest points also identified as sinks by a separately computed eight-direction (D8) flow-routing model. Across four further study areas, agreement ranged from 61% to 83%. By combining open data, explicit spatial reasoning, traceable evidence, and human oversight, the framework enables transparent first-pass flood screening while keeping consequential recommendations inspectable and user-controlled.
authors: Yutian Tao, Haoan Feng, Xin Xu, Leila De Floriani
bullets: Accepts place names, drawn regions, or uploaded boundaries and returns ranked candidate basins with maps and reports.
Uses public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure data to identify terrain depressions and compute relative flood-priority scores.
Restricts the language model to traceable decision points: threshold selection, evidence-based recommendations, and recommendation review.
Provides three human checkpoints for revising the persistence threshold, factor weights, or recommendations.
In the case studies, basin identification agreed with D8 flow-routing sinks for 61%–83% of basins, including 77% in College Park, Maryland.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a topology-guided GeoAI framework for spatial reasoning and flood screening, directly utilizing spatial intelligence concepts like topology and spatial analysis.
papers.title: A Topology-Guided GeoAI Agentic Framework for Urban Flood Screening
papers.tldr: A topology-guided GeoAI agent combines deterministic spatial analysis, constrained language-model reasoning, and human oversight to provide transparent first-pass urban flood screening.

papers.abstract: Scaling large language models has substantially improved linguistic fluency, yet reliable autonomous agents require more than fluent generation. In multi-turn inference, current agentic systems often produce semantically plausible but structurally ungrounded reasoning, especially under incomplete observations. We propose Structure-Grounded Uncertainty Reduction (SGUR), a training-free framework that complements token-level generation with active uncertainty reduction over structured hypothesis spaces. SGUR represents incomplete observations as a query graph and aligns them with candidate hypothesis graphs through a prior-weighted partial graph matching mechanism, where database-derived empirical priors assign greater importance to decision-relevant relations rather than treating all graph edges uniformly. The resulting inference state is iteratively refined by an active information-gain strategy that selects the next most informative node to query, systematically pruning the candidate space. We instantiate SGUR on a challenging PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark, demonstrating that structural grounding can partially substitute for model scale: starting from only two observed symptoms, SGUR achieves 92.5% Hit@3, outperforming the strongest Graph-RAG baseline by 9.4 percentage points while using approximately 5x fewer tokens. Notably, SGUR enables smaller backbone models to match or exceed the performance of models up to 10x larger, suggesting that structural grounding provides a more robust and efficient paradigm for scaling agent performance than relying exclusively on increasing model size.
authors: Amirhossein Aghaei, Liangyan Li, Shiyi Yang, Shaohua Wang, Yan Wang
bullets: Targets structurally ungrounded reasoning in agentic systems operating with incomplete observations.
Uses a query graph, prior-weighted partial graph matching, and active information-gain queries to prune hypotheses.
Evaluated on a PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark from two observed symptoms.
Reports 92.5% Hit@3, 9.4 percentage points above the strongest Graph-RAG baseline, with about 5× fewer tokens.
Findings suggest structural grounding can let smaller models match or exceed models up to 10× larger.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a structure-grounded framework using graph matching and active information gain for reasoning, which aligns with spatial intelligence and graph-based reasoning.
papers.title: Better Reasoning, Not Just Bigger Models: A Structure-Grounded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Inference
papers.tldr: SGUR improves efficient, reliable multi-turn reasoning by actively reducing uncertainty over structured hypothesis graphs instead of relying only on larger language models.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Anchor-centric multimodal memory for open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation in dynamic scenes; combines spatial understanding with embodied memory.
papers.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: OASIS enables efficient open-vocabulary object retrieval and navigation in dynamic environments using a sparse, multimodal memory built around stable semantic scene anchors.

papers.abstract: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.
authors: Bangpu Chen, Yaxuan Li, Shirui Peng, Xiangtian Si, Liuxin Chu, Xitong Cao, Hongbo Jin, Jiayu Ding
bullets: Addresses temporal, multi-target, reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor referring expressions in dynamic 4D scenes.
Introduces R4D-Bench-QA with structured query annotations for evaluating referring segmentation.
ReferGaussian converts dynamic Gaussians into persistent language-addressable entities stored in an EntityBank.
MLLMs decompose queries into object phrases and referring constraints, enabling constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization.
Shows improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol.
papers.selection_reason: Grounds referring language in dynamic 4D Gaussian scenes via MLLM-guided decomposition and spatial entity grounding; directly relevant to spatial intelligence and 3D vision.
papers.title: R4DGS: Referring Segmentation in 4D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: R4DGS introduces a benchmark and training-free framework for grounding complex language references to dynamic objects in 4D Gaussian Splatting scenes.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
bullets: Addresses the need for models to describe designated regions and localize them from language using a shared objective rather than separate task-specific supervision.
Generates a description for a region, relocalizes that description, and uses reconstruction overlap plus localization rewards for self-verifiable training.
Extends a common region-space formulation to image masks/boxes, video intervals, and timestamped spatial evidence without reference captions or an external judge during RL.
Introduces DOVE, a human-verified benchmark for evaluating whether video descriptions distinguish a target event from similar recurrences.
Reports improved spatial grounding and temporal localization, including 68.2% gIoU on GroundingSuite, 78.7% on GRES, 51.9% tIoU on Charades, and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE.
papers.selection_reason: Unified region-text cycle RL for fine-grained multimodal understanding and spatial grounding directly fits MLLM and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
papers.tldr: Generalized CycleGRPO unifies multimodal region understanding and localization through reinforcement learning with region-text cycle consistency across images and videos.

papers.abstract: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.
authors: Zhichao Zhai, Menglei Zhao, Guikun Chen, Zihao Yan, Kanzhi Wu, Wenguan Wang, Jun Xiao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating implicit spatial instructions into explicit geometric references for 3D placement.
Uses a language model to generate executable evidence and pose programs over local voxel views with coordinates and neighborhood relations.
Computes target SE(3) poses from selected scene geometry and revises programs using visual and numerical execution feedback.
Introduces the 71-task VoxProg-Bench and evaluation metrics for Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity.
Outperforms relation-, keypoint-, and mesh-based baselines across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Language-model-driven voxel programming for 3D object placement; directly relevant to spatial reasoning and 3D-aware multimodal understanding.
papers.title: VoxProg: 3D Spatial Reasoning through Voxel Programming
papers.tldr: VoxProg enables language models to perform 3D object placement by programming over voxelized scene surfaces with iterative execution feedback.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image generation models do not explicitly receive the syntactic structure of the prompt, i.e., which word modifies which and where each phrase attaches. Consequently, they often struggle to bind attributes to the correct objects, to depict spatial relations and counts correctly, and to render syntactically ambiguous prompts in the intended interpretation. Existing syntax-based control methods mainly address attribute binding and have limited ability to control spatial relations and counts or to specify the interpretation of syntactically ambiguous prompts. They rely on phrase-structure or dependency grammars and require additional rules or constraints on the tree structure to extract modification relations between words or to specify a syntactic interpretation. We propose CCG Diffusion, a training-free method that controls image generation using Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG). In CCG, the category of each word carries rich syntactic information: it specifies what the word combines with and what phrase it forms. Modification relations between words can therefore be read directly from a CCG parse. Moreover, prepositional phrase (PP) attachment ambiguity, a representative syntactic ambiguity, can be resolved simply by fixing the preposition's category. CCG Diffusion applies the same two CCG-based mechanisms, prompt rewriting and attention guidance, both to controlling attribute binding, spatial relations, and counts and to resolving PP ambiguity. On two architecturally different backbones, Stable Diffusion and Sana, CCG Diffusion achieves the highest scores among the compared methods in attribute binding and 2D spatial relations and significantly outperforms all of them in PP ambiguity resolution.
authors: Ryosuke Yamaki, Daichi Mochihashi, Nobutaka Shimada, Seitaro Shinagawa, Tadahiro Taniguchi
bullets: Addresses failures caused by text-to-image models lacking explicit prompt syntax.
Uses CCG parses to derive word-combination and modification relations directly, avoiding extra tree constraints.
Combines prompt rewriting and attention guidance to control attributes, spatial relations, counts, and PP-attachment interpretations.
Works with Stable Diffusion and Sana, achieving the best compared scores for attribute binding and 2D spatial relations.
Significantly outperforms compared methods on resolving prepositional-phrase ambiguity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CCG Diffusion, a training-free method to control text-to-image generation using syntax to handle spatial relations and ambiguity, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: CCG Diffusion: Combinatory Categorial Grammar-Driven Compositional and Syntactically Disambiguated Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: CCG Diffusion uses Combinatory Categorial Grammar to guide text-to-image models toward syntactically correct attribute binding, spatial relations, counts, and interpretations of ambiguous prompts without training.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.
authors: Yifan Zhou, Ziyang Gong, Xiaojun Ye, Yifei Liu, Donggang Li, Xiaolong Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Xue Yang
bullets: Separates scene evidence from experience about reasoning strategies.
Uses 3DFusionMemory to build queryable spatial relations from current observations.
Provides a Spatial Skill Library and Spatial Cognition for selecting reusable procedures and resources.
Abstracts completed task trajectories into process records for consolidation across task blocks.
Improves over direct answers from the same backbone on four of five benchmarks and ties on one.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial reasoning framework with a vision-language backbone, queryable 3D spatial relations, and reasoning experience growth; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience
papers.tldr: SpatialBrain improves spatial reasoning by retaining experience about when and how to use spatial memories and tools while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation. Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models. Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features. Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.
authors: Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Jiabing Yang, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: WAMs lack explicit constraints on the 3D geometry needed for precise manipulation.
Pointwise alignment with 3D foundation-model features can help video representations but hurt compact action representations.
RGF aligns intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations to transfer geometry, correspondences, and scene-action dynamics.
The method is training-only and adds no explicit geometry branch or inference module.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show consistent gains across diverse manipulation settings and WAM paradigms.
papers.selection_reason: Relational geometry forcing for world action models targets manipulation, action-conditioned world dynamics, and geometry-aware multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Relational Geometry Forcing for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Relational Geometry Forcing improves world action models for precise robot manipulation by transferring 3D geometric structure through relational rather than pointwise feature alignment.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.
authors: Junjie Wang, Zhihao Yuan, Yunhan Tang, Sheng Xu, Jiaqi Mao, Xiaoyu Ye, Yueru Luo, Xu Yan, Chun-Mei Feng, Zhen Li
bullets: Targets spatial hallucinations caused by occlusion, perspective changes, and sparse viewpoints.
Identifies task-critical objects, lifts their zero-shot masks into a shared 3D frame, and compresses geometry into structured text.
Uses hierarchical GRPO to teach the VLM when to trust geometric tools and when to rely on visual evidence.
Think-Capture-4B improves over its backbone by 21.5, 7.9, and 5.2 points on MindCube-Tiny, MMSI-Bench positional, and ViewSpatial, respectively.
The system remains robust to coordinate and mask perturbations, fits on one 24 GB GPU, and runs as an asynchronous reasoner on an Agibot G1.
papers.selection_reason: Query-conditioned active 3D geometry acquisition for VLM spatial reasoning; strongly fits spatial intelligence and 3D-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Think-Capture improves VLM spatial reasoning by selectively acquiring and symbolically representing 3D geometry when it is useful, rather than densely processing every view.
