papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained instance-level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine-grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool-use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly-zoo/LocalAgent-main.
authors: Jiachen Guo, Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin, Ajian Liu
bullets: Targets instance-level consistency under viewpoint, illumination, and background changes, where differences may appear only in small regions.
The MLLM identifies suspicious areas and delegates them to lightweight Local Evidence Verifiers for detailed analysis.
LAC evaluates local appearance consistency, while LGC measures local geometric correspondence; their structured evidence guides the final decision.
An auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning strategy teaches the model when verification is necessary while prioritizing answer correctness.
Reports a 4.9% mean-accuracy gain over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline, with verifier use on only 12.13% of samples.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic MLLM framework combining global visual reasoning with local geometric/appearance verifiers for fine-grained instance consistency; fits VLM and spatial reasoning interests.
papers.title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
papers.tldr: LocalAgent combines global MLLM reasoning with targeted local appearance and geometric verification to improve fine-grained identification of whether two images show the same physical object.

papers.abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
authors: Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
bullets: The study tests classically simulated 4- and 8-qubit quantum circuits within LLaVA-OneVision.
Quantum layers are evaluated through insertion and replacement at four model locations on Visual Spatial Reasoning.
Insertion after the visual projector achieves 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 points above classical full fine-tuning.
Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer preserves 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Explores quantum-enhanced layers in a vision-language model for spatial reasoning, relevant to multimodal foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
papers.tldr: Quantum layers can improve or compress vision-language models, but their benefits depend strongly on where they are used and do not yet establish broad security gains.

papers.abstract: Few-shot image classification (FSIC) frequently suffers from visual ambiguity, where background clutter and RGB appearance similarities hinder discriminative feature matching in data-scarce settings. To mitigate this, we propose DAFIC, a geometry-guided framework that incorporates monocular depth into representation learning, episodic adaptation, and dense support-query matching. DAFIC first learns geometry-aware token representations through RGB-D self-supervised pre-training. Subsequently, the Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation (DGA) module uses depth-derived geometry to refine patch representations with geometry-enriched class context while suppressing background interference. Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching (SBiM) then performs bidirectional dense matching on the refined features, reducing sensitivity to spurious correspondences and background clutter. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show that DAFIC achieves strong performance against existing methods, with ablation and robustness analyses supporting the effectiveness of coupling geometry-conditioned episodic adaptation with bidirectional matching for few-shot visual recognition.
authors: Zhiqi Miao, Estefan\'ia Talavera, Weichuan Zhang, Jiapan Guo
bullets: Addresses visual ambiguity from background clutter and similar RGB appearances in data-scarce classification.
Uses RGB-D self-supervised pre-training to learn geometry-aware token representations.
Applies Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation to refine patch features with class context while suppressing background interference.
Uses Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching for more robust dense support-query correspondence.
Experiments on four benchmarks, including ablation and robustness analyses, support the framework’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Depth-guided geometric adaptation for few-shot classification incorporates geometric priors into visual representations.
papers.title: Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation for Few-shot Image Classification
papers.tldr: DAFIC improves few-shot image classification by using monocular depth to make feature adaptation and dense patch matching more geometry-aware and less sensitive to clutter.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models' embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model's capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon across instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
All models perform strongly on instruction following and spatial reasoning, but general manipulation is consistently weaker.
Astra leads instruction following and robustness; Opus leads spatial reasoning, manipulation, and overall performance in the tested configurations.
Harness design influences task success, planning cost, and execution time.
Astra case studies examine whole-body coordination, cross-embodiment manipulation, precision and dexterous manipulation, and real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-model evaluation of frontier multimodal LLMs for embodied robot control, including instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
papers.title: Frontier LLMs Enter the World of Robotics: A Cross-Model Evaluation on RoboColiseum
papers.tldr: A cross-model RoboColiseum evaluation finds that frontier multimodal LLMs understand robot tasks well but still struggle with reliable physical manipulation, with performance varying by model and harness design.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation. Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors. Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation. We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources. After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6. The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra's 73.68. Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios. These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.
bullets: Motivation: spatial perception links high-level reasoning with interaction in physical scenes.
Method: a unified pipeline combines robot manipulation recordings and diverse visual data, automatically annotates them, and converts them into verifiable grounding supervision.
Training: Qwen3.5-9B was fine-tuned on approximately 1.5 million generated samples.
Results: ACE-Brain-0.6 outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with average scores of 75.41 versus 73.68.
Scope: performance improves as successive data releases broaden grounding scenarios under a fixed fine-tuning setup.
papers.selection_reason: Scales verifiable visual grounding to strengthen spatial perception of physical foundation models for embodied operation.
papers.title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
papers.tldr: ACE-Brain-0.6 strengthens spatial grounding in an open 9B multimodal model by scaling diverse, verifiable supervision from robot and visual data.

papers.abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/
bullets: Covers 410 environments involving manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities.
Tests coordination of physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning under interdependent actions and execution feedback.
Provides EP-100, EP-Easy, EP-Hard, and EP-20 task selections spanning five suites and 16 task types.
Uses a shared protocol with observation/tool constraints, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent validity checks.
Evaluates task progress, intermediate constraints, plan revision, goal completion, rule compliance, and physical validity.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for foundation-model agents on long-horizon physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning in embodied environments.
papers.title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Embodied Playground benchmarks whether foundation-model agents can sustain reliable reasoning and physical action across long-horizon robotic tasks.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have substantially improved in language understanding, in-image text rendering, and visual composition, while their safety mechanisms do not always keep pace with these capabilities. This creates a cross-modal attack surface in which harmful semantics can remain inconspicuous in a serialized prompt yet emerge through image-level composition. We propose CollageAttack, an automated single-prompt black-box jailbreak that shifts semantic assembly into the image plane by combining context-relevant scenes, scene-grounded textual carriers, and spatially distributed text fragments. Experiments across multiple open-weight and commercial T2I models show that CollageAttack achieves attack success rates of up to 86.0%, outperforming the strongest baseline on the same model by 18.5 percentage points, while consistently producing more harmful outputs and preserving the source intent. We further find that distributed textual fragments can reconstruct the intended semantics after generation, with visual composition producing stronger communicative impact than text alone. These results reveal a cross-modal safety gap in which harmful meaning emerges from the composition of individually less explicit elements.
bullets: Targets a cross-modal safety gap: harmful semantics can be inconspicuous in serialized prompts but emerge through image composition.
Uses an automated, single-prompt, black-box attack combining context-relevant scenes, scene-grounded text carriers, and spatially distributed text fragments.
Evaluated across multiple open-weight and commercial T2I models, reaching attack success rates of up to 86.0%.
Distributed fragments can reconstruct the intended meaning after generation, with visual composition strengthening its communicative impact.
Shows that individually less explicit elements can combine into harmful outputs while preserving the source intent.
papers.selection_reason: CollageAttack investigates cross-modal alignment flaws in T2I models by exploiting spatial text composition, contributing to the understanding of spatial reasoning and safety in multimodal models.
papers.title: CollageAttack: Exploiting Cross-Modal Alignment Flaws in T2I Models through Spatial Text Composition
papers.tldr: CollageAttack jailbreaks text-to-image models by hiding harmful meaning across spatially composed visual and textual elements that evade prompt-level safety checks.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence has recently been assessed through generative tasks such as spatially grounded image editing, yet language-guided generation of spatially consistent views from partial multi-view observations remains underexplored. We introduce MindView, a benchmark for generative multi-view spatial intelligence with 1,500 samples from 513 scenes across three indoor datasets. Its seven tasks form two families: geometry-dominant tasks specify changes in camera position and orientation, while semantics-dominant tasks require inferring target viewpoints by grounding referred objects and interpreting spatial relations and reference-frame cues. Evaluation of eleven generators reveals substantial room for improvement on MindView. A paired context analysis further shows that all eleven generators obtain lower overall scores under the expanded context setting. These findings motivate us to investigate whether task-specific supervision can improve target-view generation and whether models can use additional multi-view evidence effectively. We therefore fine-tune BAGEL on the MindView training dataset, improving its overall score by 24.3 points and yielding gains across all seven MindView tasks. Beyond these generation gains, the fine-tuned model also yields higher scores on three spatial-understanding benchmarks without training on their annotations, suggesting that learning to generate spatially grounded views may benefit spatial understanding. To improve evidence utilization under expanded context, we propose MindCue, a training-free spatial evidence selector guided by a target-view hypothesis. MindCue reverses the drop in overall score under expanded context and outperforms the standard-context baseline. Overall, MindView provides a concrete testbed for generative multi-view spatial intelligence.
authors: Yanbo Wang, Siqi Luo, Siyu Zhang, Chenming Zhu, Wenzhao Zheng, Qian Yu, Juncheng Yan, Bin Fu, Tai Wang, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Jiwen Lu
bullets: Introduces 1,500 samples from 513 indoor scenes across seven tasks in geometry- and semantics-dominant families.
Evaluates 11 generators and finds substantial room for improvement, with performance declining when more context is provided.
Fine-tuning BAGEL on MindView improves its overall score by 24.3 points and benefits all seven tasks.
The fine-tuned model also improves three spatial-understanding benchmarks without using their annotations.
MindCue, a training-free target-view-guided evidence selector, reverses the expanded-context performance drop and surpasses the standard-context baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and a method (MindCue) for generative multi-view spatial intelligence, directly aligning with the spatial intelligence subtopic.
papers.title: MindView: Benchmarking Generative Multi-View Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: MindView benchmarks how well generative models infer and produce spatially consistent target views from partial multi-view observations, revealing major gaps and showing that task-specific fine-tuning and evidence selection help.

papers.abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
authors: Om Shivam Verma, Shaya Farahmand, Lingjun Zhao, Lu Gan
bullets: Addresses the limits of existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods, which require dense 3D voxel annotations and fixed semantic classes.
Represents scenes with sparse 3D Gaussians aligned to foundation models.
Uses Gaussians to communicate and fuse geometric and semantic information across agents.
Evaluated on Semantic-OPV2V, where it outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent methods.
Targets broader scene understanding for transportation safety and multi-robot efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary collaborative 3D scene understanding with foundation-aligned 3D Gaussians; fits spatial intelligence and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: CoGaussian: Open-Vocabulary Gaussian-based Collaborative 3D Scene Understanding
papers.tldr: CoGaussian enables multiple agents to collaboratively understand 3D scenes with open-vocabulary semantics using compact, foundation-model-aligned Gaussian representations.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning asks a model to work out where objects are in 3D space, how they relate to one another, and how they move. Agentic VLMs have recently brought large improvements on such tasks by letting the model actively gather evidence with 3D perception tools instead of answering in a single pass. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer: the gap between model and tools, where raw readings become usable conclusions, is left unfilled. We present S-Agent 2.0, a spatial reasoning agent that equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit, and we design the interface around one principle: help the VLM close the evidence loop: acquire scene evidence, remember it in a persistent scene memory, and interpret each reading in plain spatial language. This design keeps the full flexibility of a coding agent, and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools' geometry. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the toolkit improves a strong open-source model, Qwen3.8-27B, by +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, and a strong closed-source model, Gemini-3.8-Flash, by +11.2 and +9.6 points. With the open backbone S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized system SpatialClaw on the same backbone (62.6 and 74.5), and with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 against its 67.0 and 79.7. Both tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's shrinks far more on ReVSI, from +13.2 to +2.7, while ours stays at +9.6. S-Agent 2.0 also works across different general coding agent harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code.
authors: Rui Gong, Ruoyu Wang, Yalun Dai, Hao Li, Sidi Yang, Qihao Zhao, Hongyu Li, Zeyang Guan, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Kim-Hui Yap, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate 3D perception-tool readings and incorrect spatial reasoning conclusions.
Equips off-the-shelf coding agents with a command-line perception toolkit and an evidence-loop interface.
The interface supports evidence acquisition, persistent scene memory, and plain spatial-language interpretation while retaining coding-agent flexibility.
Improves Qwen3.8-27B by 13.9 and 20.5 points, and Gemini-3.8-Flash by 11.2 and 9.6 points on MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, respectively.
Works across coding-agent harnesses including Codex and Claude Code; gains decrease with stronger backbones but remain substantial.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial reasoning agent with 3D perception tools and scene memory directly targets spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: S-Agent 2.0: Spatial Reasoning with a General Coding Agent
papers.tldr: S-Agent 2.0 improves 3D spatial reasoning by helping general coding agents turn tool-derived evidence into grounded conclusions through persistent scene memory and plain-language interpretations.

papers.abstract: Geometric Relative Positional Encoding has become the primary mechanism for injecting spatial inductive biases into multi-view transformers. Existing designs condition attention on camera-level frustums or ray-marched depth, associating cross-view tokens through the sensor geometry. Such sensor-centric formulations, however, describe only where a token is observed from, leaving the rich surface geometry of the scene region depicted by the token. In this paper, we advocate a shift toward surface-aware positional encoding that explicitly grounds patch tokens in the geometry of physical surfaces. We introduce HRoPE, which represents the local geometry of each patch as a slanted 3D plane, following the slanted support-window assumption of classical multi-view stereo. We inject token-level, plane-induced homographies into attention as relative transformations. This equips the transformer with a geometric prior for rectifying perspective distortions and aligning patch features across viewpoints. Our encoding requires no ground-truth geometry: the plane parameters can be predicted end-to-end under a view-synthesis objective alone, or derived from foundation models. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV show that our best variant of HRoPE consistently outperforms the evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis. Extensive ablations and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed encoding. Please refer to our project page at: https://gaohchen.github.io/HRoPE
authors: Huachen Gao, Yang Yang, Xiaoqian Liang, Xingyu Chen, Youjia Zhang, Qi Zhang, Baorui Ma, Anpei Chen, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the limitation of sensor-centric positional encodings, which model camera rays but not the depicted surface geometry.
Represents each image patch as a locally slanted 3D plane and injects its induced homography as a relative attention transformation.
Plane parameters can be learned end-to-end from view synthesis alone or obtained from foundation models, without ground-truth geometry.
Experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV report consistent gains over evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis.
Ablations and analysis support the effectiveness of the surface-aware encoding.
papers.selection_reason: Surface-aware geometric positional encoding injecting spatial priors into multi-view transformers, relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: HRoPE: Homography Relative Positional Encoding
papers.tldr: HRoPE improves multi-view transformer geometry by using plane-induced homographies to align patch features across viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about fine-grained placement constraints, such as support and containment, is essential for realistic 3D scene creation. It remains a significant challenge for existing methods that rely on simplified object representations like oriented bounding box (OBB), which are blind to the detailed geometry. To address this limitation, we introduce GALA, a geometry-aware language model with explicit point cloud perception for controllable object placement. Our model performs autoregressively by predicting the 6D pose of one target object at a time conditioned on the scene context and placement instruction. We utilize a two-stage training strategy: the first stage aligns geometric and textual modalities through pretraining tasks, and the second stage fine-tunes the model for placement. To facilitate this task, we also curate a multi-source scene dataset covering diverse room types and fine-grained furniture arrangements, which will be open-sourced for community benefit. Experiments on our benchmark show our model significantly outperforms baselines without explicit geometric reasoning. We further develop a multi-stage plan-place-verify agent pipeline that uses the model for text-driven scene generation. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/
authors: Chucheng Xiang, Runze Wang, Zhi Deng, Ruchao Bao, Yuanwei Zhang, Yuxuan Xie, Hanliu Wang, Liangzhen Fei, Wenzheng Wu, Cheng Wan, Peifeng Li, Zhongyuan Liu, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets fine-grained constraints such as object support and containment, which simplified OBB representations may miss.
Autoregressively predicts one object’s 6D pose at a time from scene context and placement instructions.
Uses two-stage training to align geometric and textual modalities before placement fine-tuning.
Introduces a diverse multi-source scene dataset for room layouts and fine-grained furniture arrangements.
Also presents a plan-place-verify pipeline for text-driven scene generation; experiments report significant gains over methods without explicit geometric reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware language model with point cloud perception for controllable 3D object placement; directly targets spatial and geometric reasoning in multimodal models.
papers.title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Language Model for Controllable Object Arrangement
papers.tldr: GALA uses explicit point-cloud geometry and language instructions to predict controllable 6D object placements for realistic 3D scenes.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.
authors: Youwei Zhou, Bohan Hou, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lyu, Yifan Ye, Shilin Shan, Chen Guo, Jiaming Liu, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Shanghang Zhang, Jianfei Yang, Zhihe Lu
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation with a lightweight agent execution framework.
Probes depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding; the model demonstrates all three capabilities.
Tests five manipulation benchmarks across six capability dimensions, finding strengths alongside weaknesses in consequence-aware planning, precision, and coordinated motion.
Introduces LIBERO-GeoMotion, where GPT-6 Astra achieves 11.1% zero-shot success on geometry-constrained tasks; reported results also include 26.92% on RoboDojo and 76.0% on RoboTwin 2.0.
Real-world tests show simple zero-shot execution is feasible, but motion feasibility, physical safety, precise control, and inference latency remain deployment barriers.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation, probing depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile feedback.
papers.title: Large Multimodal Models for Direct Robot Control: GPT-6 as a Beginning
papers.tldr: GPT-6 Astra shows promising perception, learning, and tactile-feedback abilities for robot control, but struggles to convert semantic reasoning into precise, safe, and physically feasible manipulation.

papers.abstract: Existing feature lifting approaches for open-vocabulary segmentation rely on simple backprojection to assign features to primitives. In the case of 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction, the primitives overlap heavily, leading to suboptimal reconstructions, governed by many primitives per ray. Backprojection, however, reduces to a least-squares solvable problem, exactly when no two primitives share a ray. Motivated by this insight, we propose OV-Foam, which uses PowerFoam as the underlying representation. This representation uses a power-diagram to partition the scene, resulting in zero overlap between primitives and a substantial reduction in primitives per ray, which ultimately simplifies the lifting problem and allows for closer-to-optimal feature assignment. We show that the space partitioning primitives of OV-Foam reach near-optimal assignment, and our experiments demonstrate improved open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.
authors: Yousef Rajeh (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology), Alejandra Esparza Pelcastre (Universidad Panamericana), Ivan Viola (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology), Dominik Engel (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology)
bullets: Existing methods use backprojection, but overlapping Gaussian primitives make feature assignment difficult.
OV-Foam uses PowerFoam to partition scenes into non-overlapping primitives.
Fewer primitives per ray simplify lifting and bring it closer to the least-squares optimum.
The representation achieves near-optimal feature assignment and improves open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Improves open-vocabulary segmentation using 3D Gaussian Splatting with a PowerFoam representation to reduce overlap and optimize feature lifting. Fits 3D Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: OV-Foam: How 3D Representations Shape Semantic Feature Lifting
papers.tldr: OV-Foam improves open-vocabulary 3D feature lifting by replacing overlapping Gaussian primitives with non-overlapping power-diagram cells for more accurate feature assignment.

papers.abstract: Panoptic scene graph generation (PSGG) represents scene entities with segmentation masks and directed relations. Equirectangular projection (ERP) panoramas challenge PSGG through distortion, latitude-dependent pixel areas, and an artificial seam. We propose a two-stage spherical geometry-aware framework that fuses overlapping perspective-view predictions using observation reliability, spherical overlap, and angular proximity. Relation reasoning combines spherical-area-aware aggregation, weighted no-relation supervision, and dual-longitude score fusion. We also construct a dataset of 340 high-resolution panoramas with 10,571 nodes and 6,632 directed relations. Against corresponding baselines, spherical fusion improves PQ by 36.03% under matched views, while relation reasoning improves mR@50 by 11.20% under PredCls with ground-truth masks and object labels. The full framework improves mR@50 by 52.99% under SGDet with predicted panoptic segments. These results demonstrate the value of spherical geometry for panoramic PSGG.
authors: Zhe Wu, Xiaoyan Fei, Xinyi Jiang, Yanxu Wei, Junming Rao, Yihong Yan, Xuewei Li
bullets: Addresses ERP panorama challenges including distortion, latitude-dependent pixel areas, and seam artifacts.
Fuses overlapping perspective-view predictions using observation reliability, spherical overlap, and angular proximity.
Uses spherical-area-aware relation aggregation, weighted no-relation supervision, and dual-longitude score fusion.
Introduces a dataset of 340 high-resolution panoramas containing 10,571 nodes and 6,632 directed relations.
Reports improvements of 36.03% in PQ, 11.20% in mR@50 under PredCls, and 52.99% in mR@50 under SGDet.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses spatial distortion and relations in equirectangular panoramas for scene graph generation, introducing spherical geometry-aware methods. Fits Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: Spherical Geometry-Aware Panoptic Scene Graph Generation for Equirectangular Panoramas
papers.tldr: A spherical geometry-aware framework substantially improves panoptic scene graph generation for distorted equirectangular panoramas.

papers.abstract: Examining existing benchmarks for grounding in 3D VLMs reveals a pervasive "semantic leakage" in the evaluation and prompting protocols: a heavy reliance on bounding boxes as spatial prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes are highly informative of object categories, they introduce a shortcut for the models to neglect visual information during 3D VLM training. We demonstrate this with a "blind" LLM that, prompted only with the box coordinates, can perform surprisingly well. To further analyze this shortcut, we propose point-based grounding prompting - querying models with a single 3D point instead of a box. Under this protocol, the accuracy of the blind LLM drops from 36.4% to 18.0% on ScanNet's Nr3D, and similarly degrades for 3D VLMs (e.g. LL3DA). Building on this insight, we introduce P$^3$-VLM, a novel tri-pathway 3D VLM that supports point-based prompts and achieves 52.1% state-of-the-art accuracy on location-grounded captioning under this setting. To achieve this, we redesign the architecture while keeping it detector-free, scene-centric, and suitable for 3D GS inputs. P$^3$-VLM utilizes three complementary pathways (location-, task-, and context-aware), enabling strong reasoning about scenes without any bounding box dependencies. The key benefit of point-based learning is a consistent improvement across settings: P$^3$-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance under point-based grounding while also improving robustness, OOD generalization, and performance on ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA benchmarks, reflecting its reduced reliance on bounding-box shortcuts and resulting stronger visual-spatial reasoning.
authors: Anna-Maria Halacheva, Jan-Nico Zaech, Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Existing 3D VLM grounding benchmarks risk semantic leakage because bounding boxes reveal object-category information.
A blind LLM using only box coordinates reaches 36.4% on ScanNet Nr3D, but falls to 18.0% with a single 3D point, exposing the shortcut.
P$^3$-VLM is a detector-free, scene-centric, tri-pathway 3D VLM designed for point prompts and 3D Gaussian Splatting inputs.
Its location-, task-, and context-aware pathways achieve 52.1% accuracy on point-based location-grounded captioning.
Point-based learning also improves robustness, out-of-distribution generalization, and ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA performance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes P$^3$-VLM, a 3D VLM that uses point-based grounding to mitigate semantic leakage in bounding boxes, improving visual-spatial reasoning and robustness. Fits Spatial Intelligence (geometry-aware VLM) and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: P$^3$-VLM: A Point-based Alternative for Grounded 3D Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: P$^3$-VLM replaces shortcut-prone 3D bounding-box prompts with point-based grounding and achieves stronger visual-spatial reasoning without box dependencies.

papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and optical imagery provide complementary structural and appearance information for remote sensing object detection. However, substantial cross-modal discrepancies and indiscriminate channel interaction inevitably introduce redundant or conflicting features. Since different feature channels encode heterogeneous semantic information and contribute unequally to cross-modal fusion, selectively highlighting task-relevant channels while suppressing redundant ones is essential. To address this issue, we propose the Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network (CSIF-Net), which performs selective channel-level cross-modal interaction. CSIF-Net first employs a frequency decomposition module to construct frequency-aware SAR inputs, facilitating the separation of structural information from noise-related responses. It then models cross-modal channel relationships through a cross-attention channel selection module and dynamically partitions the features into shared and modality-specific components. Finally, a dual-branch fusion module performs cross-modal interaction and channel realignment for shared features while independently enhancing SAR-specific features, thereby exploiting complementary information and suppressing modality interference. Extensive experiments on the OGSOD 1.0 and M4-SAR datasets demonstrate that CSIF-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance in both horizontal and oriented object detection, surpassing the existing methods by 4.01% and 3.18% gains, respectively.
authors: Haojie Li, Yuanfei Huang, Lingfei Song, Jia Li, Lizhi Wang
bullets: Addresses redundant or conflicting features caused by indiscriminate interaction between optical and SAR channels.
Uses frequency decomposition to separate SAR structural information from noise-related responses.
Applies cross-attention channel selection to identify shared and modality-specific feature components.
Employs dual-branch fusion to realign shared features and enhance SAR-specific information independently.
Experiments on OGSOD 1.0 and M4-SAR show state-of-the-art horizontal and oriented detection, with reported gains of 4.01% and 3.18%.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a channel-selective fusion network for cross-modal (Optical-SAR) data, relevant to spatial intelligence and multimodal representation learning.
papers.title: Revealing Inter-Channel Modality Discriminability: Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network for Optical-SAR Object Detection
papers.tldr: CSIF-Net improves optical-SAR object detection by selectively interacting with informative channels while separating shared and modality-specific features to reduce cross-modal interference.

papers.abstract: Medical visual grounding requires models to align clinical descriptions with spatial evidence across heterogeneous imaging domains. However, existing multi-domain post-training strategies typically rely on fixed domain sampling and shared parameter updates, overlooking the need to adapt both which domains receive training and where their updates are applied. To address this issue, we propose PACE-MoE, a policy-guided framework that jointly performs adaptive domain sampling and domain-specific adaptation for medical visual grounding. PACE dynamically assesses the training value of each imaging domain from current-policy feedback and progressively adjusts domain coverage through domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing. Meanwhile, domain-specific LoRA adapters route updates to the corresponding imaging domains while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder. This coordinated design aligns training-data allocation with parameter adaptation without modifying the original reward formulation or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Experiments across seven medical imaging domains show that PACE-MoE consistently improves grounding performance over fixed-domain training, achieving a 3.64% relative improvement in mean box IoU over the Vanilla baseline. Under matched domain-specific adapter architectures, adaptive sampling alone further improves mean box IoU by 2.07%, demonstrating the benefit of policy-guided domain allocation. These results establish coordinated data-parameter routing as an effective strategy for multi-domain medical visual grounding.
authors: Zhenxuan Wang, Jisheng Dang, Ronghao Lin, Bimei Wang, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Bin Hu, Qi Tian, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses fixed domain sampling and shared updates in heterogeneous medical imaging.
Uses policy feedback to adapt domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing.
Routes domain-specific LoRA updates while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder.
Across seven imaging domains, improves mean box IoU by 3.64% relative to the Vanilla baseline.
Adaptive sampling alone yields a further 2.07% mean box IoU improvement under matched adapters.
papers.selection_reason: Policy-guided domain sampling and domain-specific LoRA for medical visual grounding; relevant to spatial multimodal grounding and continual multi-domain adaptation.
papers.title: PACE-MoE: Adaptive Domain Sampling and Domain-Specific LoRA for Medical Visual Grounding
papers.tldr: PACE-MoE improves multi-domain medical visual grounding by jointly adapting which imaging domains are trained and where parameter updates are applied.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.
authors: Jing Wang, Yitong Yang, Hao Dou, Yaomin Wu, Shuting He, Tingfei Shen, Jia Wu, Jiaqi Li, Yinglin Wang
bullets: Covers plane, solid, analytic, function, and vector geometry from Chinese middle- and high-school exams.
Includes 12,235 figures across diverse response formats, with each item pairing LaTeX question-answer content, an RGB image, and TikZ code.
Evaluates image-to-TikZ reconstruction and multimodal geometry reasoning in open- and closed-source models.
Finds persistent challenges in fine-grained geometric structure and image-text alignment.
Human-curated TikZ oracle experiments provide complementary geometric cues but do not assess an end-to-end conversion pipeline.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-centric multimodal benchmark probing spatial and geometric reasoning in MLLMs.
papers.title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ
papers.tldr: TriGeoBench is a 7,000-question benchmark for testing multimodal models’ geometric reasoning using questions, images, and structure-preserving TikZ representations.

papers.abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg
authors: Koushik Swarna, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Lam Ngo, Wenxuan Li, Jiancheng Yang, Alan Yuille, Zongwei Zhou
bullets: Addresses broken or fragmented anatomical segmentations, especially for difficult structures.
Learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities and anatomical descriptions, without using medical images during correction.
Scales from 50 to 377 anatomical classes using existing predictions, and transfers across CT and MRI without retraining.
Across 13 public benchmarks, reported Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder CT cases and 10% for individual prostate MRI cases.
Corrected labels improve downstream segmentation, including one model’s Dice increase from 57.1% to 67.5%, and support annotation of 45,000 CT scans.
papers.selection_reason: Text-conditioned diffusion shape prior scales across anatomical classes and modalities; relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial/geometric priors.
papers.title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
papers.tldr: DART uses text-guided diffusion to share anatomical shape knowledge across classes and imaging modalities, correcting implausible segmentation predictions without new voxel-level training annotations.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.
authors: Rohit Saxena, Alessandro Suglia, Marek Rei, Pasquale Minervini
bullets: Analyzes 19 models from four families across eight benchmarks and nine evaluation splits.
Finds 375 inverse-scaling subtask–model-pair combinations involving 4,342 queries where smaller models succeed and larger ones fail.
The effect replicates across independently developed architectures and appears in 13 subtasks spanning multiple model families.
Multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge are most affected; diagram understanding is comparatively resistant.
Results support task-aware model selection rather than assuming the largest model is always best.
papers.selection_reason: Studies inverse scaling in vision-language model families across multimodal benchmarks including spatial-reasoning subtasks.
papers.title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Larger vision-language models can perform worse than smaller ones on specific multimodal subtasks, so scaling does not guarantee uniform improvement.

papers.abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.
authors: Yuchi Wang, Rongyao Fang, Weihao Yu, Xilin Wei, Tiancheng Gu, Dingkang Yang, Hang Zhang, Dayiheng Liu, Hongsheng Li, Shuai Bai
bullets: Introduces 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks combining natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages.
Requires agents to interpret references, render webpages, visually inspect outputs, and iteratively refine them.
Evaluates open-ended artifacts with independently verifiable keypoints plus programmatic and vision-language-model judges.
Across nine frontier MLLMs, the strongest system scores 52.12/100, showing the task remains challenging.
papers.selection_reason: A benchmark for visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation, which requires models to understand and utilize spatial relationships and layouts from reference images.
papers.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
papers.tldr: RefCraft benchmarks how well AI agents can build webpages by selectively using multiple visual references, revealing substantial limitations in current models.

papers.abstract: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.
bullets: Targets implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract information inferred at a glance.
Uses diverse visual inputs with a structured taxonomy and human-written prompts.
Humans achieve 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest reported model reaches 53.6%.
Agentic visual manipulation narrows the gap but does not eliminate it.
Highlights intuitive reasoning as an under-tested capability for multimodal models.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning in MLLMs including spatial reasoning; fits multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Humanity's Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models
papers.tldr: HSS benchmarks intuitive visual reasoning in images and videos, revealing a large gap between human and frontier multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework. Project page: https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream-page/
authors: Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yu-Lun Liu, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited novelty and simplicity of VLM-generated 3D assets and the API constraints of existing procedural systems.
Uses Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation to combine existing procedural algorithms with novel, photorealistic, seed-diverse assets.
Introduces an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline with semantic scene planning and deterministic frustum-guided grid placement.
Supports precise object placement, procedural population, animation, editability, and large-scale world construction.
Evaluations across 100 object and 20 scene tasks show improvements on four perceptual metrics, supported by diversity, ablation, and human-preference analyses.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-driven procedural 3D world generation with spatial scene planning, relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation
papers.tldr: InfiniDream is a VLM-driven framework for generating open-ended, photorealistic, editable 3D assets and large-scale worlds through procedural methods.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
authors: Zhaoxi Zhang, Hao Liang, Linxuan Wu, Yiming Wu, Yifu Yuan, Kun Liang, Chenming Tang, Meiyi Qiang, Wentao Zhang, Weikang Li
bullets: Evaluates active 3D mapping across 80 indoor scenes with 3,140 target objects.
Agents control a camera using object inventories, RGB observations, camera calibration, and poses.
Success requires viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction.
The strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches a 41.71% mean overlap score; 47.23% of targets exceed IoU 0.5, but only 3.25% exceed IoU 0.9.
Results show a gap between recovering coarse layouts and producing complete, precise metric maps.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for VLM agents performing active 3D scene exploration and metric mapping; directly targets spatial intelligence and embodied navigation.
papers.title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?
papers.tldr: SpatialScout benchmarks whether VLM agents can actively explore indoor 3D scenes and build accurate, complete object-level metric maps.

papers.abstract: Image-based spatial reasoning requires perception, decomposition, and inference, but the stage that limits accuracy can change during training. Answer-level rewards neither localize failures to individual stages nor provide discriminative group-relative feedback when all rollouts receive the same reward. Process supervision provides intermediate feedback, but fixed weights cannot adapt reward allocation to these changing bottlenecks. To address this gap, we propose CALIPER, an adaptive process-reward framework supported by SpatialTrace, a corpus of stage-decomposed spatial reasoning traces. CALIPER jointly estimates the associations between stage-wise reference coverage and answer correctness through within-group ridge regression, using these associations as utility proxies to gradually update reward weights. The resulting process reward supervises all rollout groups, including uniformly failing ones. Because utility estimates can become unreliable when answer-discriminative groups are scarce, a closed-loop harness monitors estimator reliability and validation performance to guide checkpoint rollback, rollout diversification, and early stopping. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks and three backbones show that CALIPER achieves the highest mean under both one-shot and harness training, with consistent gains over fixed allocation across RL optimizers. Further analyses confirm the benefits of adaptive reward allocation and harness control, with favorable scaling in model/data size.
bullets: Fixed answer-level rewards cannot localize failures, while fixed process-reward weights cannot adapt to changing bottlenecks.
CALIPER uses within-group ridge regression to estimate how stage-wise reference coverage relates to answer correctness and update reward weights.
It provides process supervision even when all rollout groups fail uniformly.
A closed-loop harness monitors estimator reliability and validation performance to trigger rollback, rollout diversification, or early stopping.
Experiments across eight benchmarks and three backbones report the highest mean performance for both one-shot and harness training, with consistent gains over fixed allocation.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses image-based spatial reasoning with a Policy-Adaptive Credit Assignment framework. The method involves stage-wise decomposition and utility estimation, which is relevant to spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.
papers.title: Policy-Adaptive Credit Assignment for Spatial Reasoning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: CALIPER adaptively reallocates process-level rewards to the spatial-reasoning stages most associated with answer correctness, improving training across benchmarks and backbones.

papers.abstract: Few-shot segmentation (FSS) aims to segment target objects with limited annotated examples. Recent studies have begun to explore large foundation models to improve generalization for this task. In particular, SAM 3 provides strong visual representations and supports text-guided segmentation. However, its performance remains limited in specialized domains, where semantic prompts and visual representations are often poorly aligned. To address this challenge, we propose ViTA-SAM, a framework built upon SAM 3 that integrates visual memory and textual features through cross-modal alignment. Specifically, we construct a visual memory module that encodes support features together with their corresponding masks, providing support-aware visual guidance for query prediction. In parallel, we leverage the text encoder of SAM 3 to extract semantic features as complementary priors. To bridge the gap between semantic and visual representations, we introduce a cross-modal alignment module that conditions textual features on memory-enhanced visual representations, yielding more consistent and visually grounded predictions. In addition, we propose a pseudo-label refinement strategy that updates the memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive representation learning. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ViTA-SAM achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods, outperforming the strongest competing method by over 5% in average mIoU.
authors: Tianqi Wei, Zhi Chen, Xin Yu, Scott Chapman, Zi Huang
bullets: Addresses poor alignment between semantic prompts and visual representations in specialized domains.
Stores support features and masks in a visual memory module to guide query segmentation.
Uses SAM 3 text features as complementary semantic priors and aligns them with memory-enhanced visual features.
Refines pseudo-labels to update memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive learning.
Outperforms the strongest competing method by over 5% average mIoU across multiple benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Enhances few-shot segmentation by aligning visual memory and textual features of a foundation model (SAM), improving spatial understanding and cross-modal reasoning.
papers.title: Visual Memory and Textual Alignment for Cross-Modal Few-Shot Segmentation
papers.tldr: ViTA-SAM improves specialized-domain few-shot segmentation by aligning SAM 3’s visual memory and text features for more grounded predictions.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.
authors: Jinbae Seo, Hyeongjun Kwon, Jiyoung Lee, Hyunsung Jang, Namkoo Ha, Jungin Park, Kwanghoon Sohn
bullets: Addresses the problem that lengthy reasoning can dilute relevant visual evidence with broad scene descriptions and peripheral details.
Uses three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation from the compressed context.
Trains the framework with multi-stage GRPO and progressive rewards for structured outputs, information reduction, relevance preservation, and localization accuracy.
Evaluated on six multimodal grounding benchmarks, where it achieves substantial zero-shot performance gains.
Scope: focuses on retaining useful extended reasoning while distilling it for precise grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement-learning framework for multimodal grounding via reasoning compression in MLLMs, directly relevant to multimodal and spatial localization.
papers.title: Think, Compress, Answer: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Grounding via Reasoning Compression
papers.tldr: TCA improves multimodal grounding by compressing extended reasoning into concise, target-specific context before generating localization answers.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are asked to report what they see: to count objects, box them, parse a screen or pick a click target (GUI grounding). We argue that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. In a dense scene with 173 shapes, GPT-6.1 lists 173 records that match every shape, yet the counts it states in the same response sum to 188. From Seeing to Reporting (FSR) is a theory of visual reporting and a set of inference-time procedures that improve the reports of frozen VLMs. It models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers, linked by task-compatible matching. The chain gives exact relations for deleting records, averaging their coordinates and switching readouts, and it splits the error of one answer chosen among several calls into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices. These relations guide procedures for counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding that use the task specification and a shipped configuration, without requiring labels from the target task. On 50 dense synthetic scenes, a one-call reporting-and-decoding protocol cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a GUI-grounding tier that combines three models lowers the miss rate from 13.67% for GPT-6.1's two-stage zoom to 9.33%, against 12.67% for three such zooms combined by a cluster vote at about the same cost. A plain vote over the same three models misses 12.33%: the other models supply the candidates, and selecting among them turns those candidates into fewer misses. We release the protocols, the stored responses and the analysis code.
authors: Junzhe Shi, Yuan Gan, Shida Jiang
bullets: Frames reporting as a chain from model responses to decoded records, sets, and final task answers.
Uses task-compatible matching to identify missing candidates, lost representatives, and wrong selections.
Requires no target-task labels, relying on the task specification and a shipped configuration.
Reduces per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 on 50 dense synthetic scenes.
On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a three-model grounding tier lowers miss rate to 9.33%, outperforming the reported comparison protocols at similar cost.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time procedures for reliable visual set generation in VLMs; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial/GUI grounding.
papers.title: From Seeing to Reporting: A Theory of Reliable Visual Set Generation in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: FSR treats visual reporting as part of VLM reasoning and improves counting, detection, parsing, and GUI grounding through task-aware inference-time procedures for frozen models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how language models represent text---especially on tasks where visualization would help, like geometry questions posed in words. We distinguish weak multimodality (the model can answer questions about an input image) from strong multimodality (the model's text representations themselves become vision-aligned, improving performance on text-only tasks with latent visual structure). To test for strong multimodality, we construct a task of shape-counting problems with paired equivalent text and image specifications. This task is trivial when the image is provided, but requires visualization when specified in text as line coordinates. We compare instruction-tuned Qwen-2.5 and Mistral models against their vision-aligned counterparts on the text variant of the task. We find that the multimodal models do no better in this setting, despite strong performance on the image version of the task. Probing experiments corroborate this: vision-aligned decoder embeddings carry no more visual structure than their text-only counterparts. Finally, we provide an optimization objective that distills in-context visual embeddings into text embeddings. This alignment induces gains on the text variant of the task without explicit task supervision, even on samples more complex than seen during alignment. This suggests that VQA-style alignment leaves available cross-modal transfer untapped.
authors: Shashwat Singh, He He, Tal Linzen
bullets: The paper distinguishes weak multimodality—answering questions about images—from strong multimodality, where text representations become vision-aligned.
On paired shape-counting tasks, multimodal models perform no better than text-only models when given coordinate-based text, despite performing well with images.
Probing shows that vision-aligned decoder embeddings contain no more visual structure than embeddings from text-only models.
A self-distillation objective aligns in-context visual and text embeddings without explicit task supervision.
This alignment improves text-based shape counting, including examples more complex than those used during alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Examines vision-language models' cross-modal transfer and spatial/geometric reasoning, fitting multimodal LLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help
papers.tldr: VQA-style vision-language alignment does not make text representations visually grounded, but self-distilling visual embeddings into text representations improves reasoning over text with latent visual structure.

papers.abstract: Human memories are organized in a way that connects events with their corresponding spatial contexts. An AI assistant should also be able to memorize and recall the nexus of events and spaces. Thus we introduce SENRI, a task that studies this space--event connection in long, continuous real-life egocentric video. It contains six task types in two directions: Event$\rightarrow$Space, which recovers spatial knowledge from event cues, and Space$\rightarrow$Event, which retrieves events from regions and trajectories. To evaluate this, we build SENRI-Bench, containing 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions over 10 uninterrupted self-recorded videos with around 25.3 hours of content.
