Also, we evaluate three typical long video understanding paradigms: direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory. The task remains challenging across all three paradigms, highlighting substantial room for improvement. Then we show two representative failure modes of existing memory methods and address these evidence gaps with SENRI-Agent, a controller that uses Target-Guided Visual Check (TGVC) to propose local visual check tasks for parallel verifiers and integrate the reports into a working memory to help with reasoning. Built upon existing memory systems, SENRI-Agent improves the performance of existing baselines without modifying their stored memories. We hope SENRI will provide valuable insights into how real-life egocentric understanding should be evaluated, reveal the gaps in existing approaches, and offer a possible direction for improvement.
authors: Kehan Lan, Kaining Ying, Henghui Ding, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Covers six tasks in two directions: inferring spaces from events and retrieving events from spaces or trajectories.
SENRI-Bench contains 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions from about 25.3 hours of uninterrupted self-recorded video.
Evaluates direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory; all remain challenging.
SENRI-Agent uses Target-Guided Visual Check with parallel verifiers and working memory to address evidence gaps.
Improves existing memory-system baselines without changing their stored memories.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and method for space-event reasoning in egocentric video, directly relevant to embodied perception and learning from human video, with spatial reasoning components.
papers.title: SENRI: Understanding the Space-Event Nexus in Real-Life Videos
papers.tldr: SENRI introduces a benchmark and agent for testing and improving how AI connects events with spatial contexts in long egocentric videos.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}
authors: Junwei Wen, Deshui Miao, Guangming Lu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xin Li, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the video reference gap between language-based reasoning and visual evidence across frames.
Builds a chronological chain of video primitives linking entity references with temporal support and spatial evidence.
Uses selected primitives to generate box prompts and temporal guidance for video mask prediction.
Trains the representation with supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning.
Shows strong performance across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Spatiotemporally grounded video reasoning segmentation with video CoT; relevant to video understanding, multimodal LLMs, and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Think Visually Across Space and Time: Grounded Reasoning for Video Segmentation
papers.tldr: TCoVP grounds video reasoning in timestamped spatial and temporal evidence to improve segmentation of implicitly described targets.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model's original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.
authors: Chaoran Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Chenglin Cui, Yazhe Wan, Taein Kwon, Changjae Oh
bullets: Directly matching VLA and 3D foundation-model features can cause severe rank collapse.
The proposed method aligns pair-wise relationships rather than enforcing point-wise feature equality.
It integrates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning without compromising original expressivity.
Experiments across public benchmarks, a new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation show robust spatial understanding across diverse tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Relational spatial alignment to inject 3D awareness into VLA models; directly relevant to VLA and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Relational Spatial Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: A relational alignment method injects 3D spatial awareness into vision-language-action models while preserving their representational expressivity.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in 2D visual understanding tasks, yet the passive view-centric perception paradigm limits their capacity for 3D spatial reasoning. Such reasoning often requires actively acquiring spatial evidence beyond the currently visible views, such as camera poses and cross-view spatial relationships, to infer 3D relationships that are not explicitly represented in 2D images. However, existing methods either lack active exploration or merely provide additional views during inference, without explicitly acquiring such spatial evidence beyond 2D images. In this paper, we propose View-to-World (V2W), an active exploration framework that enables VLMs to actively explore 3D worlds and lifts VLMs from passive view-centric perception to active world-centric spatial reasoning. Given a spatial reasoning task with multi-view images, V2W first reconstructs an explicit 3D world with geometry, camera poses, and language-grounded semantics, and exposes it to VLMs through visual and linguistic interfaces. Through multi-turn interaction with these interfaces, VLMs iteratively acquire spatial evidence from the constructed 3D world, enabling active world-centric spatial reasoning. V2W can be integrated with existing VLMs in a training-free manner and can be further enhanced by optimizing the exploration policy via reinforcement learning. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks demonstrate that V2W substantially improves VLM baselines in the training-free setting and achieves state-of-the-art performance with the learned exploration policy, highlighting the importance of active exploration for spatial intelligence. Project page: \url{https://fangzhou2000.github.io/projects/v2w}.
authors: Qijian Tian, Jiayu Ying, Ke Fan, Lizhuang Ma, Xin Tan
bullets: Addresses the limits of view-centric VLMs for 3D spatial reasoning, where key cross-view relationships are not explicit in individual images.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world from multi-view images and provides visual and linguistic interfaces for interactive exploration.
Supports training-free integration with existing VLMs, with optional reinforcement learning to optimize exploration policies.
Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks show substantial gains over VLM baselines and state-of-the-art performance with learned exploration.
Scope: performance depends on the quality of the reconstructed 3D world and applies to tasks with multi-view images.
papers.selection_reason: Active 3D world exploration for VLM spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: From Views to Worlds: Active Exploration over 3D Worlds for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: V2W turns VLMs from passive image viewers into active 3D-world explorers by letting them gather spatial evidence through reconstructed geometry, camera poses, and language-grounded semantics.

papers.abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu, Kezhi Mao
bullets: Commodity RGB-D sensors produce missing, distorted, or incorrect geometry, causing a sharp performance drop in modern 3D policies.
NISE learns trustworthy spatial features using Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision with calibrated multi-view depth.
Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention propagates position uncertainty instead of treating corrupted 3D tokens as exact.
Simulated sensor-corruption benchmarks and real-robot tasks with transparent and reflective objects show improved noise robustness.
The approach targets deployment with imperfect commodity RGB-D sensors, beyond clean-depth evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial encoding for 3D manipulation policies robust to depth corruption; relevant to VLA, manipulation, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding for 3D Manipulation Policies under Depth Corruption
papers.tldr: NISE improves the robustness of 3D manipulation policies to realistic RGB-D depth corruption without sacrificing clean-depth performance.

papers.abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.
authors: unsu Kim, Naeun Kim, Dongyoon Han, Seungryul Baek
bullets: Targets ambiguous references to adjacent body parts, garments, and visually similar motions.
Uses per-avatar semantic and motion memories to connect language with persistent Gaussian regions and joint trajectories.
An MLLM selects regions by appearance, relation, or function, while composable operators identify matching motion intervals.
Selections are traceable and extensible through category choices and operator programs.
On three human-annotated benchmarks, it outperforms baselines in part, 3D, and 4D referring segmentation, with minutes of per-avatar setup.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free MLLM-based spatial and temporal querying of 3D avatars; relevant to spatial intelligence and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
papers.tldr: HumanSkill-4D enables training-free language-based selection of avatar regions and motion intervals by combining multimodal reasoning with geometric operations.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Han Zhang, Yixuan Lin, Yuyang Hou, Bin Wu, Ruike Cao, Li Xiao, Yinsheng Li
bullets: Introduces UNICORNS, a benchmark with 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans and four evidence conditions.
Tests referential ambiguity, insufficient evidence, false presuppositions, and related challenges using eight categories plus answerable controls.
Six open-source 3D-LLMs show a large reliability gap: 61.22% on controls versus 40.94% on challenge categories for the strongest zero-shot model.
Proposes HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method using task, obligation, and supervised control-replay rewards.
HORN achieves 75.1 ± 1.0% on challenges and 77.2 ± 0.8% overall, without degrading control accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and post-training for evidence-grounded 3D-LLM reasoning; directly targets 3D foundation models and spatial multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
papers.tldr: UNICORNS reveals that 3D-LLMs often fail to ground answers in available 3D evidence, while HORN substantially improves reliable reasoning without hurting answerable-question performance.

papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
authors: Savitha Sam Abraham, Marjan Alirezaie, Hossein Rahnama
bullets: Reframes T2I evaluation as constraint satisfaction over objects, attributes, and relations.
Tests nine constraint classes, including logical operators such as ∀, ∃, counting, and implication, across four T2I models.
Performance drops from 98% on single-object attributes to 53% on complex conditional multi-object relations.
Compositional generalization declines from 84% for single constraints to 20% for multiple constraints; unsatisfiable prompts are recognized correctly only 23% of the time by the best model.
On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.88–0.98 against human judgments.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LogicVal, a benchmark for evaluating logical and spatial reasoning in Text-to-Image models using constraint satisfaction.
papers.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: LogicVal evaluates text-to-image models as logical constraint solvers, revealing major weaknesses in complex, multi-constraint, and unsatisfiable prompts.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires distinguishing subtle differences in local attributes and spatial relations, yet remains challenging for existing vision-language models. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) offer a new opportunity through generation pathways that preserve rich visual information complementary to understanding. However, existing generation-assisted understanding methods mainly rely on generative supervision or explicit generation and have not systematically explored direct use of native generation-side representations. To address this gap, we systematically analyze what generation-side representations offer for fine-grained understanding, finding that they are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, capture task-relevant changes missed by understanding-side representations, and depend on correct spatial organization for this advantage. Guided by these findings, we design GAFU, a post-training framework that unlocks native generation-side information for fine-grained understanding. It compresses generation-side visual representations into compact \(G\) tokens that preserve fine-grained visual details, enabling task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway. Experiments show that GAFU consistently outperforms SFT baselines trained on the same data across diverse visual understanding tasks and UMM architectures, with maximum relative improvements of 20.00\%, 17.94\%, and 8.62\% on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and VSR-Bench, respectively. Overall, GAFU converts complementary information from the generation pathway into gains in fine-grained visual understanding, providing an effective path toward synergy between generation and understanding in UMMs.
authors: Tengju Ru, Weitong Lian, Zecong Tang, Zhiheng Liu, Lingyi Meng, Haoran Li, Kaixuan Wang, Bohao Li, Xihui Liu
bullets: Fine-grained understanding of subtle attributes and spatial relations remains difficult for vision-language models.
Generation-side representations are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, but their benefit depends on correct spatial organization.
GAFU compresses these representations into compact G tokens that preserve visual detail and support task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway.
Across multiple tasks and UMM architectures, GAFU outperforms same-data SFT baselines, with reported maximum relative gains of 20.00%, 17.94%, and 8.62%.
The approach is evaluated within unified multimodal models and focuses on improving fine-grained visual understanding through generation-understanding synergy.
papers.selection_reason: Unlocks generation-side representations for fine-grained spatial understanding in unified multimodal models.
papers.title: What Generation Knows: Unlocking Fine-Grained Understanding in Unified Multimodal Models
papers.tldr: GAFU harnesses native generation-side representations in unified multimodal models to improve fine-grained visual understanding.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.
authors: Xinyu Fang, Yuchi Wang, Weihao Yu, Rongyao Fang, Zhaohai Li, Zhixun Li, Tiancheng Gu, Xilin Wei, Yuhang Zang, Hongsheng Li, Dahua Lin, Guofeng Zhang, Shuai Bai, Zhibo Yang, Dayiheng Liu
bullets: Introduces 223 open-ended tasks across architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization.
Uses text, image, video, and structured specifications as task inputs.
Evaluates rendered Blender projects from multiple viewpoints with 2,651 binary rubrics and holistic visual-quality scores.
Among 13 frontier models, GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest reported fused score, followed by Opus-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol.
Results show broad instruction understanding but substantial weaknesses in structural accuracy and 3D spatial consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM agents on 3D creation, emphasizing spatial coherence; fits spatial intelligence and 3D foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References
papers.tldr: BlenderWorld benchmarks multimodal agents on realistic Blender-based 3D creation and finds that models still struggle with fine-grained spatial coherence and faithful reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the capacity to represent and reason about physical space, underlies embodied perception and real-world visual understanding. Existing benchmarks probe it through spatial relations, perspective-taking, and mental modeling. What remains underexamined is whether a model can maintain a coherent scene representation across views, since pairwise comparison alone cannot reveal which view departs from the truth. We thus introduce Same Space or Not (SSoN), a benchmark of cross-view contradiction resolution comprising 1,000 questions from seven indoor scene sources and six categories of controlled 3D edits. Each question presents three views of an unchanged scene and one view of an edited variant. Models must identify the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction without a designated trusted reference or a marked target. Our pipeline iteratively translates human review into generation constraints. Automated checks and exhaustive human validation screen out both trivial visual shortcuts and questions lacking sufficient evidence for a unique answer. Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, compared with 39.7% for the strongest vision-language models (VLMs), falling to 34.9% when a valid visual explanation is also required. We investigate prompting, camera information, and 3D reconstruction as interventions. On a 100-question intervention set with a 24% baseline, prompting and 3D reconstruction remain below 50% answer accuracy, except when ground-truth camera information is supplied, which reaches 61% answer accuracy but only 48% True solve accuracy. On a held-out 201-question test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 21.89% accuracy, 33.33% after answer-only fine-tuning, and 41.79% after fine-tuning on both rationales and answers. These results identify cross-view contradiction resolution as a substantial weakness of current VLMs that can be partly addressed by targeted supervision.
authors: Huizi Cao, Guanyu Xu, Zhixuan Liang, Ming Yin, Jiuxiang Gu, Manling Li, Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu
bullets: Introduces a 1,000-question benchmark spanning seven indoor-scene sources and six controlled 3D-edit categories.
Requires identifying an inconsistent view among four without a trusted reference, marked target, or reliance on trivial visual cues.
Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, versus 39.7% for the strongest tested VLMs and 34.9% when valid explanations are required.
Prompting and 3D reconstruction generally remain below 50% accuracy; ground-truth camera information improves answer accuracy to 61% but true solving to 48%.
On a held-out test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves from 21.89% to 41.79% with fine-tuning on both answers and rationales.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for cross-view spatial reasoning directly targets spatial intelligence in VLMs.
papers.title: Same Space or Not: Benchmarking Spatial Intelligence Through Cross-View Contradictions
papers.tldr: SSoN reveals that current vision-language models struggle to detect and explain contradictions across views of the same 3D scene, though targeted rationale-and-answer supervision improves performance.

papers.abstract: Enterprises run schema-guided structured field extraction on documents with frontier multimodal models, and accuracy keeps improving as new models and systems arrive. Two things have not kept pace: the evidence for each extracted value, meaning the location of the document it was read from, and how far to trust the value and that evidence. Neither is a component of most extraction systems today, so we build them as a framework that attaches to an existing extractor and leaves it untouched. We present VERDICT, a plug-in framework that uses a small Vision--Language Model (VLM) to ground/localize the evidence once per document over a fixed external extractor's output, then calibrates value and evidence confidence. Fine-tuning the VLM for evidence localization substantially improves visual evidence quality and, more importantly, expands VERDICT's selective-prediction operating range. At a strict confidence threshold $0.80$, VERDICT with the fine-tuned VLM gives usable precision--coverage trade-offs for both value and evidence confidence across the in-distribution and out of distribution datasets, whereas the frozen setting often collapses to little or no coverage. Running an open-weight VLM for localization rather than a closed API makes its internal states available to the calibrator, and they are worth more than output log-probabilities: in-distribution AUROC rises from $0.730$ to $0.914$ for value confidence and from $0.681$ to $0.906$ for evidence confidence. This advantage does not survive a distribution shift. We show that the signal is displaced rather than destroyed, and that labeling roughly $120$ fields from the target dataset takes evidence confidence from $0.641$ to $0.905$ on one dataset and from $0.675$ to $0.829$ on the other.
authors: Harikrishnan P M, Goutham Vignesh, Siva Prasad, Zishan Ahmad, Mahesh Basveshwar Deshmukhe, Varun V, Rohit Agrawal, Vishal Vaddina
bullets: A small VLM localizes evidence for each extracted field and calibrates confidence in both the value and its supporting evidence.
Fine-tuning the VLM improves evidence quality and expands selective-prediction coverage at strict confidence thresholds.
Open-weight VLM internal states substantially outperform output log-probabilities for in-distribution confidence estimation.
This advantage weakens under distribution shift, but target-domain labeling of roughly 120 fields restores evidence-confidence quality.
The framework is evaluated across in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, with scope limited by reduced cross-distribution calibration transfer.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based evidence localization in document layouts is a multimodal spatial grounding contribution.
papers.title: VERDICT: Visual Extraction-Result Decoder with Integrated Confidence and Traceable Evidence
papers.tldr: VERDICT adds calibrated value confidence and traceable visual evidence to existing document extractors without modifying them.

papers.abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.
authors: Joshua Williamson, Niall Jeffrey, Lorne Whiteway
bullets: Targets spherical physical-science datasets with no preferred position or orientation, where ignoring symmetry can require costly simulations.
Implements a gauge-equivariant architecture on HEALPix using steerable filters, parallel transport, and spin-weighted features.
Provides provably exact SO(3) equivariance under a band-limit, with full-network invariance errors at the percent level or lower.
Achieves strong benchmark performance in dense gradient regression, competitive CMB foreground removal and denoising, and tighter cosmological-lensing SBI posteriors at matched simulation counts.
Scope: equivariance and exactness depend on the band-limit, while full-network invariance is controlled by hyperparameters.
papers.selection_reason: Develops an SO(3)-equivariant CNN for spherical data, explicitly incorporating geometric symmetry to avoid relearning invariance, directly relevant to spatial intelligence and geometric reasoning.
papers.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
papers.tldr: An SO(3)-equivariant CNN for spherical data encodes rotational symmetry exactly, reducing the need to learn it from simulations and improving scientific inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Recent image generators exhibit rich visual priors that can support dense visual perception. However, existing approaches typically encode multiple perception tasks into a shared parameterization, making joint training sensitive to the mixture and weighting of heterogeneous data and prone to cross-task interference. To address this issue, we introduce ReVision, an instruction-conditioned parameter generation framework built on a frozen multimodal understanding model and a frozen image generator. Given an image and a free-form instruction, the understanding model jointly encodes them into a multimodal image--instruction representation, which a trainable parameter generator maps to transient low-rank updates for the generator. Each image--instruction pair induces a distinct set of transient prediction parameters, enabling instance-specific adaptation while both pretrained backbones remain unchanged. ReVision requires no task-specific heads, explicit task identifiers, or stored adapters. A shared RGB output interface unifies segmentation, depth estimation, and surface-normal prediction. Across diverse dense prediction benchmarks, ReVision achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods while supporting flexible task specification through natural-language instructions. Our analysis further reveals substantial gradient disagreement across tasks, highlighting the conflict introduced when heterogeneous objectives share a single parameterization. Meanwhile, the generated updates exhibit structured task- and input-dependent organization in weight space, further validating instance-level parameter generation for multi-task perception.
authors: Yitong Yang, Yinglin Wang, Xuexin Liu, Wei Chen, Zhaoyang Xu, Jiaxin Lin, Rui Chen, Shuting He, Kai Wang
bullets: Addresses cross-task interference and sensitivity to heterogeneous data mixtures in jointly trained dense perception models.
Uses a frozen multimodal understanding model to encode an image and natural-language instruction, then generates transient low-rank updates for a frozen image generator.
Supports segmentation, depth estimation, and surface-normal prediction through a shared RGB output interface without task-specific heads, task IDs, or stored adapters.
Achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods across diverse dense prediction benchmarks while enabling flexible natural-language task specification.
Gradient analysis shows substantial task conflict, while generated updates exhibit structured task- and input-dependent organization in weight space.
papers.selection_reason: Instruction-conditioned parameter generation for dense perception tasks including depth and surface-normal prediction, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: ReVision: Reprogramming Image Generators for Dense Visual Perception
papers.tldr: ReVision adapts a frozen image generator to multiple dense perception tasks by generating instruction- and image-specific low-rank parameter updates, avoiding shared-parameter task interference.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. In this paper, we build the first such suite, with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples across three progressive capabilities, Perceive, Solve, and Reason, and use it to ask how time series should enter an LLM that must master all three, and in what order. We find that a dedicated encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model surpasses GPT-4o on every perception attribute we test, whereas textualizing the series costs 8--10 points in reasoning accuracy. The capabilities then build on one another: learning them in order beats mixing the same data and rivals reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data, but only when an encoder is used. Analyses further reveal that capabilities are transferred through distinct network depths rather than simply stacked, and that a stage converged on its own benchmark is not necessarily ready for the next. Distilled into a simple recipe, these findings yield 4B TS-LLMs that, without any target-domain data, outperform four recent 7B TS-LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics, by up to 11 points. We therefore advocate treating time series as a first-class modality for LLMs, read through dedicated encoders and taught to perceive before they reason.
authors: Xin Qiu, Junlong Tong, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Introduces a suite with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples spanning Perceive, Solve, and Reason capabilities.
Finds that dedicated encoders are essential: textualizing time series reduces reasoning accuracy, while a 4B model exceeds GPT-4o on tested perception attributes.
Shows that ordered capability training outperforms mixing the same data and can rival reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data.
Reports that capability transfer occurs across distinct network depths, and benchmark convergence at one stage does not guarantee readiness for the next.
The resulting 4B models outperform four recent 7B time-series LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics without target-domain data.
papers.selection_reason: Develops Time Series-LLMs with a dedicated encoder, treating time series as a first-class multimodal modality.
papers.title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
papers.tldr: A dedicated time-series encoder and progressive training from perception to solving to reasoning substantially improve LLM-based time-series understanding.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.
authors: Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang, Jianyuan Guo
bullets: Addresses spatial fidelity degradation and target misidentification in cluttered, scale-variable remote-sensing scenes.
Introduces an Anticipatory Prior that places the [SEG] token in the initial query as a persistent spatial anchor.
Uses Location-aware Chain-of-Thought for coarse-to-fine localization with bounding boxes.
Adds a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment loss to align segmentation representations with physical image textures.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM reasoning segmentation with spatial fidelity and location-aware CoT; fits MLLM and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
papers.tldr: GeoReason improves remote-sensing reasoning segmentation by preserving visual grounding during long-form reasoning and refining target localization.

papers.abstract: Spatial context prediction requires visual grounding and spatial reasoning to identify vacant regions relative to objects in a scene. Spatial relationships and physical constraints remain challenging for large vision-language models (VLMs). Recursive reasoning has demonstrated strong performance on discrete and abstract reasoning tasks, motivating its use for improving spatial context prediction in natural images. Weight sharing enables higher accuracy with a small trainable parameter count. We introduce Spatial-TRM, a compact recursive model with frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and just 11.2M trainable parameters. This weight-tied reasoner supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects. On the RoboSpatial-Home benchmark, Spatial-TRM achieves 29.51% context accuracy, a gain of 9.02 percentage points (44.0% relative) over a separately trained single-step model with the same parameter count. Including the frozen encoders, the model has 877.8M total parameters, approximately $15\times$ fewer than the reported 13B size of RoboPoint. These results show that repeated refinement improves spatial context prediction from pretrained vision-language features at a fixed trainable parameter count on this benchmark.
authors: Wajeeha Tahir, Anna Tegon, Lionnus Kesting, Gamze \.Islamo\u{g}lu, Krist\'of Karacs, Luca Benini, Thorir Mar Ingolfsson
bullets: Targets spatial context prediction: identifying vacant regions relative to objects while handling spatial relationships and physical constraints.
Combines frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and a compact 11.2M-parameter recursive reasoner.
Supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects.
Reaches 29.51% context accuracy on RoboSpatial-Home, improving by 9.02 percentage points over a same-size single-step model.
The reported gains are demonstrated on RoboSpatial-Home and do not establish broader generalization beyond this benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive spatial reasoning for VLMs in spatial context prediction.
papers.title: Look, Reason, Draw a Region: Recursive Refinement for Spatial Context Prediction
papers.tldr: Spatial-TRM uses recursive, weight-shared refinement over frozen vision-language features to predict spatial regions with few trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: BEV tokenization compresses video MLLM visual tokens while improving embodied spatial reasoning, combining spatial intelligence, token merging, and video understanding.
papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
papers.tldr: Cambrian-BEV improves embodied spatial reasoning by aggregating multi-view video features into a compact, persistent bird’s-eye-view representation.

papers.abstract: Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.
authors: Chaoyu Li, Arka Sadhu, Yuliang Li, Hyo Jin Kim, Yuning Chai, Pooyan Fazli
bullets: Addresses unreliable multi-step spatial reasoning caused by inaccurate external tool observations.
Uses Planner and Perception teachers with Dual-LoRA to supervise a mixture-of-experts student.
Applies segment-level multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train the student on its own trajectories.
The resulting workflow adaptively asks evidence-seeking questions, stops gathering evidence, and composes final answers.
Across three benchmarks, it improves base-model accuracy by 9.2 and 7.5 points, reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8–66.3%, and achieves 1.29–1.49× speedups over the teachers.
papers.selection_reason: Internalizes plan-perceive-compose reasoning for egocentric video spatial understanding, fitting spatial intelligence and video-language reasoning.
papers.title: EgoP$^{2}$C: Internalizing Plan-Perceive-Compose for Spatial Reasoning in Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: EgoP²C teaches a single VLM to plan, selectively perceive, and compose answers for spatial reasoning in egocentric video without external tools.

papers.abstract: Recent works augment Vision-Language Models with geometry features from pretrained 3D models, expecting that the geometric signal will boost spatial reasoning. However, we find that simply fusing geometry features and training on standard spatial QA yields only marginal improvements on high-level multi-hop tasks. We attribute this gap to a training-signal problem: standard spatial QA can be largely answered from visual features and language priors, so the geometry pathway receives weak gradients and fails to integrate with the visual features. To provide a training signal that requires geometry, we propose \textbf{novel-view semantic rendering} as an auxiliary training task that requires the model to predict the semantic layout of an unobserved viewpoint, inspired by humans' ability to mentally simulate novel viewpoints during spatial reasoning. This task encourages joint use of both pathways: geometry provides pose-dependent visibility, while vision provides semantic content. Our auxiliary task yields consistent improvements over the geometry-augmented baseline across all three benchmarks (up to +1.6 on VSI-Bench, +2.2 on ReVSI, +2.9 on our 3D-Point-QA dataset) and our full model surpasses prior open-source methods on VSI-Bench and on ReVSI. Project page: https://yuqunw.github.io/Render2Reason/.
bullets: Simply adding pretrained 3D geometry features provides limited gains because standard spatial QA can rely on vision and language priors.
The proposed auxiliary task predicts the semantic layout from an unobserved viewpoint, requiring mental-style spatial simulation.
Geometry supplies pose-dependent visibility while visual features provide semantic content, encouraging pathway integration.
The method improves over the geometry-augmented baseline by up to 1.6 on VSI-Bench, 2.2 on ReVSI, and 2.9 on 3D-Point-QA.
It surpasses prior open-source methods on VSI-Bench and ReVSI.
papers.selection_reason: Improves spatial understanding in VLMs via novel-view semantic rendering.
papers.title: Render to Reason: Novel-View Semantic Prediction Improves Spatial Understanding in VLMs
papers.tldr: Novel-view semantic rendering gives geometry-augmented VLMs a stronger training signal, improving spatial reasoning across three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Traditional change detection (CD) identifies changes between bi-temporal remote sensing images, while semantic change detection (SCD) assigns predefined land-cover classes. However, mapping all changes may not meet a user's specific needs. Referring change detection (RCD) enables selective retrieval through category prompts. However, existing category-prompted RCD uses the queried category to specify the destination of a change and returns only a binary mask of the corresponding regions. Users may instead request a particular transition and paired semantic maps to understand what changed into what. Such requests require explicit source and target reasoning beyond target-class localization. To address these needs, we propose query-guided semantic change parsing (QSCP), which supports category names, synonyms, and intent-bearing sentences and returns a query-specific mask with paired temporal semantic maps. QSCP parses requests into intents and semantic slots, composes bidirectional visual evidence, and predicts both temporal states with a query-conditioned decoder. On SECOND, QSCP outperforms RCDNet on synonym, sentence, and transition queries and improves end-to-end semantic prediction over evaluated semantic baselines. WHU-CDC experiments further assess cross-dataset transfer and consistency across equivalent expressions without target-domain training. Code is available at https://github.com/qianyuancs/QSCP
bullets: Addresses the limitation of target-class-only retrieval, which cannot explicitly reason about change sources and destinations.
Parses queries into intents and semantic slots, combines bidirectional visual evidence, and uses a query-conditioned decoder.
Outputs a query-specific change mask together with semantic maps for both temporal states.
Outperforms RCDNet on synonym, sentence, and transition queries on SECOND, while improving end-to-end semantic prediction over evaluated baselines.
WHU-CDC experiments examine cross-dataset transfer and consistency across equivalent expressions without target-domain training.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a query-guided semantic change parsing method for remote sensing, utilizing VLMs for spatial reasoning and source-target transition understanding.
papers.title: QSCP: Beyond Class-Name Prompts for Query-Guided Semantic Change Parsing
papers.tldr: QSCP advances query-guided change detection by interpreting category, synonym, and sentence queries to identify specific transitions and produce paired semantic maps over time.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial supervision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token's input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model's native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28). RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, while the full model preserves general video understanding. Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/.
authors: Han Su, Meng Tian, Tianyu Huang, Mingyu Gao, Lennox Wei, Dongxu Li, Jianhua Han, Hang Xu, Xiaohe Wu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Targets VLMs’ difficulty with 3D relations across views and changing observer positions.
Uses Dual-Kernel Attention: semantic attention preserves pretrained behavior, while geometric attention uses 3D points and camera poses.
A learned gate fuses semantic and geometric attention outputs instead of directly fusing reconstruction features into visual tokens.
Introduces Reference-Frame Composition supervision with stepwise turn and heading targets for multi-step reasoning.
DK-VLM-8B reports the best average score across six spatial benchmarks, including 74.33 on VSI-Bench and 58.28 on ReVSI-32; it also preserves general video understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-as-position attention for spatial reasoning in VLMs; directly fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: DK-VLM improves multi-view 3D spatial reasoning by injecting scene geometry into attention as positional information and training explicit reference-frame updates.

papers.abstract: Spatial instructions describe how to move objects, transform regions, or modify their surroundings. When several operations are applied in sequence, each acts on a configuration shaped by earlier changes. How accurately can large language models (LLMs) predict the resulting spatial state? We introduce Grid-Bench, an executable benchmark in which eight families of operations transform discrete worlds represented as two-, three-, and four-dimensional grids. Given an initial grid, explicit rules, and an event history expressed as text, a model predicts the complete final grid. Reference execution makes every predicted value checkable, supporting comparisons across spatial operations, history lengths, and workloads. Evaluating six LLMs shows that complete-state accuracy falls sharply as histories grow, with substantial divergence among models that perform similarly on single events. Models with similar exact-match accuracy can nevertheless differ substantially in the number of incorrect cells on shared instances. Even over long histories, some models recover many correct changes beyond what copying the initial state would yield. Grid-Bench makes both complete recovery and these differences in returned states directly measurable across a range of spatial conditions.
authors: Zixiang Xu, Zirui Song, Wanrong Zheng, Chiyu Zhang, Yue Huang, Yuyang Peng, Kexin Zhang, Jinkun Chen, Xiuying Chen, Xiangliang Zhang, Yan Liu, Laurent Itti, Frank Shyu, Xiaoqiang Luo, Sandeep Pandey, Xi Liu, Luke Simon, Xiyang Hu, Yue Zhao
bullets: Benchmarks eight operation families across 2D, 3D, and 4D grid worlds.
Provides an initial grid, text-based rules, and event histories; models must output the complete final grid.
Reference execution makes every predicted cell verifiable across history lengths and workloads.
Six LLMs show sharply declining complete-state accuracy as histories grow, with differing error patterns despite similar exact-match scores.
Some models recover many correct changes in long histories, outperforming simple copying of the initial state.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM spatial state prediction over discrete grids directly targets spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Grid-Bench: Can LLMs Predict How Discrete Worlds Change?
papers.tldr: Grid-Bench evaluates how accurately LLMs execute sequences of spatial transformations and reconstruct final states in discrete grids.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.
authors: Luozheng Qin, Yuhan Zhu, Changhai Zhou, Qian Qiao, Jun Gao, Yuhua Zhou, Harry Zhang, Xiangyu Zeng, Yuxuan Liu, Kaijie Chen, Andrew Chen, Pony Ma
bullets: Targets three spatial tasks: choice-based relations, numerical distance estimation, and 2D point prediction.
Scores candidates with pretrained query/key projections, adding no parameters and requiring one forward pass per decision.
Uses coarse-to-fine classification for value bins and image regions, with jointly supervised stages and efficient heterogeneous-data batching.
Trained on 12.3M converted question-answer pairs, it ranks first on 7 of 12 benchmarks and achieves a 65.64% overall score across eight models.
Runs 2.5× faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6× faster than its autoregressive base model; scope is spatial understanding tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified classification framework for spatial understanding tasks (relations, distance, points) in a multimodal decision model.
papers.title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching
papers.tldr: MJev-Spatial converts spatial reasoning into fast, unified classification, achieving strong benchmark performance while avoiding autoregressive answer generation.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
authors: Dongjie Cheng, Ruifeng Yuan, Ran Wei, Ning Song, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed visual-imagination pipelines, such as novel-view synthesis, for diverse reasoning tasks.
Uses tools and skills to help the VLM decide whether and how to imagine, formulate generation requests, and interpret visual evidence.
Introduces co-evolution of tools, skills, and execution code from feedback while keeping model weights fixed.
Improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM across seven spatial, temporal, causal, and perceptual benchmarks.
Reports relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA; the strongest variant outperforms five evolving baselines across five benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: VWM-driven agentic reasoning for spatiotemporal and spatial tasks fits world models, video understanding, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
papers.tldr: CoWorld Reasoner equips a VLM with an evolving, tool-based video world-model harness for flexible visual imagination and stronger spatiotemporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Bohan Zhou, Jinghao Li, Yangkai Wei, Wenqian Li, Peiran Dong, Yingjie Xu, Leyi Wu, Haojian Huang, Binghui Xie, Han Yang, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng

papers.title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
papers.tldr: Anvil builds embodied spatial intelligence by recirculating verified, failure-driven knowledge across localization, relation reasoning, and action-oriented stages.

papers.abstract: Partial shape matching is a crucial yet underexplored problem in 3D vision, with significant relevance to real-world scenarios where shapes are often only partially observed. Existing feature descriptors face difficulties in this setting, as traditional representations either struggle with the boundaries of partial shapes or heavily depend on the shape's spatial position. While existing approaches have employed DINO features for partial shape matching, these features are not inherently suited for handling partial observations. In this work, we propose a method to refine DINO features using LoRA-based self-supervised learning, enabling the generation of feature descriptors that are robust to partiality. Our features substantially improve performance on partial shape matching compared to traditional or vision foundation features. Additionally, when integrated into existing partial shape matching pipelines, we achieve state-of-the-art results on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.
authors: Viktoria Ehm, Dongliang Cao, Riccardo Marin, Daniel Scholz, Weikang Wang, Florian Bernard, Daniel Cremers
bullets: Addresses partial 3D shape matching, where boundaries and spatial-position dependence challenge existing descriptors.
Refines DINO features through self-supervised learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA).
Produces geometry-aware descriptors designed to handle partial observations.
Improves partial shape matching over traditional and general vision-foundation features.
Achieves state-of-the-art results when integrated into existing pipelines on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised geometry-aware refinement of DINO features for partial 3D shape matching; relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Teaching DINOv3 About Partial 3D Geometry: A Self-Supervised Geometry-Aware Approach
papers.tldr: A LoRA-based self-supervised adaptation makes DINO features more robust for matching partially observed 3D shapes.

papers.abstract: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.
authors: Yijiang Li, Bingyang Wang, Nuno Vasconcelos
bullets: Uses one rendered image at a time, with actions such as moving and reorienting, rather than preloaded multi-view or 3D inputs.
Combines trajectory-supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning driven mainly by final-answer correctness, without viewpoint or action labels.
Achieves 53.2% average accuracy across six 3D benchmarks, improving its base Qwen model by 22.0% and using 50–70% fewer input frames than existing open-source methods.
