papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free framework for VLM adaptation to distant OOD domains by extracting spatially grounded visual traits, bridging descriptive and discriminative capabilities.
papers.title: Inductive Visual Logic for Few-Shot Out-Of-Distribution Adaptation in VLMs
papers.tldr: IVL enables few-shot adaptation to distant OOD visual domains by turning VLMs’ descriptive abilities into interpretable classification rules without training.

papers.abstract: Advancing spatial intelligence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is bottlenecked by the scarcity of complex, scalable 3D question-answer (QA) data. While manual annotation is labor-intensive, directly utilizing LLMs to synthesize these QA pairs often fails due to their inherent deficiencies in spatial and geometric computation. We introduce Exemplar2VQA, a scalable exemplar-driven visual question answering generation framework that rapidly synthesizes large-scale spatial QA pairs in simulated environments via multi-agent coding. By equipping collaborative agents with a meticulously designed library of geometric utilities, Exemplar2VQA bypasses LLMs' spatial reasoning flaws through deterministic code execution. Crucially, the framework exhibits remarkable versatility: taking diverse static object-centric spatial query templates as exemplars, it seamlessly and autonomously scales them into massive, high-fidelity synthetic datasets. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B) exclusively on Exemplar2VQA-generated synthetic indoor data yields significant performance improvements across various diverse benchmarks. Furthermore, its effectiveness is not limited to in-domain indoor datasets but also robustly extends to outdoor and mixed-scene benchmarks. These results establish Exemplar2VQA as a scalable and powerful paradigm for bridging the sim-to-real gap in Embodied AI. Our code is at https://github.com/yingjiayu12/Exemplar2VQA
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and high annotation cost of complex 3D spatial QA data.
Uses collaborative agents with deterministic geometric code execution to avoid LLM spatial-reasoning errors.
Expands diverse static object-centric spatial query templates into large synthetic datasets in simulated environments.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL models on the generated indoor data improves performance across multiple benchmarks.
Shows transfer beyond indoor scenes to outdoor and mixed-scene settings, supporting sim-to-real applications.
papers.selection_reason: Scalable spatial QA generation framework that directly targets spatial intelligence in MLLMs.
papers.title: Exemplar2VQA: A Scalable Exemplar-Driven Visual Question Answering Generation Framework via Multi-Agent Coding
papers.tldr: Exemplar2VQA uses multi-agent coding and geometric utilities to efficiently generate scalable, high-quality 3D spatial VQA data from exemplars, improving MLLM spatial intelligence across indoor, outdoor, and mixed-scene benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
authors: Xin Gao, Yifan Yang, Xin Li, Pan Wang, Yan Li, Muzhao Tian, Mingxi Cheng, Bei Liu, Kai Qiu, Qi Dai, Dong Chen, Yue Dong, Leandros Tassiulas, Rex Ying, Ji Li, Chong Luo
bullets: Targets editable, verifiable code generation for slides, posters, dashboards, and similar visual artifacts.
Represents designs as attributable design graphs covering canvas elements and their relationships.
Uses deterministic code/rendering verifiers for parsable properties and a VLM judge with sample-specific Visual Graph Rubrics for non-parsable visual qualities.
Optimizes the reward channels with reinforcement learning and per-channel normalization to improve planning, aesthetics, and correctness.

On a benchmark separating correctness from visual quality, AesCode improves visual quality over same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points for its 8B and 32B models, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AesCode, a framework for generating code for visual artifacts using a VLM judge and decoupled cross-modal rewards to improve spatial planning and aesthetic quality.
papers.title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
papers.tldr: AesCode improves code-generated visual artifacts by combining reference-image aesthetic guidance with graph-grounded, decoupled rewards for correctness and visual quality.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high-level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi-step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high-level reasoning and multi-step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high-level planners. Overall, Plan-Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan-Bench.
authors: Juntong Feng, Qingan Liu, Jingru Dong, Yue Zhu, Weiming Zheng, Yujie Cheng, Xinzhe Han, Shuai Hao, Yunzhi Zhuge, Haiwen Diao, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Evaluates VLM planning independently of action execution in embodied-world scenarios.
Covers three dimensions, 16 subclasses, and 699 curated samples.
Evaluation of 28 VLMs finds substantial room for improvement; the best reaches 75.0% accuracy.
Larger models generally perform better and show greater potential as high-level planners.
Provides a lightweight benchmark and code for assessing embodied reasoning and planning.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for VLM high-level reasoning and multi-step planning in embodied worlds, directly relevant to embodied decision making.
papers.title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?
papers.tldr: Plan-Bench shows that current VLMs still struggle with reliable multi-step reasoning and planning for embodied tasks, despite benefits from scaling.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve natural complexity, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether abilities measured in toy games correspond to real-world visual reasoning and whether game examples can support transfer. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark that studies these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We construct 1,000 procedurally generated game samples with executable verification and curate 400 real-world samples aligned by shared reasoning requirements rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs and observe strong game-to-real consistency, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. We further study one-shot game-to-real transfer on four models. Constraint reasoning improves for several models, while fine-grained perception declines with game demonstrations. We also construct Game2Real-Dataset with nearly 24K verified game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.
authors: Qingan Liu, Juntong Feng, Yue Zhu, Yujie Cheng, Xinzhe Han, Shuai Hao, Yunzhi Zhuge, Haiwen Diao, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Evaluates VLMs across fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning.
Pairs 1,000 procedurally generated, executable-verified game samples with 400 real-world samples sharing reasoning requirements.
Reports strong game-to-real consistency across 25 VLMs, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935.
One-shot game-to-real transfer improves constraint reasoning for several models but can hurt fine-grained perception.
Also releases nearly 24K verified game samples spanning 18 tasks and 65 QA families.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark studying VLM visual and spatial reasoning, including game-to-real transfer of reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?
papers.tldr: Game2Real-Bench finds that performance on verified toy-game tasks strongly reflects real-world visual reasoning, but game demonstrations transfer unevenly across capabilities.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. The dominant interface compresses it into the hidden state of a single [SEG] token, a d-dimensional vector with no spatial index, and leaves the decoder, which never sees the expression, to recover the referent's extent. We show that the VLM already computes a better signal: the [SEG] token's attention over the image tokens, which is defined on the patch grid by construction. Probing a frozen segmentation VLM, we find that this attention yields 18 to 22 more gIoU than the [SEG] hidden state when read by the same probe, that it gains nothing from the image where the hidden state does, and that it is concentrated in the late layers. Building on these findings, we introduce AttnSeg, which replaces the [SEG] embedding with this attention as the decoder's prompt. A learned, signed combination of the attention heads forms a dense spatial prompt, and an attention-guidance objective supervises it directly. A two-stage recipe first trains the VLM to localize without the decoder, then trains the decoder to refine, within the budget of standard fine-tuning. Applied to Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg by 6.4 gIoU and GS-Eval by 10.2 at 4B (4.2 and 9.6 over the same model fine-tuned on the same data), and by 8.8 and 11.3 at 14B. The gains reach 13 to 18 gIoU on object parts, multiple objects, and single objects, where the referent must be singled out, and are negligible on stuff regions, which the decoder already recovers unaided. Code and models are available at https://eslambakr.github.io/attseg_project_page/
authors: Eslam Abdelrahman, Hamza Omar Alkaf, Yuheng Li, Siddharth Srinivasan Iyer, Nanxuan Zhao, Eli Shechtman, Krishna Kumar Singh, Mohamed Elhoseiny
bullets: The standard [SEG] embedding discards spatial information, forcing the pixel decoder to infer the referent’s extent.
[SEG]-token attention over image patches is a stronger localization signal, yielding 18–22 higher gIoU with the same probe and concentrating in late layers.
AttnSeg learns a signed combination of attention heads as a dense spatial prompt and directly supervises it with attention guidance.
A two-stage training recipe separates VLM localization from decoder refinement within standard fine-tuning.
On Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg and GS-Eval, especially for single objects, multiple objects, and object parts; gains are negligible for stuff regions.
papers.selection_reason: Uses VLM attention as a spatial prompt for segmentation, improving spatial grounding and fitting multimodal LLM and spatial intelligence topics.
papers.title: Segment Where You Look: Attention as the Interface Between Language Models and Segmenters
papers.tldr: AttnSeg improves language-guided image segmentation by using the VLM’s spatial [SEG]-token attention instead of its non-spatial hidden state as the decoder interface.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.
authors: Rong Li, Shijie Li, Jiangyong Huang, Lingdong Kong, Jiaming Zhou, Dongyue Lu, Zeying Gong, Baoxiong Jia, Junwei Liang, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty with metric and multi-view relationships implicit in RGB observations.
Trains lightweight Geometric Readers to convert geometry into continuous tokens aligned with representations the frozen VLM can interpret.
Fine-tunes the VLM for question-conditioned geometry use while keeping the Readers fixed; no geometry chain-of-thought is needed at inference.
Achieves 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny and averages 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks in the reported Qwen-based settings.
Shows that reconstructible geometry features are insufficient unless the receiving VLM actually uses them.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces geometry-aware continuous tokens to improve spatial reasoning in VLMs, fitting spatial intelligence and geometry-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GeoReader teaches vision-language models to directly use learned geometric tokens for stronger spatial reasoning from RGB images.

papers.abstract: Reliable robot autonomy requires reasoning about the world from partial and noisy observations. However, many perception systems model only visible scene regions, rely on fixed semantic categories, and assume reliable sensor measurements. These assumptions break under occlusion, novel object encounters, and sensor degradation. In this paper, I present a research vision for incompleteness-aware scene understanding. I organize this vision around three fundamental challenges: incomplete evidence, incomplete knowledge, and incomplete sensor reliability. I discuss my research contributions toward addressing these challenges through amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world scene understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multi-modal fusion. Building on these contributions, I outline future research directions toward belief-centric 4D scene representations. These representations aim to jointly model geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty. I also discuss active sensing and safe adaptation strategies that allow robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction. The goal is to develop calibrated and actionable scene representations that support reliable autonomy in dynamic, open-world environments.
bullets: Identifies three challenges: incomplete observations, incomplete semantic knowledge, and uncertain sensor reliability.
Proposes addressing them with amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multimodal fusion.
Envisions belief-centric 4D scene representations combining geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty.
Highlights active sensing and safe adaptation as ways for robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction.
Focuses on calibrated, actionable representations rather than assuming complete visibility or fixed categories.
papers.selection_reason: Incompleteness-aware spatial scene understanding and belief-centric 4D representations for robot autonomy, relevant to embodied AI, spatial intelligence, world models, and 3D vision.
papers.title: Perception Beyond the Visible: Incompleteness-Aware Scene Understanding for Robot Autonomy
papers.tldr: A research vision for robot perception that explicitly models missing evidence, unknown objects, and unreliable sensors to enable safer autonomy in dynamic open-world environments.

papers.abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Petar Damjanovi\'c, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Addresses the costly trial-and-error needed to identify compatible model pairs.
Measures compatibility using two axes: pair-specific k-NN overlap and a training-paradigm compatibility ceiling.
Ranks candidate pairs and recommends whether to proceed, spend more compute, change the paradigm, or deprioritize the pair.
Across 72 cross-modal alignment experiments and 392 model merges, COMPASS correlated strongly with downstream success.
Reported average Pearson correlations were 0.91 for alignment and 0.70 for merging.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMPASS, a diagnostic tool to assess model compatibility for alignment/merging based on representational convergence (k-NN overlap), a spatial/structural metric.
papers.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
papers.tldr: COMPASS cheaply predicts whether pretrained model pairs will align or merge successfully before expensive training or merging.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.
authors: Ting Zhu, Huizhi Liang, Boguslaw Obara, Shufei Duan, Varun Ojha
bullets: Targets the lack of explicit geometric structure in predominantly Euclidean multimodal emotion recognition methods.
Uses EuclFusion for token-level cross-modal semantic fusion and HypGeoRoute for geometry-aware emotion representation routing in hyperbolic space.
Evaluated on the IEMOCAP benchmark, achieving 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy.
Reports the best performance among evaluated methods, outperforming Euclidean baselines including MemoCMT.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes GeoMER, a multimodal emotion recognition framework using a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic geometry, which fits the 'Spatial Intelligence' subtopic regarding geometry-aware multimodal models.
papers.title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.tldr: GeoMER combines Euclidean multimodal fusion with hyperbolic emotion-core routing to model both fine-grained interactions and hierarchical emotion structures.

papers.abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.
authors: Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao, Chen Liao, Daqin Luo, Yiming Ma, Baiyu Pan, Hailin Shi, Jiyuan Wang, Xiangming Xu, Xiongwei Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented world models that handle modalities and functions through separate interfaces or modules.
Uses modality-specific encoders and decoders around a shared Unified Dynamics Transformer that jointly evolves RGB, metric depth, and action representations.
Supports joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics.
A motion probe indicates that frozen visual representations retain recoverable action-related motion information.
Trained on heterogeneous egocentric-video, real-robot, and simulation data; the abstract reports top results on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad, and WorldArena.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal world model jointly modeling RGB, depth, and robot action for embodied intelligence, with strong relevance to world models, embodied action, and spatial representation.
papers.title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
papers.tldr: Thinker-WM unifies visual appearance, depth geometry, and robot actions in one shared world model for prediction, generation, and control-related tasks.

papers.abstract: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.
authors: Yu Wang, Rui Dai, Wei Chen, Yi Wang, Bo Dang, Kaikui Liu, Xiangxiang Chu, Yansheng Li
bullets: Represents scenes as interactive multi-view environments for landmark queries, zooming, oblique rendering, and bounding-box prediction.
Trains the vision-language tool-use policy with reinforcement learning using localization and exploration-efficiency rewards.
Achieves the best reported Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer while grounding without candidate boxes.
Runs substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline.
Shows improved zero-shot cross-scene robustness on STPLS3D-Refer.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic VLM spatial grounding in city-scale 3D scenes; active spatial search and RL-optimized tool use.
papers.title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
papers.tldr: Urbex reframes city-scale 3D grounding as efficient, agentic spatial search rather than ranking precomputed proposals.

papers.abstract: In this paper, our goal is to represent text embeddings as sketches for three main reasons. First, to visualize text representation and to explore their potential their potential for AI explainability. Second, to investigate the potential benefits of the sketch-based representation for information retrieval. Third, to explore their potential for reasoning, drawing inspiration from the concept of mental imagery. We propose a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches. Our approach aims to emphasis the semantics content encoded in the text embeddings through the corresponding sketch. Evaluations are conducted on the MS-COCO dataset to examine the utility of these sketches for text retrieval. The comparative study of SBERT and Sketch-based method reveals that SBERT retains an advantage in strict top-1 retrieval accuracy while achieving comparable performance to the sketch-based method in top-5 retrieval. A cascaded approach combining SBERT and the sketch-based method outperforms SBERT alone, suggesting that the Sketch-based representation could offer significant potential for information retrieval if trained directly on text.
bullets: Represents text embeddings as sketches to make semantic content more visually interpretable and explore AI explainability.
Investigates whether visual, sketch-based representations can support information retrieval and reasoning inspired by mental imagery.
Evaluated on MS-COCO for text retrieval using SBERT and the proposed sketch-based method.
SBERT performs better at strict top-1 retrieval, while sketch-based retrieval is comparable at top-5.
Combining SBERT with the sketch-based method in a cascade outperforms SBERT alone; direct training on text is identified as future potential.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text embeddings into topographic sketches, offering a novel spatial representation for multimodal information retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond Black Boxes: Visual Grounding for Text Embeddings
papers.tldr: A sketch-based visual grounding framework turns text embeddings into semantic topographic sketches, supporting interpretability and retrieval, with a cascaded system improving over SBERT alone.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models use depth information to judge which object is closer, or rely on image-plane cues? We investigate this question through controlled depth--cue conflicts, representation analysis, and interventions. Among the many image-plane cues relevant to depth perception, we focus on apparent size and vertical position. We compare depth judgments under cue-consistent and cue-conflict conditions in both rendered scenes and real-world photographs. Across model families and scales, depth judgments systematically shift toward misleading cues. Yet the correct depth order remains decodable from the queried objects' visual representations, including when the model answers incorrectly. Image and category controls support interpreting this signal as image-dependent depth information beyond the two target cues. Strengthening the model's own depth readout through object-level write-back can correct conflict decisions without updating model parameters or using ground-truth depth annotations. Interventions show that the effect of this correction depends on the direction and target tokens of the written signal, while its strength varies across architectures and domains. Together, these findings reveal a mismatch between a model's ability to represent depth and use this information when deciding the answer. VLMs can retain useful depth information while allowing competing image-plane cues to exert greater influence on their answers.
bullets: The study examines depth judgments under conflicts involving apparent size and vertical position.
Across model families, scales, rendered scenes, and real photographs, answers systematically shift toward misleading cues.
Correct depth order remains decodable from object representations even when the model answers incorrectly.
Object-level write-back can strengthen depth readout and correct decisions without parameter updates or ground-truth depth labels.
Correction effects depend on the written signal’s direction and target tokens, and vary by architecture and domain.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates depth representation and cue use in vision-language models via controlled conflicts and interventions, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Seeing Depth but Choosing Cues in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Vision-language models can represent correct depth information but often let misleading image-plane cues dominate their judgments.

papers.abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
authors: Qingchuan Ma, Yuexiao Ma, Xiang Meng, Yixuan Zou, Tianyu Xie, Wang Chen, Yuhui Zeng, Yuhang Wu, Xiawu Zheng, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Models iteratively rotate a 3D object to match a target 2D silhouette under a limited action budget.
The benchmark contains 674 solvable tasks, including a stratified 100-task test set built from 2D icons and reversible initialization.
GPT-5.6-Sol succeeded on 17% of tasks, while undergraduate participants achieved 100% success across repeated test-set completion.
Models sometimes improve silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment more often than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%).
Removing interaction history led 96.8% of model actions to use coarse 30° rotations and sharply reduced task success.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates VLMs' interactive 3D spatial reasoning via projection alignment, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
papers.tldr: RoTA-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models can use visual feedback to perform precise 3D rotation-based alignment, revealing major gaps in spatial reasoning and control.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming spatial understanding with embodied memory and active exploration; directly fits embodied memory, spatial intelligence, and vision-language-action.
papers.title: MemAct: Streaming Spatial Understanding with Memory and Active Exploration
papers.tldr: MemAct enables embodied agents to understand spaces over time by combining structured memory, on-demand retrieval, and active exploration in a unified streaming loop.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model tell left from right? Modern VLMs solve visual puzzles and follow hour-long videos, yet when asked whether the camera moved left or right, most do no better than a coin flip. Adding camera-motion data or geometric representations has been tried, separately, and neither closes the gap. We argue that camera-motion understanding needs two conditions at once: the representation must couple off-screen camera motion with on-screen flow dynamics, and it must be interpreted by the language model rather than trained as a standalone pose or depth estimator. We propose CameraVLM, which pairs a motion-state representation with state-language alignment. Camera tokens capture how the camera moves off screen, flow tokens capture how the subject and background move on screen, and a two-stage training strategy keeps language in the loop so that both are learned together with camera-motion semantics. With only 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms all open-source and camera-motion-specific models by a wide margin across three benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, and matches or surpasses GPT-6 Astra as well as human viewers in a 48-participant study. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/CameraVLM/
authors: Chong Cheng, Ran Zhang, Xinyuan Li, Alan Zhao, Hao Wang, Xi Wang
bullets: Vision-language models often perform near chance when identifying whether a camera moved left or right.
The approach combines camera tokens for off-screen motion with flow tokens for subject and background dynamics.
A two-stage training strategy aligns these motion representations with language while keeping camera-motion semantics in the loop.
Using 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms open-source and camera-motion-specific models across three benchmarks and over 20 baselines.
It reportedly matches or exceeds GPT-6 Astra and human performance in a 48-participant study.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CameraVLM, a vision-language model for understanding camera motion by coupling off-screen motion with on-screen flow, directly advancing spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: When Left Is Right? Camera-Motion Understanding beyond Screen
papers.tldr: CameraVLM improves left-versus-right camera-motion understanding by jointly modeling off-screen camera motion, on-screen optical flow, and language semantics.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.
authors: Chenlong Wei, Hanling Wang, Mingjin Lou, Yufan Shi, Yandong Sun, Sheldon Yu, Xiaohui Zhu, Xiaobo Jin, Yiwei Wang
bullets: Introduces Sonic-Bench with 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific QA pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes.
Covers source localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings.
Combines physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features with learned transitions and recurrent updates, then feeds source states into an Omni LLM.
On Sonic-Bench, improves direction accuracy and azimuth error over Spatial-Omni.
Transfers zero-shot to Spatial LibriSpeech while retaining strong localization performance.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial audio reasoning with latent source dynamics and an Omni LLM, fitting spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
papers.tldr: SonicWorld enables source-aware spatial audio reasoning by maintaining persistent latent states for moving and overlapping sound sources.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models, exemplified by GPT-6 Astra, raise the prospect of general-purpose embodied reasoning and planning. Using Internet videos for embodied pretraining calls for reliable physical-scale annotations. Yet visual geometry foundation models often recover scene structure and camera motion without reliable metric scale. We show that uncertain size priors of familiar objects can jointly constrain a reconstruction's shared scale. Building on this insight, we present UniMetric, a universal and training-free metric scale recovery framework for geometry foundation models, without additional sensors or task-specific metric supervision. Specifically, Metric Prior Acquisition elicits object height intervals from a vision-language model. Semantic-Geometric Alignment measures reconstructed object heights along the estimated support-surface normal in each frame and converts the priors into scale intervals. Global Scale Recovery reconciles these intervals through a convex objective, yielding a jointly feasible scale when they overlap and a unique compromise otherwise. The estimated sequence-level scale is applied uniformly to reconstructed points and camera translations. Controlled experiments with real VLM priors show that combining observations improves scale accuracy with exact relative object heights. To evaluate metric accuracy on GFM reconstructions without ground-truth scale alignment, we introduce MetricBench, covering twelve embodied, driving, and roadside subsets with sensor-derived ground truth. Across nine geometry foundation models, UniMetric reduces mean depth Abs Rel, reconstruction Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively, improving every model on all three tasks at the suite level. We release the UniMetric code and MetricBench data.
authors: Lei Yang, Yuner Zhang, Ziyang Liu, Ziying Song, Kai WU, Yiyang Gao, Jiangtao Su, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of reliable physical-scale annotations in geometry foundation model outputs.
Elicits object-height intervals, aligns reconstructed objects with support-surface geometry, and converts them into scale intervals.
Reconciles multiple observations with a convex global objective to estimate one sequence-level scale, applied to points and camera translations.
Introduces MetricBench, a sensor-grounded benchmark spanning 12 embodied, driving, and roadside subsets.

Across nine geometry foundation models, reduces mean depth Abs Rel, Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively. In scope: requires familiar objects with usable size priors and overlapping or reconcilable scale constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free metric scale recovery for visual geometry foundation models using VLM object priors and geometric alignment; directly relevant to spatial/geometric reasoning in multimodal systems.
papers.title: UniMetric: Universal Metric Scale Recovery for Visual Geometry Foundation Models
papers.tldr: UniMetric is a training-free framework that recovers metric scale for visual geometry foundation model reconstructions using uncertain object-size priors from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts part articulation and connectivity from images/depth and demonstrates utility for generating robot motion trajectories; view-grounded spatial representation is transferable to embodied manipulation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: ViewStruct: View-Grounded Articulation and Connectivity Inference
papers.tldr: ViewStruct infers object part connectivity and articulation from visual inputs using a view-grounded representation that transfers beyond synthetic training categories and assets.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.
authors: Xin Liu, Feng Lu, Wei Li
bullets: Maps variable EEG channels into fixed regional tokens using electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances.
Preserves fine-grained channel information through a channel-evidence injection branch.
Uses a Region-Time Transformer with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals for pretraining.
Outperforms compared methods in average balanced accuracy across six benchmark datasets.
On OpenBMI-MI, matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, while using 96.8% fewer parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Uses hyperbolic geometry for self-supervised EEG representation learning. The hyperbolic aggregation method is transferable to spatial reasoning tasks involving hierarchical data.
papers.title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
papers.tldr: HyBRA is a self-supervised EEG representation-learning framework that uses hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation to improve robustness across heterogeneous electrode montages and datasets.

papers.abstract: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.
bullets: Motivates richer probabilistic output layers to add spatial regularization without substantially increasing data requirements.
Addresses the challenge of obtaining meaningful derivatives and convergence when pairing graphical models with deep networks.
Introduces two solution approaches for pairwise conditional random fields with convergence guarantees.
Evaluates the approaches through mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, showing differences in their performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces convergent differentiable approaches for CRFs with spatial regularization. This contributes to the class of differentiable probabilistic models for spatial reasoning.
papers.title: DeepFlow: Two Convergent Differentiable Approaches for Pairwise Conditional Random Fields
papers.tldr: DeepFlow presents two provably convergent differentiable algorithms for incorporating pairwise CRF-style spatial regularization into deep image and signal classifiers.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph generation requires understanding both object semantics and metric spatial relations. However, existing open-vocabulary methods often struggle with spatial predicates because language similarity reflects semantic co-occurrence rather than explicit geometry. We propose GHOST, a Geometry-constrained Hybrid diffusion framework for Open-vocabulary 3D Scene graph generaTion. GHOST jointly models continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates, following a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to ensure geometrically consistent relation prediction. It introduces language-grounded constraint induction, which maps predicate embeddings to differentiable geometric constraints that guide both layout refinement and predicate reweighting. A Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser further couples node and edge reasoning through noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both closed-set and open-vocabulary settings, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.
authors: Changqun Feng, Wangxiandi Yin, Xin Hu, Ruiting Dai, Feiyang Yang, Jielei Wang, Tao He
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language similarity and explicit 3D spatial geometry in open-vocabulary relation prediction.
Uses a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to jointly model continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates.
Induces differentiable geometric constraints from predicate embeddings to refine layouts and reweight relation predictions.
Employs a Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser with noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 3DSSG, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation with geometry-constrained spatial reasoning fits 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GHOST: Geometry-Constrained Hybrid Diffusion for Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graph Generation
papers.tldr: GHOST improves open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation by coupling language-grounded geometric constraints with diffusion-based joint reasoning over objects and spatial relations.

papers.abstract: Current image-text evaluation often relies on a global score, which gives limited insight into which semantic details are supported by the image. Explainable metrics provide rationales, but the visual evidence supporting those rationales can still be difficult to verify. We introduce VisExMEM, a reference-free evaluator that decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence, verifies each claim, and averages claim-level support into a global score. Explanations use the same evidence and decisions. We train Qwen3.5-based 4B and 9B models on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware GDPO. Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B achieves the highest descriptive composite among open-source evaluators in our comparison, exceeding VQAScore by 11.7 points while remaining competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol. We also introduce AGITA-Bench, containing 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation. For untuned Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol controls, decomposed prompting raises the same composite by 3.6-5.1 points relative to holistic prompting. Human evaluation shows that VisExMEM explanations outperform prior explainable metrics and approach GPT-5.6 Sol.
authors: Subhadeep Roy, Christoph Leiter, Steffen Eger
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability and verifiability of global image-text evaluation scores.
Decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes supporting evidence, verifies each claim, and averages support into a global score.
Uses shared evidence and decisions to generate explanations, improving their faithfulness.
Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B reports the highest descriptive composite among compared open-source evaluators and remains competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol.
Introduces AGITA-Bench with 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a multimodal evaluation metric that grounds explanations in visual evidence, contributing to spatial intelligence and multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: VisExMEM: Visual Evidence-Based Explainable Multimodal Evaluation Metric
papers.tldr: VisExMEM is a reference-free multimodal metric that evaluates captions by verifying atomic claims against localized visual evidence and producing evidence-grounded explanations.

papers.abstract: Speech-driven visual grounding in remote sensing (RSVG) removes the typing bottleneck of text-based interaction and is intended to preserve prosodic intent, enabling hands-free target acquisition in time-critical missions. The direct-audio paradigm, mapping raw speech straight to a bounding box and bypassing automatic speech recognition (ASR), was recently adopted by RSTalker, but what such grounders actually learn about language remains unmeasured. SemEcho grafts a frozen Whisper speech pathway onto a VLTVG grounding host so that speech and text share one decoder, making the paired text, free by construction since speech corpora in this task are synthesized from DIOR-RSVG expressions, a training-time teacher and a fair, same-host text upper bound. On this instrument we dissect three semantic injection channels (feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining) with linear semantic probes, and release Audio-DIOR-R (80,973 training clips; 10 timbres x K=3; Qwen3-TTS synthesis with online sox noise lambda in [0, 0.4]) and Audio-DIOR-Comp, a re-split holding out 17 attribute-category combinations under a 2x2 acoustic-semantic protocol. Our anatomy yields four findings. (i) Whether direct alignment beats a domain-trained ASR cascade is decided by recognizer quality: against a weak in-domain cascade (CTC 0.53) direct wins by 9.0 Acc@0.5 points with transcription errors concentrated on spatial-relation words, but a strong in-domain cascade (CTC 0.029) reaches the text upper bound (80.8 vs. 81.0) and beats even the strongest direct model by 8.8 points; the anti-ASR premise holds only against weak recognizers.
bullets: Speech-driven remote-sensing grounding aims to enable hands-free target acquisition while preserving prosodic intent.
SemEcho combines a frozen Whisper speech pathway with a VLTVG grounding host, using paired text as training-time semantic supervision and an upper bound.
It evaluates feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining with linear semantic probes.
The study introduces Audio-DIOR-R and Audio-DIOR-Comp for acoustic and compositional evaluation.
Against a weak in-domain ASR cascade, direct grounding gains 9.0 Acc@0.5 points; a strong cascade nearly matches the text upper bound and exceeds the strongest direct model by 8.8 points.
papers.selection_reason: Speech-driven visual grounding with spatial-relation understanding fits multimodal spatial intelligence.
papers.title: From Sound to Sense: An Anatomy of Semantic Supervision for Speech-Driven Visual Grounding in Remote Sensing Imagery
papers.tldr: SemEcho provides a controlled framework for measuring semantic supervision in direct speech-driven visual grounding and finds that strong ASR can outperform direct audio grounding, challenging the anti-ASR premise.

papers.abstract: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used to encode relative positions in Transformers. In multi-view settings, however, patch coordinates are defined independently in each image: the same 3D point can therefore have different coordinates across views, making them insufficient for establishing cross-view correspondences. We introduce WorldRoPE, a probabilistic world-centric RoPE for multi-view attention. At each layer, WorldRoPE back-projects each patch token into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame. These primitives represent multiple plausible 3D supports for a token, jointly capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite spatial extent of its patch frustum. When a key token's support is projected into a query view, it induces a distribution over where that key may appear in the query image. WorldRoPE integrates the rotary operator over this distribution in closed form, combining rotations at the projected primitive centers according to their mixture weights with covariance-dependent attenuation. This makes attention less sensitive to uncertain key locations in the query view, without rasterizing or warping token features. The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Kyujin Lim, Bohyung Han
bullets: Per-image patch coordinates cannot reliably establish correspondences for the same 3D point across views.
Each token is back-projected into volumetric Gaussian primitives capturing alternative depths, uncertainty, and patch-frustum extent.
The method integrates RoPE over the induced projected-location distribution using mixture weights and covariance-based attenuation.
It guides cross-view attention with predicted geometry while allowing updated features to refine geometry across layers.
Experiments show effectiveness for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction.
papers.selection_reason: World-centric RoPE for multi-view attention; fits 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: WorldRoPE: Probabilistic World-Centric Rotary Embedding for Multi-View Attention
papers.tldr: WorldRoPE enables geometry-aware cross-view attention by representing uncertain 3D token locations as probabilistic supports in a shared world frame.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang, Xi Xiang, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.
Uses a training-free multiagent framework that plans steps to gather missing spatial evidence and combines it with native evidence.
Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Residual test-time agentic computation for video spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence and test-time learning.
papers.title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: ReTAC improves video spatial reasoning by directing test-time agentic computation only toward unresolved requirements and localized failures.

papers.abstract: World-action models should preserve the intended manipulation across equivalent descriptions of a spatial goal. We evaluate this consistency in 864 rollouts from three models across four RoboLab scenes, holding initial states and task goals fixed. Describing relations through the reference object rather than the object-to-move lowers the rate of reaching a stable placement by 12.2 percentage points on average. The effect of instruction rephrasing varies across spatial relations, so aggregate scores can hide sensitivity to wording. Standalone tests of the policies' language understanding identify relation reversals and show that adding images can disrupt otherwise correct text-only interpretations. Rollout analysis also distinguishes spatial placement from instruction following: moving the wrong object can satisfy the requested relation, and rates of stable placement fall from 43.2% at any time to 21.8% at episode end. These findings motivate a more thorough evaluation of world-action models' steerability, language understanding, and grounding. Evaluations should test consistency across equivalent instructions, verify that the intended object moved, and check whether the requested arrangement persists to the end of the rollout.
authors: Ali-Adeeb Abbas, Esmaeil Seraj, Behrad Toghi, Taskin Padir
bullets: Evaluates instruction consistency across 864 rollouts, three models, and four RoboLab scenes with fixed initial states and goals.
Reference-object phrasing reduces stable-placement success by 12.2 percentage points on average, with sensitivity varying by spatial relation.
Standalone language tests reveal relation reversals; adding images can disrupt interpretations that are correct from text alone.
Rollout analysis separates spatial placement from instruction following: the wrong object may be moved, and end-of-episode stability is lower than transient success.
Findings call for evaluations that test equivalent instructions, verify object identity, and assess whether arrangements persist to episode end.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates spatial instruction grounding in world-action models for manipulation, relevant to VLA and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Same Goal, Different Words: Spatial Instruction Sensitivity in World-Action Models
papers.tldr: World-action models can produce different—and sometimes incorrect—manipulations for equivalent spatial instructions, revealing weaknesses in language grounding and steerability.

papers.abstract: Situated 3D Question Answering requires models to interpret a 3D scene relative to an agent's pose. Existing methods commonly convey that pose through a natural-language situation description, which may be unavailable or costly to obtain in real-world deployments. While some methods additionally incorporate numerical pose, we find that randomly shuffling the agent pose causes little performance degradation, indicating limited functional dependence on the numerical pose. To address this gap, we introduce EgoAlign, a simple 3D language model that represents a scene in an agent-centric coordinate frame, together with a dedicated egocentric alignment stage comprising four complementary tasks: object category recognition, egocentric direction prediction, metric distance estimation, and spatial relation prediction. This stage teaches the model to consistently interpret scene geometry relative to the agent's pose before task-specific fine-tuning. EgoAlign achieves the strongest performance on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA among compared methods while remaining highly efficient. More importantly, removing textual situation descriptions yields comparable or better downstream performance, whereas shuffling EgoAlign's numerical pose causes substantial degradation. These results show that EgoAlign establishes agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose without requiring textual situation descriptions.
authors: Yiyang Li, Tianyi Ma, Zehong Wang, Yanfang Ye
bullets: Addresses the cost and unavailability of natural-language situation descriptions in real-world 3D deployments.
Represents scenes in an agent-centric coordinate frame and uses four alignment tasks: category recognition, egocentric direction, metric distance, and spatial relation prediction.
Achieves the strongest reported performance among compared methods on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA while remaining efficient.
Removing textual situation descriptions preserves or improves performance, while shuffling numerical pose substantially degrades it.
Demonstrates that numerical pose can directly establish the agent-centric context needed for situated 3D understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Agent-centric 3D language model for situated spatial reasoning, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: EgoAlign: Situated 3D Understanding without Situation Descriptions
papers.tldr: EgoAlign enables situated 3D question answering by learning agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose, without textual situation descriptions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer many geometric and physical reasoning questions correctly, yet still behave inconsistently in interaction, for example, abandoning a correct answer when confronted with a confident but incorrect user assertion. Standard single-turn accuracy cannot distinguish such capitulations from beneficial corrections because it scores each response in isolation. We introduce GRIP, a controlled benchmark with 34 procedurally generated reasoning domains, 100,000 images, and 600,000 questions spanning geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning. Each scene is generated by deterministic code, and every answer is derived directly from the underlying scene state, providing exact ground truth without human annotation. On GRIP, we propose Dual-Loop Evaluation. A closed loop probes each image with a five-step compositional question ladder to localize where reasoning fails. An open loop then re-elicits the model's answer under controlled challenges, including peer-model responses and unsupported user assertions. Because ground truth is known exactly, answer changes can be signed as corrections (wrong-to-right) or capitulations (right-to-wrong), separating two failure modes: rule absence and rule fragility. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/bilaljawaid980/GRIP-Benchmark, with further details at https://bilaljawaid980.github.io/grip-benchmark/.
authors: Bilal Jawaid, Hamza Hanif, Muhammad Maaz Uddin, Anas Zafar, Inad Alqurashi, Aizan Zafar, Osama Farooqui, Sheheryar Khan, Ferhat Sadak, Shaina Raza, Rizwan Qureshi
bullets: Introduces a procedurally generated benchmark covering 34 geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning domains.
Uses 100,000 images and 600,000 questions with exact ground truth derived from deterministic scene states.
Applies Dual-Loop Evaluation: compositional question ladders diagnose reasoning failures, while controlled challenges test answer stability.
Separates rule absence from rule fragility by labeling answer changes as corrections or capitulations.
Provides the benchmark publicly; the abstract does not report model-specific performance results or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation protocol for spatial, geometric, and physical reasoning in vision-language models.
papers.title: Geometric Parrots: Rule Absence vs. Rule Fragility in Spatial and Physical Reasoning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GRIP evaluates whether vision-language models lack spatial and physical reasoning rules or abandon correct answers under confident but unsupported challenges.

papers.abstract: Grounded spatial reasoning about indoor scenes rests on a geometric reconstruction that the multimodal system does not itself produce. Feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models operate under a fixed view budget, making frame selection a critical upstream decision. We show that under this setting the conventional preference for sharp frames can be actively harmful. Across nine handheld room scans, selecting the sharpest 16 of 200 candidate frames is the worst strategy we test, reaching 48\% room dimension error where uniform temporal sampling reaches 3\%. We trace this failure to a coupling between image quality and camera motion: sharp frames tend to occur during slow motion and therefore concentrate the selection in a narrow angular region, leaving $192^\circ$ of the room unobserved in the case we illustrate and over $300^\circ$ in the worst cells. A $2\times2$ factorial experiment that independently manipulates viewpoint spread and per-frame sharpness shows that spread has roughly three times the main effect of quality, and that blurry but well spread selections outperform sharp but clustered selections in 8 of 9 captures. The advantage also diminishes as the frame budget increases and angular coverage saturates, consistent with this mechanism. Finally, we ask whether the failure is detectable at inference: the reconstruction model's multi-view consistency score increases with reconstruction error, while a vision-language model given the same frames reports confidence unrelated to its own spatial estimation error. Under small view budgets, viewpoint coverage is a more important constraint than per-frame image quality, and neither uncertainty signal available at inference reveals this upstream failure.
bullets: Selecting the sharpest 16 of 200 frames produced the worst reconstruction, whereas uniform temporal sampling greatly reduced room-dimension error.
Sharp frames often cluster during slow camera motion, leaving large portions of the room unseen.
A factorial experiment found viewpoint spread had about three times the effect of image quality; blurry but well-spread frames beat sharp clustered frames in 8 of 9 scans.
Coverage benefits shrink as the frame budget grows and angular coverage saturates.
Neither reconstruction consistency scores nor vision-language-model confidence reliably revealed the upstream coverage failure.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes viewpoint coverage vs image quality in feed-forward 3D reconstruction and spatial reasoning; relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Sharper Frames, Worse Rooms: Viewpoint Coverage Dominates Image Quality in Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: For feed-forward 3D room reconstruction with few frames, broad viewpoint coverage matters far more than selecting the sharpest images, while common confidence signals fail to detect poor coverage.

papers.abstract: Google Earth AI is a family of geospatial AI models, together with an agent that orchestrates them. We present this agent, Google Earth AI's Geospatial Reasoning agent (GRA), a Gemini-powered research system that combines geospatial data sources, foundation models, and tools to answer questions about our planet. GRA organizes these into modular domain skills and pairs them with upfront geospatial planning to decompose complex queries into multi-stage workflows. Evaluating such systems is hard: real-world problems admit multiple valid workflows, require data discovery across large catalogs, and rely on evolving ground truth. We introduce two benchmarks and release their development splits. GeoExpertQueries poses complex analytical problems grounded in practitioner use cases and refined by geospatial experts; each is paired with a consensus golden workflow from three independent experts and scored by a human-validated, tool-agnostic autorater. GeoKTools consists of templated queries with deterministic reference solvers that systematically vary the number of required tool types. We also use two external benchmarks, CBGB and UnivEARTH; the latter we find to be saturated. To isolate the contribution of GRA's tools and its agentic orchestration, we compare four configurations, each with Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.8 Flash: a standalone LLM, the LLM with basic tools, the LLM with GRA's skills and tools but without its upfront planning and execution guidance, and GRA itself. With at most basic tools, an advanced model recovers much of the answer on templated queries but satisfies only a small fraction of the expert workflows on open-ended problems; GRA performs well on both. The largest step comes from GRA's skills and tools; on open-ended problems, its planning and execution guidance add a further gain with Gemini 3.8 Flash, letting Flash match or exceed Pro at lower cost.
