authors: Noam Slonim, Aviv Slobodkin, Gil Fidel, Gal Moshitch, Mimi Sun, Lily Mihalkova, Joydeep Paul, Per Bjornsson, Sydney Lin, Jamie McPike, Samapriya Roy, Utkarsh Patel, Gia Jung, Zachary Luna, Allison Berman, William Cai, Xiao Wu, Mohit Agarwal, Mandar Sharma, Aliza Hoffman, Mark Young, Rama Pasumarthi, Roy Lee, Ruth Alcantara, Luke Barrington, Aaron Bell, Reuven Sayag, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Tyler McHenry, Ronald Ho, Christopher Haire, Oliver Guinan, Niv Efron, Tim Thelin, Gautam Prasad, Shravya Shetty

Combines Gemini models, geospatial data sources, modular domain skills, tools, and explicit planning/execution guidance.
Introduces GeoExpertQueries and GeoKTools, alongside evaluations on CBGB and UnivEARTH; development splits are released for the new benchmarks.
GRA’s skills and tools provide the largest improvement, while planning adds further gains on open-ended problems.
With planning, Gemini 3.8 Flash matches or exceeds Pro on open-ended tasks at lower cost; UnivEARTH is found to be saturated.

papers.title: Google Earth AI Geospatial Reasoning Agent: Capabilities and a Systematic Evaluation
papers.tldr: Google Earth AI’s Geospatial Reasoning Agent combines specialized geospatial tools with upfront planning to solve complex Earth-analysis questions and is systematically evaluated through new workflow-focused benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground-level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster-mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross-view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re-ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6-27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3-8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place-specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human-centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers-VLM.
authors: Hao Li, Wenping Yin, Fabian Deuser, Jia Jia, Ziqi Liu, Levente Juh\'asz, Fan Zhang, Filip Biljecki
bullets: PhotoMappers’ archive is geographically and temporally uneven, reflecting changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities.
Cross-view geolocalization integrates volunteered geographic information, street-view imagery, and remote sensing imagery with Sinkhorn re-ranking.
The approach achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, with substantial variation across years.
Qwen3.6-27B shows higher agreement with geographic reasoning evidence than InternVL3-8B, but both struggle with localized, place-specific cues.
The study advocates human-centered GeoAI that scales candidate retrieval without replacing expert or volunteer interpretation.

papers.title: A Decade of PhotoMappers: A Longitudinal Study of Crowdsourced Disaster Photos Geolocalization with Vision-Language Models and Geospatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: A decade-long study shows that combining crowdsourced disaster photos with street-view and remote-sensing imagery can scale geolocalization, while human judgment remains essential for ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
authors: Xinnan Dai, Kaiqi Yang, Yaxin Li, Cheng Luo, Wanli Li, Mingqing Xiao, Xinyang Jiang, Daoan Zhang, Kaitao Song, Fengze Liu, Zefan Cai, Caihua Shan
bullets: Addresses the gap between static language benchmarks and real-world embodied action.
Tests LLMs with robotic arms, cameras, sensors, and a harness system receiving physical feedback.
Measures grounded perception, planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, correction, and robustness to uncertainty.
Experiments reveal failures including hallucinated state changes, weak recovery, and unstable long-horizon plans.
Provides a foundation for evaluating LLMs as agents connecting language, tools, and the physical world.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction with robotic arms and sensors, covering grounded perception, action planning, and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
papers.tldr: A benchmark evaluates how well LLMs perceive, plan, and adapt while controlling real physical systems through closed-loop interaction.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for spatial text-to-image generation, but existing work largely focuses on policy optimization, assuming accurate rewards and effective online rollouts. We observe in-domain gains with out-of-domain degradation, exposing two limitations: unreliable spatial rewards in open-world settings and rollouts lacking basic-to-complex progression. We propose a curriculum-guided RL framework. First, we introduce SpatialCritic, an agentic reward model equipped with a spatial perception harness that combines reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools. We then construct spatial preference datasets through targeted counterfactual perturbations and perform agent-harness alignment to improve tool selection and evidence integration efficiently. Second, curriculum learning organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic achieves 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming 320B GLM-5.3-Flash with a 40x smaller 8B backbone and raising average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL. Project page: https://xiaofeng-tan.github.io/projects/spatialcritic/
authors: Xiaofeng Tan, Jiaxin Lin, Haobo Yuan, Tiancheng Shen, Zihan Su, Rui Chen, Hongsong Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: SpatialCritic uses reusable verification guidance and specialized vision tools to assess spatial correctness in open-world images.
Counterfactual spatial preference data and agent–harness alignment improve tool selection and evidence integration.
A capability graph organizes basic-to-complex skills for mastery-guided rollouts, review, and targeted remediation.
On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic reaches 95.1% verification accuracy with an 8B backbone.
Average scores improve from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and from 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic spatial reward model for spatial text-to-image generation; directly targets spatial understanding and reasoning in multimodal models.
papers.title: Getting Space Right: Agentic Rewards for Image Generation
papers.tldr: A curriculum-guided RL framework improves spatial text-to-image generation by combining agentic spatial rewards with mastery-guided rollouts.

papers.abstract: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Enzhi Zhou, Junan Lin, Dulan Zhou, Weiqiang Wang, Yuge Huang, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers six dimensions: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose.
Questions target quantities such as depth, interpersonal distance, gaze angle, velocity, trajectories, blink count, and contact-deformation strength.
Labels are generated programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state rather than human annotation or model estimation.
The benchmark includes a training corpus produced by the same pipeline and evaluates both open- and closed-source MLLMs.
Results indicate that all six dimensions remain challenging and are only partially dissociable for current MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for human-centric physical and spatial perception in MLLMs; fits spatial intelligence and video understanding.
papers.title: HumanPhys: A Human-Centric Physical-World Perception Benchmark for Real-World Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: HumanPhys benchmarks whether multimodal models can infer physically grounded human- and camera-related quantities from real-world visual inputs.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.
authors: Chaoyue Li, Shoudong Han, Haoyang Wu, Boxue Yang, Sijia Chen, Yufan Chen, Ruping Zhang
bullets: Defines Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU): tracking entity continuity, forecasting future trajectories and events, and grounding predictions in observed visual evidence.
SceneForesee provides paired observed/future scenes with shared identities, including 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K evidence-linked events.
EvoSee jointly reasons over future geometry and event semantics using shared candidate states and entity assignment.
EvoSee improves over Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1.
It also improves Dyn-Bench question answering and grounding, supporting predicted entity changes as dynamic representations for spatiotemporal reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and framework for scene evolution and spatiotemporal reasoning in video with LMMs.
papers.title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
papers.tldr: SceneForesee introduces a benchmark and EvoSee framework for predicting and explaining how entities and scenes evolve over time from video.

papers.abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.
authors: Andrew Perrault (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Anmol Takiar (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Dominik Wienecki (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Arnab Nandi (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA)
bullets: Benchmarks documentation and view acceptability across 11 Blender environments modeling unconstrained tasks such as solar installation and vehicle repair.
Evaluates 26 vision-language models on whether views provide suitable proof-of-work and whether task-relevant state can be understood.
Models generally solve documentation when answers are visible as text, but struggle with measurements, small parts, and spatial relationships.
Acceptability judgments are difficult because human raters disagree; leading models perform similarly to an individual non-author rater.
Model rankings on rendered documentation frames transfer to real images for the three tested questions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating VLMs on documenting physical work, testing spatial relations and scene understanding.
papers.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
papers.tldr: RealityBench uses simulated physical-work environments to show that vision-language models struggle with visual proof-of-work quality, measurements, fine details, and spatial relations despite handling text-in-frame documentation well.

papers.abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.
authors: David R. Martin, Jared Paquet, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar, Kyle Volle, J. Humberto Ramos, Scott Nivison

Uses free-space/obstacle overlays, task classification, and task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning.
Supports role allocation, collision-free route verification, coordinated maneuvers, task division, and directional or coverage-based instructions.
Validated in Gazebo and on Turtlebot 4 hardware, achieving 84.4% average success versus 50.0% for the closest baseline.
When both methods succeed, its paths are 27% shorter on average.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based coordinated path planning for robot teams with spatial reasoning enhancements from language and image input.
papers.title: CoPlanVLM: Coordinated Path Planning for a Robot Team using Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: CoPlanVLM combines visual overlays, task-specific planning, and structured VLM reasoning to generate coordinated paths for two robots from a single instruction and image.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. Building on MOIS, we propose Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (MvFFN), which jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.
authors: Yuguang Li, Yichuan Deng, Zixuan Liu, Ivaylo Boyadzhiev, Xiuyuan Wu, Xinyu Zou, Linda Shapiro, Alex Colburn
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenges of camera pose, geometry, semantics, and global structure in multi-room reconstruction.
MOIS predicts each panorama column’s observed wall and its next two clockwise adjacent walls, keeping predictions local.
MvFFN jointly estimates coarse poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantics.
Layout Chaining aggregates overlapping local predictions into globally coordinated, connected floor plans.
Experiments report improved wall and junction accuracy over prior methods; the work also introduces the ZInD-CrossView dataset.
papers.selection_reason: Jointly reconstructs camera poses and floor-plan layouts from panoramas, advancing spatial layout understanding.
papers.title: MvFFN: Multi-view Floor plan Feed-forward Network for Unposed Wide-Baseline Panorama Layout Reconstruction
papers.tldr: MvFFN reconstructs multi-room floor plans from sparse, unposed wide-baseline panoramas by combining local wall predictions with deterministic global layout assembly.

papers.abstract: ScanRefer Multiple queries require spatial disambiguation: several instances of the target class are present, and the referencer must pick one. When per-query logits were never logged, a common substitute is cross-epoch agreement. On the full ScanRefer validation set (9,508 queries; GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals), object-level softmax is similarly miscalibrated on Unique and Multiple (ECE 0.068 vs. 0.102; the scene-bootstrap gap interval includes zero). Fixed-final agreement on the same checkpoints reports ECE 0.041 vs. 0.272 (gap +0.231). Modal-vote agreement is 0.045 vs. 0.318. Most Multiple errors are same-class wrong-instance (45.6%); geometric miss (H2) is 59.6%, and wrong-category (H1) is 16.7%. A non-monotone H1 pattern does not appear under the default fixed-final protocol, and we retract it. Logit-free thresholds rank spatially hard queries poorly. If only agreement was logged, calibrate abstention on Multiple and report wrong-instance rates with H1.
authors: Micha{\l} Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak, Volodymyr Karpiv
bullets: The study evaluates 9,508 ScanRefer validation queries using a GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals.
Object-level softmax calibration is similar on Unique and Multiple queries, while fixed-final and modal-vote agreement show much larger calibration gaps on Multiple.
Most Multiple errors select the wrong instance of the correct class (45.6%); geometric misses account for 59.6% and wrong-category errors for 16.7%.
Logit-free agreement thresholds rank spatially difficult queries poorly, and the previously suggested non-monotone H1 pattern is retracted under the default protocol.
When only agreement is available, the abstract recommends calibrating abstention specifically on Multiple queries and reporting wrong-instance rates alongside H1 errors.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of spatial disambiguation in 3D referring expressions; relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Agreement versus Softmax under Spatial Disambiguation
papers.tldr: For ScanRefer spatially ambiguous queries, cross-epoch agreement appears substantially less reliable than object-level softmax for calibration, especially on Multiple queries.

papers.abstract: Under a fixed context budget, which objects and relations should a 3D scene-grounded VLM see first? On ScanNet indoor referring benchmarks (Dai et al., 2017), matching the query to object category names outperforms pairwise geometry scoring at every reported K. The gaps are largest at high recall. Analytic pairwise cues beat per-object cue scoring and query-agnostic kNN graphs, including on paraphrases. MiniLM and BGE-small still score higher on those splits. We evaluate token-budgeted candidate retrieval with axis-aligned boxes, a token-ratio metric, training-free baselines, two small encoders that match q to each object's category name, and QCRR (Query-Conditioned Relation Retrieval), a deterministic pairwise-geometry scorer. Across ScanRefer gt_val plus a custom 20% scan-id split of Nr3D and Sr3D (35,504 queries; not official ReferIt3D val), additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 on ScanRefer against QCRR's 0.626; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911 to 0.913 on ScanRefer and 0.941 to 0.947 on Nr3D. A corrected 3DGraphLLM harness (native Acc@0.25 0.67 on the full graph, n=300 ScanRefer queries) shows that context selection changes downstream accuracy under a matched object budget (Random 0.44, QCRR 0.56, MiniLM 0.67, oracle 0.70). Semantic retrieval beats hand-designed geometry on that harness. We will release the protocol, retriever implementations, and per-query outputs so new selectors can be swapped in without rewriting the analysis.
authors: Micha{\l} Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak
bullets: Evaluates token-budgeted candidate retrieval using object category names, pairwise geometry, kNN graphs, and small text encoders.
On ScanRefer, additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 versus 0.626 for QCRR; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911–0.913.
Semantic retrieval also performs better on Nr3D and Sr3D splits, including paraphrased queries.
In a corrected 3DGraphLLM harness, downstream Acc@0.25 is 0.67 with MiniLM, versus 0.56 with QCRR and 0.44 with random selection.
The evaluation uses custom splits and a limited harness; results are scoped to the reported ScanNet-based benchmarks and budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Token-budgeted context selection for 3D scene-grounded VLMs; directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Token-Budgeted Candidate Retrieval for 3D Scene-Grounded VLMs: Category Names vs. Pairwise Geometry
papers.tldr: For token-limited 3D scene-grounded VLMs, category-name matching retrieves relevant objects more effectively than pairwise geometry, improving downstream accuracy under matched context budgets.

papers.abstract: Positional embeddings encode the spatial position of each image patch in a Vision Transformer (ViT), allowing the model to distinguish different spatial arrangements of visual content. However, we know little about how the choice of embedding shapes a vision transformer's internal representation. In this work, we show that Absolute Positional Embeddings (APE) and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) encode spatial position through different internal mechanisms: APE stores position in explicit features, while RoPE builds it inside attention and rebuilds it when it is withheld. Specifically, in APE models, sparse autoencoders recover causal row- and column-specific features, whereas interventions on RoPE reveal distinct rotary components that separately encode row and column information. Additionally, causal interventions selectively disabling RoPE's row or column rotations show that decodable row and column information can be independently removed and, once rotations are restored, partly reconstructed, in part by axis-specialized attention heads. Both mechanisms are causally important for classification: permuting APE's positional features across patches reduces top-1 accuracy by 24--31 points, and ablating the rotations of RoPE's primary rebuilding head reduces it more than ablating those of any other head. Our findings show that the choice of positional encoding fundamentally changes how spatial information is organized and processed inside Vision Transformers. More broadly, our work demonstrates how mechanistic analysis can reveal how models construct, reconstruct, and maintain structured representations, providing a basis for targeted interventions in vision models.
authors: Mahmoud Mannes, Nikhil Maturi, Parva Mehta, Jiwon Jeong, Aravind Singaram Kannappan
bullets: APE represents position in explicit, patch-specific features, while RoPE encodes it through attention-based rotary components.
Sparse autoencoders identify causal row- and column-specific features in APE models; interventions reveal separate row and column rotations in RoPE.
When RoPE rotations are removed, spatial information can be partly reconstructed, with some attention heads specializing in particular axes.
Causal disruption of APE positional features lowers top-1 accuracy by 24–31 points, while ablating RoPE’s key rebuilding head causes the largest impact among heads tested.
The study shows that positional-encoding choice fundamentally shapes how spatial information is organized and processed.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of positional encodings in ViT; transferable to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: How Vision Transformers Represent Position: A Mechanistic Comparison of Absolute and Rotary Positional Encodings
papers.tldr: APE and RoPE enable spatial reasoning in Vision Transformers through fundamentally different, causally important internal mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs report strong performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks, yet most treat perception and reasoning as a single measurable process. We introduce a five-task diagnostic experiment across physics and geometry benchmarks that isolates failures to perception, reasoning, or both. Incorrect diagram interpretation degrades performance even on problems models solve correctly from text alone, and accuracy generally rises from raw images to human-authored captions. Recovery under corrected captions is high for some models, separating perception-blocked failures from genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Which reasoning error follows a perception failure depends on domain: physics failures resolve into calculation errors, geometry into conceptual misapplication. As a discussion beyond our core experiments, InternS1-mini, despite heavy scientific pretraining and thinking capabilities, falls below the weakest model from experiments on every task, with reasoning traces frequently truncating before completion.
bullets: Incorrect diagram interpretation harms performance even when models solve the same problems from text alone.
Human-authored captions generally improve accuracy over raw images.
Corrected captions reveal which failures are perception-blocked versus genuine reasoning failures.
Perception failures tend to become calculation errors in physics and conceptual misapplication in geometry.
InternS1-mini underperforms all evaluated models across tasks, often truncating its reasoning traces.↩
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception vs reasoning failures in multimodal physics and geometry reasoning, directly relevant to MLLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Lost in Perception: Isolating Perceptual and Reasoning Failures in Multimodal Physics and Geometry Reasoning
papers.tldr: A five-task diagnostic shows that multimodal physics and geometry errors often stem from diagram perception, while remaining failures reflect domain-specific reasoning bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly analyze and reason about images, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations faithfully encode the structured relations required for such reasoning. We introduce EICS (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for testing whether representations consistently encode concepts under controlled one-concept interventions, and CASP-VL (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, we find that spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information, even when the same models score well above chance on compositional benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation, whether through the (EOS) token or by mean pooling. These findings reveal a systematic failure invisible to output-based evaluation: VLMs do not preserve, in the representation used downstream, relational information that is present in their own input.
bullets: Introduces EICS, a metric for testing concept stability under controlled one-concept interventions.
Introduces CASP-VL, a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs.
Across multiple VLM architectures, spatial information is represented less faithfully than lexical information.
Spatial relations remain identifiable at predicate tokens but are lost when representations are aggregated via EOS tokens or mean pooling.
The failure is hidden by output-based and compositional benchmark performance.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates spatial relation representations in VLMs; directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors
papers.tldr: VLMs can recognize spatial relations in outputs yet fail to preserve them reliably in their global internal representations.

papers.abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.
authors: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai, Jiaqi Wang, Yuhang Zang, Dahua Lin
bullets: Targets the underdeveloped ability of LVLMs to revisit scenes from task-relevant viewpoints during spatial reasoning.
Uses training-time spatial simulation with an allocentric novel-view generator grounded in visual evidence.
Provides explicit Active Spatial Mentalization trajectories and automatically constructed perspective-taking tasks as supervision.
Improves average accuracy across seven spatial benchmarks and four LVLM backbones while preserving general vision capabilities.
Offers a scalable way to reduce reliance on scarce spatial chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Enhances LVLMs' active spatial mentalization, viewpoint planning, and spatial reasoning, fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: SpatialASM trains vision-language models to actively plan viewpoints and mentally simulate scenes, improving spatial reasoning across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.
authors: Jasin Cekinmez, Addison J. Wu, Ryo Mitsuhashi, Linrong Cai, Xingyu Fu, Zhuang Liu
bullets: Benchmark separates direct cases, relying on shadows or reflections, from inferential cases based on broader scene context.
Across five VLMs, accuracy was 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases; humans showed no significant gap.
OccludeTrace identifies recovering the hidden object from its projection in the full image as the main bottleneck.
Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting provide inconsistent improvements.
Inpaint-then-confront reduces the direct–inferential gap to a statistically non-significant difference for models with image-generation capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: VLM benchmark for recovering occluded objects; relevant to multimodal LLM and spatial/visual reasoning.
papers.title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?
papers.tldr: OccludeBench shows that VLMs struggle to recover fully occluded objects from direct physical cues, and an inpaint-then-confront strategy can reduce this reasoning gap.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models (MLLMs) exhibit promising spatial reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms supporting them remain poorly understood. We uncover S-Space, a linear representation subspace in which object-token representations encode continuous coordinates along horizontal, vertical, and distance axes. Although we identify these axes by differentiating spatial-answer scores with respect to object-token activations, S-Space is intrinsic rather than induced by specific data or prompts, remaining readable under non-spatial questions. We show that S-Space functions as an internal spatial workspace of MLLMs. Perception encodes object locations into it, forming spatial representations that can be directly read out to support accurate spatial judgments. Internal reasoning transforms it for changing viewpoints. Verbal responses selectively access it, evidenced by causal interventions that alter spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses. Case studies further show that S-Space assigns locations to unseen entities and the observer, and connects physical directions with abstract linguistic meanings, suggesting both the capabilities and limitations of large-scale language training. Finally, we use S-Space as a diagnostic tool for spatial reasoning failures. Direction-word readouts reveal systematic coupling between cardinal and image-relative reference frames. More importantly, a perception-computation decomposition exposes a key bottleneck: MLLMs can form capable spatial representations, yet fall short in the spatial transformations required to reason reliably across viewpoint changes.
authors: Zhiyuan Shi, Xiang Li, Xingzhuo Guo, Shangchen Miao, Weiliang Chen, Qiyu Dai, Jinshan Ren, Jiangran Lyu, Fangfu Liu, Mingsheng Long, Jialong Wu
bullets: Object-token representations encode continuous horizontal, vertical, and distance coordinates in a linear subspace.
The subspace is intrinsic and remains readable across prompts, including non-spatial questions.
Perception writes locations into S-Space, reasoning transforms them across viewpoints, and verbal responses selectively read from it.
Causal interventions show that modifying S-Space changes spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses.
Diagnostics indicate that unreliable spatial reasoning stems mainly from deficient viewpoint-related spatial transformations, not representation formation.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies S-Space, a linear subspace for spatial reasoning in MLLMs, directly contributing to 'Spatial Intelligence' and multimodal understanding.
papers.title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models
papers.tldr: S-Space is an intrinsic spatial workspace in multimodal language models that represents object coordinates and supports spatial reasoning, while revealing failures in viewpoint transformations.

papers.abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.
authors: Zheng Ren, Yanning Wang, Ziheng Huang, Fei Huang, Shiqi Wang, Ziqian Ye, Yang Yue
bullets: Benchmarks an escalating range of spatial cognition, from relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing.
Uses urban data from six geographically diverse cities across GeoJSON and map-image modalities, covering 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations.
Ground-truth references and editing constraints are verified with GIS operations.
Models perform better on qualitative topological and ordering relations than on quantitative metric relations.
GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images; editing, especially for ordering relations, often violates specified constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM spatial reasoning and constrained spatial editing; directly fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
papers.tldr: GeoSpatialBench evaluates whether multimodal LLMs can understand and edit real-world spatial configurations under explicit geometric constraints, revealing a substantial gap between recognition and reliable spatial manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.
authors: Amirhossein Vahdat, Thierry Badard, Luc Lamontagne
bullets: Targets a gap in LLM evaluation: geospatial data-requirements elicitation for retrieval-oriented analysis.
Evaluates two reasoning dimensions: Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding.
Uses a fixed, provider-independent schema to encode ground-truth resource and attribute requirements.
In minimal-prompt experiments across seven models, GPT-5.4 Thinking recovered all required resources for 66.67% of requests.
Resource identification was more achievable than accurate fitness-for-use specification, especially when inference demands increased.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM geospatial data requirements elicitation, relevant to spatial reasoning evaluation.
papers.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks
papers.tldr: GeoFitBench-LLM benchmarks how well LLMs identify the geospatial datasets, resources, and constraints needed for natural-language geo-analytic tasks.

papers.abstract: Spatial coding agents significantly improve spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by using external tools to generate verified execution traces. However, this paradigm inherently suffers from prohibitive inference-time overhead and external dependencies. In this paper, we explore whether an MLLM can internalize this agentic capability to operate entirely tool-free. We begin with a simple observation: prompting an MLLM with summarized execution traces of a spatial coding agent naturally unlocks the model's internal spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Motivated by this, we introduce SpatialOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework that internalizes spatial reasoning into a standalone MLLM by formulating verified agent traces as privileged information. To mitigate privileged-information leakage during distillation, we introduce Repetition-Aware Distillation, which combines repetition masking with unlikelihood regularization. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that self-distilling SpatialOPSD achieves higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO on both spatial and OOD datasets, exhibiting superior performance and generalization.
bullets: Targets the inference overhead and external dependencies of tool-using spatial coding agents.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to treat verified agent traces as privileged reasoning information.
Introduces Repetition-Aware Distillation with repetition masking and unlikelihood regularization to reduce privileged-information leakage.
Experiments report higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO across spatial and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
Scope: focuses on internalizing spatial reasoning in standalone MLLMs without external tools.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets spatial reasoning in MLLMs via self-distillation from coding agent traces, fitting spatial intelligence and multimodal LLM subtopics.
papers.title: SpatialOPSD: Self-Distilling Spatial Intelligence from Verified Coding Agent Traces
papers.tldr: SpatialOPSD distills verified spatial coding-agent traces into an MLLM, enabling tool-free spatial reasoning with improved benchmark performance and generalization.

papers.abstract: Multimodal AI, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), is transforming assistive technologies by enabling simultaneous processing of visual and textual data. This advancement holds significant promise for over 43 million visually impaired and neuro-divergent individuals worldwide who face persistent challenges in navigating indoor and outdoor environments due to limited spatial awareness and insufficient environmental cues. Existing navigation aids often lack comprehensive 3D scene understanding, relying on constrained route-based strategies that hinder user autonomy. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework that integrates LLMs, VLMs and digital twin technologies to deliver a spatially cognitive navigation support for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users. Our system captures video input via standard mobile phone cameras, and employs SLAM3R to generate dense 3D point clouds from monocular RGB sequences in real-time. Our custom post-processing algorithm ensures accurate point cloud alignment across multiple viewpoints without requiring predefined reference points. This enhances the capabilities of SpatialLM to produce structured 3D representations, including architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes. The enriched spatial data is then processed by a locally deployed LLM, which interprets 3D contexts to generate detailed scene descriptions and precise distance measurements between users and surrounding objects. We evaluated our approach across diverse video scenarios featuring various perspectives, looped walking views and captured in multiple environments. The evaluation results demonstrate consistent accuracy in 3D scene interpretation and object localisation, underscoring the potential of our system as a transformative assistive navigation solution that combines advanced visual perception with spatial reasoning
bullets: Addresses the limited spatial awareness and environmental cues provided by conventional route-based navigation aids.
Uses monocular video, SLAM3R, and custom point-cloud alignment to construct dense, consistent 3D environments without predefined reference points.
Extends SpatialLM with structured representations of architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes.
A locally deployed LLM converts 3D context into scene descriptions and user-to-object distance estimates.
Evaluation across varied viewpoints, walking sequences, and environments reports consistent 3D scene interpretation and object-localisation accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates VLMs and LLMs for spatial cognition and navigation of visually impaired users, utilizing 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Assisted Spatial Cognition Through Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A mobile-camera system combines VLMs, LLMs, SLAM, and digital twins to build 3D scene understanding for more autonomous navigation by visually impaired and neuro-divergent users.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often struggle to identify and use geometric relations in diagrams. Recent methods address this challenge by converting geometric entities, relations, and constraints into explicit textual representations for the model to reason over. However, effective formalization is highly non-trivial: on Geometry3K, structure injection fixes 28 errors but introduces 13 new ones among 200 examples. Redundant relations can distract the model, while ambiguous references to diagram elements can lead it to apply constraints incorrectly. This suggests that the key challenge is not merely extracting more geometric facts, but organizing them into representations that support downstream reasoning. To fully exploit the power of formalization, we further propose GeoReform, a reflective formalization evolution framework that treats formalization as an optimizable policy rather than a fixed parser output. GeoReform executes the full reasoning pipeline, collects failed rollouts, diagnoses defects in the current representation, and mutates the policy to better select, ground, group, and present geometric entities, relations, constraints, and targets. On Geometry3K, GeoReform improves Qwen3VL-2B accuracy from 42.0\% to 56.0\%. Extensive experiments and analyses across geometry reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that effective formalization is crucial for improving multimodal geometry reasoning.
authors: Jialu Wang, Ruichen Zhang, Xiaoou Liu, Hua Wei, Tianlong Chen
bullets: MLLMs often struggle to identify and correctly use geometric relations in diagrams.
Fixed formalization can add distracting or ambiguous relations, sometimes creating new errors.
GeoReform treats formalization as an optimizable policy rather than a fixed parser output.
It diagnoses failed reasoning rollouts and mutates how entities, relations, constraints, and targets are selected, grounded, grouped, and presented.
Experiments across geometry benchmarks show that effective formalization is important for multimodal geometry reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Reflective formalization policy for multimodal geometry reasoning directly targets spatial and geometric reasoning in MLLMs.
papers.title: GeoReform: Reflective Formalization Evolution for Multimodal Geometry Problem Solving
papers.tldr: GeoReform improves multimodal geometry solving by iteratively refining how diagrams are formalized for reasoning, raising Qwen3VL-2B accuracy on Geometry3K from 42.0% to 56.0%.

papers.abstract: World-action models have recently improved autonomous driving by jointly learning future scene prediction and trajectory generation. Most existing approaches model the future primarily through RGB appearance, and recent works have begun to incorporate geometric prediction to improve spatial understanding. However, dense geometry describes the spatial layout of the entire scene without indicating which parts are most relevant to the ego vehicle's action. For driving, the model must also identify and anticipate where it can safely move and which regions may pose collision risks. Jointly modeling action-relevant regions and future geometry can provide the policy with both driving-relevant cues and their corresponding spatial structure. We therefore propose AffordDrive3D, an affordance- and geometry-aware world-action model that jointly learns future action-relevant regions and spatial structure. In order to capture the scene semantics and driving context needed for driving affordance prediction, we build AffordDrive3D on a VLM backbone to forecast drivable areas and collision-critical regions that directly affect ego motion, while predicting future geometry from RGB world-model latents. On NAVSIM, AffordDrive3D achieves state-of-the-art performance with 91.3 PDMS and 89.9 EPDMS, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly modeling future affordances and geometry for trajectory planning.
authors: Tianhui Cai, Xinglong Sun, Chao Fang, Zhenxin Li, Rui Song, Jose M. Alvarez, Yunxiang Mao, Jiaqi Ma, Langechuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of RGB- and geometry-focused world-action models that lack action-relevant spatial cues.
Uses a VLM backbone to forecast drivable areas and collision-critical regions affecting ego motion.
Predicts future geometry from RGB world-model latents alongside future affordances.
Achieves 91.3 PDMS and 89.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM, reported as state-of-the-art.
Focuses on affordance and geometry prediction for driving-relevant spatial understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Affordance- and geometry-aware world-action model for autonomous driving trajectory planning with spatial understanding.
papers.title: AffordDrive3D: Affordance-Aware World-Action Modeling with Spatial Understanding
papers.tldr: AffordDrive3D improves autonomous-driving trajectory planning by jointly predicting future driving affordances and scene geometry.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal foundation models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra) have recently shown strong potential for direct robotic control, yet their performance on fine manipulation remains limited. We argue that an important source of failure is not necessarily insufficient policy capability, but insufficient spatial observability, where task-critical spatial relationships may be poorly revealed by the existing physical camera setup. We introduce SpatialHarness, a test-time embodied harness that provides test-time spatial scaffolding for fine robotic manipulation without policy fine-tuning or changes to the physical sensing setup. SpatialHarness maintains an online simulated scene synchronized with real-world execution, identifies task-critical spatial relationships, and renders complementary virtual views that expose them to a frozen multimodal policy. To keep the simulated scene aligned during interaction, we develop interaction-aware scene synchronization that distinguishes static, held, and transition modes. We evaluate SpatialHarness on four real-robot manipulation tasks spanning precise geometric alignment, object-relative placement, and articulated-object interaction. Using the same frozen GPT-6 Astra policy, SpatialHarness substantially improves task success, including from 26.7% to 66.7% on plug insertion and from 0% to 100% on Tower of Hanoi. These results indicate that improving spatial observability at test time can unlock fine-manipulation capabilities already present in strong multimodal foundation models. Project website: https://emilia113.github.io/SpatialHarness/.

papers.title: SpatialHarness: Test-Time Spatial Scaffolding for Fine Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SpatialHarness improves fine robotic manipulation by giving a frozen multimodal policy complementary virtual views of task-critical spatial relationships at test time.

papers.abstract: We present Pumpire, a unified benchmark for evaluating metric point-pair distance estimation capability of both image- and video-level 3D foundation models, with or without depth priors. In contrast to previous approaches that normally evaluate depth and camera intrinsics separately or evaluate point-clouds with geometric similarity metrics, which cannot directly reflect models' point-to-point distance estimation capability, Pumpire directly assesses point-to-point distances from the reconstructed geometry. To this end, we collect a large-scale and diverse dataset (pumpire-6k) comprising 100 real-world scenes, each annotated with physically measured point-pair distances and containing 64 frames, for a total of 6,400 frames. Building on this dataset, we establish a holistic evaluation protocol that covers both image- and video-level 3D foundation models and enables direct assessment of point-pair distance errors and cross-setting comparison. We conduct extensive experiments across 29 baseline configurations of representative 3D foundation models and provide a comprehensive analysis of the results. By offering this benchmark, we target the more fundamental ability to perceive and estimate physical scale in the reconstructed 3D space, which prior evaluation protocols have largely overlooked. The project page can be found at https://pumpire.github.io/
authors: Siyu Chen, Zehan Wang, Jiayang Xu, Yihan Wu, Jialei Wang, Junming Chen, Ziang Zhang, Yutong Ying, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Addresses a gap in evaluations that separately assess depth, camera intrinsics, or geometric similarity rather than physical distance estimation.
Introduces pumpire-6k: 100 diverse real-world scenes with measured point-pair distances across 6,400 frames.
Provides a unified protocol for comparing image- and video-level 3D foundation models, with or without depth priors.
Evaluates 29 representative baseline configurations and analyzes their distance-estimation performance.
Focuses on physical-scale perception in reconstructed 3D space, which prior protocols largely overlook.

papers.title: Pumpire: Unified Benchmark for Metric Distance Estimation
papers.tldr: Pumpire is a benchmark for directly evaluating how accurately 3D foundation models estimate physical point-to-point distances from reconstructed image or video geometry.

papers.abstract: Dense correspondence matching has historically been bounded by simplifying spatio-temporal priors, such as smooth motion and rigid geometry. While effective for classical tasks, these assumptions break down in image editing and reference-guided generation (IEG), where transformations can preserve visual identity while breaking physical continuity. To establish identity-preserving correspondence across such transformations, we introduce FreeMatching, a generalizable framework combining generative and semantic foundation representations with heterogeneous supervision from classical datasets, tracked videos, and synthetic scenes. Teacher-guided iterative refinement further improves correspondence in IEG without dense correspondence annotations. Experimentally, a single FreeMatching model substantially improves correspondence quality on challenging IEG image pairs while retaining competitive performance on classical benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility as a quantitative metric for evaluating identity preservation, with scores that correlate with human judgment. The code is available at https://github.com/luping-liu/FreeMatching.
authors: Luping Liu, Bingyi Kang, Yifan Wang, Dong Xu
bullets: Targets image editing and reference-guided generation, where visual identity may persist despite broken physical continuity.
Combines generative and semantic foundation representations with heterogeneous supervision from classical datasets, tracked videos, and synthetic scenes.
Uses teacher-guided iterative refinement to improve correspondence without requiring dense correspondence annotations for IEG.
Improves correspondence quality on challenging IEG pairs while remaining competitive on classical benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Dense correspondence matching with foundation representations is a spatial correspondence technique transferable to geometry-aware multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Beyond Spatio-Temporal Priors: A Generalizable Approach for Dense Correspondence Matching
papers.tldr: FreeMatching enables identity-preserving dense correspondence across transformations that violate conventional motion and geometry assumptions.

papers.abstract: Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks mainly test spatial perception: reading off relations already visible in the input. Yet real-world spatial intelligence demands predictive spatial reasoning: constructing a scene from observations, anticipating how an intervention changes it, and reasoning about the unseen outcome. We introduce SpaceCast-Bench, the first benchmark to directly and diagnostically evaluate this capability. Built around an observe-transform-infer framework, its 3,862 questions from 182 real-world scenes span 16 task types at three levels: static perception, local prediction, and global prediction, progressively requiring scene understanding, spatial state updating, and relational inference over unobserved outcomes. Evaluating 21 models exposes a stark gap: the strongest model reaches only 58.0% against 87.2% human performance, while spatially specialized models remain near random chance. Controlled analyses further reveal that bridge views are critical for integrating distributed observations, and that explicit 3D evidence benefits models more reliably than generated outcome images or videos. Fine-tuning on our programmatically generated data lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 34.0% to 65.7% with macro-average gains across six out-of-domain benchmarks.
authors: Hongxing Li, Jinyue Su, Dingming Li, Wenqi Zhang, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yueting Zhuang, Yongliang Shen

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for predictive spatial reasoning in vision-language models; directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpaceCast-Bench: Evaluating Predictive Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SpaceCast-Bench reveals that vision-language models struggle with predictive spatial reasoning, especially when inferring unseen outcomes from scene changes.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning remains a persistent weakness of vision-language models (VLMs), because RGB inputs do not directly provide geometric evidence. Existing remedies either inject 3D into the model at inference, paying architecture and latency costs, or train with outcome rewards that supervise only the final answer. Spatial errors originate in perception: a misjudged depth or direction can be corrected only by the scene's true geometry, which the 3D-scanned sources of spatial training corpora already provide. We propose GPD (Geometry-Privileged Distillation), which makes geometric evidence the privilege in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). For each question, depth, semantic, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) cues are rendered as compact text and routed to the teacher alongside the reference answer; a privileged KL, applied only to incorrect trajectories, augments GRPO, and the deployed model remains RGB-only. On the 4B backbone, GPD achieves 57.1 on VSI-Bench and 37.6 average across MindCube, SPARBench, MMSI-Bench, and ViewSpatial, outperforming both GRPO and answer-privileged OPSD across spatial reasoning benchmarks. Ablations confirm the complementarity of 3D and answer privilege, the advantage of question-conditioned routing over full-context injection, and the benefit of restricting distillation to incorrect trajectories.
authors: Hongxing Li, Yixin Li, Dingming Li, Zixuan Wang, Yuchen Yan, Wenqi Zhang, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
bullets: Addresses errors caused by missing depth and directional geometry in RGB-based VLMs.
Uses on-policy self-distillation with depth, semantic, and bird’s-eye-view cues rendered as text for a teacher model.
Applies privileged KL distillation only to incorrect trajectories while retaining an RGB-only deployed model.
Reports 57.1 on VSI-Bench and 37.6 average across four additional spatial benchmarks on a 4B backbone.
Ablations support question-conditioned routing, complementary 3D and answer privileges, and incorrect-trajectory-only distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets spatial reasoning in vision-language models using 3D geometric priors, fitting the configured spatial intelligence interest.
papers.title: Distilling Routed 3D Privilege for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GPD improves RGB-only VLM spatial reasoning by distilling routed 3D geometric cues into the model during training.

papers.abstract: Large Multi-modality Models (LMMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding and generation, but still face challenges in visual editing, particularly in following complex instructions, preserving appearance consistency, and supporting flexible input formats. To study this gap, we introduce RISEBench, the first benchmark for evaluating Reasoning-Informed viSual Editing (RISE), and extend it to RISEBench++, a more comprehensive and fine-grained benchmark for this emerging task. RISEBench++ extends the taxonomy into a hierarchical scheme spanning six reasoning dimensions: Temporal, Causal, Spatial, Logical, and Counterfactual Reasoning, together with Hybrid Reasoning integrating multiple reasoning types across multi-turn edits. These dimensions are further decomposed into 12 subcategories and 65 fine-grained task types. We expand input formats to include multi-image conditioning and scale the benchmark to 1000 human-annotated test cases, released in English and Chinese. We also improve our evaluation framework, assessing Instruction Reasoning, Appearance Consistency, and Visual Plausibility with human judges and an LMM-as-a-judge approach for more reliable and calibrated judgements. Beyond benchmarking, we introduce RISE-Agent, a training-free agentic framework integrating reasoning-driven planning, tool-augmented execution, and verifier-guided refinement, outperforming most strong existing approaches across diverse RISE tasks. We evaluate 58 visual editing approaches, including 34 open-source models, 19 closed-source models, and 5 agentic methods. The results reveal substantial challenges in reasoning-based visual editing, with even the strongest evaluated approach, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, achieving only 56.6% accuracy. RISEBench++ highlights the limitations of contemporary editing models, provides insights, and indicates future directions for reasoning-aware visual editing.
authors: Xue Yang, Peiyuan Zhang, Yilun Zhu, Qihao Yang, Mingxin Liu, Xiangyu Zhao, Ziqian Fan, Zhaokai Wang, Yan Li, Yifan Yang, Xu Yang, Xiaosong Jia, Yue Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Junchi Yan

papers.title: Reasoning-Informed Visual Editing
papers.tldr: RISEBench++ evaluates reasoning-intensive visual editing across diverse tasks, while RISE-Agent uses planning, tools, and verification to improve performance, revealing substantial limitations in current models.

papers.abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can describe increasingly complex visual scenes, token-level grounding becomes crucial. Yet, when an MLLM generates "the yellow banana on the left", established grounding approaches focus on what is in the image ("banana"), overlooking tokens that help describe which instance is meant ("yellow", "left"). In this work, we ask whether frozen MLLM representations contain decodable grounding information about the referred instance across generated tokens, extending to modifiers such as attributes, spatial expressions, and relational/action terms. To address this question, we introduce OTTER, a lightweight supervised probe over frozen MLLM representations that uses Optimal Transport (OT) to align generated tokens with visual regions and produce compact grounding maps. Our results show that (i) instance-discriminative visual information can be decoded from modifier tokens, with the clearest evidence for spatial terms, but (ii) is not confined to them, as contextualized object nouns also carry referential information; (iii) the recovered grounding remains informative under context perturbations, while selected regions remain relevant to generation; and (iv) the learned OT-based grounding extends beyond the controlled setting to free generation and cross-dataset transfer.
authors: Barbara Toniella Corradini (AI for Good), Caterina Gallegati (University of Siena, Italy), Ludovica Genovese (AI for Good), Vittorio Murino (AI for Good)
bullets: Problem: Existing grounding methods emphasize object nouns and overlook modifier tokens that disambiguate the intended instance.
Method: OTTER uses a lightweight supervised probe with Optimal Transport to align generated-token representations with visual regions and create grounding maps.
Finding: Spatial modifiers provide the clearest instance-discriminative signals, while attributes, relations/actions, and contextualized nouns also carry referential information.
Robustness: Grounding remains informative under context perturbations, and selected regions remain relevant to generation.
Scope: The learned grounding generalizes from controlled experiments to free generation and cross-dataset transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Probes modifier grounding in frozen MLLMs, including spatial expressions, relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: From What to Which: Decoding Modifier Grounding in Frozen MLLMs
papers.tldr: OTTER shows that frozen MLLMs encode which visual instance is referred to not only in object nouns, but also in modifiers such as spatial and attribute terms.

papers.abstract: Text prompting is an indirect interface for poster generation, requiring users to encode inherently two-dimensional composition intent into a one-dimensional sequence of words. We introduce a Spatial Canvas Interface that enables users to directly compose generation intent in space through four complementary binding types: semantic, identity, text, and pixel, together with Text Specifications for individual elements and global appearance. Based on this interface, we develop Compo, a poster generation model adapted from a pretrained image editing model to understand Spatial Canvas inputs and Text Specifications. Compo supports both direct inference, where users explicitly construct the canvas, and agentic mode, where a high-level request is automatically translated into a planned Spatial Canvas. To train Compo, we develop a scalable pipeline that automatically constructs supervision data for different binding types and their combinations, enabling efficient adaptation without training a specialized poster generator from scratch. We further introduce a benchmark that evaluates adherence to individual binding types and their joint composition. Experiments show that Compo achieves stronger compositional controllability than both general-purpose image generation models and dedicated poster generation systems while maintaining high visual quality. By decoupling intent specification from visual generation, our work shifts poster generation from prompting toward composing.
authors: Yitong Wang, Fangyun Wei, Jinjing Zhao, Sirui Zhang, Hongyang Zhang, Dong Chen, Bo Dai, Yan Lu
bullets: Users express poster intent spatially through semantic, identity, text, and pixel bindings, plus element-level and global text specifications.
Compo adapts a pretrained image-editing model to interpret Spatial Canvas inputs in direct and agentic generation modes.
An automated supervision pipeline supports training across binding types and their combinations without building a specialized poster generator from scratch.
A new benchmark evaluates adherence to individual bindings and their joint composition.
Experiments report stronger compositional controllability than general-purpose image generators and dedicated poster systems while preserving visual quality.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a spatial canvas interface for poster generation, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: From Prompting to Composing: A Spatial Canvas Interface for Poster Generation
papers.tldr: Compo replaces one-dimensional text prompting with a spatial canvas for more controllable, high-quality poster generation.

papers.abstract: In text-guided image editing, describing the desired change is often straightforward, but identifying the intended object or region can be cumbersome, especially when several objects look alike. We introduce a new image editing interface that lets users place spatial marks and optional short notes directly on the image. Together, these annotations form a canvas instruction that specifies where to edit and what to change. Our editor, VibeEdit, follows these instructions to perform object addition, removal, replacement, attribute modification, and movement without a separate text prompt. We construct 1.55 million source-target edit pairs with object masks and structured edit descriptions, from which we render canvas instructions during training. We adapt Qwen-Image-Edit with layer-decoupled conditioning that separately encodes source images and canvas instructions for image editing. We train the model with region-weighted supervised fine-tuning, followed by rubric-guided reinforcement learning to improve edit completion, local edit quality, and preservation of unedited regions. We evaluate VibeEdit on an independently constructed, human-curated benchmark of 419 cases emphasizing target selection among similar objects. VibeEdit achieves a VLM rubric score of 79.9 and an outside-region PSNR of 32.8 dB, compared with 67.4 and 24.0 dB for FireRed, the highest-scoring text-instructed baseline in our evaluation.
authors: Jinjing Zhao, Fangyun Wei, Yitong Wang, Xiuyu Wu, Yunuo Chen, Yang Yue, Sirui Zhang, Wenbo Wang, Hongyang Zhang, Dong Chen, Yan Lu, Chang Xu

Supports adding, removing, replacing, modifying, and moving objects through canvas instructions.
Trains a Qwen-Image-Edit-based model with separate source-image and canvas-instruction conditioning, region-weighted fine-tuning, and rubric-guided reinforcement learning.
On a 419-case human-curated benchmark, VibeEdit scores 79.9 on a VLM rubric and 32.8 dB outside-region PSNR, outperforming the reported text-instructed baseline.

papers.title: VibeEdit: Image Editing with Canvas Instructions
papers.tldr: VibeEdit enables precise text-free image editing by combining spatial marks with optional brief notes on the canvas.

papers.abstract: Interactive scene exploration requires frequent view updates, although small camera motions preserve much of the visible content. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting nevertheless renders each target view, leaving this image overlap unexploited. Reusing rendered images offers an alternative. Geometric warping alone cannot recover newly exposed content and remains sensitive to depth errors.
